title: How innovations in methodology offer new prospects for volume electron microscopy
authors: Arent J. Kievits; R. Lane; Elizabeth C. Carroll; J. Hoogenboom

ocar.opportunity: Volume electron microscopy already delivers nanometer-scale 3D structure from tissues, but conventional microscope throughput has limited both the size and the number of samples. Method innovations are now making whole organs and small organisms structurally imageable.
ocar.challenge: Faster acquisition shifts bottlenecks onto sample preparation, image analysis, and data management. Automatic segmentation and server-based annotation have progressed, yet several challenges in those downstream stages remain.
ocar.action: Kievits, Lane, Carroll, and Hoogenboom review in Journal of Microscopy (2022) recent trends in volume EM, emerging routes to higher throughput (including multi-beam SEM), and implications for preparation, analysis, and data handling. They place current practice in a lineage from 1940s TEM protocols and 1950s serial-section TEM through computer-assisted reconstruction.
ocar.resolution: The review argues that acquisition gains are driving a volume-EM revolution while stressing remaining pipeline bottlenecks, and it surveys how automatic segmentation and shared annotation tools have changed analysis even as data-management and preparation constraints grow.
ocar.future_work: Sustained progress will require matching sample-preparation, analysis, and storage methods to the new acquisition rates rather than treating imaging speed as the sole remaining problem.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopes can show tissue in three dimensions at nanometer detail, but they used to be too slow for whole organs. This review explains newer, faster microscopes and warns that preparing samples, analyzing the pictures, and storing the data become the new traffic jams.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopes can show tissue in three dimensions at nanometer detail, but they used to be too slow for whole organs. This review explains newer, faster microscopes and warns that preparing samples, analyzing the pictures, and storing the data become the new traffic jams.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Microscopy (2022), Kievits, Lane, Carroll, and Hoogenboom review methodology innovations for volume EM. They argue that throughput limits of conventional instruments are being lifted enough to image whole organs and small organisms, which in turn stresses sample preparation, image analysis, and data management. They highlight automatic segmentation and server-based annotation as rapidly advancing, while listing remaining challenges and emerging acquisition methods such as multi-beam SEM.
summaries.advanced: This is an invited methods review, not a new instrument or dataset. Claims about whole-organ imaging cite the field’s trajectory rather than a single benchmark in this paper. J. P. Hoogenboom discloses co-founding Delmic, which sells integrated microscopes including FAST-EM; readers should treat commercial mentions in that light. No quantitative throughput table is given in the extracted text.

title: Multi-layered maps of neuropil with segmentation-guided contrastive learning
authors: S. Dorkenwald; Peter H. Li; Michał Januszewski; D. Berger; Jeremy B. Maitin-Shepard; A. Bodor; F. Collman; C. Schneider-Mizell; N. D. da Costa; J. Lichtman; Viren Jain

ocar.opportunity: Dense maps that name cells, their subcellular parts, and their connections would reveal circuit principles, but annotating the vast number of objects in neuropil is the bottleneck even after nanometer-scale EM and automated instance segmentation.
ocar.challenge: Supervised networks for cell-fragment annotation need large labeled sets and do not transfer easily across tasks. Many reconstructed neurites in current volumes are truncated at the imaging boundary, so type inference from short fragments is especially valuable.
ocar.action: Dorkenwald, Li, Januszewski, Berger, Maitin-Shepard, Bodor, Collman, Schneider-Mizell, da Costa, Lichtman, and Jain introduce SegCLR in Nature Methods (2023): segmentation-guided contrastive learning of representations from 3D imagery and segmentations, applied to human and mouse cortical volumes. They train without per-task labels, then use lightweight classifiers on the embeddings.
ocar.resolution: SegCLR enabled accurate classification of cellular subcompartments and matched a supervised approach while requiring 400-fold fewer labeled examples. Cell types could be inferred from fragments as small as 10 μm. Applications include exploring layer 5 pyramidal subtypes and automated large-scale synaptic-partner analysis in mouse visual cortex. Embeddings, code, and pretrained weights are released.
ocar.future_work: The authors emphasize fragment typing for incomplete reconstructions and invite community use of the released human and mouse embedding datasets.

plain_language_summary: Once a computer has colored in the cells in a 3D brain picture, it still does not know what part of a cell it is looking at or what cell type it is. This method learns a compact description of each snippet from the pictures themselves, so a few human labels can name parts and types even on very short broken pieces.

summaries.beginner: Once a computer has colored in the cells in a 3D brain picture, it still does not know what part of a cell it is looking at or what cell type it is. This method learns a compact description of each snippet from the pictures themselves, so a few human labels can name parts and types even on very short broken pieces.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature Methods (2023), Dorkenwald, Li, Jain and colleagues present SegCLR, a self-supervised contrastive method that embeds cells from 3D EM imagery plus segmentations. On human and mouse cortex it classifies subcompartments at supervised-level performance with 400-fold fewer labels and infers cell type from fragments as small as 10 μm. They demonstrate layer 5 pyramidal subtype exploration and automated synaptic-partner analysis in mouse visual cortex, and they release embeddings and code. A linear classifier on embeddings trains in minutes on one CPU with a few hundred labels, versus GPU-days for prior deep networks on related tasks.
summaries.advanced: Equivalence to supervised performance is for the subcompartment task with 400-fold fewer labels, not every possible annotation layer. The 10 μm fragment result is a reported operating point, not a guarantee on all morphologies. Large-scale partner analysis and L5 subtype exploration are demonstrations on the published volumes. Self-supervision still depends on the quality of the input segmentation.

title: neuPrint: An open access tool for EM connectomics
authors: Stephen M. Plaza; Jody Clements; Tom Dolafi; L. Umayam; Nicole N. Neubarth; Louis K. Scheffer; S. Berg

ocar.opportunity: EM and deep learning now yield connectomes with tens of thousands of neurons and tens of millions of connections that interest non-specialists, not only the reconstructing lab. Publication of a paper is not enough: the data must be queryable in a browser and by APIs without downloading entire graphs.
ocar.challenge: Earlier reconstructions were small enough for experts to download. New graphs break that model; performance, public query languages, and reconstruction-quality checks become first-class requirements. Hosting such data online also has real cost.
ocar.action: Plaza, Clements, Dolafi, Umayam, Neubarth, Scheffer, and Berg introduce neuPrint in Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2022): a web interface for typical biological queries plus programmer APIs, with reconstruction-quality features. Internally, connectome data are a graph in neo4j, queried with Cypher. The paper also analyzes preprint versus journal-publication usage as an open-science experiment.
ocar.resolution: NeuPrint made Janelia FlyEM-style connectomes usable from a browser worldwide. The authors find that a significant fraction of readers proceed to examine the data directly; preprint posting triggered data inquiries and PDF downloads immediately, with little change at formal publication, implying many users wanted the data more than the narrative. They also report that keeping data available online imposes substantial additional costs on connectomics research.
ocar.future_work: The graph-in-neo4j design is argued to extend to still larger databases; sustaining public hosting and documentation is an ongoing operational challenge.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram with tens of millions of connections is useless to most scientists if they have to download a giant file. neuPrint is a website and programming interface that lets anyone ask ordinary biology questions of a connectome in a web browser.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram with tens of millions of connections is useless to most scientists if they have to download a giant file. neuPrint is a website and programming interface that lets anyone ask ordinary biology questions of a connectome in a web browser.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2022), Plaza, Scheffer, Berg and colleagues present neuPrint, combining a browser UI, APIs, and quality-assessment tools over connectomes stored as neo4j graphs queried with Cypher. The system targets EM reconstructions with tens of thousands of neurons and tens of millions of synapses. Analyzing their own usage, they report that preprints drove immediate data access largely unaffected by later formal publication, and that public online hosting adds substantial cost. Code repositories for HTTP, Python, and related clients are cited.
summaries.advanced: Performance claims are qualitative (“typical queries”) without latency benchmarks in the extracted text. The open-science usage analysis is of this project’s readership, not a general trial of all data journals. neo4j/Cypher will not automatically solve every motif query at future scales. Organism is unspecified in the abstract; the motivating deployment is Janelia FlyEM connectomes.

title: Rapid reconstruction of neural circuits using tissue expansion and light sheet microscopy
authors: Joshua L. Lillvis; H. Otsuna; Xiaoyu Ding; I. Pisarev; Takashi Kawase; Jennifer Colonell; Konrad Rokicki; Cristian Goina; Ruixuan Gao; Amy Hu; Kaiyu Wang; J. Bogovic; D. Milkie; Linus Meienberg; B. Mensh; E. Boyden; S. Saalfeld; P. Tillberg; B. Dickson

ocar.opportunity: Physiology can be measured in many animals, but synaptic structure is usually mapped with low throughput, blocking studies of how circuit variation relates to behavior. EM yields dense connectomes slowly; light microscopy is high-throughput and molecularly specific but historically lacked synaptic resolution.
ocar.challenge: That methodological gulf leaves individual differences, sex differences, and experience-dependent rewiring hard to quantify at single synapses across many animals.
ocar.action: Lillvis, Otsuna, Ding, Pisarev, Kawase, Colonell, Rokicki, Goina, Gao, Hu, Wang, Bogovic, Milkie, Meienberg, Mensh, Boyden, Saalfeld, Tillberg, and Dickson in eLife (2022) combine tissue expansion with lattice light-sheet microscopy (ExLLSM) and a high-throughput analysis pipeline to reconstruct selected Drosophila circuits at single-synapse resolution with molecular contrast. Protocols allow one sample to be prepared and analyzed within a week and several samples in parallel; software is released.
ocar.resolution: In Drosophila the method yielded synaptic counts similar to EM, enabled comparison of synaptic connectivity across sex and experience, and could correlate structural connectivity, functional connectivity, and behavior in the same animal. The authors argue it fills a gap for studying variability within and between species using relatively affordable microscopes.
ocar.future_work: Better fluorescent continuity for automated single-neuron (not just cell-type) segmentation, denser labeling, and genetic reagents for specific chemical and electrical synapse components are identified as next developments; the pipeline is intended to transfer where neurons can be labeled and tissue expanded.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopes map every synapse but too slowly to compare many animals. This method swells the tissue, photographs it with a light-sheet microscope, and counts synapses in chosen fly circuits fast enough to compare sex, experience, and behavior.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopes map every synapse but too slowly to compare many animals. This method swells the tissue, photographs it with a light-sheet microscope, and counts synapses in chosen fly circuits fast enough to compare sex, experience, and behavior.
summaries.intermediate: Published in eLife (2022), Lillvis, Tillberg, Dickson and colleagues present an ExLLSM pipeline for rapid, targeted synaptic reconstruction. Using Drosophila, they report synapse counts similar to EM, comparisons across sex and experience, and correlation of structure, function, and behavior in the same animal. A sample can be prepared and analyzed within a week and multiplexed; 8× expansion is discussed in the context of light-sheet imaging. Software tools for multi-terabyte volumes are released. Other light-sheet microscopes besides LLSM can image the expanded samples.
summaries.advanced: “Similar to EM” synaptic counts are a validation claim for selected Drosophila circuits, not a dense whole-brain connectome. Current analysis is largely at cell-type rather than fully automated single-cell resolution, as the authors note. Transfer to nematodes, rodents, zebrafish, and organoids is prospective, based on existing expansion and labeling literature. CNN synapse/neuron models may need retraining for new species.

title: RoboEM: automated 3D flight tracing for synaptic-resolution connectomics
authors: Martin Schmidt; Alessandro Motta; Meike Sievers; M. Helmstaedter

ocar.opportunity: Mapping networks from 3D EM still struggles with thin axons. Even strong automated segmentations usually need human proofreading before they support more demanding connectomic analyses.
ocar.challenge: Analyses differ in required error-free path length: local synaptic configurations may need only ~10 µm of axon, whereas neuron-to-neuron cortical connectomes need an additional order of magnitude of faithful axonal reconstruction, which has not been fully automatic.
ocar.action: Schmidt, Motta, Sievers, and Helmstaedter introduce RoboEM in Nature Methods (2024): an AI self-steering 3D flight system trained to navigate along neurites from EM alone. Applied to mouse and human cortical 3D-EM, it is used as automated proofreading to improve state-of-the-art segmentations, including flood-filling-network outputs.
ocar.resolution: RoboEM substantially improved automated segmentations and could replace manual proofreading for more complex connectomic analysis problems, with computational annotation cost for cortical connectomes about 400-fold lower than manual error correction. Split reduction was 3.5-fold better than state-of-the-art FFN agglomeration. The authors estimate that soma-seeded iterative use could extend fully automated axon reconstruction by multiple millimeters per neuron in petascale volumes. Compute cost increased by less than 2× in the discussed setting.
ocar.future_work: They argue RoboEM makes fully automated cortical connectomes at the scale of thousands to ten thousand neurons plausible by focusing on long, locally thin axons.

plain_language_summary: Computers still lose thin axons in 3D electron-microscope volumes, so people spend huge effort correcting maps. RoboEM is a virtual pilot that flies along those axons from the pictures alone, fixing breaks cheaply enough that much of that human proofreading can be skipped.

summaries.beginner: Computers still lose thin axons in 3D electron-microscope volumes, so people spend huge effort correcting maps. RoboEM is a virtual pilot that flies along those axons from the pictures alone, fixing breaks cheaply enough that much of that human proofreading can be skipped.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature Methods (2024), Schmidt, Motta, Sievers, and Helmstaedter present RoboEM, a self-steering 3D flight tracer using only EM as input. On mouse and human cortex it improves automated segmentations and can replace manual proofreading for more complex analyses, with about 400-fold lower computational annotation cost than manual correction and 3.5-fold better split reduction than FFN agglomeration. Calibration used volumes around 100–150 µm on a side; projections to millimeter axons in petascale data are estimated from soma-seeded iterative application.
summaries.advanced: The 400-fold cost figure compares computational annotation to manual error correction for cortical connectomes as stated by the authors, not wall-clock of a whole pipeline. Performance on 100–150 µm cubes is measured; millimeter-to-centimeter axon claims are estimates. FFN similarity is discussed: RoboEM traces centerlines with “growth inertia,” which the authors say solves problems volume methods miss. It does not eliminate all human work for every analysis type.

title: The connectome of an insect brain
authors: Michael Winding; B. Pedigo; C. L. Barnes; Heather G. Patsolic; Youngser Park; Tom Kazimiers; Akira Fushiki; Ingrid V. Andrade; Avinash Khandelwal; Javier Valdes-Aleman; Feng Li; N. Randel; E. Barsotti; Ana Correia; R. Fetter; V. Hartenstein; Carey E. Priebe; J. Vogelstein; Albert Cardona; Marta Zlatic

ocar.opportunity: Knowing network architecture is essential for understanding brain function. Drosophila larva offers rich behavior—learning, value computation, action selection—in a brain small enough for a complete synaptic-resolution map.
ocar.challenge: Without a whole-brain synapse-level connectome, claims about hubs, feedback, multisensory integration, and resemblance to machine-learning architectures remain incomplete. Axon versus dendrite compartmentalization also changes how connections should be counted.
ocar.action: Winding, Pedigo, Barnes, Patsolic, Park, Kazimiers, Fushiki, Andrade, Khandelwal, Valdes-Aleman, Li, Randel, Barsotti, Correia, Fetter, Hartenstein, Priebe, Vogelstein, Cardona, and Zlatic in Science (2023) map the synaptic-resolution connectome of an entire Drosophila larva brain. They split each neuron into axon and dendrite, yielding four connection types, cluster neurons from connectivity, and track polysynaptic pathways from synapse numbers.
ocar.resolution: The reconstruction comprises 3,016 neurons and 548,000 synapses. Connectivity clustering yielded 93 neuron types with internally consistent morphology and, where known, function. Most connections were axon-to-dendrite (66.4%), with axon-to-axon 26.4%, dendrite-to-dendrite 5.4%, and dendrite-to-axon 1.8%; noncanonical types were pronounced in learning and action-selection circuits. The authors report pervasive multisensory and interhemispheric integration, high recurrence, abundant feedback from descending neurons, and novel motifs; the most recurrent circuits involved learning-center input and output neurons. Some structural features resembled powerful machine-learning architectures (multilayer shortcuts, nested recurrent loops).
ocar.future_work: The map is offered as a basis for experimental and theoretical circuit studies; many connectivity-defined clusters still lack gene-expression and functional characterization.

plain_language_summary: This paper maps every neuron and synapse in a fruit-fly maggot’s brain. The wiring is highly recurrent, mixes the senses, and uses extra connection styles beyond the usual axon-to-dendrite pattern, especially in the learning center.

summaries.beginner: This paper maps every neuron and synapse in a fruit-fly maggot’s brain. The wiring is highly recurrent, mixes the senses, and uses extra connection styles beyond the usual axon-to-dendrite pattern, especially in the learning center.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Science (2023), Winding, Pedigo, Cardona, Zlatic and colleagues report a complete Drosophila larva brain connectome of 3,016 neurons and 548,000 synapses. Neurons were split into axon and dendrite compartments (four connection types). Unbiased connectivity clustering produced 93 types. Architecture analysis finds widespread multisensory and interhemispheric integration, recurrence concentrated at learning-center input/output neurons, descending-neuron feedback, and motifs including multilayer shortcuts and nested loops. Axon–axon connections are 26.4% of synapses and are discussed in the context of mushroom-body teaching signals and possible lateral inhibition.
summaries.advanced: Abstract and PDF neuron/synapse totals differ slightly (3,013 / 544,000 versus 3,016 / 548,000); figures here follow the reconstructed PDF. “Entire insect brain” is the larva CNS brain, not adult Drosophila. Functional interpretations of a-a synapses (e.g., inhibitory mAChR-B) draw on adult literature. Clustering by connectivity is one type definition; many clusters remain uncharacterized. Machine-learning architecture resemblance is analogical.

title: The neuropeptidergic connectome of C. elegans
authors: Lidia Ripoll-Sánchez; Jan Watteyne; Haosheng Sun; Robert W. Fernandez; Seth R. Taylor; Alexis Weinreb; Marc Hammarlund; David M. Miller; O. Hobert; Isabel Beets; P. Vértes; W. Schafer

ocar.opportunity: Synaptic wiring diagrams miss extrasynaptic neuropeptide signaling, which is widespread and essential in all nervous systems. C. elegans offers single-cell anatomy, gene expression, and a growing biochemical map of peptide–receptor pairs, so a draft peptidergic connectome is feasible.
ocar.challenge: Neuropeptidergic networks are largely uncharacterized as graphs. Diffusion range is uncertain, many receptors remain orphan, and topology may differ radically from synaptic networks.
ocar.action: Ripoll-Sánchez, Watteyne, Sun, Fernandez, Taylor, Weinreb, Hammarlund, Miller, Hobert, Beets, Vértes, and Schafer in Neuron (2023) integrate GPCR deorphanization (51 GPCRs, 49 neuropeptide precursors, 92 ligand–receptor pairs), scRNA-seq of 302 neurons, and anatomical contacts to build a draft C. elegans neuropeptide connectome. They analyze density, cascades, autocrine foci, communities, hubs, and rich-club structure under conservative diffusion assumptions.
ocar.resolution: The peptidergic network is over 10-fold denser than the synaptic connectome even with conservative diffusion assumptions. It is decentralized, with a large interconnected core of three communities sharing similar input patterns. Several of the most important nodes are little-studied neurons specialized for peptidergic neuromodulation. Degree correlates with synaptic degree (r = 0.54, p = 3.1e−14). A rich club of 156 neurons is reported for the short-range model (166 for mid-range).
ocar.future_work: The authors anticipate this draft as a prototype for organizational principles of neuroendocrine networks; additional deorphanization and spatial diffusion measurements would refine edges.

plain_language_summary: Worms—and likely all brains—send many messages not across tight synapses but as chemical broadcasts. This paper draws a first whole-animal map of those peptide signals and finds a dense, less hub-dominated network than the classic synaptic wiring diagram.

summaries.beginner: Worms—and likely all brains—send many messages not across tight synapses but as chemical broadcasts. This paper draws a first whole-animal map of those peptide signals and finds a dense, less hub-dominated network than the classic synaptic wiring diagram.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Neuron (2023), Ripoll-Sánchez, Beets, Vértes, Schafer and colleagues assemble a draft C. elegans neuropeptidergic connectome from 51 GPCRs, 49 peptide genes, 92 validated pairs, and expression in 302 neurons. Even under conservative diffusion assumptions the graph is over 10-fold denser than the synaptic connectome, with extended cascades, autocrine foci, and a decentralized core of three input-similarity communities. Hubs include little-studied peptidergic specialists. Synaptic and peptidergic degrees correlate (r = 0.54); a short-range rich club contains 156 neurons.
summaries.advanced: Edges are model-based (expression × biochemically validated pairs × assumed range), not imaged peptide release. Conservative diffusion still yields >10× density; true range could change topology. Orphan receptors and peptides are missing by construction. Correlation r = 0.54 leaves much unmatched variance between synaptic and peptidergic importance. Behavioral examples (e.g., FLP-20) illustrate timescales, not a full functional validation of the graph.

title: A connectomic study of a petascale fragment of human cerebral cortex
authors: Alexander Shapson-Coe; Michał Januszewski; D. Berger; Art Pope; Yuelong Wu; T. Blakely; R. Schalek; Peter H. Li; Shuohong Wang; Jeremy B. Maitin-Shepard; N. Karlupia; Sven Dorkenwald; Evelina Sjostedt; Laramie Leavitt; Dongil Lee; Luke Bailey; A. Fitzmaurice; Rohin Kar; Benjamin Field; Hank Wu; J. Wagner-Carena; David Aley; J. Lau; Zudi Lin; D. Wei; H. Pfister; A. Peleg; Viren Jain; J. Lichtman

ocar.opportunity: Human association cortex is rarely available as rapidly preserved, high-quality tissue for nanometer-scale circuit reconstruction. A cubic-millimeter, full-thickness volume would let researchers see all layers, white matter, and intra-cortical axons that may travel over a hundred microns before the first synapse.
ocar.challenge: Access, preservation, petascale imaging, and automated segmentation with remaining split/merge errors all stand between a surgical sample and a usable human cortical connectome. Epilepsy history and medications are additional confounds even when the resected piece is “in the way” rather than the focus of disease.
ocar.action: Shapson-Coe, Januszewski, Berger, Pope, Wu, Blakely, Schalek, Li, Wang, Maitin-Shepard, Karlupia, Dorkenwald, Jain, Lichtman and colleagues (bioRxiv 2021) rapidly preserved a human temporal-lobe surgical sample, stained ~1 mm³, cut more than 5,000 slices at ~30 nm, and imaged with multibeam SEM. Computational reconstruction yielded 57,216 cells, hundreds of millions of neurites, and 133.7 million synapses in a 1.4-petabyte volume; 104 cells were manually proofread. Data are available to browse online.
ocar.resolution: Glia outnumbered neurons 2:1, with oligodendrocytes the most common cell type. Excitatory spiny neurons were 69% of neurons; excitatory synapses 76%. Synaptic drive onto spiny neurons was 70% excitatory versus 48% onto inhibitory interneurons. Despite incomplete automated segmentation, validated connections could be generated among most excitatory and inhibitory types within and between layers. Deep-layer excitatory cells split into new structural/connectivity subsets; chandelier cells innervated one another’s axon initial segments as well as those of excitatory neurons. Rare axons made up to ~20 synapses onto a target, among thousands of weak inputs, suggesting outsized influence.
ocar.future_work: The authors argue that rapid immersion of fresh tissue can match perfusion quality and that further scale-up toward mouse-brain-scale volumes is becoming realistic; interpreting findings in light of possible epilepsy-related or pharmacological effects remains necessary.

plain_language_summary: A cubic millimeter of human temporal cortex was sliced thousands of times, photographed with a fast electron microscope, and reconstructed into a digital tissue with tens of thousands of cells and more than a hundred million synapses. Among many findings, glia outnumber neurons, and a few axons make unusually many contacts onto the same cell.

summaries.beginner: A cubic millimeter of human temporal cortex was sliced thousands of times, photographed with a fast electron microscope, and reconstructed into a digital tissue with tens of thousands of cells and more than a hundred million synapses. Among many findings, glia outnumber neurons, and a few axons make unusually many contacts onto the same cell.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2021), Shapson-Coe, Januszewski, Jain, Lichtman and colleagues reconstruct a 1 mm³ human temporal-cortex sample: >5,000 sections at ~30 nm, 1.4 PB, 57,216 cells, 133.7 million synapses, and 104 manually proofread cells. Glia:neuron is 2:1; oligodendrocytes are most common; 69% of neurons are excitatory spiny cells; 76% of synapses are excitatory (70% of synapses onto spiny neurons versus 48% onto interneurons). They describe new deep-layer excitatory subsets, chandelier-to-chandelier AIS innervation, and rare multi-synaptic axons (up to ~20 contacts). Online browsing of the H01 volume is provided.
summaries.advanced: Automated segmentation is explicitly incomplete (splits/merges). The donor had epilepsy; the sample was access-path tissue judged not primarily pathological, but pharmacology and disease effects cannot be excluded. 1 mm³ is argued as sufficient for layer-spanning local circuits, not a whole area. Multi-synaptic “powerful” inputs are anatomical multiplicity, not measured EPSP amplitude. Comparison to a 2015 mouse saturated reconstruction is a scale-up narrative (~4 years, ~660,000-fold voxels), not a matched biology study.

title: A multiscale brain map derived from whole-brain volumetric reconstructions
authors: C. Brittin; Steven J. Cook; D. Hall; S. W. Emmons; N. Cohen

ocar.opportunity: Nervous-system organization spans synapses, neuronal morphology, and brain-region connectivity, but a complete structure–function model integrated across those scales had not been achieved even in a small animal. C. elegans offers a compact nerve ring plus existing synaptic and gap-junction connectomes.
ocar.challenge: The nerve ring was long treated as a densely packed process tract without an internal spatial model that could explain which synapses are possible. Connectomes were often treated as invariant, hiding core versus variable wiring.
ocar.action: Brittin, Cook, Hall, Emmons, and Cohen in Nature (2021) integrate volumetric reconstructions of the nerve ring from two animals with corresponding chemical-synapse and gap-junction connectomes. They analyze local neighborhoods, variability versus a core circuit, and propose a modular structure–function architecture.
ocar.resolution: Local neighborhoods spatially constrain and support the synaptic connectome. The C. elegans connectome is not invariant: a precisely wired core is embedded in variable connectivity, from which they derive a candidate reference core connectome. On that reference they propose modules supporting sensory computation and integration, sensorimotor convergence, and brain-wide coordination, arguing these are scalable, robust features that may be universal across phyla.
ocar.future_work: The model is a template for asking which spatial and modular principles generalize; more animals would better separate core from variable edges.

plain_language_summary: The worm’s central nerve bundle was thought to be a packed tangle of wires. Reconstructing it in 3D in two animals shows orderly neighborhoods, a shared core circuit, and extra connections that differ between individuals.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s central nerve bundle was thought to be a packed tangle of wires. Reconstructing it in 3D in two animals shows orderly neighborhoods, a shared core circuit, and extra connections that differ between individuals.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature (2021), Brittin, Cook, Hall, Emmons, and Cohen present a structure–function model of the C. elegans nerve ring from two complete volumetric reconstructions aligned to synaptic and gap-junction connectomes. They show internal spatial neighborhoods that constrain synapses, reject strict invariance in favor of a core circuit plus variable background, and propose a modular architecture for sensory integration, sensorimotor convergence, and brain-wide coordination.
summaries.advanced: n = 2 animals limits statistical separation of core versus variable synapses. Universality across phyla is an interpretive claim. Gap junctions are included in the integrated model but chemical-synapse analyses dominate many narratives of variability. The extracted PDF is an accepted manuscript with figure placeholders; quantitative neighborhood statistics are not in the truncated text beyond the abstract-level findings.

title: AxonEM Dataset: 3D Axon Instance Segmentation of Brain Cortical Regions
authors: D. Wei; Kisuk Lee; Hanyu Li; R. Lu; J. Bae; Zequan Liu; Lifu Zhang; M'arcia dos Santos; Zudi Lin; T. Uram; Xueying Wang; Ignacio Arganda-Carreras; Brian Matejek; N. Kasthuri; J. Lichtman; H. Pfister
journal: International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention

ocar.opportunity: EM can reconstruct circuits at synaptic resolution, but cortical axons are morphologically hard and there was no public large-scale cortical EM dataset with dense axon instance ground truth for training and evaluation.
ocar.challenge: Broken membranes, tight axon bundles, invaginations, thin segments, and image defects cause merge and split errors. Without dense axon labels, methods cannot be compared at scale.
ocar.action: Wei, Lee, Li, Lu, Bae, Liu, Zhang, dos Santos, Lin, Uram, Wang, Arganda-Carreras, Matejek, Kasthuri, Lichtman, and Pfister introduce AxonEM at MICCAI (2021): two 30 × 30 × 30 µm³ EM volumes from human and mouse cortex with dense 3D axon instance segmentation. They proofread over 18,000 axon instances and densely annotate nine ground-truth subvolumes per volume for training, then reimplement affinity U-Net and flood-filling network baselines.
ocar.resolution: The dataset enables large-scale axon evaluation. Affinity U-Net expected run length reached 88% of ground truth on mouse (AxonEM-M) and 65% on human (AxonEM-H). An FFN baseline without the original multi-scale consensus and agglomeration steps was substantially worse (reported as 34% and 22% of GT ERL). Code and data are public.
ocar.future_work: The authors expect the set to foster better axon methods and to serve as a testbed for other applications; a more faithful FFN baseline remains future work.

plain_language_summary: Thin axons in cortex are among the hardest objects to color in automatically, and there was no big public test set. AxonEM hands the community two cubes of human and mouse cortex with more than 18,000 carefully checked axons so algorithms can be scored fairly.

summaries.beginner: Thin axons in cortex are among the hardest objects to color in automatically, and there was no big public test set. AxonEM hands the community two cubes of human and mouse cortex with more than 18,000 carefully checked axons so algorithms can be scored fairly.
summaries.intermediate: In MICCAI (2021), Wei, Lee, Pfister and colleagues release AxonEM: two 30 × 30 × 30 µm³ cortical EM volumes (human and mouse) with dense proofreading of over 18,000 axons and nine densely annotated training subvolumes per volume. Reimplemented affinity U-Net agglomeration achieved axon expected run length of 88% of GT on mouse and 65% on human. A partial FFN reimplementation lagged (22–34% of GT ERL) because multi-scale consensus and FFN agglomeration were omitted. Data and code are at the Connectomics Bazaar AxonEM page.
summaries.advanced: Volumes are 30 µm cubes, not cortical columns. FFN numbers are not a reproduction of Januszewski et al.’s full pipeline; the authors warn against treating them as SOTA FFN performance. ERL percentages are relative to GT axon ERL in these volumes. Human versus mouse difficulty (65% vs 88%) should not be over-interpreted as a species law. Some authors disclose Zetta AI financial interests.

title: Connectomes across development reveal principles of brain maturation
authors: Daniel K. Witvliet; Ben Mulcahy; James K. Mitchell; Y. Meirovitch; D. Berger; Yuelong Wu; Yufang Liu; Wan Xian Koh; Rajeev Parvathala; D. Holmyard; R. Schalek; N. Shavit; A. Chisholm; J. Lichtman; Aravinthan D. T. Samuel; Mei Zhen

ocar.opportunity: As an animal grows, its nervous system and behaviors mature, but how much a complete brain’s wiring diagram remodels after birth was unknown. C. elegans is isogenic and small enough that full brains can be reconstructed at multiple ages.
ocar.challenge: Prior connectomes were essentially snapshots, so stable, variable, and developmental edges could not be separated. Gap-junction visibility and limited animals per stage further constrain developmental inference.
ocar.action: Witvliet, Mulcahy, Mitchell, Meirovitch, Berger, Wu, Liu, Koh, Parvathala, Holmyard, Schalek, Shavit, Chisholm, Lichtman, Samuel, and Zhen in Nature (2021) used serial-section EM to reconstruct the full brain of eight isogenic C. elegans individuals across postnatal stages. They compared geometry, chemical synapses among individuals, and consistent wiring changes across maturation.
ocar.resolution: Overall brain geometry is preserved from birth to adulthood, while chemical synaptic connectivity changes substantially on that scaffold. Individuals differ enough that each brain is partly unique, yet many neuron-pair changes are consistent across maturation, altering existing weights and adding connections. Central decision-making circuitry is maintained while sensory and motor pathways remodel; with age the brain becomes more feedforward and discernibly modular. Most connectivity asymmetry present at birth is eliminated during L1. Relative neurite-length proportions correlate between L1 and adult (Spearman r = 0.75, n = 947).
ocar.future_work: The authors note that gap junctions were not included at the same confidence, and that most time points have only one animal, so age-specific variability remains undersampled; higher throughput per stage is needed.

plain_language_summary: Eight worm brains, from baby to adult, were fully mapped in the electron microscope. The overall layout stays the same, but many chemical connections change in a coordinated way, and the adult network looks more one-way and more modular.

summaries.beginner: Eight worm brains, from baby to adult, were fully mapped in the electron microscope. The overall layout stays the same, but many chemical connections change in a coordinated way, and the adult network looks more one-way and more modular.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature (2021), Witvliet, Lichtman, Samuel, Zhen and colleagues reconstruct complete brains of eight isogenic C. elegans across postnatal life. Geometry is stable while chemical synapses remodel: individual uniqueness plus stereotyped developmental additions and weight changes. Decision-making cores persist; sensory and motor pathways change more. Networks become more feedforward and modular with age. Left–right asymmetry and missing connections drop most during L1. An online database (nemanode.org) hosts the connectomes, including electrical synapses where visible.
summaries.advanced: Gap junctions are a stated limitation of the analysis. Typically one connectome per time point prevents measuring within-age variability. Chemical-synapse scoring is higher confidence than electrical. Isogenic animals reduce genetic noise but not all environmental or stochastic developmental effects. Spearman r = 0.75 describes relative neurite-length preservation, not synapse-by-synapse invariance.

title: Connectomic features underlying diverse synaptic connection strengths and subcellular computation
authors: Tony X. Liu; Pasha A Davoudian; Kristyn M. Lizbinski; James M. Jeanne

ocar.opportunity: EM connectomes list every synapse location and neuron shape, which might let researchers infer physiological connection weights and when axons versus dendrites must be modeled as separate compartments. Doing so requires pairing anatomy with subthreshold physiology on the same cell classes.
ocar.challenge: Network models often treat synaptic weights and compartmentalization as free parameters. Anatomy–physiology links known for one synapse type (for example mouse neocortex PSD size versus uEPSP) may not generalize across diverse neurons. Drosophila hemibrain offers morphological diversity but needs matched physiology.
ocar.action: Liu, Davoudian, Lizbinski, and Jeanne (bioRxiv 2021) compare anatomy and physiology at subcellular, subthreshold resolution in a stereotyped Drosophila olfactory network (projection neurons to lateral horn neurons). They relate synapse number, density, and location to somatic unitary EPSP amplitude and fit biophysical models of axonal versus dendritic integration.
ocar.resolution: Synapse density and location jointly predict the amplitude of the somatic postsynaptic potential evoked by a single presynaptic spike. Number of synapses and LHN surface area predict somatic uEPSPs for dendritic connections but severely underpredict when input is axonal. Models predict that electrical compartmentalization lets axon and dendrite arbors balance independent and interacting computations.
ocar.future_work: The authors frame this as a step from connectivity maps toward activity maps; testing whether the same anatomical predictors hold beyond PN–LHN pairs is the next generalization.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram says how many synapses two cells share, but not how strong the message feels. In the fly olfactory system, counting synapses and noting whether they sit on the dendrite or the axon predicts the electrical bump recorded at the cell body after one spike.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram says how many synapses two cells share, but not how strong the message feels. In the fly olfactory system, counting synapses and noting whether they sit on the dendrite or the axon predicts the electrical bump recorded at the cell body after one spike.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2021), Liu, Davoudian, Lizbinski, and Jeanne pair Drosophila hemibrain-style anatomy with subthreshold physiology in olfactory projection-neuron to lateral-horn-neuron connections. Synapse density and location jointly predict somatic uEPSP amplitude from a single presynaptic spike. Dendritic connections are predicted by synapse number and LHN surface area; axonal input is not. Compartmental models indicate axons and dendrites can compute somewhat separately while still interacting.
summaries.advanced: Results are for a stereotyped olfactory subnetwork, not a brain-wide weight table. Predictors are of somatic uEPSP, which can miss local axonal computations the models themselves emphasize. Hemibrain anatomy is from published reconstructions, not necessarily the same individual as the physiology. No single scalar R² is given in the extracted text. Mouse PSD–uEPSP linearity is cited as motivation, not a result of this paper.

title: Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex
authors: J. Alexander Bae; Mahaly Baptiste; A. Bodor; D. Brittain; J. Buchanan; D. Bumbarger; M. Castro; Brendan Celii; Erick Cobos; F. Collman; N. D. da Costa; S. Dorkenwald; L. Elabbady; Paul G. Wong; Jingpeng Wu; Chris Xu; Runzhe Yang; Dimitri Yatsenko; Fei Ye; W. Yin; Szi-chieh Yu

ocar.opportunity: Understanding the brain requires relating each neuron’s functional responses to the synaptic architecture that shapes them. Crick’s 1979 “impossible” request—a cubic millimeter with both wiring and firing—is now approachable by combining dense calcium imaging with volumetric EM.
ocar.challenge: Prior structure–function studies were fragmentary (single cells, slices, or viral tracing). Co-registering awake visual physiology with a millimeter-scale EM volume spanning multiple cortical areas, then proofreading enough axons to count thousands of cell-to-cell connections, is a massive alignment and reconstruction problem.
ocar.action: The MICrONS Consortium in Nature (2025) recorded activity from around 75,000 neurons in VISp, VISrl, VISal, and VISlm of an awake mouse viewing natural movies and synthetic stimuli, co-registered to an EM reconstruction with more than 200,000 cells and 0.5 billion synapses. Proofreading of a subset yielded complete dendritic trees plus local and inter-areal axons. They release the dataset and retrieval tools; accompanying papers analyze cell types, a cortical-column connectivity diagram, inhibitory motifs linked to gene expression, visual integration, neuronal invariances, and excitatory wiring within and across areas.
ocar.resolution: The resource includes Neuroglancer visualizations of proofread examples (layer 5 thick-tufted and near-projecting cells, layer 4, layer 2/3). Reporting materials specify a male Slc17a7-Cre × Ai162 mouse, IACUC approval at Allen Institute or Baylor, no experimental replication, and exclusion of neurons without proofread axons from a subset of analyses.
ocar.future_work: Continued proofreading is described as making the reconstruction increasingly accurate; accompanying papers are the venue for the biological conclusions built on this release.

plain_language_summary: A mouse watched movies while thousands of its visual-cortex cells lit up, and the same cubic millimeter was later reconstructed in an electron microscope with hundreds of millions of synapses. The public dataset lets anyone match those firing patterns to actual wiring.

summaries.beginner: A mouse watched movies while thousands of its visual-cortex cells lit up, and the same cubic millimeter was later reconstructed in an electron microscope with hundreds of millions of synapses. The public dataset lets anyone match those firing patterns to actual wiring.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature (2025), the MICrONS Consortium releases a functional connectomics resource: dense two-photon calcium imaging of ~75,000 neurons across VISp and higher visual areas (VISrl, VISal, VISlm) in an awake mouse, co-registered with serial-section TEM of >200,000 cells and 0.5 billion synapses. Proofread neurons include full dendrites and inter-areal axons with up to thousands of connections per cell. Companion papers address cell types, column connectivity, inhibitory motifs, visual computation, invariances, and excitatory wiring rules. Tools for retrieval and Neuroglancer viewing are included.
summaries.advanced: This is a resource-and-consortium paper; many biological claims are deferred to accompanying studies. n = 1 male mouse; reporting summary states no replication, randomization, or blinding. Functional sampling aimed to include primary and secondary visual areas rather than a pre-specified power calculation. Analyses that need axons exclude non-proofread neurons. Calcium imaging and EM co-registration inherit residual alignment error not quantified in the extracted text.

title: Partial connectomes of labeled dopaminergic circuits reveal non-synaptic communication and axonal remodeling after exposure to cocaine
authors: Gregg A. Wildenberg; A. Sorokina; J. Koranda; A. Monical; C. Heer; M. Sheffield; X. Zhuang; D. McGehee; B. Kasthuri

ocar.opportunity: Dopaminergic axons strongly influence behavior including addiction, but how they communicate in nucleus accumbens—point synapses versus volume transmission—and how that anatomy changes after cocaine remain poorly resolved at EM scale.
ocar.challenge: Light-level varicosity counts cannot show vesicles, synapses, spinules, or mitochondrial remodeling. Cell-type-specific EM labeling is needed to follow identified DA axons in large volumes before and after drug exposure.
ocar.action: Wildenberg, Sorokina, Koranda, Monical, Heer, Sheffield, Zhuang, McGehee, and Kasthuri in eLife (2021) combine genetic labeling (mito-Apex2 in DAT+ neurons) with large-volume serial EM of mouse NAc in controls and after a brief cocaine-sensitization protocol. They classify varicosities by vesicle content, score synapses versus spinule-like interdigitations, and quantify branching, glial ensheathment, bulbs, and mitochondrial length.
ocar.resolution: Individual DA axons contain mixed varicosity types that appear non-randomly ordered. Classic synapses were rare (<2%, 6/410), whereas spinule-like structures with neighbors were more common (15%, 61/410). Days after cocaine, DA axons were more branched, formed mitochondria-filled blind-ended bulbs, and were surrounded by elaborated glia. Mitochondrial length increased ~2.2-fold relative to control only in DA axons and NAc spiny dendrites. The authors conclude NAc DA transmission is unlikely to be classical synaptic and that anatomical plasticity after cocaine is largely axonal rearrangement with correlated mitochondrial change.
ocar.future_work: Follow-up in self-administration or longer abstinence, and tests of whether DAT+ subclasses differ, are needed; the authors treat sensitization as a minimal acute model, not full addiction.

plain_language_summary: Dopamine cables in the mouse reward center almost never make textbook synapses. They more often interleave with neighbors and, after a short cocaine exposure, sprout extra branches and swollen, mitochondria-packed endings.

summaries.beginner: Dopamine cables in the mouse reward center almost never make textbook synapses. They more often interleave with neighbors and, after a short cocaine exposure, sprout extra branches and swollen, mitochondria-packed endings.
summaries.intermediate: Published in eLife (2021), Wildenberg, Kasthuri and colleagues reconstruct labeled dopaminergic axons in mouse nucleus accumbens with serial EM, with and without cocaine sensitization. Varicosity types differ by vesicle content and are non-randomly ordered along axons. Specific synapses were 6/410 (<2%); spinule-like interdigitations 61/410 (15%). After cocaine, axons branched more, formed mitochondria-filled bulbs, and attracted elaborated glia; mitochondrial length rose ~2.2× only in DA axons and NAc spiny dendrites.
summaries.advanced: Synapse rarity is 6/410 scored varicosities in this labeled NAc sample, not all DA systems. Cocaine protocol is sensitization, which the authors distinguish from addiction models. Labeling uses DAT-driven AAV; subclass bias cannot be fully excluded despite matched virus batches. Mitochondrial 2.2× is a length increase in specified compartments, not a metabolic assay. Volume-transmission inference is from lack of synaptic specializations plus spinules, not measured extrasynaptic concentrations.

title: Petascale neural circuit reconstruction: automated methods
authors: T. Macrina; Kisuk Lee; R. Lu; N. Turner; Jingpeng Wu; S. Popovych; W. Silversmith; N. Kemnitz; J. Bae; M. Castro; S. Dorkenwald; A. Halageri; Z. Jia; C. Jordan; Kai Li; E. Mitchell; S. Mondal; S. Mu; Barak Nehoran; W. Wong; Szi-chieh Yu; A. Bodor; D. Brittain; J. Buchanan; D. Bumbarger; Erick Cobos; F. Collman; L. Elabbady; Paul G. Fahey; E. Froudarakis; D. Kapner; S. Kinn; G. Mahalingam; S. Papadopoulos; Saumil S. Patel; C. Schneider-Mizell; Fabian H. Sinz; Marc M. Takeno; R. Torres; W. Yin; X. Pitkow; J. Reimer; A. Tolias; R. Reid; N. D. Costa; H. Seung

ocar.opportunity: 3D EM has mapped invertebrate nervous systems but only small chunks of mammalian brain. Serial-section EM of a near cubic millimeter produces petascale images that need a computational pipeline for alignment, segmentation, semantics, and synapses.
ocar.challenge: Serial sections contain numerous cracks and folds, so alignment cannot assume smooth transforms. Boundary detection, semantic labeling (axon, dendrite, soma), synapse assignment, and agglomeration must run in distributed cloud workflows whose intermediates remain inspectable.
ocar.action: Macrina, Lee, Lu, Turner, Wu, Popovych, Silversmith, Kemnitz, Bae, Castro, Dorkenwald, Seung and the MICrONS consortium (bioRxiv 2021) describe a pipeline of convolutional nets for nonsmooth serial-section alignment, neuronal boundary detection, semantic voxel labels, and synapse detection/assignment, followed by mean-affinity agglomeration with semantic and size constraints. Intermediate results live in cloud storage as viewable images. They apply it to ~1.5 petapixels from a P87 male mouse spanning four visual cortical areas (Yin et al. 2020 acquisition).
ocar.resolution: The pipeline produced a public automated reconstruction of that multi-area visual-cortex volume, with publicly available code. Discussion emphasizes remaining errors at residual misalignments, mitochondria or ER contacting plasma membrane, low contrast, and missing/thick sections, and sketches scaling hierarchical agglomeration toward an exascale whole-mouse brain (~1000× larger).
ocar.future_work: Automated error detection/correction is cited as not yet deployed at scale in this pipeline; reducing cracks/folds in future acquisitions or considering block-face EM are discussed as complementary paths.

plain_language_summary: Photographing a cubic millimeter of mouse cortex on thousands of slices creates a mountain of images full of cracks and folds. This paper is the factory software that lines the slices up, finds cell borders and synapses, and glues fragments together in the cloud so people can browse an automated reconstruction.

summaries.beginner: Photographing a cubic millimeter of mouse cortex on thousands of slices creates a mountain of images full of cracks and folds. title: PyTorch Connectomics: A Scalable and Flexible Segmentation Framework for EM Connectomics
authors: Zudi Lin; D. Wei; J. Lichtman; H. Pfister

ocar.opportunity: Connectomics depends on segmenting neurons, synapses, and organelles such as mitochondria from nanometer-scale volumetric microscopy before structural or functional analysis can proceed. Deep learning is now the default for both semantic and instance segmentation on biomedical volumes.
ocar.challenge: Open-source segmentation packages are typically built for standard benchmarks, so adapting them to connectomics data of different scales and formats takes substantial work on hardware and preprocessing. Specialized architectures and learning targets are cumbersome to implement, and expensive expert labels sit beside large unlabeled volumes that most packages do not exploit.
ocar.action: Lin, Wei, Lichtman, and Pfister present PyTorch Connectomics (PyTC), an open-source PyTorch framework for 2D and 3D semantic and instance segmentation. Configuration options, without new code, enable multi-task and semi-supervised learning and retargeting to other tissues and imaging modalities.
ocar.resolution: On the CREMI challenge, PyTC reports the best synaptic-cleft segmentation, outperforming the previous best result by a relative 6.1%, with competitive performance on mitochondria and neuronal nuclei. Code and tutorials are released at connectomics.readthedocs.io.
ocar.future_work: The selected extract does not specify a follow-on reconstruction campaign; the natural next uses are applying the same configuration-driven pipeline to additional organelles, volumes, and imaging modalities.

plain_language_summary: Computers must paint every pixel of a brain microscope volume before anyone can follow the wiring. This paper shares an open toolbox, PyTorch Connectomics, that trains those painting models on big three-dimensional images without rewriting code for each new dataset.

summaries.beginner: Computers must paint every pixel of a brain microscope volume before anyone can follow the wiring. This paper shares an open toolbox, PyTorch Connectomics, that trains those painting models on big three-dimensional images without rewriting code for each new dataset.
summaries.intermediate: In an arXiv preprint (2021), Lin, Wei, Lichtman, and Pfister introduce PyTorch Connectomics (PyTC) for semantic and instance segmentation of volumetric microscopy. The toolbox is aimed at connectomics-scale neuron, synapse, and organelle segmentation and supports multi-task and semi-supervised training so scarce expert labels can be combined with unlabeled data. On CREMI synaptic-cleft segmentation it reports a relative 6.1% improvement over the previous best result, with competitive mitochondria and neuronal-nuclei scores.
summaries.advanced: The 6.1% figure is a relative CREMI synaptic-cleft gain, not a neuron-instance score; mitochondria and nuclei results are described only as competitive. The selected PDF extract is dominated by front matter and references, so claims about production-scale reconstructions or other tasks rest on the abstract and introduction rather than a full results section. Generalization beyond the reported benchmarks is asserted via configuration, not quantified here.

title: Structure and function of axo-axonic inhibition
authors: C. Schneider-Mizell; A. Bodor; F. Collman; D. Brittain; Adam A. Bleckert; S. Dorkenwald; N. Turner; T. Macrina; Kisuk Lee; R. Lu; Jingpeng Wu; J. Zhuang; Anirban Nandi; Brian Hu; J. Buchanan; Marc M. Takeno; R. Torres; G. Mahalingam; D. Bumbarger; Yang Li; Thomas Chartrand; N. Kemnitz; W. Silversmith; Dodam Ih; J. Zung; A. Zlateski; Ignacio Tartavull; S. Popovych; W. Wong; M. Castro; C. Jordan; E. Froudarakis; Lynne Becker; S. Suckow; J. Reimer; A. Tolias; C. Anastassiou; H. Seung; R. Reid; N. D. da Costa

ocar.opportunity: Cortical inhibitory neurons come in many physiological, morphological, molecular, and connectivity flavors. Mapping how a defined interneuron class innervates identified targets at synaptic resolution is a route to linking cell type, structure, and function.
ocar.challenge: Average connectivity of several interneuron classes is known, but the synaptic-resolution distribution of a distinct inhibitory type, how that distribution relates to target-cell properties, and how it affects function remain poorly understood.
ocar.action: Schneider-Mizell and colleagues used dense electron microscopy in layer 2/3 of mouse visual cortex plus cell-type-specific calcium imaging in awake animals. They mapped complete chandelier-cell input onto 153 pyramidal neurons and simulated the observed axo-axonic pattern.
ocar.resolution: Chandelier synapse number is highly variable across pyramids, correlates with target structural features, and varies more than perisomatic inhibition; simple perisomatic features already accounted for approximately half the variance in chandelier synapse count. Simulations indicate the pattern is especially effective when excitation and inhibition are co-active. In vivo, chandelier cells fire in highly correlated bouts that track pupil dilation, a proxy for arousal.
ocar.future_work: The authors flag a larger volume (Bae et al., 2021) to reduce truncation and add morphology, activity, and excitatory-network covariates. Whether P36 connectivity is adult-mature, and whether remaining filopodia mark plasticity or incomplete maturation, needs older-animal datasets.

plain_language_summary: Some inhibitory cells grab the axon of a neighbor right where it starts its output spike. This paper maps those chandelier connections onto many visual-cortex pyramids in a mouse and shows the cells fire together when the animal is aroused.

summaries.beginner: Some inhibitory cells grab the axon of a neighbor right where it starts its output spike. This paper maps those chandelier connections onto many visual-cortex pyramids in a mouse and shows the cells fire together when the animal is aroused.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2021), Schneider-Mizell, da Costa, and colleagues reconstructed chandelier input onto 153 layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons in mouse visual cortex from dense electron microscopy and imaged chandelier activity in awake mice. Synapse counts vary widely, more than perisomatic inhibition, and correlate with target structure; perisomatic features explained about half of chandelier-count variance. Biophysical simulations suggest axo-axonic inhibition is especially effective when excitation and inhibition coincide. Population calcium signals are highly correlated and track pupil dilation.
summaries.advanced: The EM volume is from postnatal day 36, just after the critical period; adulthood is usually taken as P56, and occasional chandelier filopodia leave open whether the map is fully mature. Functional imaging and EM are not from the same cells. Volume truncation and missing whole-cell morphology are explicit limits; about half the chandelier-count variance remains unexplained by the simple features used here.

ocar.action: Scheffer, Xu, Januszewski, Plaza, and a large Janelia–Google collaboration present the adult Drosophila central-brain (hemibrain) connectome. They summarize pipeline improvements, define cell types, refine compartments, and release public circuits of neurons and chemical synapses.

plain_language_summary: This paper delivers a wiring diagram for a large part of an adult fruit-fly brain, cell by cell and synapse by synapse. Finding who talks to whom, a job that used to take months, is now a public lookup.

summaries.beginner: This paper delivers a wiring diagram for a large part of an adult fruit-fly brain, cell by cell and synapse by synapse. Finding who talks to whom, a job that used to take months, is now a public lookup.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2020), Scheffer, Xu, Januszewski, Plaza, and colleagues report the hemibrain connectome of the adult Drosophila central brain. They improve preparation, imaging, alignment, segmentation, synapse finding, and proofreading, then define cell types and computational compartments and release neuron-and-chemical-synapse circuits. Analyses cover strength distributions, motifs, compartmental electrical effects, and packing-density constraints. The data are public so upstream and downstream partners can be queried rather than rediscovered experimentally.
summaries.advanced: The map is chemical synapses in a large fraction of the central brain of one animal, not a whole-animal nervous system and not gap junctions. Completeness varies by region; central complex and mushroom body were prioritized. The authors themselves note that synaptic richness far exceeds identified behaviors, so many pathways remain uninterpreted. Sex differences are acknowledged as unfinished.

title: A connectome of the Drosophila central complex reveals network motifs suitable for flexible navigation and context-dependent action selection
authors: B. Hulse; H. Haberkern; R. Franconville; D. Turner-Evans; Shin-ya Takemura; T. Wolff; M. Noorman; M. Dreher; Chuntao Dan; Ruchi Parekh; A. Hermundstad; G. Rubin; V. Jayaraman

ocar.opportunity: Flexible, long-timescale behaviors are thought to use recurrent networks in deep brain regions. In insects, the central complex (CX) supports directed locomotion, sleep, and context- and experience-dependent navigation, but a complete synaptic map had been missing.
ocar.challenge: Deep circuits are hard to interpret because inputs and outputs are usually difficult to identify, and attractor dynamics and vector computations are thought to depend on structured recurrence rather than simple sensory-to-motor chains.
ocar.action: Hulse, Haberkern, Franconville, Turner-Evans, Jayaraman, and colleagues report the first complete electron-microscopy connectome of the Drosophila CX, including all its neurons and circuits at synaptic resolution, from the hemibrain volume.
ocar.resolution: They identify new CX neuron types, sensory and motor pathways, and network motifs argued to extract head direction, maintain it with attractor dynamics, and combine it with other sensorimotor information for vector-based navigation, plus pathways that may select CX-driven actions by context and internal state.
ocar.future_work: Many proposed computations remain models. The authors treat a 90° PFN phase shift and excitatory LNO types as simplifying assumptions, note unknown functional significance of type-to-type phase variability, and leave the information carried by nodulus inputs to be determined.

plain_language_summary: Flies steer, sleep, and navigate using a deep midline brain region called the central complex. This paper maps every neuron and chemical synapse in that region so the loops that could hold a heading and pick an action can be read from the wiring.

summaries.beginner: Flies steer, sleep, and navigate using a deep midline brain region called the central complex. This paper maps every neuron and chemical synapse in that region so the loops that could hold a heading and pick an action can be read from the wiring.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (updated 2021; 2020 preprint), Hulse, Haberkern, Franconville, Turner-Evans, Jayaraman, and colleagues present a complete synaptic connectome of the adult Drosophila central complex. They report new cell types and motifs proposed to support head-direction extraction, attractor maintenance, and vector navigation, and pathways that may gate CX-driven behavior by context and state. Discussion of PFN phase shifts treats a precise 90° shift and excitatory LNO input as working assumptions for forward models of coordinate transformation.
summaries.advanced: Completeness is for CX neurons and synapses in this EM volume, not a demonstration that the motifs implement the named computations in vivo. Phase-shift and LNO-sign assumptions are explicit simplifications; vΔ and hΔ columnar variability is likewise reduced to keep-or-flip-by-180° in the models. Rotational-velocity content of nodulus input is described as still unknown.

title: Combined membrane potential imaging and connectome of behavioral circuits in an annelid worm
authors: M. Ashaber; Yusuke Tomina; Pegah Kassraian-Fard; E. Bushong; W. Kristan; Mark Ellisman; D. Wagenaar

ocar.opportunity: A motor neuron can play different dynamical roles in different behaviors without rewiring. Joint functional imaging and synaptic anatomy in the same specimen can show how converging pathways support that flexibility.
ocar.challenge: No current technology comprehensively records activity and reconstructs synapses in brains the size of a mouse or human. Even in smaller systems, obtaining both from the same tissue remains rare.
ocar.action: Ashaber, Tomina, Kassraian, Wagenaar, and colleagues recorded most neurons in a medicinal-leech segmental ganglion with a voltage-sensitive dye during fictive swimming, crawling, and local-bend escape, then imaged the same ganglion with serial block-face electron microscopy. They traced motor neuron DE-3 and all of its presynaptic partners to their somata.
ocar.resolution: Input synapses important for all of the behaviors were widely distributed over DE-3's branches, yet functional synapse clusters differed during fictive swimming versus crawling. Data are released publicly.
ocar.future_work: The reconstruction is a proof of concept centered on one motor neuron rather than a complete ganglion connectome; extending tracing and matching more functional assemblies is the obvious next step.

plain_language_summary: One leech motor neuron helps swimming, crawling, and a local escape bend without changing its wiring. This paper records the ganglion's activity, then traces that cell's incoming synapses in the electron microscope to see how the same anatomy supports different jobs.

summaries.beginner: One leech motor neuron helps swimming, crawling, and a local escape bend without changing its wiring. This paper records the ganglion's activity, then traces that cell's incoming synapses in the electron microscope to see how the same anatomy supports different jobs.

They fully traced dorsal excitor motor neuron DE-3 and all of its presynaptic partners. Synapses used in all behaviors were spread over DE-3's arbor, but spatial clusters of co-active inputs differed between swimming and crawling.
summaries.advanced: The EM reconstruction is thorough for DE-3 and its presynaptic partners, not for every neuron in the ganglion. Behaviors are fictive motor patterns. Clustering results depend on chosen neighborhood parameters (tables explore several (dNN, dext) settings). Catalog organism tags that list mouse do not match the leech specimen in the paper.

title: Comparative Connectomics Reveals How Partner Identity, Location, and Activity Specify Synaptic Connectivity in Drosophila
authors: Javier Valdes-Aleman; R. Fetter; Emily C. Sales; Emily L. Heckman; L. Venkatasubramanian; C. Doe; M. Landgraf; Albert Cardona; Marta Zlatic

ocar.opportunity: How synaptic partners recognize each other and set appropriate connection numbers during embryonic development is a route to understanding circuit assembly. Comparative connectomics after experimental perturbations can separate identity, place, and activity.
ocar.challenge: The relative roles of partner identity, axon-terminal location, and developmental activity in setting synapse numbers, excitation–inhibition balance, and behavior are poorly resolved at synaptic resolution.
ocar.action: Valdes-Aleman, Zlatic, Cardona, and colleagues combined electron-microscopy reconstruction, functional imaging, and behavior in the embryonic Drosophila nerve cord. They shifted partner axons to ectopic locations or silenced them and compared connectivity and function with controls.
ocar.resolution: Postsynaptic cells still found and connected to partners that had been moved or silenced. Orderly positioning and synaptic activity were nonetheless required for appropriate synapse numbers between specific partners, for excitation–inhibition balance, and for normal functional connectivity and behavior.
ocar.future_work: The study is grounded in identified mechanosensory and downstream cell types in the larval nerve cord; whether the same weighting of identity, location, and activity holds in other circuits or stages is not established here.

plain_language_summary: Developing fly neurons can still find their partners even if those partners sit in the wrong place or are quiet. This paper shows that getting the right number of connections, and therefore the right behavior, still depends on location and on activity during development.

summaries.beginner: Developing fly neurons can still find their partners even if those partners sit in the wrong place or are quiet. This paper shows that getting the right number of connections, and therefore the right behavior, still depends on location and on activity during development.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuron (January 2021), Valdes-Aleman, Fetter, Cardona, Zlatic, and colleagues used EM reconstruction, calcium imaging, and behavior in the embryonic Drosophila nerve cord. Partners connected even when axons were shifted ectopically or silenced. Correct synapse numbers, excitation–inhibition balance, functional connectivity, and behavior nonetheless required orderly terminal positioning and developmental synaptic activity.
summaries.advanced: Connectivity is scored as fraction of postsynaptic input and compared with chi-square tests; calcium and behavior use rank-sum, chi-square, and t tests as specified in STAR Methods. The result is circuit-specific (mechanosensory partners including Basin and A08a) rather than a universal assembly rule. Silencing and ectopic-shift experiments do not imply that identity cues are unnecessary—only that they are not sufficient for proper numbers and function.

title: Complete Connectomic Reconstruction of Olfactory Projection Neurons in the Fly Brain
authors: A. S. Bates; P. Schlegel; Ruairí J. V. Roberts; N. Drummond; Imaan F. M. Tamimi; R. Turnbull; X. Zhao; E. Marin; P. D. Popovici; S. Dhawan; Arian Jamasb; A. Javier; F. Li; G. Rubin; S. Waddell; D. Bock; M. Costa; G. Jefferis

ocar.opportunity: Sensory, local, projection, and motor neurons are the building blocks of circuits, but those classes must be split into cell types with known synapses. A complete inventory of second-order olfactory projection neurons would give holotypes for a model system.
ocar.challenge: Even in Drosophila, circuitry beyond the second olfactory layer is much less known than antennal-lobe logic. Light-level studies likely undercount projection neurons and cannot resolve axo-axonic and feedback motifs.
ocar.action: Bates, Schlegel, Jefferis, and colleagues reconstructed, in a whole-adult-brain EM volume, the full set of olfactory projection neurons from antennal lobe to higher centers, linking morphologies to the literature as synaptic-resolution holotypes.
ocar.resolution: They report 346 such projection neurons, about twice as many as light-level counts, and finalize 51 olfactory glomeruli. Types are stereotyped but not identical in cell and synapse number across hemispheres; some uniglomerular types vary by up to 50% (for example 2 versus 4 VA1d cells) in about 17% of cases, with axonal synapse totals often compensated. The lateral horn is the main target and contains hierarchical axo-axonic PN networks plus local-neuron and memory-related feedback; the mushroom-body calyx is organized differently.
ocar.future_work: The reconstructions are holotypes from one brain; whether numerical compensation and axo-axonic communities are identical in other individuals remains to be tested in additional volumes.

plain_language_summary: Smell information leaves the fly's antennal lobe on projection neurons headed for higher brain centers. This paper traces all of those cells in an electron-microscope whole brain and finds about twice as many as light microscopy had suggested.

summaries.beginner: Smell information leaves the fly's antennal lobe on projection neurons headed for higher brain centers. This paper traces all of those cells in an electron-microscope whole brain and finds about twice as many as light microscopy had suggested.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2020), Bates, Schlegel, Jefferis, and colleagues reconstruct a complete inventory of 346 adult Drosophila olfactory projection neurons in a whole-brain EM volume. Uniglomerular types can differ by up to 50% in cell number between hemispheres in about 17% of types, yet total axonal synapse counts can match, as for DA1 and DA2. New motifs in the lateral horn include axo-axonic PN communities and feedback onto PN axons, unlike the mushroom-body calyx.
summaries.advanced: Counts and motifs come from one EM brain (Zheng et al. volume). Multiglomerular PNs are numerous but have fewer axonal output synapses than uniglomerular PNs, so influence as individual feedforward units may be limited. Hemisphere compensation is shown for selected types, not proven as a universal rule. Functional roles of the axo-axonic hierarchy are inferred from anatomy.

title: Connectomics Analysis Reveals First-, Second-, and Third-Order Thermosensory and Hygrosensory Neurons in the Adult Drosophila Brain
authors: E. Marin; Ruairí J. V. Roberts; Laurin Büld; Maria Theiss; M. W. Pleijzier; Tatevik Sarkissian; Willem J. Laursen; R. Turnbull; P. Schlegel; A. S. Bates; Feng Li; M. Landgraf; Marta Costa; D. Bock; P. Garrity; G. Jefferis

ocar.opportunity: Animals have innate and learned preferences for temperature and humidity, but the central circuits are far less mapped than olfaction. A whole-brain EM volume lets first-, second-, and third-order thermo- and hygrosensory neurons be reconstructed together.
ocar.challenge: Antennal thermo- and hygrosensory neurons target ventroposterior (VP) glomeruli whose full projection-neuron set, higher-order partners, and integration with olfaction and the clock were incomplete.
ocar.action: Marin, Roberts, Jefferis, and colleagues reconstructed VP glomeruli and their projection neurons in an adult Drosophila whole-brain EM volume, then densely mapped neurons downstream of heating- and cooling-responsive PNs in the mushroom-body lateral accessory calyx (lACA).
ocar.resolution: They add two VP glomeruli to the five known (suggesting VP1l cool/cooling and VP1m humidity pending physiology), reconstruct 19 novel VP PN types, and show that a few Kenyon cells are purely thermosensory while most mix olfactory and thermo- or hygrosensory input. The lACA is a hub including DN1 clock neurons; a descending neuron mainly postsynaptic to dry-responsive VP PNs implies as few as two synapses from hygrosensory input to nerve-cord motor neurons.
ocar.future_work: Valence and function of novel glomeruli and PN types need physiology and sparse driver lines. Specific DAN/MBON partners of lACA Kenyon cells, and partners of lACA output neurons, remain unidentified.

plain_language_summary: Flies sense heat, cold, and humidity with antenna cells that look a lot like smell cells. This paper traces those pathways through the brain and finds a temperature hub that even talks to the circadian clock.

summaries.beginner: Flies sense heat, cold, and humidity with antenna cells that look a lot like smell cells. This paper traces those pathways through the brain and finds a temperature hub that even talks to the circadian clock.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2020), Marin, Jefferis, and colleagues reconstruct thermo- and hygrosensory circuitry in an adult Drosophila whole-brain EM volume. They identify two additional VP glomeruli, 19 novel VP projection-neuron types, and a connectome of the lateral accessory calyx. A few α'/β' Kenyon cells receive only thermosensory input; DN1a and DN1p clock neurons innervate the lACA. A descending neuron fed mainly by dry-responsive VP PNs sits two synapses from hygrosensory afferents toward the nerve cord.
summaries.advanced: Novel glomeruli VP1l and VP1m are assigned cool/humidity roles from receptor expression, not from recordings in this paper. Average sensory-neuron counts per VP glomerulus are about one-quarter of olfactory glomeruli; many VP PNs are biglomerular. Integration hypotheses (pooling similar valences in PNs, mixing at third order) are anatomical. The two-synapse claim is a shortest anatomical path, not a demonstrated motor reflex.

title: FlyWire: Online community for whole-brain connectomics
authors: Sven Dorkenwald; Claire E. McKellar; T. Macrina; N. Kemnitz; Kisuk Lee; R. Lu; Jingpeng Wu; S. Popovych; E. Mitchell; Barak Nehoran; Z. Jia; J. Bae; S. Mu; Dodam Ih; M.
