title: A visual motion detection circuit suggested by Drosophila connectomics
authors: Shin-ya Takemura; A. Bharioke; Zhiyuan Lu; Aljoscha Nern; S. Vitaladevuni; P. Rivlin; W. Katz; D. J. Olbris; Stephen M. Plaza; Philip Winston; Ting Zhao; J. Horne; R. Fetter; Satoko Takemura; Katerina Blazek; Lei-Ann Chang; Omotara Ogundeyi; M. Saunders; Victor L. Shapiro; Christopher Sigmund; G. Rubin; Louis K. Scheffer; I. Meinertzhagen; D. Chklovskii

ocar.opportunity: Local motion detection in insect vision is thought to compare signals offset in space and time, but without a medulla connectome the cellular implementation remained elusive.
ocar.challenge: Intensive behavioral, physiological, and anatomical work had not identified which medulla cell types form the two arms of a correlation-type detector.
ocar.action: Takemura, Chklovskii, Meinertzhagen and colleagues developed a semi-automated EM pipeline and reconstructed a Drosophila optic medulla volume containing 379 neurons and 8,637 chemical synaptic contacts, matching cells to light-microscopy types.
ocar.resolution: Within the repeating medulla module they identified a candidate motion circuit: Mi1 and Tm3 as inputs to T4, with connection geometry consistent with T4 direction selectivity. They predict which arm should introduce a longer delay given synaptic polarities. Analogous L2-pathway candidates (Tm1, Tm2, Tm4) are suggested pending T5 reconstruction in the lobula.
ocar.future_work: Anatomy cannot probe the nonlinear operation or time delay needed to distinguish correlation models; T5/lobula confirmation is left explicit.

plain_language_summary: Flies see motion with a repeating column of cells behind the eye, but which cells do the comparison was unknown. This paper maps thousands of synapses in that column and points to a short list of cell types that look like a motion detector.

summaries.beginner: Flies see motion with a repeating column of cells behind the eye, but which cells do the comparison was unknown. This paper maps thousands of synapses in that column and points to a short list of cell types that look like a motion detector.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2013), Takemura et al. reconstruct Drosophila medulla connectome modules (379 neurons; 8,637 chemical synapses) with a semi-automated EM pipeline and light-microscopy type matching. Mi1 and Tm3 onto T4 are proposed as the two arms of a correlation-based detector; Tm3 had been easy to miss from arbor overlap in stratum M10. Comprehensiveness is used to argue both pathway importance and absence of alternatives. Parallels to vertebrate direction-selective ganglion cells and starburst amacrine cells are discussed with differences in preferred-direction geometry.
summaries.advanced: This is chemical synapses in medulla, not a full optic-lobe connectome including T5. Direction selectivity of T4 is aligned with dendritic orientation but preferred direction is away from dendritic tips, unlike SACs. Model class (Hassenstein–Reichardt versus others) cannot be chosen from anatomy alone. Sparse overlap-based connectivity estimates are argued to be inferior to synaptic counts.

title: Cellular-resolution connectomics: challenges of dense neural circuit reconstruction
authors: M. Helmstaedter

ocar.opportunity: Volume electron microscopy can now acquire circuits of a few hundred to a few thousand neurons, so cellular-resolution connectomics is limited less by imaging than by turning those volumes into graphs.
ocar.challenge: Neuronal networks are high-dimensional graphs packed at extreme density in 3D tissue; comprehensively mapping them is a major challenge, and data analysis was massively lagging acquisition.
ocar.action: Helmstaedter’s perspective aims to summarize and quantify data-analysis challenges in cellular-resolution connectomics and to describe then-current solutions based on online crowd-sourcing and machine learning.
ocar.resolution: The piece frames dense reconstruction as an analysis-scale problem once volume EM data exist for circuits of hundreds to thousands of neurons, and it points to crowd and algorithmic approaches as the practical responses.
ocar.future_work: Closing the analysis gap is presented as the central remaining task for cellular-resolution connectomics.

plain_language_summary: Taking the pictures for a brain wiring map is getting easier; turning those pictures into a list of who talks to whom is the hard part. This perspective explains why tracing densely packed neurons at cellular resolution is so demanding and how crowds and machine learning were being used to catch up.

summaries.beginner: Taking the pictures for a brain wiring map is getting easier; turning those pictures into a list of who talks to whom is the hard part. This perspective explains why tracing densely packed neurons at cellular resolution is so demanding and how crowds and machine learning were being used to catch up.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Methods (2013), Moritz Helmstaedter reviews cellular-resolution connectomics as a data-analysis problem. Volume EM had made acquisition feasible for circuits of a few hundred to a few thousand neurons, but analysis lagged. The perspective sets out to quantify those challenges and to describe online crowd-sourcing and machine-learning approaches then in use.

No original reconstructions, error rates, or software benchmarks should be inferred beyond what the abstract states. It is a perspective, not an empirical methods paper.

title: Connectomic reconstruction of the inner plexiform layer in the mouse retina
authors: M. Helmstaedter; K. Briggman; Srinivas C. Turaga; Viren Jain; H. Seung; W. Denk

ocar.opportunity: The inner plexiform layer is the retina’s main computational neuropil, so a dense map of neurons and contacts can test whether co-stratification predicts connectivity and can generate functional hypotheses.
ocar.challenge: High resolution and large extent are both required; fully manual labeling of the volume was estimated at about US$10 million, and automated segmentation still fragmented cells even at few-percent voxel error.
ocar.action: Helmstaedter, Briggman, Seung, Denk and colleagues applied crowd-sourced skeletons plus machine-learning volume segmentation to serial block-face EM dataset e2006 (>1 million μm³), covering layers with intra-retinal synapses and stained for plasma-membrane contrast.
ocar.resolution: They densely reconstructed 950 neurons and their mutual contacts, confirmed ten known bipolar types, discovered the XBC, and subdivided a known type by connectivity. Motifs suggested a mechanism for localized-motion detection in one ganglion cell and predicted motion sensitivity in another. Contact could be used to augment type classification; neurite co-stratification did not always predict contact.
ocar.future_work: The functional role of the sparse, sharp-stratifying XBC remains unclear (possible luminance adaptation is speculated); an OFF-side cell with similarly sharp stratification was not found.

plain_language_summary: This team mapped 950 nerve cells in the mouse retina’s inner computing layer with a 3D electron microscope, volunteers, and computer vision. They found a new bipolar cell type and used the wiring pattern to guess how some ganglion cells detect motion.

summaries.beginner: This team mapped 950 nerve cells in the mouse retina’s inner computing layer with a 3D electron microscope, volunteers, and computer vision. They found a new bipolar cell type and used the wiring pattern to guess how some ganglion cells detect motion.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2013), Helmstaedter et al. densely reconstruct the mouse inner plexiform layer from SBEM (e2006, more than 1 million μm³) using crowd-sourced annotation and ML segmentation. They report 950 neurons and contacts, a new bipolar type (XBC), connectivity-based splitting of a known type, and circuit motifs tied to a localized-motion ganglion cell plus a predicted motion-sensitive ganglion cell. SBEM’s z-resolution and low distortion are cited as aiding humans and computers. Peters-style inference from proximity is treated as frequently violated.
summaries.advanced: “Dense” refers to this IPL-centered volume, not the entire retina. Completely automatic reconstruction was not achieved; skeletons supply long-range continuity while segmented contacts supply area. The ~US$10 million fully manual cost is an estimate used to motivate the hybrid pipeline. XBC homology to primate giant bipolar cells is considered and argued against because of small dendritic fields. Contact-area percentages in figures (e.g., ON/OFF SAC) should be read from the paper’s panels rather than over-generalized.

title: From the connectome to brain function
authors: Cori Bargmann; E. Marder

ocar.opportunity: Small invertebrate circuits whose connectivity is already known can teach what else is required to go from a wiring diagram to function, informing how to study large vertebrate circuits.
ocar.challenge: A connectome by itself does not specify dynamics, neuromodulation, or which of several parallel circuits is in use.
ocar.action: Bargmann and Marder, in a historical perspective, review invertebrate circuits with known connectivity and compare them with the vertebrate retina.
ocar.resolution: They highlight neuronal dynamics, neuromodulation, and parallel circuits as necessary ingredients beyond connectivity, argue that the retina shares these features, and suggest approaches for large circuits based on knowledge of small ones.
ocar.future_work: The piece is a conceptual program for studying functional organization, not a new reconstruction.

plain_language_summary: A complete list of who is connected to whom is not enough to know what a nervous system will do. This perspective uses well-mapped small animal circuits—and the retina—to argue that timing, chemical modulators, and spare parallel pathways also matter.

summaries.beginner: A complete list of who is connected to whom is not enough to know what a nervous system will do. This perspective uses well-mapped small animal circuits—and the retina—to argue that timing, chemical modulators, and spare parallel pathways also matter.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Methods (2013), Bargmann and Marder ask what information beyond connectivity diagrams is needed to understand nervous-system function. Drawing on invertebrate circuits with known wiring, they emphasize neuronal dynamics, neuromodulation, and parallel circuits. They note that the vertebrate retina shares these properties, suggesting generality, and they outline how lessons from small circuits might scale to large ones.
summaries.advanced: The selected PDF extract does not match this article (it is a 2026 European Journal of Neuroscience paper on engrams and reductionism). This card therefore uses only the catalog abstract. No new empirical connectome or quantitative comparison is claimed. Catalog tags linking the record to mouse retina describe the comparison case in the abstract, not a retinal reconstruction by these authors.

title: The Rich Club of the C. elegans Neuronal Connectome
authors: Emma K. Towlson; P. Vértes; S. Ahnert; W. Schafer; E. Bullmore

ocar.opportunity: Graph measures from human neuroimaging suggested rich-club organization; a complete cellular connectome can test whether the same cost–value tradeoff appears at synaptic resolution.
ocar.challenge: Most brain-network topology work used large-scale neuroimaging without cellular resolution, so it was unclear whether rich clubs were a general, scale-invariant principle.
ocar.action: Towlson, Vértes, Ahnert, Schafer, and Bullmore applied graph theory to the C. elegans neuronal connectome treated as 2,287 synaptic connections among 279 neurons.
ocar.resolution: An 11-neuron rich club (conservative 3σ definition) was highly efficient, long-distance, and almost entirely locomotor command interneurons (10 of 11), with DVA the remaining proprioceptive modulator. Rich-club cells are connector hubs; shortest paths between peripheral neurons most often traverse the club. Those neurons are born early, before visible movement and body elongation. Network efficiency was 47% of maximum at 4% connection density.
ocar.future_work: A more liberal club adds a few head interneurons (AIBR, RIBL, RIAR); the authors interpret high wiring cost as justified by coordinated movement, paralleling human imaging.

plain_language_summary: In the worm’s tiny nervous system, a handful of highly connected cells form a “rich club” that other cells use as a shortcut. Those club members are mostly the command cells for crawling, and they appear early in development.

summaries.beginner: In the worm’s tiny nervous system, a handful of highly connected cells form a “rich club” that other cells use as a shortcut. Those club members are mostly the command cells for crawling, and they appear early in development.
summaries.intermediate: In the Journal of Neuroscience (2013), Towlson et al. analyze C. elegans as a graph of 279 neurons and 2,287 synapses. They identify an 11-node rich club with high efficiency, high betweenness, high participation, and relatively long physical connection distance. Ten of eleven conservative club members are locomotor command interneurons; DVA is proprioceptive. The connectome is small-world (Watts–Strogatz) with efficiency 47% of maximum at 4% density, and wiring cost is strongly but not strictly minimized.
summaries.advanced: The analysis is uninformed by prior functional labels yet recovers locomotor interneurons—an alignment, not an independent causal test. Synaptic connections are treated as undirected/unweighted in the simple graphical model described. Laser-ablation literature is cited for function, not re-done here. Human neuroimaging parallels are analogical across scale.

title: TrakEM2 Software for Neural Circuit Reconstruction
authors: Albert Cardona; S. Saalfeld; J. Schindelin; Ignacio Arganda-Carreras; S. Preibisch; M. Longair; P. Tomančák; V. Hartenstein; R. Douglas

ocar.opportunity: For Drosophila and C. elegans, image acquisition was no longer the limiting step; extracting circuits from terascale EM and optical volumes on desktop hardware was.
ocar.challenge: Laboratories needed open tools to compose deformed serial tiles into browsable volumes, reconstruct arbors, annotate synapses, and manage huge image and annotation collections.
ocar.action: Cardona, Saalfeld, Douglas and colleagues built TrakEM2, an open-source package for volume composition, fast manual and semi-automatic arbor and synapse annotation, and export of 3D circuits in NeuroML and other formats.
ocar.resolution: The software had already been used for Drosophila larval CNS EM, array tomography, LSM lineage reconstruction, cat thalamocortical connections, and an inhibitory network in a 10-terabyte mouse visual-cortex EM set, among other projects. Sketching types (balls, pipes, connectors, area lists) support synapses and vesicle counts.
ocar.future_work: The output is framed as analysis-ready circuit structure rather than a finished biological connectome in this methods paper.

plain_language_summary: Huge stacks of electron-microscope pictures are useless until someone traces the cells. TrakEM2 is a free program that stitches those pictures, lets people draw neurons and synapses, and exports a 3D wiring sketch.

summaries.beginner: Huge stacks of electron-microscope pictures are useless until someone traces the cells. TrakEM2 is a free program that stitches those pictures, lets people draw neurons and synapses, and exports a 3D wiring sketch.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS ONE (2012), Cardona et al. present TrakEM2 for neural circuit reconstruction from large EM and optical volumes. It targets image-volume composition from deformed tiles, arbor reconstruction, synapse annotation, and management of tera-scale collections on consumer computers. Demonstrated uses include Drosophila larval CNS, array tomography, optical lineage work, cat visual cortex, and a 10 TB mouse visual-cortex inhibitory-network reconstruction. Export includes NeuroML.
summaries.advanced: This is software and workflow, not a new complete connectome; biological results live in the cited applications. Catalog organism/dataset tags pointing at C. elegans reflect the paper’s motivating model systems, not a worm reconstruction in this article. Performance claims are qualitative (expeditious reconstruction) without benchmark tables in the extracted text.

title: Volume electron microscopy for neuronal circuit reconstruction.
authors: K. Briggman; D. Bock

ocar.opportunity: New SEM methods and scaled, automated TEM made large EM volumes newly available for extracting neuronal wiring diagrams.
ocar.challenge: There is no single best volume-EM method: size, resolution, completeness, speed, and reliability trade off, and dendrite spine necks (~40 nm) or Drosophila neurites (~50 nm) set resolution needs, while a mouse cortical column is ~100 times an adult C. elegans volume.
ocar.action: Briggman and Bock review volume EM acquisition methods, their tradeoffs, and applicability to anatomical connectivity, arguing that wiring diagrams are necessary but not sufficient.
ocar.resolution: They conclude volume EM is best combined with molecular biology, optogenetics, and physiology. In the short term, sparse reconstruction of subsets of connections will keep yielding insight; dense mammalian millimeter-scale reconstruction awaits analysis automation. Data analysis times already dwarf acquisition for complete dense reconstruction.
ocar.future_work: They anticipate that progress in automating acquisition will carry over to analysis, eventually permitting complete mammalian circuit reconstruction across millimeter scales.

plain_language_summary: Scientists now have several ways to take 3D electron-microscope pictures of brain tissue, each with different speed and sharpness. This review says those pictures can give a wiring diagram, but you still need other tools—genes, light, and electrical recordings—to understand what the circuit does.

summaries.beginner: Scientists now have several ways to take 3D electron-microscope pictures of brain tissue, each with different speed and sharpness. This review says those pictures can give a wiring diagram, but you still need other tools—genes, light, and electrical recordings—to understand what the circuit does.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2012), Briggman and Bock survey SEM and TEM volume methods for circuit reconstruction. Required volume depends on the circuit (adult C. elegans ~50 × 50 × 1000 μm versus a mouse cortical column ~400 × 400 × 1000 μm). Voxel size must follow the finest processes (mammalian spine necks as fine as 40 nm; Drosophila neurites as thin as 50 nm). Completeness matters because lost sections mix thin processes. They argue connectomes are necessary but not sufficient without multimodal physiology.
summaries.advanced: This is a review/opinion, not a new dataset. Cited TEMCA volume (450 × 350 × 50 μm) is from Bock et al. 2011, used as an example of combined two-photon and EM. “No best method” is the explicit stance. Dense millimeter-scale mammalian reconstruction is a projected future, not a result.

title: High-accuracy neurite reconstruction for high-throughput neuroanatomy
authors: M. Helmstaedter; K. Briggman; W. Denk

ocar.opportunity: Volume EM can image densely stained neuropil fast enough that reconstruction, not acquisition, limits connectome throughput.
ocar.challenge: In dense data even experts err, especially at branches; a missed branch can misattribute thousands of synapses, and conventional proofreading of skeletons is tiresome.
ocar.action: Helmstaedter, Briggman, and Denk introduced KNOSSOS for rapid manual skeletonization (~50-fold faster than volume labeling) and RESCOP, a redundant-skeleton consensus procedure with a statistical model of annotation decisions.
ocar.resolution: RESCOP detects inconsistencies across redundant skeletons, estimates consensus reliability, and supports focused re-annotation of difficult locations (vote ratios near 0.5 are rare). Annotators without prior neurobiology knowledge can be used if redundancy and focused review are applied. The optimal vote threshold can differ from majority voting.
ocar.future_work: Error-rate estimates for large redundancy N are somewhat uncertain because difficult locations are rare; the assumption that infinite annotators converge to truth limits ultimate validity.

plain_language_summary: When every nerve fiber is stained, even experts mix up branches. This paper has people quickly draw stick-figure traces of the same cell several times, then a statistical method (RESCOP) votes out the mistakes much faster than painting every voxel.

summaries.beginner: When every nerve fiber is stained, even experts mix up branches. This paper has people quickly draw stick-figure traces of the same cell several times, then a statistical method (RESCOP) votes out the mistakes much faster than painting every voxel.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Neuroscience (2011), Helmstaedter, Briggman, and Denk present KNOSSOS skeletonization and RESCOP consensus for densely labeled SBEM data. Manual skeletons are ~50 times faster than volume labeling. Redundant traces plus a model of how true continuity becomes votes yield consensus skeletons and reliability estimates. Focused re-annotation of ambiguous sites is predicted to raise reliability steeply with average redundancy. Neurite continuity errors are treated as far more costly than single synapse-ID errors.
summaries.advanced: The ~50-fold speedup is versus volume labeling, not versus later machine segmentation. Expert errors at branches are demonstrated; synapse identification errors are acknowledged but not the main quantification. Infinite-annotator convergence is an explicit limiting assumption. Denk/Helmstaedter disclose patent and SBEM license income. Sparse Golgi-like data are described as assumed reliable with little published validation.

title: Network anatomy and in vivo physiology of visual cortical neurons
authors: D. Bock; W. Lee; Aaron Kerlin; M. Andermann; Greg Hood; A. Wetzel; S. Yurgenson; E. Soucy; Hyon-Suk Kim; R. Reid

ocar.opportunity: Cortical wiring diagrams are incomplete without knowing each neuron’s function; combining in-vivo physiology with network anatomy can test how geometry and tuning shape connections.
ocar.challenge: Past synaptic studies sampled few cells, so the structure of highly interconnected cortical networks was only partially known.
ocar.action: Bock, Lee, Reid and colleagues measured preferred orientation in mouse V1 with two-photon calcium imaging, then used a custom TEM camera array (TEMCA) on serial thin sections to trace local axons of those pyramids and their postsynaptic targets.
ocar.resolution: Inhibitory interneurons received convergent anatomical input from nearby excitatory neurons spanning a broad range of preferred orientations, consistent with physiological predictions that inhibitory cells are less selective, although weak biases could not be rejected. In the sample, 51% of synapses were onto inhibitory targets. The imaged series was 350 × 450 μm wide and only 52 μm in the sectioning dimension, so only 245 of the thousands of synapses made by characterized neurons could be traced.
ocar.future_work: Larger EM volumes were anticipated; subtype-specific inhibitory selectivity was not classified and could still exist.

plain_language_summary: Researchers first watched mouse visual-cortex cells respond to oriented bars, then traced some of their connections in electron-microscope slices. Inhibitory cells collected input from neighbors that preferred many different orientations, which may help explain why those inhibitory cells are less picky.

summaries.beginner: Researchers first watched mouse visual-cortex cells respond to oriented bars, then traced some of their connections in electron-microscope slices. Inhibitory cells collected input from neighbors that preferred many different orientations, which may help explain why those inhibitory cells are less picky.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2011), Bock et al. combine two-photon orientation mapping with large-scale serial-section EM (TEMCA) in mouse V1. Reconstructed pyramidal axons synapse onto inhibitory neurons with broadly distributed orientation preferences; strong bias is excluded, weak bias is not. 51% of sampled synapses were onto inhibitory targets, higher than 10–20% reports from cat and macaque, possibly species or proximal-axon sampling. The public volume is noted at Whole Brain Catalog and UCSD CCDB (MP8448).
summaries.advanced: Sampling is partial: 245 synapses from proximal arbors in a 52 μm-thick volume. Interneuron subtypes were not classified. Geometry appeared to dominate over function for excitatory-to-inhibitory connections in this analysis. The 51% inhibitory-target fraction should not be read as a whole-cortex synapse census. Alignment between in-vivo imaging and EM is a prerequisite that limits which cells enter the anatomical sample.

title: Wiring specificity in the direction-selectivity circuit of the retina
authors: K. Briggman; M. Helmstaedter; W. Denk

ocar.opportunity: Direction-selective ganglion cells (DSGCs) compute motion direction, but the wiring that creates asymmetric inhibition from starburst amacrine cells (SACs) was unresolved at scale.
ocar.challenge: Light-microscopy proximity studies conflicted, and earlier EM could not reconstruct large fractions of SACs and DSGCs together; physiology alone cannot locate which SAC dendrite branches contact which DSGC.
ocar.action: Briggman, Helmstaedter, and Denk combined two-photon calcium imaging of DSGCs in mouse retina with serial block-face EM and targeted reconstructions of SAC–DSGC synapses.
ocar.resolution: SAC dendrites selectively synapse onto a DSGC when oriented along that cell’s null direction, providing a structural substrate for asymmetric inhibitory currents. Among 831 synapses, dendrite angle contributed beyond soma–soma geometry, consistent with SAC dendrites as independent computational units. Incidental touches (n = 3,481) were distinguished from synapses. Synapses occur across the DSGC field, so some strongly connected SAC somata can lie on the preferred side.
ocar.future_work: The same SBEM data are expected to support dense retinal circuit reconstruction; development must use local dendrite geometry or activity, not cell identity alone, to place synapses.

plain_language_summary: Some retinal cells fire only when a spot moves one way. This paper shows that starburst cells wire most strongly onto those motion cells along the opposite, “null” direction, which can shut them down when motion goes the wrong way.

summaries.beginner: Some retinal cells fire only when a spot moves one way. This paper shows that starburst cells wire most strongly onto those motion cells along the opposite, “null” direction, which can shut them down when motion goes the wrong way.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2011), Briggman, Helmstaedter, and Denk pair two-photon calcium imaging (Oregon Green 488 BAPTA-1; bars in eight directions at 0.5 mm s⁻¹) with SBEM in C57BL/6 mouse retina. SAC-to-DSGC synapses (n = 831) follow null-direction dendrite orientation more than soma angle alone. The asymmetry supports models with null-direction inhibition and rules out purely symmetric wiring with only strength differences. SBEM is contrasted with artifact-prone serial-section EM.
summaries.advanced: Reconstructions are targeted, not a full IPL connectome (that is anticipated). Synapse versus touch classification is central (3,481 incidental touches). Preferred-direction excitation asymmetry is not the primary structural claim. Developmental mechanism is constrained, not identified. Motion speed and stimulus details in Methods Summary should not be generalized to all DSGC subtypes without the paper’s cell-class definitions.

title: Ultrastructural analysis of hippocampal neuropil from the connectomics perspective
authors: Y. Mishchenko; Tao Hu; J. Špaček; J. Mendenhall; K. Harris; D. Chklovskii

ocar.opportunity: Vertebrate synaptic circuits cannot be completed by unaided manual ssTEM, so automated reconstruction must be tested on real neuropil, and light-microscopy “potential synapse” rules need ultrastructural checks.
ocar.challenge: It was unclear when axo-dendritic proximity or membrane touches predict actual synapses, i.e., when Peters’ rule holds.
ocar.action: Mishchenko, Hu, Harris, Chklovskii and colleagues densely reconstructed four rat hippocampus volumes totaling 670 μm³ with automated ssTEM registration/segmentation plus RECONSTRUCT proofreading.
ocar.resolution: Axon density within reach of spines did not predict synaptic density because the fraction of axons that synapse varied. An axo-dendritic touch did not predict a synapse, yet synapse density was a universal fraction 0.2 of touch density along hippocampal dendrites. The largest bouton–spine touch predicted actual synapses with about 80% precision but would miss about half of synapses. Synaptic density scaled with dendrite caliber (universal shaft membrane area 0.66 μm² per synapse), not with local axon availability.
ocar.future_work: Proofreading speed and error rates were satisfactory for these small volumes but need radical improvement to reconstruct complete vertebrate circuits. Datasets lacking ultrastructural synapse cues will poorly predict connectivity.

plain_language_summary: In a bit of rat hippocampus, this team outlined every nearby axon and dendrite in electron-microscope slices. Simply sitting next to each other does not mean two cells are connected; you still need the synapse’s fine structure to tell a real contact from a near miss.

summaries.beginner: In a bit of rat hippocampus, this team outlined every nearby axon and dendrite in electron-microscope slices. Simply sitting next to each other does not mean two cells are connected; you still need the synapse’s fine structure to tell a real contact from a near miss.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuron (2010), Mishchenko et al. densely reconstruct 670 μm³ of rat hippocampal neuropil (four volumes) with automated ssTEM methods. Peters’ rule fails for predicting synaptic density from nearby axon density. Touches outnumber synapses; synapses are about 0.2 of touches along dendrites. Largest-touch inference is ~80% precise but misses about half of synapses. Caliber, not local axon crowding, correlates with synapse density (0.66 μm² shaft membrane per synapse).
summaries.advanced: Volumes are too small for complete circuits; they are proving grounds. Mean connectivity fraction matching light-microscopy theory coexists with enough dendrite-to-dendrite variation to break Peters’ rule. The 80%/50% largest-touch result cautions against LM or low-resolution EM connectivity inference. Catalog organism “other” is rat hippocampus in the paper.

title: Structural Properties of the Caenorhabditis elegans Neuronal Network
authors: L. Varshney; Beth L. Chen; Eric Paniagua; D. Hall; D. Chklovskii

ocar.opportunity: Even for C. elegans, published wiring diagrams were neither accurate nor complete and self-consistent, yet statistical network properties might generalize if a cleaned map existed.
ocar.challenge: Prior assemblies made unjustified assumptions that some reconstructed neurons represented others, and analyses used incomplete or inconsistent diagrams.
ocar.action: Varshney, Chen, Hall, Chklovskii and colleagues assembled whole, self-consistent gap-junction and chemical-synapse networks of hermaphrodite C. elegans from White et al. materials plus new electron micrographs, then computed topology, motifs, linear-systems activity modes, and gap-versus-chemical interactions.
ocar.resolution: They propose a signal-flow visualization, identify central neurons and candidate functional motifs, find activity patterns that could underlie known behaviors, and note that multiplicity and motif statistics resemble mammalian neocortex. The diagram is meant to generate predictions for genetic perturbations, laser ablations, and activity monitoring.
ocar.future_work: Connectivity alone is stated as not sufficient to explain function; the resource is a substrate for experiments rather than a completed mechanistic account of behavior.

plain_language_summary: The worm’s wiring list had gaps and inconsistencies. This paper rebuilds a coherent map of chemical synapses and gap junctions for the hermaphrodite and then asks what the network’s shape can tell us about signal flow and behavior.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s wiring list had gaps and inconsistencies. This paper rebuilds a coherent map of chemical synapses and gap junctions for the hermaphrodite and then asks what the network’s shape can tell us about signal flow and behavior.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Computational Biology (2011), Varshney et al. curate self-consistent C. elegans hermaphrodite chemical and gap-junction networks from the White et al. archive and new EM. Similarities to neocortical multiplicity/motif statistics are taken as candidate general principles.
summaries.advanced: The catalog year is 2009; the selected PDF is the 2011 PLoS Computational Biology article. Linear-systems “activity patterns” are models, not measured calcium or voltage. Completeness is relative to prior published diagrams, not a claim of zero remaining EM ambiguity. GABAergic-conditioned likelihood ratios for gap/chemical co-occurrence are in the supporting analysis, not a physiological proof of interaction rules.

title: Serial Block-Face Scanning Electron Microscopy to Reconstruct Three-Dimensional Tissue Nanostructure
authors: Winfried Denk; H. Horstmann

ocar.opportunity: Completely reconstructing neuronal connectivity needs 3D tissue structure over hundreds of micrometers at a resolution that follows the thinnest processes and identifies synapses, a gap between conventional EM of tiny volumes and light microscopy.
ocar.challenge: Serial ultrathin TEM is laborious and hard to automate; SEM was mostly a surface tool; charging of uncoated block faces and sectioning chatter limit in-chamber imaging.
ocar.action: Denk and Horstmann combined automated diamond-knife serial sectioning inside an SEM with backscattered-electron imaging of heavy-metal-stained, TEM-style blocks under low vacuum (20–60 Pa H2O).
ocar.resolution: Resolution sufficed to trace the thinnest axons and identify synapses. Stacks of several hundred sections 50–70 nm thick were obtained with typical lateral position jitter under 10 nm, enabling automated EM-level 3D datasets without slice-to-slice distortion correction that needs manual landmarks.
ocar.future_work: They discuss thinner sections (toward ~20 nm), lower beam energies, oscillating knives, and nonmechanical ablation, while noting radiation damage and charging tradeoffs relative to TEM.

plain_language_summary: This paper shows how to put a tiny diamond knife inside a scanning electron microscope so the machine can shave a stained tissue block and photograph each new face automatically. The resulting 3D stack is sharp enough to follow the thinnest nerve fibers and see synapses.

summaries.beginner: This paper shows how to put a tiny diamond knife inside a scanning electron microscope so the machine can shave a stained tissue block and photograph each new face automatically. The resulting 3D stack is sharp enough to follow the thinnest nerve fibers and see synapses.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Biology (2004), Denk and Horstmann introduce serial block-face SEM. Backscattered electrons image routine heavy-metal stains; 20–60 Pa water vapor prevents charging of the uncoated face. They report stacks of several hundred 50–70 nm sections with typically <10 nm lateral jitter and registration good enough to skip landmark-based alignment. The method is positioned to supply the volumes needed for complete local-circuit reconstruction.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods demonstration, not a completed connectome. 50 nm is described as a practical thickness limit in their hands then; 20 nm isotropic is aspirational. Dose, heating at low kV, and BSE angular/contrast differences versus TEM are discussed as constraints. Oscillating-knife and ion-milling alternatives are prospective in the discussion.

title: The structure of the nervous system of the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans
authors: J. White; Erica L. Southgate; J. Thomson; S. Brenner
journal: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences

ocar.opportunity: An essentially invariant, complete cellular anatomy would let connectivity of a whole nervous system be described neuron by neuron.
ocar.challenge: Reconstructing that structure required serial electron micrographs through an entire small animal and consistent identification of processes, synapses, and neuromuscular junctions.
ocar.action: White, Southgate, Thomson, and Brenner reconstructed the hermaphrodite C. elegans nervous system from serial-section EM.
ocar.resolution: The hermaphrodite has 302 neurons in 118 morphological/connectivity classes. Neurons are simple, sparsely branched, and synapse en passant in stereotyped process bundles. Muscle arms reach motoneuron axons. A typical animal has about 5,000 chemical synapses, 2,000 neuromuscular junctions, and 600 gap junctions. Most morphologically identifiable connections are described, including amphids, nerve-ring and ventral-cord motoneurons, tail circuitry, and egg-laying.
ocar.future_work: Conclusions address process placement and synaptic specificity as organizing principles for this invariant nervous system.

plain_language_summary: This classic monograph maps every nerve cell in a tiny roundworm—302 of them—and lists how they connect with chemical synapses, muscle junctions, and electrical gap junctions. It is the original whole-animal wiring diagram.

summaries.beginner: This classic monograph maps every nerve cell in a tiny roundworm—302 of them—and lists how they connect with chemical synapses, muscle junctions, and electrical gap junctions. It is the original whole-animal wiring diagram.
summaries.intermediate: In Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B (1986), White et al. deduce C. elegans hermaphrodite nervous-system structure from serial EM. They report 302 neurons, 118 classes, simple morphologies, en passant synapses in longitudinal and circumferential bundles, and muscle arms onto motoneuron axons. Typical synapse counts are about 5,000 chemical, 2,000 neuromuscular, and 600 gap junctions. Reliability, nomenclature, and circuit chapters (amphids, ventral cord, egg-laying) structure the 340-page account.
summaries.advanced: The selected PDF extract is largely front matter and contents (pdf_chars_body is short relative to the 340-page work); counts in the abstract are the quantitative spine of this card. “Most” identifiable synapses in a typical animal are described, not a modern digital adjacency matrix. Structure is of the hermaphrodite; males differ. Later revisions of the worm connectome exist beyond this 1986 reconstruction.

title: ConnectomeBench2: A Unified Benchmark for Automated Connectomic Proofreading
authors: Jeff B. Brown; Tim Farkas; Gleb Razgar; Edward S. Boyden

ocar.opportunity: Proofreading split and merge errors is the rate-limiting step in synapse-resolution connectomics, so a shared multi-species training set could let one vision model serve mouse, human, zebrafish, and fly volumes.
ocar.challenge: Proofreading labels are fragmented by species and error type, and it is unclear whether a single model can reach human-level accuracy, stay calibrated, and adapt cheaply when the next brain looks different.
ocar.action: Brown, Farkas, Razgar, and Boyden (arXiv, 2026) release ConnectomeBench2, with over 716,485 expert-labeled proofreading decisions and more than 4,500,000 associated images spanning four open connectomes, then train a Vision Transformer with shared encoders for mesh geometry and electron microscopy on split correction, merge identification, and merge-correction mask generation.
ocar.resolution: A single ViT reaches human-level accuracy across species for split error correction and merge error identification, with performance scaling with data size and modality. The model is well-calibrated in distribution; distribution-distance measures predict degradation on unseen data; connectomics-specific pretraining outperforms ImageNet for new species; and at a budget of K = 300 operations on leave-one-species-out mouse, facility-location and batch-Fisher selection beat random sampling on merge identification, though absolute performance at that budget remains well below deployment.
ocar.future_work: The authors flag lossy 2D slice rendering versus full 3D EM cutouts, Vision-Transformer-only architectural coverage, and species imbalance, and they present the benchmark as infrastructure for 3D embeddings, other architectures, and cheaper adaptation to new regions.

plain_language_summary: Fixing computer mistakes in 3D brain maps still takes huge amounts of human time. This team released a shared test set from mouse, human, zebrafish, and fly brains and showed that one vision model can match people on many of those fixes.

summaries.beginner: Fixing computer mistakes in 3D brain maps still takes huge amounts of human time. This team released a shared test set from mouse, human, zebrafish, and fly brains and showed that one vision model can match people on many of those fixes.
summaries.intermediate: Brown, Farkas, Razgar, and Boyden (arXiv, 2026) introduce ConnectomeBench2, a unified proofreading benchmark with over 716,485 expert decisions and more than 4.5 million images from four open connectomes. A Vision Transformer with shared mesh and EM encoders is trained on split correction, merge identification, and merge-correction masks. Joint training matches or exceeds species-specific models; in-distribution calibration is strong; Mahalanobis distance provides a label-free shift signal; and connectomics pretraining plus active learning reduce the labels needed to touch a new species. Data and code are released on Hugging Face and GitHub.
summaries.advanced: Human-level claims are for split correction and merge identification, not a blanket claim that merge-mask generation matches experts. Active-learning gains at K = 300 on held-out mouse still leave performance far below a deployable proofreader for a new species. 2D slice renders are lossy relative to 3D cutouts; evaluations emphasize ViTs rather than 3D CNNs or point-cloud models; and sample counts are unbalanced across species, which the authors say should temper leave-one-species-out claims.

title: Connectomic Analysis of Mitochondria in the Central Brain of Drosophila
authors: Kit D Longden; P. Rivlin; M. Januszewski; Erika Neace; Louis K. Scheffer; Christopher Ordish; Jody Clements; Elliott Phillips; Natalie Smith; Satoko Takemura; L. Umayam; Claire Walsh; Emily A Yakal; Timothy F. Musial; Michael J. Devine; Michael B. Reiser; Stephen M. Plaza; S. Berg

ocar.opportunity: Electron-microscopy volumes collected for fly connectomics already contain mitochondria, so the same images can be mined for subcellular metabolism without a new acquisition.
ocar.challenge: How mitochondrial size, placement, and appearance vary by cell type, synapse polarity, and brain region at whole-central-brain scale has not been measured.
ocar.action: Longden, Rivlin, Januszewski, Neace, Scheffer, Berg and colleagues (bioRxiv, 2026) extract, classify, and measure approximately 6 million mitochondria from the Drosophila Hemibrain, annotate location, orientation, voxel size, and appearance (dark/dense, light/sparse, or medium), link each synapse to its closest mitochondrion, and add the objects to neuPrint.
ocar.resolution: Mitochondria are larger and closer at presynapses than postsynapses, and presynapses typically have a mitochondrion within one micron, but Kenyon cells have unusually small, sparse mitochondria near only about half of presynapses. Inhibitory neurons devote a greater fraction of cell volume to mitochondria than excitatory cells; dopaminergic and glutamatergic neurons show distinctive positioning or light appearance; and synapses with more postsynaptic partners have larger presynaptic mitochondria and more distant postsynaptic mitochondria.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the neuPrint release as a public substrate for further cell-type and regional analyses rather than a finished physiological account of why these patterns exist.

plain_language_summary: Connectome pictures of the fly brain also show mitochondria, the cell’s energy factories. This team catalogued millions of them, found that different neuron types place and size them differently, and put the catalog online so others can search it.

summaries.beginner: Connectome pictures of the fly brain also show mitochondria, the cell’s energy factories. This team catalogued millions of them, found that different neuron types place and size them differently, and put the catalog online so others can search it.
summaries.intermediate: Longden et al. (bioRxiv, 2026; Janelia FlyEM and collaborators) mine the Drosophila Hemibrain for approximately 6 million mitochondria, most of them among more than 20 thousand neurons and over 5500 cell types. Each organelle is labeled for location, orientation, size, and appearance, and each synapse is linked to its nearest mitochondrion. Presynaptic mitochondria are typically larger and closer (within one micron) than postsynaptic ones, while Kenyon cells are an exception with small, sparse mitochondria near only about half of presynapses. Inhibitory, dopaminergic, and glutamatergic classes show further differences in occupancy, placement, or appearance. The objects are queryable in neuPrint as neuronal subcellular components.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint reuse of Hemibrain EM, not a new volume or live imaging of mitochondrial dynamics. Appearance classes (dark/dense, light/sparse, medium) are morphological, not direct metabolic assays. Kenyon-cell and transmitter-class claims are correlative with Hemibrain cell types; causal links to learning, memory, or synapse strength are not tested here. Coverage is the central brain Hemibrain, not a complete adult CNS.

title: Convergence-divergence circuits for multimodal integration of innate and learned opponent valences
authors: Wenjing Wang; Yaokai Yang; Qiong Liu; Yunming Gao; Qiantao Lv; Kaiqi Zhang; Jing Ning; Yi Sun

ocar.opportunity: Flies must judge attraction versus aversion in messy natural scenes, not only in simple lab odors, so a brain-wide wiring map could show where innate and learned valences meet.
ocar.challenge: Prior valence work in Drosophila has focused on the lateral horn (LH) and mushroom body (MB) with synthetic stimuli, leaving the circuit for natural multimodal objects unclear.
ocar.action: Wang, Yang, Liu, Sun and colleagues (Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience, 2026) use brain-wide connectome analysis to place the superior protocerebrum (SP) as a convergence–divergence bottleneck that collects LH and MB inputs and broadcasts especially to the central complex.
ocar.resolution: They argue that SP resembles an autoencoder bottleneck: LH neurons pool ethologically related innate valences (unimodal food odors, or multimodal wind and temperature as ‘lousy weather’), opponent attraction and aversion are combined in SP, and MB learned valences update innate LH signals. Attractive versus aversive inputs arrive via excitatory versus inhibitory synapses onto single SP neurons with opposite dendritic organizations.
ocar.future_work: The paper highlights SP as a candidate general motif for complex valence; physiological tests of the autoencoder analogy and of dendritic opponent integration are left open.

plain_language_summary: Fruit flies must decide what is good or bad in a messy world, not just in a simple lab smell. This study uses a whole-brain wiring map to argue that a region called the superior protocerebrum mixes inborn and learned likes and dislikes before sending a compact signal onward.

summaries.beginner: Fruit flies must decide what is good or bad in a messy world, not just in a simple lab smell. This study uses a whole-brain wiring map to argue that a region called the superior protocerebrum mixes inborn and learned likes and dislikes before sending a compact signal onward.
summaries.intermediate: Wang et al. (Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience, 2026) analyze Drosophila connectomes to argue that the evolutionarily conserved superior protocerebrum (SP) integrates brain-wide multimodal inputs mainly via the lateral horn and mushroom body and sends widespread outputs, especially to the central complex. They describe a convergence–divergence layout resembling an autoencoder, with SP as the bottleneck for low-dimensional valence. LH inputs can be unimodal (diverse food odors) or multimodal (wind and temperature as poor weather); MB learned valences update innate LH signals; and single SP neurons combine attraction and aversion through excitatory versus inhibitory synapses with opposite dendritic organization. The work is a circuit-anatomy study of valence integration, not a new EM volume.
summaries.advanced: The autoencoder analogy is an architectural reading of connectivity, not a trained model or a demonstration that SP activity is low-dimensional. Claims about ‘robust valence detection in natural environments’ are inferred from wiring and known LH/MB roles rather than new freely behaving physiology in this paper. Opponent dendritic organization is anatomical; whether it computes a signed valence sum in vivo is untested here.

title: DRIFT-EM enables direct wafer retrieval of ultrathin serial sections for large-volume electron microscopy
authors: Nelson D. Medina; Joseph V Gogola; Kevin M. Boergens; Fuming Yang; Y. Meirovitch; J. Lichtman; Narayan Kasthuri; Gregg A. Wildenberg

ocar.opportunity: Large-volume serial electron microscopy needs reliable libraries of ultrathin sections, but existing tape- and magnet-based collectors (ATUM, MagC, GAUSS-EM) often demand specialized hardware or infrastructure.
ocar.challenge: Cost, hardware, and setup still limit who can collect wafer-scale serial sections for connectomics.
ocar.action: Medina, Gogola, Wildenberg and colleagues (Cell Reports Methods, 2026) introduce DRIFT-EM (direct retrieval by ionizer-facilitated transfer): off-the-shelf static ionizers clear sections from the knife, a thermoplastic boundary confines them on silicon wafers, 3D-printed parts complete the boat, and open-source software maps regions of interest.
ocar.resolution: They report section packing densities comparable to established magnetic methods with minimal setup cost and maintenance, and they frame the platform as modular and complementary to tape- and magnet-based systems. ROI scripts currently emit Zeiss ATLAS-compatible XML.

plain_language_summary: Making a big electron-microscope map of a brain requires collecting thousands of extremely thin slices, which usually needs expensive special gear. This team shows a cheaper way to float those slices onto silicon wafers using ordinary static ionizers, 3D-printed parts, and open software.

title: Organization of circuits linking descending input to motor output in the Drosophila Male Adult Nerve Cord connectome
authors: H. S. Cheong; K. Eichler; T. Stürner; Samuel K Asinof; A. Champion; E. Marin; T. Oram; M. Sumathipala; L. Venkatasubramanian; S. Namiki; I. Siwanowicz; Marta Costa; S. Berg; Janelia FlyEM Project Team; G. Jefferis; G. Card

ocar.opportunity: A dense Male Adult Nerve Cord (MANC) connectome makes it possible, for the first time at synaptic resolution, to ask how descending brain neurons reach motor neurons in the fly ventral nerve cord.
ocar.challenge: Direct brain-to-muscle paths are expected to be rare, but the community organization of walking, flight, and mixed wing–leg control has not been surveyed at this scale.
ocar.action: Cheong, Eichler, Stürner, Jefferis, Card and colleagues (eLife, 2026) proofread and curate all descending neurons (DNs) and motor neurons (MNs), match morphologies to light microscopy, and analyze DN-to-MN networks using companion MANC connectivity and lineage papers.

Direct DN–MN connections are infrequent (typically <10% of MN input synapses), though about 80% of MN groups receive some direct DN input at a 1% threshold; neck and some abdominal MNs are outliers with DN input up to 60%. Anatomical DN subclasses target dorsal, ventral, or mixed neuropils, including walking, flight steering/power, and coordinated wing–leg communities.
ocar.future_work: Unmatched DN and MN types remain to be linked at the light level; the authors treat the maps as hypotheses for physiology and as a resource for others to query VNC circuits.

plain_language_summary: To move, a fly’s brain must talk to motor neurons in the nerve cord, but those paths are hard to see. Using a complete male nerve-cord wiring map, this team shows that brain cells rarely plug straight into muscles and instead work through communities that look like walking, flight, and mixed wing–leg control.

Using a complete male nerve-cord wiring map, this team shows that brain cells rarely plug straight into muscles and instead work through communities that look like walking, flight, and mixed wing–leg control.

(2024) and cell-type/lineage annotations of Marin et al. (2024). title: Organizational principles governing synapse types in a whole-brain connectome
authors: A. Gross; Majd Farah; Subhajit Jana; S. Dorkenwald; D. Bock; David S. Deutsch

ocar.opportunity: Many neurons mix presynaptic and postsynaptic sites on the same arbor, so a complete brain connectome can ask how often wiring is not simply axon-to-dendrite.
ocar.challenge: Non-canonical synapse types (axo-axonic, dendrodendritic, dendro-axonic) are known in selected circuits, but their brain-wide organization has not been quantified.
ocar.action: Gross, Farah, Jana, Dorkenwald, Bock, and Deutsch (bioRxiv, 2026) map synapse types across compartments, cell types, and regions in an adult Drosophila brain connectome of approximately 140,000 neurons and more than 80 million synapses.
ocar.resolution: Mixed polarity is widespread but structured: about one third of synapses between polarized neurons are non-canonical. Synapse type is predictable from a morphology-and-connectivity complexity axis—low-complexity early visual neurons interact more through dendrites, larger highly connected central neurons more through axons. Mixed polarity promotes reciprocal connectivity dominated by non-canonical motifs, and postsynaptic terminals on presynaptic boutons are a common local motif.
ocar.future_work: How these anatomical rules translate to physiology, and whether they hold in other complete brains, is left open; the preprint cites emerging CNS and vertebrate volumes as natural tests.

plain_language_summary: Textbooks say dendrites take messages in and axons send them out, but many neurons mix both on the same branches. Using a complete fly-brain wiring map, this team shows that mixed wiring is common, follows simple complexity rules, and often makes two-way connections.

summaries.beginner: Textbooks say dendrites take messages in and axons send them out, but many neurons mix both on the same branches. Using a complete fly-brain wiring map, this team shows that mixed wiring is common, follows simple complexity rules, and often makes two-way connections.
summaries.intermediate: Gross et al. (bioRxiv, 2026) classify synapse types across the complete adult Drosophila brain connectome (~140,000 neurons, >80 million synapses). About one third of synapses between polarized neurons are non-canonical (axo-axonic, dendrodendritic, or dendro-axonic). A simple neuronal-complexity axis from morphology and connectivity predicts synapse type: low-complexity neurons that dominate early vision prefer dendritic interactions, whereas larger, more connected central-brain neurons prefer axonal interactions. Mixed polarity strongly promotes reciprocal connectivity, and postsynaptic terminals on presynaptic boutons emerge as a widespread local motif. The paper is a whole-brain anatomical census, not a new EM acquisition.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint. ‘Polarized’ versus mixed-polarity labels depend on how axonal and dendritic compartments are assigned in the reconstruction. The one-third non-canonical figure is for synapses between polarized neurons, not all synapses. Complexity-axis prediction is correlative. Reciprocal and bouton-terminal motifs are structural; inhibitory versus excitatory function is not resolved from synapse-type geometry alone here.

title: Comparative connectomics of Drosophila descending and ascending neurons
authors: T. Stürner; Paul Brooks; Laia Serratosa Capdevila; Billy J. Morris; A. Javier; Siqi Fang; Marina Gkantia; S. Cachero; Isabella R. Beckett; E. Marin; Philipp Schlegel; A. ocar.challenge: Those neurons are split across separate EM volumes, sexes, and light-level driver libraries, so matching types has been incomplete.
ocar.action: Stürner, Brooks, Jefferis, Eichler and colleagues (Nature, 2025) integrate three EM datasets to reconstruct female descending and ascending neurons, compare them to the male nerve cord, match types across hemispheres, datasets, and sexes, link 51% of DN cell types to light-level driver lines, and classify all ascending populations.

plain_language_summary: A fly’s brain and body are linked by a thin neck cable of neurons that send commands down and senses back up. This Nature paper stitches three electron-microscope maps to finish that cable in the female, compare it with the male, and tie many cell types to genetic tools used in experiments.

summaries.beginner: A fly’s brain and body are linked by a thin neck cable of neurons that send commands down and senses back up. This Nature paper stitches three electron-microscope maps to finish that cable in the female, compare it with the male, and tie many cell types to genetic tools used in experiments.
summaries.intermediate: Stürner et al. (Nature, 2025) combine three EM volumes to give a complete connectomic description of descending neurons (DNs), ascending neurons (ANs), and sensory ascending neurons in the Drosophila female nervous system, matched to the male nerve cord. Proofread reconstructions are matched across hemispheres, datasets, and sexes; 51% of DN cell types are linked to light-level driver lines, and all ascending populations are classified. They describe DN–AN chains spanning the neck and analyze sexually dimorphic circuits for courtship (DNa12/aSP22), song (08B ANs), and ovipositor extrusion (DNp13). The work supplies EM-level analyses spanning the adult central nervous system rather than a single neuropil.
summaries.advanced: Sample size remains small (a handful of EM specimens), a limitation the authors themselves emphasize even while using more datasets than typical single-volume studies. 51% of DN types—not all—are matched to driver lines. Functional labels (courtship, song, oviposition) rest on prior genetics plus new connectivity, not new physiology in this paper. Truncation and cross-alignment issues persist until full-CNS volumes; male–female comparisons inherit those matching uncertainties.

summaries.intermediate: Nern et al. (Nature, 2025) present a FIB-SEM connectome of the right optic lobe of a male Drosophila melanogaster. Cross-dataset matching to FlyWire uses bidirectional NBLAST after transforming optic-lobe skeletons into FAFB space, followed by independent morphological review. Transmitter identity is predicted, not biochemically confirmed; 170 types remain unclear. Some groups (ONIN, ONCN) are hard to distinguish by morphology alone and needed connectivity clustering. title: Light-microscopy-based connectomic reconstruction of mammalian brain tissue
authors: Mojtaba R. Tavakoli; Julia Lyudchik; M. Januszewski; Vitali Vistunou; Nathalie Agudelo Dueñas; Jakob Vorlaufer; C. Sommer; Caroline Kreuzinger; Bárbara Oliveira; Alban Cenameri; Gaia Novarino; Viren Jain; Johann G. Danzl

ocar.opportunity: Light microscopy can show specific molecules, but dense synapse-level circuit reconstruction has been an electron-microscopy specialty because diffraction-limited light cannot separate packed neurites.
ocar.challenge: Resolution, contrast, and volumetric imaging have kept light-based dense connectomics out of reach, so molecular identity and full wiring are usually collected in different experiments.
ocar.action: Tavakoli, Lyudchik, Januszewski, Danzl and colleagues (Nature, 2025) introduce LICONN (light-microscopy-based connectomics): engineered hydrogel embedding and expansion plus deep-learning segmentation and connectivity analysis, demonstrated on mammalian brain tissue including thick hippocampal CA1 slices and multi-round block-face imaging.
ocar.resolution: They argue LICONN can incorporate molecular information directly into synapse-level reconstructions and will allow synapse-level phenotyping in a more adoptable optical workflow. Extended data illustrate iterative imaging/sectioning of expanded hydrogel (for example two-round fusion of a 6×6×2 grid and a 3×3×12 grid whose fused axial extent is 205 µm at original tissue scale).
ocar.future_work: The authors present LICONN as enabling biological experiments rather than as a finished whole-brain mammalian connectome; scaling, tracing completeness, and molecular multiplexing limits remain the practical next tests.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopes can map every connection, but they do not easily show which molecules sit at those connections. This team expands brain tissue in a gel, images it with light, and uses machine learning to trace cells and synapses while keeping molecular labels.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopes can map every connection, but they do not easily show which molecules sit at those connections. This team expands brain tissue in a gel, images it with light, and uses machine learning to trace cells and synapses while keeping molecular labels.
summaries.intermediate: Tavakoli et al. (Nature, 2025) describe LICONN, integrating hydrogel expansion with deep-learning segmentation so light microscopy can reconstruct densely labeled mammalian neuropil at synapse level and attach molecular information to those reconstructions. Conventional light resolution (best-case hundreds of nanometres laterally, often ~1 µm axially) is treated as too coarse for dense tracing; expansion plus computational segmentation is the proposed route. Extended data show multi-tile, multi-round block-face imaging of expanded CA1 tissue with seamless fusion, including a fused volume of 205 µm original-tissue axial extent from 12 imaging rounds. The claim is adoptable synapse-level phenotyping, not replacement of all EM connectomics.
summaries.advanced: This is not a whole-brain mammalian connectome. Expansion factor, residual distortion, and automated versus manual tracing completeness should be read from the full figures rather than assumed from the slogan. Molecular incorporation is a design goal of the hydrogel/labeling strategy; the selected extract does not quantify how many molecular channels survive expansion at connectomic density. Comparison with EM error rates on the same tissue is the natural external benchmark and is not fully settled by the front matter alone.

title: Building and Integrating Brain-Wide Maps of Nervous System Function in Invertebrates
authors: Talya S. Kramer; S. Flavell

ocar.opportunity: Brain-wide activity maps, connectomes, and cell atlases now exist for C. elegans and Drosophila, so structure and function can be compared at nervous-system scale rather than one circuit at a time.
ocar.challenge: How activity is coordinated across regions, and which structural motifs must enter whole-brain models, remains open even in these small animals.
ocar.action: Kramer and Flavell (Current Opinion in Neurobiology, 2024) review recent whole-brain calcium imaging in behaving worms and flies, maps of connectivity, transmitter/receptor identity, and neuromodulation, and circuit motifs with known structure–function links, largely from the past few years.
ocar.resolution: C. elegans now has an atlas of how most neurons encode spontaneous behavior, and Drosophila activity maps give a global view of dynamics, alongside genetic and synaptic maps in both species. The authors argue that flexibility, degeneracy, extrasynaptic signaling, and receptor kinetics are still missing ingredients for accurate whole-brain models.
ocar.future_work: They call for brain-wide recordings across behavioral states and motivated contexts, large-scale views of transmitter and neuropeptide dynamics, and models that generate testable predictions rather than assuming fixed activity maps.

plain_language_summary: For tiny animals like worms and fruit flies, scientists can now record almost the whole brain while the animal moves, and they also have wiring diagrams. This review asks how to put those maps together so we can explain real behavior, not just one circuit at a time.

summaries.beginner: For tiny animals like worms and fruit flies, scientists can now record almost the whole brain while the animal moves, and they also have wiring diagrams. This review asks how to put those maps together so we can explain real behavior, not just one circuit at a time.
summaries.intermediate: Kramer and Flavell (Current Opinion in Neurobiology, 2024) review brain-wide maps of structure and function in C. elegans and Drosophila. They cover whole-brain calcium imaging in immobilized and freely moving animals, connectomes, genetic identity, and neuromodulation, then walk through circuit motifs that show why whole-brain models must capture more than a static wiring diagram. They note that C. elegans has an atlas of how most neurons encode spontaneous behavior, while fly activity maps provide a global dynamical view, and that both species now have synaptic and receptor/transmitter maps. Mammalian brain-wide imaging is treated as still incomplete despite recordings of over a million mouse cortical neurons.
summaries.advanced: This is a review, not a primary reconstruction or a new activity dataset. Species parallels are suggestive, not proof of shared algorithms. The authors explicitly say current activity maps will not be fixed across states. Citations to ‘most neurons’ in the worm atlas and to million-neuron mouse cortex are pointers to other papers; readers should not treat this article as the source of those measurements.

title: EM and XRM Connectomics Imaging and Experimental Metadata Standards
authors: Miguel E. Wimbish; Nicole K. Guittari; Victoria A. Rose; Jorge L. Rivera; P. Rivlin; Mark A. Hinton; Jordan K. Matelsky; Nicole Stock; Brock Andrew Wester; Erik C. Johnson; William Gray-Roncal

ocar.opportunity: Petascale EM and X-ray micro/holographic-nano tomography volumes are multiplying across species, regions, and techniques, and shared metadata would make comparative connectomics and software interoperability realistic.
ocar.challenge: Neuroinformatics standards that work for other modalities have not covered EM and XRM/XHN connectomics, so datasets remain isolated with idiosyncratic metadata.
ocar.action: Wimbish, Guittari, Rose, Johnson, Gray-Roncal and the BENCHMARK working group (arXiv preprint, version 1.1 dated December 30, 2025 in the PDF) specify Image and Experimental Metadata Standards for EM and XRM/XHN, including classes such as contributors, license, funder, projects, taxonomy, coordinate frame, publication, and links, with a companion document for derived annotations.
ocar.resolution: The document is a community standard (v1.1) intended to support metadata services and future software, with definitions on a community GitHub page and an acronym table covering ATUM-SEM, FIB-SEM, SB-SEM, XRM, and identifier schemes (ORCID, RRID, ROR, and others).
ocar.future_work: The authors hope the standards will be refined by the community; adoption, not a new dataset, is the measure of success.

plain_language_summary: Giant microscope maps of brains are hard to compare if every lab describes the experiment differently. This working-group paper proposes shared labels for how electron-microscope and X-ray volumes were made, so the files can be found, combined, and reused.

summaries.beginner: Giant microscope maps of brains are hard to compare if every lab describes the experiment differently. This working-group paper proposes shared labels for how electron-microscope and X-ray volumes were made, so the files can be found, combined, and reused.
summaries.intermediate: Wimbish et al. (arXiv, BENCHMARK standards v1.1) present imaging and experimental metadata standards for electron microscopy and X-ray micro / holographic-nano tomography connectomics. They argue that FAIR-style standardization, already common in other neuroinformatics modalities, has not reached these volumetric datasets. Version 1.1 defines required and optional fields (contributors, license, taxonomy, coordinate frame, publication, links, and others) to support metadata services; annotation standards are deferred to a companion document. A stakeholder working group is listed, and technique abbreviations span ATUM-SEM, FIB-SEM, serial block-face SEM, TEM variants, and XRM.
summaries.advanced: This is a standards preprint, not a validation that labs have adopted the schema. Many fields in the excerpted table are optional. Interoperability gains depend on uptake by repositories and tools. The selected extract is partly a field dictionary; it does not benchmark completeness of metadata on existing public volumes.

title: NeuroSC: Exploring Neurodevelopment via Spatiotemporal Collation of Anatomical Networks
authors: Noelle L. Koonce; Sarah E. Emerson; Dhananjay Bhaskar; Manik Kuchroo; Mark W. Moyle; Pura Arroyo-Morales; Nabor Vázquez Martínez; Jamie I Emerson; Smita Krishnaswamy; William Mohler; Daniel A. Colón-Ramos

ocar.opportunity: Volume-EM connectomes contain not only synapses but also cell-biological contacts that can be compared across developmental stages if graph analytics stay linked to the underlying anatomy.
ocar.challenge: High-dimensional adjacency and contact measurements are hard to inspect without a platform that moves between abstract graphs and neuropil features.
ocar.action: Koonce, Emerson, Colón-Ramos, Mohler and colleagues (bioRxiv, 2024; version posted May 27, 2025) introduce NeuroSC/NeuroSCAN, an open-source online platform, and apply it to a series of published C. elegans brain neuropils spanning larval stages through adult.
ocar.resolution: Integrated graphical representations of neuronal relationships are used to compare connectomes and to prompt structure–function and developmental insights. Supplemental adjacency tables quantify contacts and pixel-weighted adjacencies at L1 (5 h post hatching), L2 (23 h), L3 (27 h), L4 (36 h), and adult (48 h).
ocar.future_work: The platform is framed as a way to keep synthesizing abstractions with cell-biological detail as more staged connectomes appear.

plain_language_summary: Worm brains have been mapped at several ages, but the tables of who touches whom are hard to browse. This team built a website that lets you jump from a simplified graph of neuron relationships down to the actual cell contacts that change as the worm grows.

summaries.beginner: Worm brains have been mapped at several ages, but the tables of who touches whom are hard to browse. This team built a website that lets you jump from a simplified graph of neuron relationships down to the actual cell contacts that change as the worm grows.
summaries.intermediate: Koonce, Emerson et al. (bioRxiv, 2024) present NeuroSC (also called NeuroSCAN), an open-source platform linking data-science graph views of neuronal relationships to cell-biological features in volume-EM connectomes. They analyze published C. elegans brain neuropils across development and argue that these integrated representations make cross-connectome comparison tractable. Supplemental resources include searchable adjacency counts (number of EM sections in contact and summed pixel weights) for L1 through adult, with times such as 5, 23, 27, 36, and 48 hours post hatching. The contribution is visualization and collation infrastructure plus developmental comparison, not a new EM volume.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint methods/resource paper on published worm neuropils. Insights into structure–function are catalyzed by the representations; they are not independently validated with new physiology here. title: Serotonergic modulation of swallowing in a complete fly vagus nerve connectome
authors: Andreas Schoofs; Anton Miroschnikow; P. Schlegel; I. Zinke; Casey M. Schneider-Mizell; A. Cardona; Michael J. Pankratz

ocar.opportunity: A whole-animal scanning transmission EM volume of Drosophila can, in principle, map every gut–brain path through the insect vagus at synaptic resolution.
ocar.challenge: How the body tells the brain that swallowing succeeded, and how serotonin then values that act, has not been reconstructed as a complete circuit.
ocar.action: Schoofs, Miroschnikow, Pankratz and colleagues (Current Biology, 2024) reconstruct enteric-to-brain circuits in a whole-larva STEM volume and combine that anatomy with functional arguments about Piezo mechanosensors and serotonergic modulation.
ocar.resolution: Piezo-expressing esophageal mechanosensory neurons (EGpost on the myogenic esophagus) report food passage to a cluster of six central serotonergic neurons, which, together with food-value information, enhance serotonin-receptor-7 motor neurons that drive swallowing. Glutamatergic esophageal motor neurons make axo-axonic synapses onto those mechanosensors. The authors interpret this as a neuromodulatory loop that strengthens ongoing swallowing when a biologically meaningful act is completed, possibly an ancient form of motor learning.
ocar.future_work: They separate ‘mission accomplished’ sensing, value encoding, and reinforcement as conceptual questions still to be tested beyond this larval swallowing system.

plain_language_summary: Swallowing is the moment food is truly taken in, but how the gut tells the brain ‘that worked’ is usually guessed, not wired out. Using a whole-larva fly electron-microscope map, this team finds stretch sensors in the esophagus that talk to six serotonin cells, which then boost the motor neurons that swallow.

summaries.beginner: Swallowing is the moment food is truly taken in, but how the gut tells the brain ‘that worked’ is usually guessed, not wired out. Using a whole-larva fly electron-microscope map, this team finds stretch sensors in the esophagus that talk to six serotonin cells, which then boost the motor neurons that swallow.
summaries.intermediate: Schoofs et al. (Current Biology, 2024) map the Drosophila enteric nervous system’s links to the brain via the insect vagus in a whole-animal STEM volume. They describe a feedback loop: Piezo-positive esophageal mechanosensors, especially EGpost on the myogenic esophagus, signal completed food passage to six serotonergic brain neurons that modulate 5-HT7 motor neurons. An axo-axonic synapse from glutamatergic esophageal motor neurons onto the mechanosensors is part of the architecture. Discussion contrasts neurogenic initiation at the pharynx–esophagus junction with myogenic peristalsis and treats EGpost as a ‘mission accomplished’ sensor rather than a deglutition trigger. Anatomy is paired with the claim that serotonin reinforces high-value completed swallows.
summaries.advanced: The volume is larval Drosophila, not adult. Piezo expression and activity-during-feeding arguments support the stretch hypothesis but do not fully substitute for in vivo force measurements in the selected text. The ‘ancient motor learning’ framing is interpretive. Completeness claims refer to feeding-relevant body–brain connections in this STEM volume; they should not be read as a complete adult autonomic connectome.

title: WASPSYN: A Challenge for Domain Adaptive Synapse Detection in Microwasp Brain Connectomes
authors: Yicong Li; Wanhua Li; Qi Chen; Wei Huang; Yuda Zou; Xin Xiao; Kazunori Shinomiya; Pat Gunn; Nishika Gupta; A. Polilov; Yongchao Xu; Yueyi Zhang; Zhiwei Xiong; Hanspeter Pfister; D. Wei; Jingpeng Wu

ocar.opportunity: Connectomic EM volumes reach tera- to petascale with appearance that shifts by sample preparation, so synapse detectors must work when labeled training data are a tiny fraction of the volume.
ocar.challenge: Domain-adaptation methods are common in natural images but lacked a public synapse-detection benchmark on biological EM domains.
ocar.action: Li, Wu, Wei, Pfister and colleagues (IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging, 2024) annotated 14 volumes from biologically diverse Megaphragma viggianii brain regions across three whole-brain datasets and ran the WASPSYN challenge at ISBI 2023, with 3D pre- and postsynaptic coordinates plus one-to-many connectivity, a two-step baseline, and CodaLab evaluation.
ocar.resolution: The paper reports the dataset, tasks, baseline, evaluation, challenge results, and limitations. The challenge remains open at the CodaLab URL given in the text. Ground-truth annotators and imaging (Pang and Xu in the Hess lab at Janelia) are acknowledged.
ocar.future_work: The authors hope winning algorithms will generalize to real-world connectomics; they discuss challenge limits and neuroscience impact rather than declaring a solved detector.

plain_language_summary: Computers that find synapses in brain pictures often fail when the next sample was prepared a little differently. This team labeled synapses in tiny wasp brains from three different datasets and ran a public contest so methods can be compared fairly when the pictures change.

summaries.beginner: Computers that find synapses in brain pictures often fail when the next sample was prepared a little differently. This team labeled synapses in tiny wasp brains from three different datasets and ran a public contest so methods can be compared fairly when the pictures change.
summaries.intermediate: Li et al. (IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging, 2024) describe WASPSYN, an ISBI 2023 challenge for domain-adaptive synapse detection in Megaphragma viggianii. Fourteen annotated EM volumes from three whole-brain samples provide pre- and postsynaptic 3D coordinates and one-to-many connectivity. Labeled training data in typical connectomics applications are described as often smaller than 0.001% of the target volume, motivating out-of-domain evaluation. A two-step baseline, public starter code, and online CodaLab scoring (https://codalab.lisn.upsaclay.fr/competitions/9169) are provided. Imaging and alignment were done by Pang and Xu in Harald Hess’s Janelia lab.
summaries.advanced: This is a benchmark and challenge report, not a claim that domain shift is solved. The 0.001% figure characterizes the general labeling problem, not necessarily the fraction labeled in these 14 volumes. Success on microwasp appearance shift may not transfer to mammalian EM. One-to-many connectivity annotations add task richness but also annotation noise risk; the paper discusses limitations of the challenge design.
