title: A complete reconstruction of the early visual system of an adult insect.
authors: Nicholas J. Chua; Pat Gunn ... Anastasia A Makarova; Harald F. Hess; A. Polilov; D. Chklovskii; Pat Gunn; S. Villani; Ben Cohen; Myisha Thasin; Jingpeng Wu; Deena Shefter; Song Pang; Shan Xu

ocar.opportunity: The microinsect Megaphragma viggianii is small enough for whole-head electron microscopy while still flying, so its early visual system could expose a minimal flying-insect circuit.
ocar.challenge: Most neuroscience model species lack a complete high-resolution map of the compound eye and first visual neuropil, which blocks compact computational models of insect vision.
ocar.action: Chua, Polilov, Chklovskii and colleagues (Current Biology, 2023), as described in the catalog abstract, image the whole head with serial EM, reconstruct the compound eye, analyze ommatidial optics, and reconstruct the lamina connectome.
ocar.resolution: Relative to fruit fly and honeybee, the visual system is highly simplified: 29 ommatidia per eye and 6 lamina neuron types, with both stereotyped and specialized ommatidial features. The authors argue this ‘barebones’ flying-insect circuit will aid computational models of visual processing.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents the reconstruction as a substrate for models; how specializations map onto behavior is left to subsequent analysis.

plain_language_summary: Some tiny wasps have very small eyes but can still fly, which makes them a good place to look for the simplest flying visual circuit. This paper maps one such wasp’s eye and the first brain station behind it, finding only 29 facets per eye and six cell types in that first station.

summaries.beginner: Some tiny wasps have very small eyes but can still fly, which makes them a good place to look for the simplest flying visual circuit. This paper maps one such wasp’s eye and the first brain station behind it, finding only 29 facets per eye and six cell types in that first station.

They analyze ommatidial optics and the lamina connectome, reporting 29 ommatidia per eye and six lamina neuron types—far simpler than Drosophila or honeybee. Features that are shared across most ommatidia are distinguished from specialized ones. The stated goal is to identify circuits critical for flying insects and to facilitate computational models. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.

title: A Novel Semi-automated Proofreading and Mesh Error Detection Pipeline for Neuron Extension
authors: Justin Joyce; Rupasri Chalavadi; Joey Chan; Sheel Tanna; Daniel Xenes; Nathanael Kuo; Victoria A. Rose; Jordan K. Matelsky; Lindsey M. Kitchell; Caitlyn Bishop; Patricia K. Rivlin; Marisel Villafañe-Delgado; Brock Andrew Wester

ocar.opportunity: False splits at neurite tips hide many synapses from their parent cell, so cheap geometric flags for those tips could speed both human and automated extension.
ocar.challenge: Manual proofreading of petascale EM segmentations is still required, and existing extension tools do not first cheaply rank likely error locations.
ocar.action: Joyce, Chalavadi, Chan, Tanna, Wester and colleagues (bioRxiv, 2023) use mesh processing to find likely errors near neuronal tips and embed that detector in a semi-automated proofreading pipeline, including an attempt at fully automated extension seeded by those endpoints using Sofima optical flow.
ocar.resolution: Guiding proofreaders to flagged locations improved average edit rate even with loading-time overhead. Fully automated extension often chose the correct candidate but struggled when more than three consecutive slices were blacked out or when misalignments were large.
ocar.future_work: They suggest adding geometric features or machine learning for higher-precision localization, cutting UI loading time, and using GAN or other large models where alignment fails.

plain_language_summary: When a computer map of a neuron is cut off too early, many of that cell’s connections are missing. This team looks at the shape of those dead ends, points proofreaders at the likely breaks, and shows that people fix mistakes faster when they are pointed in the right direction.

summaries.beginner: When a computer map of a neuron is cut off too early, many of that cell’s connections are missing. This team looks at the shape of those dead ends, points proofreaders at the likely breaks, and shows that people fix mistakes faster when they are pointed in the right direction.
summaries.intermediate: Joyce et al. (bioRxiv, 2023; JHU APL) detect likely false splits near tips of EM neuron meshes and route those locations into a semi-automated proofreading workflow aimed at neurite extension. They motivate the problem with hemibrain- and MICrONS-scale volumes and contrast the approach with tools such as RoboEM and NEURD. In their implementation, proofreader efficiency (edit rate) rose when tasks were oriented to predicted error sites, despite loading delays between tasks. A fully automated extension attempt using mesh-based Sofima optical flow often selected the correct continuation but failed on stretches with more than three blacked-out slices or large misalignments.

Automated extension is explicitly not robust to severe missing-section and misalignment artifacts. Results depend on the segmentation and alignment quality of the host volume (MICrONS-related in the funding and introduction). Improving loading time is acknowledged as a confounder of human-rate measurements.

title: Cyclic structure with cellular precision in a vertebrate sensorimotor neural circuit
authors: Runzhe Yang; Ashwin Vishwanathan; Jingpeng Wu; N. Kemnitz; Dodam Ih; N. Turner; Kisuk Lee; Ignacio Tartavull; W. Silversmith; C. Jordan; Celia David; Doug Bland; A. Sterling; Marc S. Goldman; Emre R. F. Aksay; H. Seung

ocar.opportunity: EM wiring diagrams invite cross-species comparison of sensorimotor organization, using C. elegans feedforwardness as the classic foil.
ocar.challenge: Whether vertebrate circuits show the opposite—overrepresented cellular cycles—had not been shown in any EM connectome.
ocar.action: Yang, Vishwanathan, Wu, Aksay, Seung and colleagues (Current Biology, 2023) analyze a larval zebrafish brainstem wiring diagram, focusing on the oculomotor module, counting three-cell cycles against feedforward loops (U3 and C3), and fitting a stochastic block model.
ocar.resolution: Three-cycles are highly overrepresented, a first among EM neuronal wiring diagrams they survey. Cellular cycles align with a three-cycle of neuronal groups in the SBM but are more specific than group structure can explain, with surprisingly common recurrence to the same neuron. Most three-cycles lack inhibitory Ve2 cells and are therefore expected to be all-excitatory. The cyclic structure coexists with the classic horizontal vestibulo-ocular reflex arc and is discussed in light of recurrent integrator models.
ocar.future_work: The functional meaning of cellular (not just group) specificity remains unclear; the authors note that a three-block cycle would already suffice for positive feedback.

plain_language_summary: Worm wiring is often described as a one-way path from sensors to muscles. In a young zebrafish eye-movement circuit, this team instead finds many three-cell loops, including loops that return to the same cell, which may help the brain hold a signal over time.

summaries.beginner: Worm wiring is often described as a one-way path from sensors to muscles. In a young zebrafish eye-movement circuit, this team instead finds many three-cell loops, including loops that return to the same cell, which may help the brain hold a signal over time.
summaries.intermediate: Yang et al. (Current Biology, 2023) contrast the feedforward C. elegans sensorimotor connectome with a larval zebrafish brainstem reconstruction. In the oculomotor module, the three-cycle motif is highly overrepresented relative to feedforward loops, reported as a first for EM wiring diagrams (invertebrate or mammalian) in their comparison set. Cycles align with a three-group cycle in a stochastic block model but show extra cellular specificity. Bidirectional connections are less overrepresented than in C. elegans, consistent with mostly axodendritic synapses that do not invite nearby reciprocal contacts. Registration to Z-Brain gene expression had previously suggested most module cells are excitatory except Ve2.
summaries.advanced: Comparing an entire worm connectome to one zebrafish module is a principled but coarse analogy, which the authors defend at the level of general organization rather than cell homology. Motif overrepresentation depends on the null model (they discuss CFG versus ER). Excitatory-loop inference uses atlas registration plus Ve2 as the inhibitory exception, not paired physiology. Whether cycles implement a neural integrator is a theoretical link, not a causal test in this report.

title: Data-driven motif discovery in biological neural networks
authors: Jordan K. Matelsky; Michael S. Robinette; Brock Andrew Wester; William Gray-Roncal; Erik C. Johnson; E. Reilly

ocar.opportunity: Connectomes are usually one-of-a-kind, so discovering repeated subgraphs cannot wait for large samples of host graphs, and exhaustive subgraph search is intractable.
ocar.challenge: Standard motif tests can mislead if the random-graph null is wrong, and listing all subgraphs does not scale.
ocar.action: Matelsky, Robinette, Wester, Gray-Roncal, Johnson, and Reilly (bioRxiv, 2023) propose improved randomization for significance, a progressive-refinement discovery procedure for directed or undirected motifs from a single graph, sampling corrections, and an open-source Python package, demonstrated on the C. elegans connectome and the Drosophila ellipsoid body.
ocar.resolution: They show that standard random-graph models can produce misleading significance calls, that their sampling correction supports testing of target motifs, and that discovered motifs include biologically familiar recurrence, feedback, and feedforward loops. Code, data, and infrastructure—including unsuccessful forays—are released for reuse.
ocar.future_work: Whether motifs are conserved across individuals, how to separate core from periphery, and how structure maps to attractor dynamics are posed as community-scale next questions.

plain_language_summary: Scientists want to know which small wiring patterns repeat in a brain map, but each map is usually one of a kind and too big to search blindly. This team offers a method and open software to find those patterns in a single connectome and to test whether they are really unusual.

summaries.beginner: Scientists want to know which small wiring patterns repeat in a brain map, but each map is usually one of a kind and too big to search blindly. This team offers a method and open software to find those patterns in a single connectome and to test whether they are really unusual.
summaries.intermediate: Matelsky et al. (bioRxiv, 2023) tackle data-driven motif discovery on single biological graphs. They critique common statistical pitfalls in motif enrichment, propose better randomization, and use progressive refinement to control computational cost while returning directed or undirected motifs with counts versus randomized graphs. Preliminary demonstrations use the C. elegans connectome and the ellipsoid body of Drosophila. An open-source Python package is provided. The discussion treats familiar motif classes (recurrence, feedforward/feedback) as expected and asks whether they are conserved across individuals.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint methods paper with ‘preliminary’ biological results. Enrichment is always relative to the chosen null; the authors’ point is that naive nulls mislead, so readers should inspect which generator was used. Discovery on one C. elegans graph and one fly subnetwork does not establish species-wide conservation. Functional interpretation of motifs is explicitly deferred.

title: Learning to Correct Sloppy Annotations in Electron Microscopy Volumes
authors: Minghao Chen; Mukesh Bangalore Renuka; Lu Mi; J. Lichtman; N. Shavit; Y. Meirovitch
journal: 2023 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Workshops (CVPRW)

ocar.opportunity: Fully automatic 3D instance segmentation of EM still fails on thin processes, so labs need a way to sketch neurons quickly and let a network clean the shapes.
ocar.challenge: Even painstaking proofreading leaves small errors, and marker-based 2-D region growing on EM has lagged other instance-segmentation settings.
ocar.action: Chen, Bangalore Renuka, Mi, Lichtman, Shavit, and Meirovitch (CVPR Workshops, 2023) introduce EMProof, learning to shrink and expand sloppy manual annotations via a marker-based 2-D instance segmentation network, tested on public benchmarks, large-scale neuron problems, a new octopus dataset, and a super-resolution setting on mouse cortex AC3.
ocar.resolution: They report near-ground-truth morphology while cutting annotation time about 8× on several connectomics examples, a new state of the art among region-growing algorithms on challenging EM stacks, and, on AC3, 16-fold XY super-resolution from coarse low-resolution segmentation with a majority of regions reaching VI under 0.04 and many improvement factors of 4–8×. Architecture ablations (U-Net plus hypercolumns, two-branch, and the full proposed model) are tabulated on skeletal inputs.
ocar.future_work: They suggest the same primitive may apply to other reconstruction tasks where a coarse human sketch is refined by learning.

plain_language_summary: Drawing every neuron perfectly in electron-microscope pictures is slow, so people often sketch roughly. This team trains a network to tidy those sloppy sketches into accurate shapes, cutting tracing time on several examples and even working from blurrier, lower-resolution pictures.

summaries.beginner: Drawing every neuron perfectly in electron-microscope pictures is slow, so people often sketch roughly. This team trains a network to tidy those sloppy sketches into accurate shapes, cutting tracing time on several examples and even working from blurrier, lower-resolution pictures.
summaries.intermediate: Chen et al. (CVPRW, 2023) present EMProof, which takes imperfect instance annotations—skeletons or tiny seeds—and learns to correct them by shrinking and expanding objects. They claim state-of-the-art among region-growing methods on hard EM stacks and about an 8× annotation-time reduction on several connectomics examples, including an octopus volume they say existing automatic segmenters cannot handle at scale. On the AC3 mouse-cortex benchmark, coarse low-resolution segmentations are super-resolved 16-fold in X and Y, with a large fraction of the data showing 4–8× VI improvement and most achieving VI under 0.04. The framework is 2-D marker-based instance segmentation used to accelerate manual 3-D reconstruction.
summaries.advanced: Headline 8× time savings are for ‘several examples,’ not a universal multiplier. VI under 0.04 and 16-fold super-resolution are AC3-specific. The octopus claim is that existing algorithms cannot automatically segment that dataset at scale; it is not a public leaderboard win against all later methods. EMProof addresses morphological reconstruction quality, not synapse graph correctness by itself. Funding from Thermo Fisher is disclosed.

title: Virtual Fly Brain—An interactive atlas of the Drosophila nervous system

Results include linked 2D/3D browsers, ontology-backed term pages (for example WEDPN2), curated split-GAL4s, and bulk downloads with licenses. The authors suggest the pattern could extend to vertebrate atlasing.

plain_language_summary: Fly neuroscience now has wiring maps, gene-expression maps, and thousands of pictures of labeled neurons, but they live in different websites. The adult brain template is described as integrating almost 100,000 images from 64 datasets, including EM and light-level neurons, clones, and expression patterns from FlyCircuit, FlyLight, CATMAID, and neuPrint. title: Edge-colored directed subgraph enumeration on the connectome
authors: Brian Matejek; D. Wei; Tianyi Chen; Charalampos E. Tsourakakis; Michael; Mitzenmacher; H. Pfister

ocar.opportunity: Connectomes can be treated as directed graphs with colored edges (for example excitatory versus inhibitory), so enumerating all small subgraphs could reveal motifs nobody hypothesized.
ocar.challenge: Exact subgraph enumeration is expensive on dense wiring diagrams, and most tools ignore edge types that change a motif’s function.
ocar.action: Matejek, Wei, Chen, Tsourakakis, Mitzenmacher, and Pfister (Scientific Reports, 2022) present a parallel general-purpose enumerator, a divide-and-conquer community strategy for per-region counts, and edge-type differentiation, run on eleven connectomes.

Ten connectomes come from two C. elegans longitudinal studies; they also discuss a fruit-fly graph with over 21,000 neurons and 800,000 moderate and strong synaptic connections. Known frequent motifs such as feed-forward loops and reciprocal connections are noted as cross-species regularities they hope to complement with new discoveries from the public counts.
ocar.future_work: Larger brains will need further algorithmic ideas, including dividing by functional region; the authors offer the motif tables for longitudinal and comparative follow-up.

plain_language_summary: Once a brain map is a network of cells and connections, you can count every small repeating pattern, including whether a connection is a ‘go’ or ‘stop’ type. This team did that counting at huge scale on eleven wiring diagrams and posted the catalogs so others can look for unexpected motifs.

This team did that counting at huge scale on eleven wiring diagrams and posted the catalogs so others can look for unexpected motifs.
summaries.intermediate: Matejek et al. (Scientific Reports, 2022) develop parallel subgraph enumeration for connectomes, including edge colors and a community-based divide-and-conquer mode for regional counts. They run the method on eleven connectomes and release summaries of 26 trillion subgraphs, using about 9.25 years of compute. Ten datasets are C. elegans longitudinal reconstructions; discussion also cites a fruit-fly connectome with over 21,000 neurons and 800,000 moderate/strong connections. The scientific goal is un-hypothesized motif discovery rather than only testing classic feed-forward and reciprocal motifs. Runtime relates non-linearly to neighborhood size, which they try to control by reducing neighborhood-size variance.

Edge-color meaning depends on how excitatory/inhibitory labels were obtained in each source connectome. 26 trillion subgraphs and 9.25 compute-years are aggregate engineering figures, not a claim of 26 trillion distinct biological circuits. Community splits can miss motifs that cross region boundaries. Exact enumeration remains sensitive to proofreading state and synapse-threshold choices in the input graphs.

title: Hierarchical Modular Structure of the Drosophila Connectome
authors: Alex Kunin; Jiahao Guo; K. Bassler; X. Pitkow; K. Josić

ocar.opportunity: A synapse-resolution adult fly reconstruction with tens of thousands of neurons lets community detection ask how modules nest from thousands of cells down to tens, without choosing a single scale in advance.
ocar.challenge: Prior descriptions of brain organization traded coarse large-scale maps against fine small-scale wiring, and analyzing >20,000 neurons and 10 million synapses needs scalable, interpretable clustering.
ocar.action: Kunin, Guo, Bassler, Pitkow, and Josić (bioRxiv, 2022) maximize a generalized modularity density to resolve Hemibrain communities across scales, recovering sensory pathways, layered fan-shaped-body structure, and a modular superior neuropil with distinct up- and downstream clusters.
ocar.resolution: They find hierarchical organization in which large communities contain smaller ones, automatically recover known anatomy, and report finer fan-shaped-body connectivity to upstream and downstream areas plus a novel superior-neuropil pathway layout. Adding node labels reveals cell-type-specific wiring; an example at χ = 0.75 shows spatial tiling of MC61 cells converging on TuBu cells. They validate the approach on the larval mushroom body against prior structure.
ocar.future_work: They treat other community-detection methods as complementary, warn that reconstruction errors and volume incompleteness (for example a cluster at the cut edge of the volume) can bias clusters, and offer the partitions as hypotheses for physiology and genetics.

plain_language_summary: A fly hemibrain wiring map is so big that it is hard to see the natural groups of cells. This team uses a clustering method that looks at many zoom levels and finds nested communities, including known sensory paths and a layered navigation center, plus some new groupings.

summaries.beginner: A fly hemibrain wiring map is so big that it is hard to see the natural groups of cells. This team uses a clustering method that looks at many zoom levels and finds nested communities, including known sensory paths and a layered navigation center, plus some new groupings.
summaries.intermediate: Kunin et al. (bioRxiv, 2022) apply generalized-modularity-density community detection to the adult female Drosophila Hemibrain (>20,000 neurons, 10 million synapses). Communities are resolved from thousands of neurons down to tens, revealing hierarchy. The method recovers sensory pathways and the layered fan-shaped body, and it proposes modular pathways in the superior neuropil. With cell-type labels, clusters can match known types (for example MC61 mosaics onto TuBu). Comparison with spectral embedding is that modularity tends to yield mixed-type anatomical communities rather than single-type clusters. A larval mushroom-body check is used as validation against prior work.
summaries.advanced: The PDF is a bioRxiv preprint (catalogued under Journal of Neuroscience). Modularity maximization finds densely connected groups relative to a random null; other algorithms would highlight different structure. Incompleteness of Hemibrain (truncated neurons at volume edges) can create spurious clusters; the authors discuss keeping an edge cluster because it marks a lobula-plate fragment. Small communities of a few nodes could be noise unless they show reliable cell-type composition. Functional predictions are unsupervised and need physiology.

title: Igneous: Distributed dense 3D segmentation meshing, neuron skeletonization, and hierarchical downsampling
authors: Y. Kubota; M. Raghavan; W. Silversmith; A. Zlateski; J. Bae; Ignacio Tartavull; N. Kemnitz; Jingpeng Wu; H. Seung

plain_language_summary: Once a computer has colored in every cell in a giant brain picture, you still need 3D surfaces and stick-figure skeletons to look at and analyze those cells. Igneous is open software that builds those objects in bulk on a computing cluster or in the cloud.

summaries.beginner: Once a computer has colored in every cell in a giant brain picture, you still need 3D surfaces and stick-figure skeletons to look at and analyze those cells. Igneous is open software that builds those objects in bulk on a computing cluster or in the cloud.

title: Imaging whole-brain activity to understand behavior
authors: Albert Lin; Daniel K. Witvliet; Luis Hernandez-Nunez; Scott W. Linderman; Aravinthan D. T. Samuel; Vivek Venkatachalam

ocar.opportunity: Whole-brain cellular-resolution imaging in C. elegans, Drosophila, and larval zebrafish now records sensory, decision, and motor circuits during behavior, opening a physics-facing theory problem of joint brain and behavioral dynamics.
ocar.challenge: Most neuroscience still studies small circuits, yet natural behaviors (navigation, mating, hunting) only fully exist in freely moving animals whose sensations depend on their own actions.

ocar.future_work: Continued sensor, optics, and modeling advances are needed to close remaining gaps between ethology and high-dimensional neural data.

plain_language_summary: To understand real behavior, it helps to watch almost every brain cell while an animal moves, not just a few cells in a dish. This review explains how that is now possible in worms, flies, and young fish, and why theories must include both the wiring diagram and the animal’s changing actions.

title: Joint reconstruction of neuron and ultrastructure via connectivity consensus in electron microscope volumes
authors: Bei Hong; Jing Liu; Hao Zhai; Jiazheng Liu; Lijun Shen; Xi Chen; Qiwei Xie; Hua Han

ocar.future_work: They plan tests on other organelles and want to add long-range (lifted multicut) relationships between non-adjacent nodes.

plain_language_summary: Computers usually color neurons and their inner parts as separate jobs, even though a mitochondrion should not jump between two cells. This paper ties those jobs together so membrane and organelle clues vote in one step, which they say makes the neuron maps more accurate.

summaries.beginner: Computers usually color neurons and their inner parts as separate jobs, even though a mitochondrion should not jump between two cells. This paper ties those jobs together so membrane and organelle clues vote in one step, which they say makes the neuron maps more accurate.

title: Scalable graph analysis tools for the connectomics community
authors: Jordan K. Matelsky; Erik C. Johnson; Brock Andrew Wester; William Gray-Roncal

ocar.opportunity: Synaptic-resolution graphs now exceed laptop RAM, and comparative queries across regions and species need reusable algorithms rather than one database per dataset.
ocar.challenge: neuPrint and FlyBrainLab work well for specific volumes, but general larger-than-RAM analysis and low-maintenance comparative search remain gaps.
ocar.action: Matelsky, Johnson, Wester, and Gray-Roncal (bioRxiv, 2022) describe a tool suite: MossDB for immutable annotations, Grand for larger-than-RAM graph prototyping with NetworkX/Cypher/DotMotif dialects, GrandIso-Cloud for out-of-core motif queries, and Motif Studio for public cross-connectome queries, interfacing with neuPrint, Neo4j, Pandas, and NetworkX.
ocar.resolution: They emphasize write-once/run-anywhere algorithm design and include a table of connectome sizes from Bock through H01 (Hemibrain v1.2: 21,692 sources; MICrONS Minnie65: 106,126 sources; H01: 1,268,187 sources), noting that density tends to fall as graphs grow. Operational cost and expertise barriers are treated as first-class design constraints.
ocar.future_work: The preprint offers recommendations for community tooling rather than a single production hosted connectome; uptake depends on maintaining the backends as datasets grow.

plain_language_summary: Modern wiring diagrams are too big to hold in a normal computer’s memory, and they live in different databases. This team shares a set of open tools so scientists can search for repeated connection patterns across those huge graphs without building a new system each time.

summaries.beginner: Modern wiring diagrams are too big to hold in a normal computer’s memory, and they live in different databases. This team shares a set of open tools so scientists can search for repeated connection patterns across those huge graphs without building a new system each time.
summaries.intermediate: Matelsky et al. (bioRxiv, 2022) present scalable graph-analysis tools for connectomics: MossDB, Grand, GrandIso-Cloud, and Motif Studio, plus visualization and query services that wrap existing stores. Grand translates NetworkX-style operations, Cypher, and DotMotif into backends (SQLite, Pandas, graph toolkits) so prototypes can move from laptops to cloud graphs. They contrast persistent graph databases (fast but costly to keep up) with on-disk edgelists (cheaper but expert-heavy). A size table lists unique sources/targets and densities for datasets from White/Kasthuri/Helmstaedter/Takemura through Hemibrain, MICrONS Minnie65, and H01. The goal is algorithm and dataset reuse for comparative connectomics.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint software framework, not a new biological finding. Table densities mix proofread and unproofread graphs and omit synaptic isolates, as the caption states. Interoperability claims depend on community maintenance of adapters as neuPrint schemas evolve. Larger-than-RAM performance is architectural; the selected text does not quote a single latency SLA. Motif Studio’s public query power is only as complete as ingested graphs.

title: SyConn2: dense synaptic connectivity inference for volume electron microscopy
authors: Philipp J Schubert; Sven Dorkenwald; Michał Januszewski; Jonathan Klimesch; Fabian Svara; Andrei Mancu; Hashir Ahmad; M. Fee; Viren Jain; Joergen Kornfeld

ocar.opportunity: Volume EM is producing ever larger annotated tissues, so labs need an open, cost-aware pipeline that turns dense segmentations into queryable synaptic connectomes on HPC or rented clouds.
ocar.challenge: Prior tools covered pieces of reconstruction, proofreading, and organelle detection, but an efficient annotated-connectome toolkit that neuroscientists can run on existing clusters was lacking.
ocar.action: Schubert, Dorkenwald, Januszewski, Kornfeld and colleagues (Nature Methods, 2022) introduce SyConn2, which starts from dense neuron reconstructions and semantic voxel classes (cells, extracellular space, synapses, organelles), detects contact sites, scores synapses with ultrastructural features, and supports point-cloud morphology, cell-type classification, and a web client, tested on datasets with more than 10 million synapses including zebra finch tissue.
ocar.resolution: Cloud cost is estimated at about US$2,000 per teravoxel of 8-bit raw VEM at 10 × 10 × 25 nm³ (about US$800 per million µm³) on Google Cloud for a zebra finch dataset. Analyses include synapse-to-mitochondrion distance CDFs in pallidal-like versus striatal-like neurons and supervised putative cell-type classification. The package is a major upgrade of earlier SyConn software.
ocar.future_work: SyConn2 assumes existing dense neuron reconstructions; scaling queries and classification as volumes grow remains an operations problem the authors address with chunked CPU/GPU workers (SLURM).

plain_language_summary: After cells in an electron-microscope volume are colored in, someone still has to find the synapses and ask which cell types they belong to. SyConn2 is open software that does that bookkeeping at large scale, including on songbird brain data with more than ten million synapses.

summaries.beginner: After cells in an electron-microscope volume are colored in, someone still has to find the synapses and ask which cell types they belong to. SyConn2 is open software that does that bookkeeping at large scale, including on songbird brain data with more than ten million synapses.
summaries.intermediate: Schubert et al. (Nature Methods, 2022) present SyConn2, an open-source toolkit for dense synaptic connectivity inference from volume EM that runs on HPC or cloud clusters. Processing uses semantic voxel maps, contact-site detection, and additional ultrastructural features around candidate clefts rather than overlap alone. Morphology is analyzed with point clouds instead of only dense volumes. The authors report tests on connectomes with more than 10 million synapses, a web visualizer, and a Google Cloud cost of about US$2,000 per teravoxel at 10 × 10 × 25 nm³ on zebra finch data. Example analyses include cell-type classification and mitochondria–synapse distances in songbird basal ganglia-like circuitry.
summaries.advanced: SyConn2 requires a dense neuron segmentation as input; it does not replace proofreading of that segmentation. Cost figures are approximate cloud estimates for a specific voxel size and dataset. Putative cell types (LTS, FS, TAN, NGF, STN-like, GP-like, MSN) are classifier outputs. Feature-based synapse decisions can still err where ultrastructure is ambiguous. The brief communication format limits methodological detail relative to a full pipeline paper; see the supplement for comparisons to SyConn1.

title: Towards a Comprehensive Optical Connectome at Single Synapse Resolution via Expansion Microscopy
authors: Madison Sneve; Kiryl D Piatkevich

ocar.opportunity: Expansion microscopy can physically magnify tissue so diffraction-limited light microscopes resolve synapses, potentially yielding optical connectomes with molecular labels that EM struggles to provide.
ocar.challenge: Synapses are small and dense; EM connectomes are limited to small samples and heavy tracing, while ordinary light microscopy cannot separate packed contacts.
ocar.action: Sneve and Piatkevich (Frontiers in Synaptic Neuroscience, 2022) review ExM-compatible fluorescent probes and labeling strategies for postsynaptic scaffolds and receptors, presynaptic terminals and vesicles, and snapshots of synaptic activity in mouse, zebrafish, Drosophila, and C. elegans, including delivery vectors and practical limits.
ocar.resolution: They argue ExM plus multicolor neuronal and synaptic labeling could enable more automated circuit tracing than EM. The perspective stresses that one connectome cannot represent a species, sex, stage, or mutant, and that zebrafish and rodents still lack anything like a complete connectome because EM remains slow and costly.
ocar.future_work: Emerging probes and ExM variants are discussed as the path to multiple optical connectomes per species; the review does not itself reconstruct a circuit.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopes can see every synapse but not easily the molecules in them, and they are slow. This review surveys dyes and genetic tags that still work after brain tissue is swollen in a gel, so ordinary light microscopes might map connections with molecular color.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopes can see every synapse but not easily the molecules in them, and they are slow. This review surveys dyes and genetic tags that still work after brain tissue is swollen in a gel, so ordinary light microscopes might map connections with molecular color.
summaries.intermediate: Sneve and Piatkevich (Frontiers in Synaptic Neuroscience, 2022) review expansion microscopy as a route to synapse-resolution optical connectomics. They catalog genetically encoded and other fluorescent probes, compatible with current ExM protocols, for labeling postsynaptic scaffolds/receptors, presynaptic terminals/vesicles, and activity snapshots in mouse, zebrafish, Drosophila, and C. elegans, plus vectors and experimental caveats. EM is acknowledged as the nanoscale gold standard but is limited by sample size and tracing burden. The outlook is that ExM could let many labs generate connectomes, including many individuals, if labeling and automated tracing mature.
summaries.advanced: This is a review and perspective, not a demonstrated whole-brain optical connectome. Probe performance after expansion (brightness, linkage error, completeness) is species- and protocol-dependent; the authors discuss limitations rather than a single recommended stack. ‘Fully automated’ tracing is aspirational. Claims about EM sample-size limits reflect the literature at writing time (worm, tadpole, fly, small mammalian pieces).

title: A scalable and modular automated pipeline for stitching of large electron microscopy datasets
authors: G. Mahalingam; R. Torres; D. Kapner; Eric T. Trautman; Tim Fliss; S. Seshamani; E. Perlman; R. Young; S. Kinn; J. Buchanan; Marc M. Takeno; W. Yin; D. Bumbarger; R. Gwinn; J. Nyhus; E. Lein; Stephen J. Smith; Clay Reid; K. Khairy; S. Saalfeld; F. Collman; Nuno Maçarico da Costa

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section EM produces tens of terabytes per day, so 2D stitching and 3D alignment must keep up with the microscope if reconstruction is not to stall.
ocar.challenge: Assembling up to on the order of 10^8 tiles into a high-fidelity volume, including a cubic millimeter of cortex, requires automation, distributed compute, and quality control without rendering every intermediate image.
ocar.action: Mahalingam, Torres, Collman, da Costa and colleagues (bioRxiv, 2021) present ASAP (Assembly Stitching and Alignment Pipeline), built on Janelia Render services from the adult Drosophila brain assembly, operating on image metadata and transforms in a database, with BlueSky-triggered workflows, automated QC, 3D alignment (EM aligner), and final render-to-disk, plus multi-channel support for fluorescence and array tomography.
ocar.resolution: They report continuous processing of mouse visual cortex and human samples, including one cubic millimeter of mouse visual cortex, at speeds exceeding imaging. A cubic millimeter at 4 × 4 × 40 nm³ is described as more than a petabyte and more than 100 million tiles. Modularity is intended so new algorithms can be swapped without redesigning the workflow.
ocar.future_work: The pipeline is a production stitching/alignment stack; downstream segmentation and proofreading remain separate. Multi-modal array-tomography support is demonstrated as an extension path.

plain_language_summary: A cubic millimeter of brain imaged at synapse scale is more than a million gigabytes of overlapping snapshots that must be sewn into one volume. This team’s ASAP software stitches and aligns those pictures as fast as the microscope can take them, using a database of positions instead of rewriting every image at each step.

summaries.beginner: A cubic millimeter of brain imaged at synapse scale is more than a million gigabytes of overlapping snapshots that must be sewn into one volume. This team’s ASAP software stitches and aligns those pictures as fast as the microscope can take them, using a database of positions instead of rewriting every image at each step.
summaries.intermediate: Mahalingam et al. (bioRxiv, 2021; Allen Institute, Janelia, and collaborators) describe ASAP, a modular, distributed stitching and alignment pipeline for large serial-section EM. Built on Render services previously used for adult Drosophila, it stores per-tile transforms in a database so intermediate volumes need not be fully rendered. Components include stitching, automated quality control, 3D section alignment, and export. They deployed it on mouse visual cortex and human EM, including the MICrONS-scale cubic millimeter, claiming throughput above imaging rates of tens of terabytes per day. Multi-channel processing extends to fluorescence and array tomography. Example numbers: >1 PB and >100 million tiles for 1 mm³ at 4 × 4 × 40 nm³.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint infrastructure paper. ‘Speeds that exceed imaging’ is a deployment claim for their production setting, not a portable benchmark. Alignment quality for connectomics still depends on sectioning artifacts and QC thresholds not fully reproduced in the selected extract. ASAP does not segment neurons. Catalog organism tags include fly because Render originated on Drosophila; the flagship deployments described are mouse and human ssEM.

title: Circuits for integrating learned and innate valences in the insect brain
authors: Claire Eschbach; Akira Fushiki; Michael Winding; Bruno Afonso; Ingrid V. Andrade; Benjamin T. Cocanougher; K. Eichler; Ruben Gepner; Guangwei Si; Javier Valdes-Aleman; R. Fetter; Marc H. Gershow; G. Jefferis; Aravinthan D. T. Samuel; J. Truman; Albert Cardona; Marta Zlatic

ocar.opportunity: Animals mix innate and learned values of cues when they choose to approach or avoid. A synaptic map of how mushroom-body (learned) and lateral-horn (innate) pathways meet would show how experience can override instinct.
ocar.challenge: Innate and learned valences are thought to be computed in distinct brain areas, but the circuit mechanisms that integrate them, and by which learned valences can override innate ones, are poorly understood.
ocar.action: Eschbach, Fushiki, and colleagues in eLife (2021) use electron microscopy in Drosophila larva to map all neurons downstream of all mushroom-body output neurons and their interactions with lateral-horn neurons, then test functional connectivity and behavior for selected convergence cells.
ocar.resolution: They identify 62 neurons per hemisphere as direct MB–LH convergence points, including a subtype of 10 that receive excitatory input from positive-valence MB and LH pathways and inhibitory input from negative-valence MB pathways. Two of these encode integrated odor value and bidirectionally regulate turning; for one, aversive learning skews inputs toward inhibition.
ocar.future_work: The authors speculate that learning could skew excitation–inhibition onto these neurons and thereby modulate turning; broader tests of remaining convergence subtypes and of how learning rewires them are the implied next steps.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly larvae have one brain area for inborn likes and dislikes and another for learned ones. This study maps how those two systems meet, and shows that some meeting-point cells control turning when an odor is attractive.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly larvae have one brain area for inborn likes and dislikes and another for learned ones. This study maps how those two systems meet, and shows that some meeting-point cells control turning when an odor is attractive.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2021), Eschbach, Fushiki et al. reconstruct larval Drosophila circuits downstream of all mushroom-body output neurons and their contacts with lateral-horn neurons. They report 62 MB–LH convergence neurons per hemisphere and a 10-cell subtype with mixed positive excitation and negative inhibition. Two cells encode integrated odor value, suppress turning when activated, and increase turning when inactivated; aversive learning was verified to shift one cell toward inhibition.
summaries.advanced: Functional and behavioral tests cover two of 10 cells in one subtype, not all 62 convergence neurons. The claim that learning could modulate turning via E/I balance is partly speculative; only one neuron is shown to receive more inhibition after aversive learning. The map is larval, not adult. Optogenetic valence assignment of many MBONs is part of the study but is not a whole-brain connectome.

title: CONFIRMS: A Toolkit for Scalable, Black Box Connectome Assessment and Investigation
authors: Caitlyn Bishop; Jordan K. Matelsky; Miller Wilt; Joseph Downs; P. Rivlin; Stephen M. Plaza; Brock Andrew Wester; William R. Gray Roncal
journal: Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society

ocar.opportunity: Automated EM reconstructions now produce terabyte- and petabyte-scale wiring diagrams, so the community needs a way to judge whether a connectome product is accurate enough to reuse without redoing years of proofreading.
ocar.challenge: Segmentation, anisotropic alignment, and synapse classification all inject merge and split errors. Exhaustive human proofreading does not scale: MICrONS visual cortex and the Janelia Hemibrain already required many staff years. Graph reconstructions are becoming too large for exhaustive checking.
ocar.action: Bishop, Matelsky, Wilt, Downs, Rivlin, Plaza, Wester, and Gray-Roncal present CONFIRMS at EMBC (2021): a scalable toolkit that marries human-in-the-loop inquiry with large-scale graph analysis for black-box quality assessment, illustrated on a recent reference dataset. Forced-choice tasks support focused rather than exhaustive proofreading.
ocar.resolution: The toolkit is released to assess reconstruction quality via targeted inquiry and network-based measures, with source code at github.com/aplbrain/. The authors argue this workflow can characterize large connectomes more quickly for reuse.
ocar.future_work: They note that as graphs grow, exhaustive proofreading may become infeasible; future evaluators should keep pairing focused human checks with automated graph measures and community adoption of the toolkit.

plain_language_summary: Huge automated brain maps can hide tracing mistakes that ruin the wiring list. This paper offers free software to spot-check a finished map with people and with graph tests, instead of rechecking every cell.

summaries.beginner: Huge automated brain maps can hide tracing mistakes that ruin the wiring list. This paper offers free software to spot-check a finished map with people and with graph tests, instead of rechecking every cell.
summaries.intermediate: At the 2021 IEEE EMBC, Bishop et al. introduce CONFIRMS for scalable, black-box assessment of nanoscale connectomes. Motivated by staff-year proofreading on MICrONS and Hemibrain, they combine supervised forced-choice inquiry with automated graph analysis on a reference dataset. Code is public; the paper is a methods toolkit rather than a new reconstruction.
summaries.advanced: The reference dataset used for illustration is not named in the selected text. No numeric precision/recall or merge/split rates are reported here. Clinical-relevance language about disease is prospective. Quality measures still depend on some human input; exhaustive proofreading is explicitly treated as increasingly infeasible.

title: Neural architectures in the light of comparative connectomics
authors: E. Barsotti; A. Correia; Albert Cardona

ocar.opportunity: Whole-brain connectomics is becoming feasible for small representative species, which opens a comparative program: recover the archetypal neural architecture of each animal bauplan and detect circuits that converged independently onto a shared layout.
ocar.challenge: It is unknown how each species' connectome differs from close relatives versus whether distant lineages converged on an optimal architecture. Research has concentrated on mouse, fruit fly, C. elegans, and zebrafish, unlike earlier neuroscience that sampled many animals.
ocar.action: Barsotti, Correia, and Cardona review in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2021) how molecular, microscopy, storage, and computational advances lower barriers to whole-brain maps, and argue for comparative connectomics across relatively small species spanning the phylogenetic tree.
ocar.resolution: They conclude that comparing maps across representative species can identify fundamental circuit architecture per bauplan and any shared yet nonhomologous circuits from convergent evolution, now that technology makes broader sampling realistic.
ocar.future_work: The review's destination is exploratory comparative mapping across the tree of life, not another single-species flagship volume.

plain_language_summary: Most detailed wiring maps come from a handful of animals. This essay argues we should map more species so we can tell which circuit designs are ancient body-plan features and which evolved more than once.

summaries.beginner: Most detailed wiring maps come from a handful of animals. This essay argues we should map more species so we can tell which circuit designs are ancient body-plan features and which evolved more than once.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2021), Barsotti, Correia, and Cardona survey comparative connectomics. They note conservation of neuroblasts and pallial divisions across deep clades, and that current maps cluster on mouse, fly, nematode, and zebrafish, with additional work in Platynereis and Ciona. They argue small representative species can reveal archetypal bauplan circuits and convergent optima.
summaries.advanced: This is an opinion/review, not new data. 'Optimal' architecture is a hypothesis to test, not a demonstrated result. Existing-connectome coverage is cited at the level of species lists, not quantitative completeness. Catalog tags are infrastructure; the scientific claim is evolutionary comparison.

title: Three-Dimensional Structure of Dendritic Spines Revealed by Volume Electron Microscopy Techniques
authors: L. Parajuli; Masato Koike

ocar.opportunity: Quantitative 3D ultrastructure of synapses, especially dendritic spines, is the basis for estimating how strongly circuits transmit and for building accurate wiring diagrams. Volume EM now makes long dendritic reconstructions realistic.
ocar.challenge: Light microscopy cannot systematically resolve synaptic morphology. Serial-section TEM can, but reconstructing long dendrites by hand is extremely slow. Inhibitory (symmetric) synapses are harder to score than spine synapses because they lack prominent postsynaptic thickenings.
ocar.action: Parajuli and Koike review in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy (2021) volume-EM studies of three-dimensional synaptic ultrastructure, focusing on rodent dendritic-spine synapses: structural diversity, dendritic organization, presynaptic wiring, and activity-dependent remodeling. They also discuss correlative light-EM, including near-infrared branding as an alternative to immunoperoxidase labeling.
ocar.resolution: Automated EM tools are presented as having addressed low-throughput imaging enough to reconstruct dendritic segments in a realistic time frame. The review compiles principles of spine organization and remodeling from key 3D EM studies.
ocar.future_work: They call for sample-preparation protocols that visualize symmetric inhibitory synapses more clearly and for SEM resolution improvements to support large-scale 3D studies of inhibition.

plain_language_summary: Tiny bumps on brain-cell branches are where many connections sit, but their true 3D shape is only clear in electron-microscope stacks. This review gathers what those 3D pictures have shown about how the bumps are built and how they change with activity.

summaries.beginner: Tiny bumps on brain-cell branches are where many connections sit, but their true 3D shape is only clear in electron-microscope stacks. This review gathers what those 3D pictures have shown about how the bumps are built and how they change with activity.
summaries.intermediate: Parajuli and Koike in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy (2021) review volume EM of dendritic-spine synapses in rodent brain. They contrast slow serial-section TEM with automated volume EM, cover spine diversity, wiring, and activity-dependent remodeling, and discuss correlative two-photon plus EM, including near-infrared branding. Inhibitory shaft synapses are flagged as under-studied because they are harder to identify.
summaries.advanced: This is a review, not a new reconstruction. Throughput claims are qualitative ('appreciable degree', 'realistic time frame'). Focus is excitatory spine synapses; inhibitory volume-EM evidence is explicitly thinner. Organism is rodent in the review's emphasis, not a named registry volume.

title: VICE: Visual Identification and Correction of Neural Circuit Errors
authors: Felix Gonda; Xueying Wang; Johanna Beyer; Markus Hadwiger; J. Lichtman; H. Pfister

ocar.opportunity: Automatic EM segmentation and synapse prediction now make nanometer-scale neuron reconstructions possible, but large cells still need human proofreading. Focusing that effort on connectivity errors in a single cell's local circuit could finish usable graphs faster.
ocar.challenge: General proofreading inspects large volumes at pixel level and is visually intensive. Automatic segmentation struggles on large neurons. Users also need to understand evolving connectivity graphs, not only to paint voxels.
ocar.action: Gonda, Wang, Beyer, Hadwiger, Lichtman, and Pfister present VICE in Computer Graphics Forum / EuroVis (2021): an analytics framework with automated likely-error detection, synapse clustering, and interactive 3D views aimed at proofreading one cell's local circuit. They evaluate with a user study versus VAST++.
ocar.resolution: Participants found VICE more efficient for proofreading, understanding evolving graphs, and sharing correction strategies, and easier to learn than VAST++ (which required three separate tools). The authors conclude local-circuit proofreading plus automated likely-error detection reduces human effort, especially when many synapses are already known.
ocar.future_work: They release the application and note the approach works best when synapse detections are dense enough for bulk proofreading and automatic classification.

plain_language_summary: Computers that color neurons in electron-microscope stacks still glue or split big cells. This tool points people at likely wiring mistakes around one cell at a time, with 3D views, so they do not have to hunt through the whole volume pixel by pixel.

summaries.beginner: Computers that color neurons in electron-microscope stacks still glue or split big cells. This tool points people at likely wiring mistakes around one cell at a time, with 3D views, so they do not have to hunt through the whole volume pixel by pixel.
summaries.intermediate: Gonda et al. in Computer Graphics Forum (EuroVis 2021) introduce VICE for connectivity-focused proofreading of EM segmentations. The workflow uses automated likely-error detection and synapse clustering on a single cell's local circuit, demonstrated on Drosophila brain output circuitry. A user study reported efficiency and learnability advantages over VAST++. Software is at fegonda.github.io/vice.
summaries.advanced: User-study ratings are subjective; quantitative error-rate reductions versus VAST++ are not given in the selected text. The method assumes a high degree of known synapses. Single-cell local circuits reduce clutter but do not by themselves yield a complete volume connectome. Comparison baseline is VAST++, not all contemporary proofreading clients.

title: Accelerated EM Connectome Reconstruction using 3D Visualization and Segmentation Graphs
authors: Philip M. Hubbard; S. Berg; Ting Zhao; D. J. Olbris; L. Umayam; Jeremy B. Maitin-Shepard; Michał Januszewski; W. Katz; Erika Neace; Stephen M. Plaza

ocar.opportunity: Automatic EM segmentation and synapse prediction make connectivity reconstruction faster than tracing raw pixels, but large neurons still need human correction. Semi-automated 3D merge and split tools could keep reconstruction pace with much larger volumes.
ocar.challenge: Segmentation networks work well in narrow fields of view yet fail on large, complex arbors that need more context. Prior editors (NeuTu, webKnossos) often force scrolling through extensive imagery. Split operations on huge bodies can be slow.
ocar.action: Hubbard, Berg, Zhao, Olbris, Umayam, Maitin-Shepard, Januszewski, Katz, Neace, and Plaza on bioRxiv (2020) introduce Neu3 workflows: affinity-driven merging and cleaving (splitting along supervoxel boundaries), plus focused merging, emphasizing top-down 3D morphology. They measure split processing on 18 bodies from 89 thousand to 90 million voxels.
ocar.resolution: They report average split processing of about 1.4 million voxels per second and argue the tools enabled a connectome on an unpublished dataset of unprecedented scale. Because large false merges are easier to cleave, agglomeration can be tuned toward fewer false splits. Proofreaders often decide from 3D shape alone.
ocar.future_work: Wait times for multi-million-voxel bodies remain; the authors frame further protocol and agglomeration-parameter tuning as the production lesson.

plain_language_summary: After a computer paints neurons in a giant 3D brain picture, people still must glue pieces and cut wrongly joined blobs. This preprint describes a 3D editor that uses the computer's own confidence scores to speed those cuts and joins.

summaries.beginner: After a computer paints neurons in a giant 3D brain picture, people still must glue pieces and cut wrongly joined blobs. This preprint describes a 3D editor that uses the computer's own confidence scores to speed those cuts and joins.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2020), Hubbard et al. present Neu3: 3D visualization plus segmentation-graph operations (merge, cleave, focused merge) driven by affinity scores. Split timing on 18 bodies (89k–90 million voxels) averaged about 1.4 million voxels per second. They report the workflows supported a large unpublished FlyEM-scale connectome and encourage more aggressive agglomeration because large merges are cheaper to undo.
summaries.advanced: The production dataset is unpublished; 'unprecedented scale' is not quantified here. 'Superior performance compared to prior work' is not given as a named metric in the selected extract. Split speed is hardware- and implementation-specific. Catalog method tags include structured-loss affinity segmentation, consistent with affinity-driven edits but not a new affinity net in this paper.

title: DotMotif: an open-source tool for connectome subgraph isomorphism search and graph queries
authors: Jordan K. Matelsky; E. Reilly; Erik C. Johnson; J. Stiso; D. Bassett; Brock Andrew Wester; William Gray-Roncal

ocar.opportunity: Nanoscale connectomes are graphs too large to search by hand. A readable query language over graph databases would let neuroscientists find motifs and test hypotheses without becoming graph-theory specialists.
ocar.challenge: Converting imagery to graphs shrinks petabytes to megabytes or gigabytes but drops morphology. Even simple neighborhood questions are hard at this scale. Query runtime can explode with graph diameter, limiting how many questions a lab can ask.
ocar.action: Matelsky, Reilly, Johnson, Stiso, Bassett, Wester, and Gray-Roncal introduce DotMotif (bioRxiv 2020; catalog venue Scientific Reports): a neuroscience-oriented grammar over graph databases and analysis libraries for subgraph isomorphism and motif search, demonstrated on simulated graphs and public connectomes.
ocar.resolution: They show motif search on simulated and real public datasets, share example structures, and release DotMotif plus GrandIso and Grand at bossdb.org/tools/. The software is positioned to let scientists query nanoscale networks at scale.
ocar.future_work: Planned work includes automated query-cost validators, a public motif encyclopedia so expensive queries are run once and reused, and faster isomorphism engines.

plain_language_summary: A finished wiring diagram is a huge list of who talks to whom. This software lets scientists ask, in almost plain language, 'find me this little wiring pattern' across those giant lists.

summaries.beginner: A finished wiring diagram is a huge list of who talks to whom. This software lets scientists ask, in almost plain language, 'find me this little wiring pattern' across those giant lists.
summaries.intermediate: Matelsky et al. (bioRxiv 2020; Scientific Reports in this catalog) present DotMotif, combining graph databases with a neuroscience query grammar for subgraph isomorphism. They demonstrate motif searches on simulated data and public connectomes and release code at bossdb.org/tools/dotmotif (plus GrandIso and Grand). Conversion of EM imagery to graphs is framed as reducing terabytes or petabytes to much smaller networks at the cost of morphology.
summaries.advanced: Catalog journal is Scientific Reports while the extracted PDF is the bioRxiv version of the same title. No motif counts or runtime tables appear in the selected extract. Queries remain computationally sensitive to graph diameter. Motif hits are structural, not proof of function.

title: Light microscopy based approach for mapping connectivity with molecular specificity
authors: Fred Y. Shen; M. Harrington; Logan A. Walker; Hon Pong Jimmy Cheng; E. Boyden; Dawen Cai

ocar.opportunity: Electron microscopy resolves synapses unambiguously but usually loses the molecular labels that name cell types. A light-microscopy strategy that keeps molecular identity while still scoring putative synapses would let ordinary labs map defined circuits.
ocar.challenge: Synapses span hundreds of nanometers, so diffraction-limited light microscopy is not gold-standard connectivity. Dense tracing needs distinguishable arbors, multiplexed protein markers, and both nano- and microscale views. Small-caliber axons (for example some glutamatergic cells) are harder than the PV axons reconstructed here.
ocar.action: Shen, Harrington, Walker, Cheng, Boyden, and Cai in Nature Communications (2020) combine Brainbow with multi-round immunostaining expansion microscopy (miriEx), a strategy they call spectral connectomics, applied in mammalian brain sections including basolateral amygdala interneurons.
ocar.resolution: They reconstructed morphology and molecular subtype for 53 BLA interneurons in one section; traced 8 postsynaptic PV neurons, 189 innervating PV axons, and 422 PV–PV inhibitory synapses (~40 hours; 422 of about 60,000 inhibitory synapses in the dataset, ~0.7%). Correlative Brainbow plus PSD immunostaining mapped putative inhibitory and excitatory inputs onto aspiny interneurons.
ocar.future_work: They envision routine lab use on other Cre lines and synaptic proteins (transporters, receptors, gap junctions, ion channels); Brainbow titer, expression time, and imaging must be tailored per cell class.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopes see connections but often lose the name tags that say which cell type is which. These authors expand tissue and paint cells many colors so a light microscope can both name cells and guess where they touch.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopes see connections but often lose the name tags that say which cell type is which. These authors expand tissue and paint cells many colors so a light microscope can both name cells and guess where they touch.
summaries.intermediate: Shen et al. in Nature Communications (2020) introduce spectral connectomics: Brainbow plus miriEx expansion microscopy. In mammalian sections they link 53 BLA interneuron identities to morphology and score putative synapses via synaptic-protein stains. A PV–PV analysis comprises 8 postsynaptic cells, 189 axons, and 422 synapses. Putative synapses required membrane-targeted fluorescent proteins plus pre- and postsynaptic immunostaining.
summaries.advanced: Connections are putative, not EM-verified. The 422 PV–PV synapses are a molecularly targeted subset (~0.7% of inhibitory synapses in that dataset), not a dense connectome. Expansion and Brainbow parameters may not transfer to thinner glutamatergic axons. Catalog method tags include electron microscopy, but this paper is a light-microscopy alternative.

title: Toward a scalable framework for reproducible processing of volumetric, nanoscale neuroimaging datasets
authors: Erik C. Johnson; Miller Wilt; Luis M. Rodriguez; Raphael Norman-Tenazas; Corban Rivera; Nathan Drenkow; D. Kleissas; Theodore J. LaGrow; Hannah P. Cowley; Joseph Downs; Jordan K. Matelsky; Marisa J. Hughes; Elizabeth P. Reilly; Brock A. Wester; Eva L. Dyer; Konrad P. Kording; William R. Gray-Roncal

ocar.opportunity: EM, optical microscopy, and X-ray microtomography now generate gigabytes to petabytes of structural brain data. Shared, reproducible pipelines would let labs without local supercomputers still estimate synapse-level graphs or cell distributions.
ocar.challenge: Many neuroscience labs lack compute for this scale. Computer-vision tools are often not portable, and results are hard to reproduce or extend. General workflow engines are built for many small records, not few huge volumetric bricks.
ocar.action: Johnson, Wilt, Rodriguez, Norman-Tenazas, Rivera, Drenkow, Kleissas, LaGrow, Cowley, Downs, Matelsky, Hughes, Reilly, Wester, Dyer, Kording, and Gray-Roncal present in GigaScience (2020) an ecosystem (SABER) of containerized, standardized modules and end-to-end pipelines, with exemplars for EM synapse-level connectomes and X-ray microtomography cell maps, plus large-scale storage and workflow engines.
ocar.resolution: They argue that approaches can be standardized across neuroimaging experiments and applied to diverse datasets. SABER is compared with TOIL, CWL-Airflow, Galaxy, and Air-tasks, emphasizing volumetric blocks, containerized tools, and pipeline optimization.
ocar.future_work: Future work targets usability, GUIs, more reference pipelines, and integration with stores such as bossDB so storage, processing, and visualization share one ecosystem.

plain_language_summary: Brain pictures at synapse scale are so large that many labs cannot even run the analysis software. This paper packages those programs so they can be rerun the same way on big computers, with recipes for electron-microscope wiring maps and X-ray cell counts.

summaries.beginner: Brain pictures at synapse scale are so large that many labs cannot even run the analysis software. This paper packages those programs so they can be rerun the same way on big computers, with recipes for electron-microscope wiring maps and X-ray cell counts.
summaries.intermediate: In GigaScience (2020), Johnson et al. describe SABER, a containerized workflow framework for volumetric nanoscale neuroimaging. Exemplars estimate synapse-level connectomes from EM and cell distributions from X-ray microtomography. They position SABER against general scientific workflow managers that lack neuroimaging-specific volumetric deployment and optimization.

Cross-domain applicability outside neuroimaging is asserted, not demonstrated here. bossDB integration is planned rather than completed in the selected discussion.

title: Biologically-Constrained Graphs for Global Connectomics Reconstruction
authors: Brian Matejek; Daniel Haehn; Haidong Zhu; D. Wei; T. Parag; H. Pfister

ocar.opportunity: Connectome pipelines typically over-segment to avoid catastrophic merges, leaving many split errors for proofreaders. A third stage that uses neuron shape and global context could close remaining splits without creating new merges.
ocar.challenge: Affinity-plus-watershed and region-merging methods decide locally and ignore global consequences. A few merges can fuse several processes, so algorithms favor over-segmentation. Global graph optimization is computationally heavy if applied too early.
ocar.action: Matejek, Haehn, Zhu, Wei, Parag, and Pfister at CVPR (2019) extract a graph from an over-segmentation, prune nodes and edges with morphology-based geometric constraints and two neural nets that learn neuronal shapes, then partition the graph (lifted multicut) instead of greedy merging. They test on four real connectomics datasets.
ocar.resolution: They report an average variation-of-information improvement of 21.3% over input segmentations. Global optimization reduced VI-merge by 15.1% on average versus greedy merging (maximum 23.6% on PNI Test Two). Edge-CNN accuracies are 96.4%, 97.2%, and 93.4% on PNI and Kasthuri sets; recall of true split errors is about 80%.
ocar.future_work: The graph formulation is meant to accept other partitioners and future neuron-type constraints (for example forbidding excitatory–inhibitory merges). Code is pointed at rhoana.org/biologicalgraphs.

plain_language_summary: Computers tracing brain cells often cut one cell into many pieces to avoid gluing two cells together. This method looks at cell shape across the whole volume and decides which pieces to join, using rules inspired by how neurons actually look.

summaries.beginner: Computers tracing brain cells often cut one cell into many pieces to avoid gluing two cells together. This method looks at cell shape across the whole volume and decides which pieces to join, using rules inspired by how neurons actually look.
summaries.intermediate: Matejek et al. at CVPR (2019) add a biology-constrained graph-partitioning stage after standard over-segmentation. Geometric filters and two shape-learning nets shrink the graph; lifted multicut then agglomerates with global context. On four datasets they report 21.3% average VI improvement and 15.1% average VI-merge reduction versus a 95%-threshold greedy baseline.
summaries.advanced: VI numbers are dataset-specific (PNI, Kasthuri named in tables). Average 21.3% and per-dataset merge decreases should not be generalized to anisotropic serial-section pipelines not in the test set. Edge-CNN accuracy is not the same as final VI. The third stage assumes a reasonable over-segmentation already exists.

title: Enabling FIB-SEM Systems for Large Volume Connectomics and Cell Biology
authors: Shan Xu; Song Pang; K. Hayworth; H. Hess

ocar.opportunity: Isotropic FIB-SEM below 10 nm in x, y, and z traces fine neurites with little alignment burden, but conventional systems are too slow and too unreliable for connectomic volumes. Making FIB-SEM run for years would open large-volume isotropic imaging.
ocar.challenge: Standard FIB-SEM is unreliable beyond a few days and volume-capped. A fly central complex plus mushroom body needs about 250 × 250 × 250 µm³, beyond an 80 µm standard-resolution milling limit, so samples must be partitioned without losing traceable processes.
ocar.action: Xu, Pang, Hayworth, and Hess on bioRxiv (2019) describe enhanced FIB-SEM: expanding image volume more than four orders of magnitude from 10³ µm³ to 3 × 10⁷ µm³ at 8 × 8 × 8 nm³ voxels, optional 4 nm voxels, and years of continuous imaging. Hot-knife slabs (~20–25 µm) are imaged in parallel and stitched.
ocar.resolution: A male Drosophila VNC was cut into 25 slabs of 25 µm (220 × 200 × 600 µm³, ~2.6 × 10⁷ µm³) and imaged on six machines in about six months. A female hemi-brain of 250 × 250 × 250 µm³ (~1.6 × 10⁷ µm³) is described as containing ~25 × 10³ neurons and ~60 × 10⁶ synapses after segmentation. Estimated material loss between slabs is ~30 nm.
ocar.future_work: Maximum volume remains time-limited; hot-knife is described as incompatible with some heavy-metal stains and Durcupan, while PLT-LTS staining is noted to enable faster imaging. Mammalian volumes still exceed these fly examples.

plain_language_summary: A microscope that shaves tissue a few nanometers at a time makes beautiful 3D pictures but used to break down after days. This work keeps it running for months to years so much larger fly-brain pieces can be photographed at even detail in every direction.

summaries.beginner: A microscope that shaves tissue a few nanometers at a time makes beautiful 3D pictures but used to break down after days. This work keeps it running for months to years so much larger fly-brain pieces can be photographed at even detail in every direction.
summaries.intermediate: Xu et al. on bioRxiv (2019) enhance FIB-SEM for long, isotropic 8 nm (optionally 4 nm) imaging from 10³ to 3 × 10⁷ µm³. Hot-knife partitioning produced a Drosophila VNC (~2.6 × 10⁷ µm³, six machines, ~six months) and a hemi-brain (~1.6 × 10⁷ µm³). They argue high z-resolution aids automated tracing and cuts proofreading. Platforms are described as years-stable versus days for conventional FIB-SEM.
summaries.advanced: Neuron and synapse counts for the hemi-brain (~25,000 neurons, ~60 million synapses) refer to a segmented product, not proven in this methods preprint alone. Hot-knife adoption is limited by resin/stain compatibility as the authors state. 'Largest connectome in the world' is their 2019 framing. 4 nm mode trades speed for resolution.

title: A resource for the Drosophila antennal lobe provided by the connectome of glomerulus VA1v
authors: J. Horne; Carlie Langille; Sari McLin; Meagan Wiederman; Zhiyuan Lu; Zhiyuan Lu; C. Xu; Stephen M. Plaza; Louis K. Scheffer; H. Hess; I. Meinertzhagen; I. Meinertzhagen

ocar.opportunity: A complete synaptic inventory of one identified Drosophila antennal-lobe glomerulus, including local interneurons that had been hard to reconstruct, would be a template for the remaining glomeruli and for functional genetics of smell.
ocar.challenge: Local interneurons have dense multidirectional arbors that serial-section EM reconstructs poorly. Genetic screens of projection neurons may be unsaturated. Light-level candidate partners do not reliably equal synapses.
ocar.action: Horne, Langille, McLin, Wiederman, Lu, Xu, Plaza, Scheffer, Hess, and Meinertzhagen in eLife (2018) densely reconstruct all neurons in right-antennal-lobe glomerulus VA1v from FIB-SEM, including local interneurons, and publish a connectivity matrix.
ocar.resolution: They report more than 11,140 presynaptic sites and about 38,050 postsynaptic dendrites connecting 51 ipsilateral and 56 contralateral ORNs, 18 PNs, and 56 of more than 150 previously reported LNs. A matrix of 192 bodies with more than 50 connections accounts for 88% of the glomerulus's pre/postsynaptic sites. LNs are largely reciprocal and mixed pre/post except LN2V; PNs outnumber genetic-screen counts.
ocar.future_work: The resource is offered as proof of principle for the remaining ~50 glomeruli and as a heuristic for imaging, physiology, and computational models of insect olfaction.

plain_language_summary: One smell-processing bead in a fruit-fly antenna brain was mapped so every connection inside it is listed, including hard-to-trace local cells. The map is meant as a recipe for the rest of the smell center.

summaries.beginner: One smell-processing bead in a fruit-fly antenna brain was mapped so every connection inside it is listed, including hard-to-trace local cells. The map is meant as a recipe for the rest of the smell center.
summaries.intermediate: Horne et al. in eLife (2018) report a FIB-SEM dense connectome of Drosophila glomerulus VA1v: >11,140 presynaptic sites, ~38,050 postsynaptic dendrites, 51+56 ORNs, 18 PNs, and 56 LNs. 192 bodies with >50 connections hold 88% of sites. ORNs are mostly presynaptic, PNs mostly postsynaptic; most LNs are reciprocal except LN2V. FIB-SEM z-resolution is credited for reconstructing LN arbors.
summaries.advanced: This is one glomerulus of the right antennal lobe, not the full lobe. 'Entire synaptic connectome' is within VA1v as reconstructed. PN counts exceeding genetic screens imply those screens were unsaturated, not that extra PNs were missed by EM. Reciprocity highlights in the matrix use a ≥3-synapse-each-way rule.

title: Analyzing Image Segmentation for Connectomics
authors: Stephen M. Plaza; Jan Funke

ocar.opportunity: Automatic EM segmentation is the bottleneck for large connectomes, but challenge metrics (CREMI, SNEMI) on small ground-truth cubes often fail to predict whether a reconstruction preserves synapses and is usable at production scale.
ocar.challenge: Common scores ignore connectivity and can over-rate segmentations. Ground truth is scarce, so large-volume evaluation needs unsupervised clues. Edit-distance costs also depend on how proofreading is actually done.
ocar.action: Plaza and Funke in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2018) introduce connectivity-aware metrics (synapse connectivity and completeness), unsupervised cues (orphan-fragment percentage, self-loop concentrations from failures), and a scalable DVID/Spark software-and-visualization stack. They evaluate on two relatively large public ground-truth datasets.
ocar.resolution: Connectivity-based metrics indicate that fully automatic reconstructions still need substantial improvement, matching practical experience. They find data can be downsampled without large effects on important metrics, and that two segmentations can be compared without ground truth by inspecting the largest metric-driven differences.
ocar.future_work: They advocate more failure-mode metrics rather than a single champion score; choice of metric should follow the application (edit distance for proofreading cost, fragmentation for over-segmentation).

plain_language_summary: Scoreboards that grade computer tracings of brain pictures often ignore whether the wiring list is still right. This paper adds tests that ask whether connections survive, and software to run those tests on bigger volumes.

summaries.beginner: Scoreboards that grade computer tracings of brain pictures often ignore whether the wiring list is still right. This paper adds tests that ask whether connections survive, and software to run those tests on bigger volumes.
summaries.intermediate: Plaza and Funke in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2018) argue CREMI/SNEMI-style metrics miss downstream connectivity. They add synapse connectivity/completeness scores, orphan and self-loop measures usable without ground truth, and a scalable evaluation/visualization framework tested on two large public ground-truth sets. They conclude automatic segmentation is not yet sufficient for fully automatic reconstructions.
summaries.advanced: The paper is agnostic about a single best metric. Unsupervised orphan/self-loop measures can flag problems but are not a substitute for synapse-level truth. 'Two relatively large' ground-truth sets are not named in the selected extract. Downsampling invariance is stated qualitatively.

title: Convergence of monosynaptic and polysynaptic sensory paths onto common motor outputs in a Drosophila feeding connectome
authors: Anton Miroschnikow; P. Schlegel; Andreas Schoofs; Sebastian Hueckesfeld; Feng Li; C. Schneider-Mizell; R. Fetter; J. Truman; Albert Cardona; M. Pankratz

ocar.opportunity: Food intake and metabolic homeostasis depend on how many sensory paths are funneled onto shared motor, modulatory, and neuroendocrine outputs. A synaptic map of those paths in a whole larval CNS would show whether reflexes are simple one-hop circuits or stacked on longer routes.
ocar.challenge: How one path is selected among many possible outputs remains open. Nervous-system complexity usually forces partial maps. Feeding mixes enteric, pharyngeal, and external senses with motor, serotonergic, and endocrine effectors, plus a separate memory circuit.
ocar.action: Miroschnikow, Schlegel, Schoofs, Hueckesfeld, Li, Schneider-Mizell, Fetter, Truman, Cardona, and Pankratz in eLife (2018) reconstruct from a whole-CNS EM volume the synaptic map of Drosophila larval feeding-related input and output neurons.
ocar.resolution: Inputs converge on seven sensory synaptic compartments in the CNS (SEZ). Monosynaptic connections from a subset of compartments cover motor, modulatory, and neuroendocrine targets in overlapping domains (ACa, AVa, AVp). Polysynaptic routes overlay those reflexes; a different sensory set reaches mushroom-body calyx, with MB output neurons targeting interneurons that contact feeding outputs.
ocar.future_work: They interpret the architecture as an elemental feeding reflex plus superimposed control paths, a template for other instinctive behaviors.

plain_language_summary: A young fruit fly must eat using sensors in the gut, mouth, and skin that all talk to pumping muscles and hormone cells. This map shows some sensors plug straight into those outputs while other routes wander through extra cells, including a learning center.

summaries.beginner: A young fruit fly must eat using sensors in the gut, mouth, and skin that all talk to pumping muscles and hormone cells. This map shows some sensors plug straight into those outputs while other routes wander through extra cells, including a learning center.
summaries.intermediate: Miroschnikow et al. in eLife (2018) reconstruct a Drosophila larval feeding connectome from a whole-CNS EM volume. Seven SEZ sensory compartments receive enteric, pharyngeal, and external inputs. Overlapping monosynaptic domains target pharyngeal motor, serotonergic, and neuroendocrine neurons; polysynaptic paths and a distinct MB-calyx sensory set are superimposed. Most elemental-circuit sensors are enteric.
summaries.advanced: This is the feeding-related sensory–output map, not the entire larval connectome. 'Elemental circuit' is an interpretive label for irreducibly short connections. Small somatosensory monosynaptic paths to mouth-hook/head-tilt motor neurons mix feeding and locomotion. Functional path selection is inferred from anatomy.
