title: Petascale pipeline for precise alignment of images from serial section electron microscopy
authors: S. Popovych; T. Macrina; N. Kemnitz; M. Castro; Barak Nehoran; Z. Jia; J. Bae; E. Mitchell; S. Mu; Eric T. Trautman; S. Saalfeld; Kai Li; Sebastian Seung

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section EM reconstructions are accelerating via automatic segmentation, but that accuracy often stalls on the preceding alignment of 2D sections into a 3D stack—especially at petascale.
ocar.challenge: Artifacts, missing sections, and the cost of global optimization make precise, robust alignment of whole brains or cubic millimetres difficult.
ocar.action: Popovych, Macrina, Seung and colleagues present a pipeline: self-supervised convolutional nets trained by metric learning to encode and align pairs, iterative fine-tuning, vector voting against artifacts, block-wise distributed alignment, and composing transformations with decay instead of a global solve.
ocar.resolution: Applied to a whole fly brain (FAFB), the pipeline improved accuracy relative to prior state of the art and scaled to a cubic millimetre of mouse visual cortex (MICrONS). Two open-source Python packages (including metroem and Corgie) are released.
ocar.future_work: The work is a production alignment system; several authors disclose financial interests in Zetta AI LLC.

plain_language_summary: Before computers can color neurons in a stack of electron-microscope slices, those slices must be lined up. This paper’s software learns to align neighboring pictures, votes to ignore damaged patches, and stitches blocks of a whole fly brain—and a cubic millimetre of mouse cortex—without a slow whole-volume optimization.

summaries.beginner: Before computers can color neurons in a stack of electron-microscope slices, those slices must be lined up. This paper’s software learns to align neighboring pictures, votes to ignore damaged patches, and stitches blocks of a whole fly brain—and a cubic millimetre of mouse cortex—without a slow whole-volume optimization.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (2024; from a 2022 bioRxiv), Popovych and colleagues describe a petascale ssEM alignment pipeline. Self-supervised convnets initialize pairwise alignment; vector voting adds robustness to artifacts or missing data; the series is split into blocks for distributed workers; blocks are joined by composing transformations with decay. They report improved accuracy on FAFB relative to prior art and demonstrate scaling to MICrONS mouse visual cortex. Software is public (metroem, Corgie).
summaries.advanced: The selected extract does not quote a numeric alignment-error table versus named baselines. Author contributions assign FAFB coarse/fine alignment and mouse-cortex/MICrONS runs to specific coauthors. Competing interests: Seung, Kemnitz, Popovych, and Macrina disclose financial interests in Zetta AI LLC. Catalog metadata lists bioRxiv 2022; the PDF is the 2024 Nature Communications article (15:289).

title: Synaptic wiring motifs in posterior parietal cortex support decision-making
authors: Aaron T. Kuan; Giulio Bondanelli; Laura N. Driscoll; Julie Han; Minsu Kim; David Grant Colburn Hildebrand; Brett J. Graham; Logan A. Thomas; S. Panzeri; C. Harvey; W. Lee

ocar.opportunity: Posterior parietal cortex shows choice-selective activity during decision-making, but how that selectivity is implemented in synaptic wiring was unknown.
ocar.challenge: Without jointly measured activity and synapse-resolution connectivity in the same neurons, models with selective versus non-selective inhibition could not be distinguished.
ocar.action: Kuan, Bondanelli, Harvey, Lee, Panzeri and colleagues combine virtual-reality behavior, two-photon calcium imaging, high-throughput serial TEM, and circuit modeling in mouse PPC.
ocar.resolution: Excitatory pyramids preferentially target inhibitory interneurons of the same selectivity; those interneurons preferentially target pyramids of opposite selectivity, forming an opponent-inhibition motif that models show amplifies selective inputs and improves trial-type encoding.
ocar.future_work: They note a modest sample of functionally characterized neurons, missing synapses outside the volume, and caution that synapse-size versus strength correlations are best established for E-to-E connections.

plain_language_summary: When a mouse chooses left or right, some parietal neurons fire for one choice. This study lines up those recordings with an electron-microscope wiring map and finds a push–pull motif: cells that like the same choice excite local inhibitors, which then suppress the opposite-choice cells.

summaries.beginner: When a mouse chooses left or right, some parietal neurons fire for one choice. This study lines up those recordings with an electron-microscope wiring map and finds a push–pull motif: cells that like the same choice excite local inhibitors, which then suppress the opposite-choice cells.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2024), Kuan and colleagues analyze mouse PPC during a virtual-reality decision task with two-photon imaging followed by large-volume serial TEM of the same tissue. Excitatory-to-inhibitory connections are more frequent and larger among co-selective pairs; inhibitory-to-excitatory connections are more frequent onto anti-selective pyramids. Circuit models indicate that this opponent-inhibition motif amplifies selective inputs, induces competition between opposite-selectivity populations, and improves encoding of trial type.
summaries.advanced: Sample size of functionally characterized neurons and within-volume synapses is described as modest; arbors and synapses outside the EM block are missing. No difference in I-to-E synapse size between co- and anti-selective pairs was detected. Synapse-size interpretation is caveated because size–strength correlation in cortex has been directly measured mainly for E-to-E synapses. The motif is contrasted with reports of non-selective E-to-I connectivity in mouse V1. Catalog metadata lists 2022 bioRxiv; the PDF is Nature 627, 367–373 (2024). A GridTape-related patent/licensing disclosure involves Lee, Hildebrand, and Graham.

title: Bridging the Gap: Point Clouds for Merging Neurons in Connectomics
authors: Jules Berman; D. Chklovskii; Jingpeng Wu
journal: International Conference on Medical Imaging with Deep Learning

ocar.opportunity: Deep networks segment EM volumes well except where consecutive sections are missing, which splits neurons across the gap and creates a dedicated proofreading problem.
ocar.challenge: UNet data augmentation can hide a few lost slices, but large consecutive gaps leave fragment identity as a matching problem that voxel methods handle poorly and expensively.
ocar.action: Berman, Chklovskii, and Wu represent neuron fragments as point clouds and train CurveNet, a point-cloud classifier, to decide which fragments should be merged across the gap.
ocar.resolution: They report strong performance that scales to gaps larger than prior methods attempted, using far less data than voxel approaches would need, and they argue point clouds are a viable representation for other proofreading tasks.
ocar.future_work: They suggest extending the method to merged and split neurons throughout entire datasets.

plain_language_summary: When several electron-microscope slices in a row are unusable, automatic neuron coloring breaks into pieces above and below the hole. This paper turns those pieces into sparse 3D point clouds and trains a geometric network to guess which pieces belong to the same cell.

summaries.beginner: When several electron-microscope slices in a row are unusable, automatic neuron coloring breaks into pieces above and below the hole. This paper turns those pieces into sparse 3D point clouds and trains a geometric network to guess which pieces belong to the same cell.
summaries.intermediate: In a MIDL 2022 submission (arXiv 2021), Berman, Chklovskii, and Wu treat gap-crossing fragment agglomeration as point-cloud classification with CurveNet. Consecutive missing sections are a common ssEM defect; they argue point-cloud representations remain accurate with an amount of data that would be unfeasible for competing methods and scale to larger gaps than prior work attempted. Keywords frame the task as neuron-fragment agglomeration and deep geometric learning.
summaries.advanced: The selected extract does not report accuracy percentages, gap thicknesses in sections, or named baseline scores. ‘Scales reasonably to gaps well beyond what other methods have attempted’ is the authors’ qualitative claim. The paper is a conference/arXiv methods piece, not a deployed whole-dataset proofreader. Catalog venue is the International Conference on Medical Imaging with Deep Learning; uuid in the catalog is the work_id because no DOI is stored.

title: Desmosomal connectomics of all somatic muscles in an annelid larva
authors: S. Jasek; C. Verasztó; Emelie A. Brodrick; R. Shahidi; Tom Kazimiers; A. Kerbl; G. Jékely

ocar.opportunity: Animal tissues are networks of synaptic, chemical, and adhesive links; for muscles, desmosomes transmit force, but whole-body adhesive networks have not been mapped like neuronal connectomes.
ocar.challenge: It was unknown how hundreds of diverse muscles in an appendage-bearing larva attach to epithelia, glia, chaetae, and basal lamina, or how motoneuron synapses map onto that force network.
ocar.action: Jasek, Verasztó, Jékely and colleagues skeletonize 853 muscle cells and their desmosomal partners in a whole Platynereis larva volume-EM dataset and overlay motoneuron synapses.
ocar.resolution: They obtain a desmosomal connectome of over 2,000 cells; aciculae are highly connected hubs, matching their many degrees of freedom in video microscopy; motoneuron synapses let them infer tissue territories influenced by each motor class. The larva has 853 muscles of 53 types versus 95 similar body-wall muscles in C. elegans and 36 muscles of 10 types in Ciona tadpoles.
ocar.future_work: Together with the synaptic connectome from the same volume, they present the larva as a system for modeling crawling and parapodial motor control.

plain_language_summary: Muscles do not float; they glue to skin, bristles, and skeleton-like rods through tiny adhesive junctions. This team maps every such glue point in a whole marine-worm larva and shows that the internal bristle rods are the busiest attachment hubs, matching how freely those rods move on video.

summaries.beginner: Muscles do not float; they glue to skin, bristles, and skeleton-like rods through tiny adhesive junctions. This team maps every such glue point in a whole marine-worm larva and shows that the internal bristle rods are the busiest attachment hubs, matching how freely those rods move on video.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2021 bioRxiv preprint (October 2022 version), Jasek and colleagues reconstruct a whole-body desmosomal connectome in a Platynereis larva. Skeletonizing 853 muscle cells and partners yields a network of over 2,000 cells linking muscles to epithelial, glial, ciliated, and chaetal cells and basal lamina. Aciculae emerge as hubs, consistent with video-microscopy degrees of freedom. Mapping motoneuron synapses onto this adhesive graph infers the tissue domain each motoneuron can influence. Muscle diversity (53 types) is contrasted with C. elegans and Ciona.
summaries.advanced: ‘Connectome’ here means adhesive junctions, not chemical synapses, though motoneuron synapses are overlaid from the same volume (Verasztó et al. 2020). Stereotypy across segments is used to infer a specified connectivity code; that is an anatomical observation, not a developmental mechanism. Functional interpretations of attachments to ciliary cells are explicitly speculative. The selected extract does not quote synapse or desmosome counts beyond the cell totals (853 muscles; >2,000 cells; 53 types).

title: Methods for analyzing neuronal structure and activity in Caenorhabditis elegans.
authors: S. W. Emmons; Ev Yemini; Manuel Zimmer

ocar.opportunity: Caenorhabditis elegans has a stereotyped neuron complement, consistent synaptic wiring, and a transparent body, so structure, synapses, and activity can be studied in identified cells of a complete nervous system.
ocar.challenge: Neuron identification, electron-microscopic connectivity, fluorescent synapse labeling, and whole-nervous-system calcium imaging have each advanced, and workers need an up-to-date methods synthesis rather than scattered protocols.
ocar.action: In a WormBook chapter in Genetics (2021), Emmons, Yemini, and Zimmer review fluorescent neuron identification, recommended EM connectomic methods, fluorescent probes for single synapses and connections, and microscopy plus genetically encoded Ca2+ indicators for activity in single neurons across the nervous system.
ocar.resolution: They argue these methods now support new C. elegans connectomic work, verification of EM reconstructions, experimental approaches to synapse formation, and observation of activity within single neurons nervous-system-wide.
ocar.future_work: They caution that globally expressed GECIs in cell bodies can miss or distort neurite-restricted Ca2+ signals unless compartmentalization is independently validated, and they point readers to recommended analysis pipelines such as Kaplan et al. (2018).

plain_language_summary: The tiny worm C. elegans is see-through and has a simple, stereotyped set of nerve cells. This methods chapter explains how to name those cells with fluorescent tags, map their connections, and watch them fire with calcium sensors.

summaries.beginner: The tiny worm C. elegans is see-through and has a simple, stereotyped set of nerve cells. This methods chapter explains how to name those cells with fluorescent tags, map their connections, and watch them fire with calcium sensors.
summaries.intermediate: In Genetics (2021), Emmons, Yemini, and Zimmer survey methods for C. elegans nervous-system structure and activity. Transparency plus neuron-specific reporters allows identification in living animals; EM remains the gold standard for synaptic connectivity, now with more powerful techniques they recommend for new reconstructions. Fluorescent synapse probes verify EM maps and enable experiments on synapse formation, while Ca2+ imaging can report activity in single neurons across the entire nervous system. They also discuss limits of somatic GECI signals given thin neurites versus large cell-body volume.
summaries.advanced: This is a WormBook methods review, not a new connectome or activity atlas. The claim that activity can be observed across the entire nervous system describes capability opened by microscopy and GECIs, not a dataset released here. The selected extract warns against over-interpreting compartmentalized Ca2+ from globally expressed indicators without further validation (citing Liu et al. 2018b on AWA).

title: An anatomical substrate of credit assignment in reinforcement learning
authors: Joergen Kornfeld; Michał Januszewski; Philipp J Schubert; Viren Jain; W. Denk; M. Fee

ocar.opportunity: Credit assignment—deciding which of trillions of synapses to change after an outcome—is solved in machine learning by backpropagation, but biology lacks a plausible implementation of that algorithm.
ocar.challenge: A biologically workable alternative such as node perturbation needs circuit structures that inject exploratory variability, correlate it with reward, and assign credit locally; those structures had not been demonstrated anatomically in vertebrate basal ganglia.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv, Kornfeld, Wang, Januszewski, Fee, Denk and colleagues use automated connectomics on two volume-EM datasets of songbird Area X (j0126 and j0251, processed with SyConn2) plus a biophysical model. They test a node-perturbation-style reinforcement-learning architecture in which LMAN axons (exploratory variability) and HVC axons (song timing/context) should target different dendritic compartments of medium spiny neurons.
ocar.resolution: The predicted synaptic dichotomy holds: variability-encoding axons terminate predominantly on dendritic shafts, context-encoding axons predominantly on spines. The biophysical model built from the EM data suggests that this dichotomy facilitates efficient local credit assignment, which the authors present as strong evidence for a general basal-ganglia solution.
ocar.future_work: Code for the biophysical model is on GitHub; analysis code is promised upon final publication. The work is a preprint (this extract is the 27 October 2025 version of a 2020 posting) and does not claim that backpropagation is thereby ruled out in other circuits.

plain_language_summary: When a bird practices song, the brain must decide which tiny contacts to strengthen after a better or worse attempt. This study maps those contacts in a song-learning region and finds two kinds of incoming wires land on different parts of the same cells, which a model says could let learning happen locally.

summaries.beginner: When a bird practices song, the brain must decide which tiny contacts to strengthen after a better or worse attempt. This study maps those contacts in a song-learning region and finds two kinds of incoming wires land on different parts of the same cells, which a model says could let learning happen locally.
summaries.intermediate: In a bioRxiv preprint, Kornfeld, Wang, Januszewski, Rother, Schubert, Goldman, Jain, Denk, and Fee reconstruct songbird Area X with automated volume EM and SyConn2, then test a node-perturbation model of reinforcement learning. LMAN axons that encode exploratory vocal variability terminate mainly on dendritic shafts of medium spiny neurons, while HVC axons that encode song timing terminate mainly on spines. A biophysical model using those morphologies argues that the shaft/spine split supports efficient local credit assignment, an alternative to backpropagation. Datasets are public on SyConn Web as j0126 and j0251.
summaries.advanced: The anatomical claim is a predominance of shaft versus spine targeting, not a numeric percentage in the selected text. The biophysical model uses specified conductances (for example g_NMDA = 0.2 nS, g_LMAN_MSN = 30 nS) and a plasticity threshold; those are modeling choices. “Strong evidence for a general, biologically plausible credit assignment model in vertebrate basal ganglia” is the authors’ interpretation of one specialized song-learning nucleus. title: Molecular topography of an entire nervous system
authors: Seth R. Taylor; G. Santpere; Alexis Weinreb; Alec Barrett; Molly B. Reilly; Chuan Xu; E. Varol; P. Oikonomou; Lori Glenwinkel; Rebecca D. McWhirter; Abigail J. Poff; Manasa Basavaraju; Ibnul Rafi; Ev Yemini; Steven J. Cook; Alexander Abrams; Berta Vidal; Cyril C Cros; Saeed Tavazoie; N. Šestan; Marc Hammarlund; O. Hobert; David M. Miller

ocar.opportunity: A molecular model of a nervous system needs gene-expression maps at the same single-cell resolution as anatomy and wiring, which few animals can provide for every neuron.
ocar.challenge: Prior C. elegans profiling covered embryonic or early-larval stages only in part, and incomplete qualitative expression data had limited computational links from genes to the wiring diagram.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv (2020), Taylor, Santpere, Weinreb, Barrett, Reilly, Xu and colleagues (CeNGEN; Hammarlund, Hobert, Miller corresponding) produce expression profiles matching all 302 neurons of the mature C. elegans nervous system, with a thresholding approach for high-confidence per-type profiles, then computationally recover cis-regulatory motifs and adhesion-protein codes.
ocar.resolution: They report that neuron classes can be identified by combinatorial expression of specific gene families: each class expresses unique codes of about 23 neuropeptide-encoding genes and about 36 neuropeptide receptors, implying an expansive “wireless” network. Neuropeptide genes are among the most abundant detections, and even at the most stringent threshold each neuron expresses at least four neuropeptide-encoding genes. Data are at cengen.org and CengenApp.
ocar.future_work: They present the catalog as a foundation for experiments on gene regulation, process placement, and connectivity, including extending adhesion-code hypotheses to other gene families and neuron groups.

plain_language_summary: To understand how each worm nerve cell gets its identity, this team measured which genes are on in every one of the 302 neurons. The catalog shows each cell type has its own mix of chemical-messenger genes and points to DNA switches and sticky proteins that may help cells wire up.

summaries.beginner: To understand how each worm nerve cell gets its identity, this team measured which genes are on in every one of the 302 neurons. The catalog shows each cell type has its own mix of chemical-messenger genes and points to DNA switches and sticky proteins that may help cells wire up.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2020 bioRxiv preprint, Taylor and colleagues report what they describe as the first transcriptome of every neuron type in an entire nervous system, complementing earlier partial embryonic and larval C. elegans profiles. Combinatorial codes in gene families distinguish classes; neuropeptide and receptor combinations (~23 and ~36 genes per class) suggest widespread extrasynaptic signaling conserved with reports in Hydra, Drosophila, and mouse cortex. Computational analyses identify cis-regulatory elements and adhesion proteins with potential roles in synaptic specificity and process placement. Transcription-factor families show distinct nervous-system patterns (T-box underrepresented; zinc finger broad; homeodomains tracking identity; nuclear hormone receptors enriched in sensory neurons).
summaries.advanced: The ~23/~36 figures are class-level unique codes as stated, not proof that those peptides form functional synapses. “At least four” neuropeptide genes per neuron is at the most stringent threshold examined. Adhesion codes “likely contribute” to neuropil formation; they are computational hypotheses. This extract is the December 2020 preprint, not a later journal version.

title: Neuronal Subcompartment Classification and Merge Error Correction
authors: Hanyu Li; M. Januszewski; Viren Jain; Peter H. Li

ocar.opportunity: Large 3D EM reconstructions now contain thousands of neurons and millions of synapses, so automated morphological interpretation—including axon versus dendrite versus soma—is needed to read the connectome and to catch agglomeration mistakes.
ocar.challenge: Prior classifiers used hand-designed features plus organelles, or 2D projections in Cellular Morphology Networks, rather than the full 3D voxel neighborhood of a neurite.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv (2020), Li, Januszewski, Jain, and Li train 3D convolutional networks on voxels to label reconstructed fragments as axonal, dendritic, or somal, then use localized predictions to detect and correct inter-class merge errors, including soma-branch geometry sampled within the first 10 µm from the soma.
ocar.resolution: Mean F1 for subcompartment classification is 0.972, above a previous state of the art of 0.955. Combined branch and soma merge analyses detect 90.6% of inter-class merge errors at a 2.7% false-positive rate. Soma-near branch classification reaches F1 0.923 at slope 0.78.
ocar.future_work: They expect finer-grained labels (spine versus shaft versus AIS) and neuronal subtype identification, and they note that processing efficiency falls as field of view grows because the neurite occupies a shrinking voxel fraction—mitigable with sparse 3D representations.

plain_language_summary: Computers that glue bits of nerve cells together sometimes fuse an axon onto a dendrite by mistake. This method looks at the 3D shape of each bit, labels it as axon, dendrite, or cell body, and uses those labels to find and cut many of those bad fusions.

summaries.beginner: Computers that glue bits of nerve cells together sometimes fuse an axon onto a dendrite by mistake. This method looks at the 3D shape of each bit, labels it as axon, dendrite, or cell body, and uses those labels to find and cut many of those bad fusions.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2020 bioRxiv paper, Li, Januszewski, Jain, and Li introduce voxel-based 3D CNNs for axon/dendrite/soma classification of reconstructed neuron fragments, exceeding CMN-style 2D projection methods (mean F1 0.972 versus 0.955). Fine localization of those labels supports automated merge-error detection and correction: 90.6% of inter-class merges found at 2.7% false positives. Best soma-exit branch performance uses skeleton nodes in the first 10 µm from the soma. Training data and the EM volume were shared by Schubert and Kornfeld.
summaries.advanced: Metrics are for inter-class merges and the reported test setting, not all merge types. The 0.955 comparator is the previous CMN state of the art they cite, not a multi-challenge leaderboard. Efficiency versus field of view is an explicit limitation. Organism is not named in the abstract; the volume acknowledgment points at songbird EM used with CMN.

title: Joint Deformable Registration of Large EM Image Volumes: A Matrix Solver Approach
authors: K. Khairy; Gennady Denisov; S. Saalfeld

ocar.opportunity: Connectomic EM volumes are mosaics of thousands to millions of overlapping 2D tiles that must be registered into one coherent stack before segmentation or tracing.
ocar.challenge: Existing deformation solvers were inadequate for the largest volumes and inefficient even for small jobs, and a least-squares system without a usable regularization prior cannot be applied beyond trivial cases.
ocar.action: In an April 2018 arXiv paper, Khairy, Denisov, and Saalfeld formulate joint deformable registration as a linear system that minimizes feature-pair square distances with explicit constraints, constructing a rigid-model approximation as prior when none is available, then delegate the solve to standard linear-algebra packages (direct methods, including PaStiX for systems with more than one million tiles).
ocar.resolution: They jointly align 2.67 million images with more than 200 million point-pairs and report successful alignment of the first full adult fruit fly brain (FAFB). Direct solvers outperform iterative ones on time, residual error, and precision in their tests; a λ sweep on a 536-tile montage shows the deformation–prior tradeoff.
ocar.future_work: They present the matrix formulation as decoupling EM registration from solver engineering so future scalable linear solvers apply automatically; Matlab code estimates translation, rigid, affine, and polynomial (up to third degree) models.

plain_language_summary: A whole fly brain is photographed as millions of slightly overlapping snapshots that must be stitched and stacked without tearing the tissue digitally. This paper turns that puzzle into a large math problem a standard linear solver can handle, and uses it on the first complete adult fruit-fly brain volume.

summaries.beginner: A whole fly brain is photographed as millions of slightly overlapping snapshots that must be stitched and stacked without tearing the tissue digitally. This paper turns that puzzle into a large math problem a standard linear solver can handle, and uses it on the first complete adult fruit-fly brain volume.
summaries.intermediate: On arXiv (2018), Khairy, Denisov, and Saalfeld describe a matrix-based solver for montage, rough, and fine alignment of serial-section EM. The system combines point-match residuals with regularization; a rigid-model approximation supplies a prior. They apply it to 2.67 million images and more than 200 million point-pairs for FAFB. Intro scale context: imaging a ~500 µm fly brain at 4×4×40 nm³ with 10% tile overlap would generate about 21 million images. On a 32-CPU Broadwell node, direct methods beat iterative ones; PaStiX excelled above 1 million tiles.
summaries.advanced: “Successfully aligning the first full adult fruit fly brain” credits this solver’s use on FAFB; residual error tables are summarized qualitatively in the extract. Hardware timings are for their Matlab/PaStiX setup, not a multi-package bakeoff of all EM aligners. The ~21 million image figure is an illustrative whole-brain acquisition estimate from Zheng et al. 2017, not the 2.67 million they jointly solved.

title: Plasticity of the electrical connectome of C. elegans
authors: A. Bhattacharya; U. Aghayeva; Emily G. Berghoff; O. Hobert

ocar.opportunity: Electrical synapses help define how a nervous system processes information, but unlike chemical synapses they are hard to map in high-throughput EM, so an “electrical connectome” is missing for most animals.
ocar.challenge: Even in C. elegans only a single adult hermaphrodite chemical connectome had been fully reconstructed, which blocks nervous-system-wide views of how gap junctions change with environment or state.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv (2018), Bhattacharya, Aghayeva, Berghoff, and Hobert map genome-wide innexin expression across the nervous system, then track how those codes change in the dauer diapause, combine that with dauer locomotion and chemosensory assays, and dissect intersectional regulation by terminal selectors and FoxO.
ocar.resolution: Fourteen of 25 innexin genes are expressed in complex neuronal codes; 12 of those 14 change in a neuron-type-specific way in dauer, affecting 86 of 118 neuron classes, and non-neuronal inx-6 turns on in the dauer nervous system. ASK and RIM express up to 11 innexins; I6 expresses one. Remodeling of identified electrical synapses accounts for aspects of dauer locomotion and chemosensation; upregulation of inx-6 in AIB generates novel electrical connections.
ocar.future_work: They hypothesize that combinatorial innexin codes specify partners and synapse-specific conductance, including possible directionality. Full EM reconstruction of the dauer electrical connectome is noted as still needed to see partner gain and loss versus composition change at existing contacts.

plain_language_summary: Worms can change how their nerve cells are electrically coupled when they enter a hardy “dauer” state. This study maps which gap-junction proteins each neuron makes, shows those recipes change in most cell types in dauer, and links some of those changes to crawling and smell.

summaries.beginner: Worms can change how their nerve cells are electrically coupled when they enter a hardy “dauer” state. This study maps which gap-junction proteins each neuron makes, shows those recipes change in most cell types in dauer, and links some of those changes to crawling and smell.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2018 bioRxiv preprint, Bhattacharya, Aghayeva, Berghoff, and Hobert treat innexin expression as a proxy for the C. elegans electrical connectome. Fourteen innexins form combinatorial neuronal codes that are not static: dauer entry alters 12 of 14 neuronal innexins across 86 of 118 classes, with isoform-specific and on/off flips, plus inx-6 induction. An intersectional terminal-selector plus FoxO mechanism explains neuron-type- and environment-specific changes. Functional tests of individual electrical synapses tie remodeling to dauer locomotion and chemosensory behavior, including new AIB connections via inx-6.
summaries.advanced: Innexin expression is not the same as an EM gap-junction map; the authors emphasize EM’s difficulty detecting electrical synapses. Partner changes versus conductance changes at existing contacts are both possible and only partly resolved (inx-6 in AIB is a gain-of-connection example). Dauer is one environmental trajectory, not all plasticity. This is the 31 August 2018 preprint.

title: Robust neural circuit reconstruction from serial electron microscopy with convolutional recurrent networks
authors: Drew Linsley; Junkyung Kim; D. Berson; Thomas Serre

ocar.opportunity: Deep networks have been reported to segment neurons from serial EM at “super-human” accuracy, which could make connectomics usable far beyond the labs that collect each volume.
ocar.challenge: Those algorithms, the authors argue, do not generalize beyond the source and tissue they were trained on, so the broader neuroscience community still cannot apply them off the shelf.
ocar.action: On arXiv (2018, this extract v4 January 2020), Linsley, Kim, Berson, and Serre introduce the STAR challenge (source- and tissue-agnostic reconstruction of neurons), show that current state-of-the-art segmenters perform poorly on it, and propose fGRU, a convolutional recurrent module with short-range horizontal connections plus long-range top-down feedback that they contrast with hGRU’s strained horizontal dynamics.
ocar.resolution: fGRU establishes state of the art on STAR and is presented as a step toward widely usable, fully automated connectomics. The paper also cites a reported 250-fold reduction in processing time versus brute-force manual annotation for a 100³ µm³ volume from prior work, while arguing the field should shift from volume-specific fitting to cross-volume generalization.
ocar.future_work: They hope STAR and fGRU become building blocks for generalization-focused connectomic vision rather than dataset-specific leaderboard fitting.

plain_language_summary: Computer programs that outline nerve cells in electron-microscope pictures often work well only on the pictures they were trained on. This paper sets a harder test that mixes sources and tissues, shows leading methods stumble, and offers a new network that does better on that test.

summaries.beginner: Computer programs that outline nerve cells in electron-microscope pictures often work well only on the pictures they were trained on. This paper sets a harder test that mixes sources and tissues, shows leading methods stumble, and offers a new network that does better on that test.
summaries.intermediate: In an arXiv computer-vision paper, Linsley, Kim, Berson, and Serre argue that published super-human EM neuron segmentation does not transfer across imaging sources and tissues. They define STAR to favor generalization, document poor SOTA transfer, and introduce fGRU, which gates horizontal interactions with top-down feedback to suppress pathological dynamics seen in a single hGRU layer. fGRU is reported as STAR state of the art. The work is framed as shifting emphasis from fitting one volume to generalizing across volumes.
summaries.advanced: STAR results are the authors’ challenge, not a community bakeoff with independent organizers in this extract. The 250-fold speedup is cited from other work [18], not measured here. “Fully automated connectomics” is a stated direction, not a claim that proofreading is obsolete. No numeric STAR scores appear in the selected text.

title: Morphological Error Detection in 3D Segmentations
authors: D. Rolnick; Y. Meirovitch; T. Parag; H. Pfister; Viren Jain; J. Lichtman; E. Boyden; N. Shavit

ocar.opportunity: Automated EM segmentation must handle merge errors, which humans spot from overall neuronal shape even when local membrane classification looks fine.
ocar.challenge: Neurons sprout highly variable branches, so correct morphology cannot be catalogued, and merge errors take many forms; existing connectomics nets emphasize local boundary classification rather than high-level shape.
ocar.action: In a 2017 arXiv paper, Rolnick, Meirovitch, Parag, Pfister, Jain, Lichtman, Boyden, and Shavit introduce MergeNet: a 3D ConvNet trained without supervision to detect merge errors from morphology alone, ignoring the raw image at inference in the “zoom out” regime they describe, and they also test on merged MNIST digits.
ocar.resolution: MergeNet generalizes without retraining across connectomics datasets, can flag errors inside its own training set, and enables automatic comparison of segmentation methods and pipeline integration without extra annotation. It localizes merges (including some parallel-touch cases) but does not by itself correct them.
ocar.future_work: Exact automatic cuts would need the microscope image or membrane probabilities, because morphology often cannot say which continuation is which after a contact or how to split multi-object tangles. They sketch morphology-based typing and anomaly detection as longer-term uses.

plain_language_summary: When a computer accidentally glues two nerve cells into one, people can often see that the shape looks wrong. This network learns that kind of shape sense without extra hand labels and can flag glued cells in new datasets, though it cannot always cut them apart by itself.

summaries.beginner: When a computer accidentally glues two nerve cells into one, people can often see that the shape looks wrong. This network learns that kind of shape sense without extra hand labels and can flag glued cells in new datasets, though it cannot always cut them apart by itself.
summaries.intermediate: On arXiv (2017), Rolnick and colleagues show that 3D ConvNets can detect merge errors from neuronal morphology. MergeNet is trained unsupervised, operates across datasets without retraining, and is also demonstrated on a merged-MNIST control. The authors stress that merges, not only splits, are a central remaining barrier given millimeter-scale path lengths versus zettabyte-scale human-brain imaging estimates they cite. Failure modes include coincident branch points that resemble crosses and parallel processes without morphological clues at some boundary locations.
summaries.advanced: No numeric precision/recall on named EM volumes appears in the selected extract. The zettabyte human-brain figure is an estimate they cite [17], not a result. MergeNet detects and localizes; correction is explicitly out of scope. Unsupervised training does not mean the method needs no segmented objects—it uses existing segmentations without extra merge labels.

title: NeuroBlocks – Visual Tracking of Segmentation and Proofreading for Large Connectomics Projects
authors: Ali K. Al-Awami; Johanna Beyer; Daniel Haehn; N. Kasthuri; J. Lichtman; H. Pfister; Markus Hadwiger
journal: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics

ocar.opportunity: Nanometer-scale EM volumes used to reconstruct wiring diagrams are often hundreds of terabytes and must be segmented for cell boundaries, synapses, and organelles.
ocar.challenge: Segmentation of a single volume is complex, time-intensive, and spread across a diverse tool set and many users, which makes it hard to track state, progress, provenance, and accountability.
ocar.action: In IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (2016), Al-Awami, Beyer, Haehn, Kasthuri, Lichtman, Pfister, and Hadwiger present NeuroBlocks, a multi-user web application designed from a domain-task analysis to integrate manual and semi-automatic segmentation, proofreading, visualization, and analysis tools used in large connectomics projects.
ocar.resolution: They describe NeuroBlocks as the first system that integrates this heterogeneous tool set with support for management, provenance, accountability, and auditing of large-scale segmentations, and they demonstrate the design in two case studies with different user roles in a real-world project.
ocar.future_work: The paper is a visualization-system design study; broader adoption and quantitative throughput gains versus prior lab practice are left to those case studies and later use rather than a public benchmark in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: When many people edit a giant brain-map project with different computer programs, it is easy to lose track of what is done and who changed what. This paper describes a shared website that follows segmentation and proofreading progress across those tools.

summaries.beginner: When many people edit a giant brain-map project with different computer programs, it is easy to lose track of what is done and who changed what. This paper describes a shared website that follows segmentation and proofreading progress across those tools.

title: A resource from 3D electron microscopy of hippocampal neuropil for user training and tool development
authors: K. Harris; J. Špaček; Maria Elizabeth Bell; Patrick H. Parker; Laurence Lindsey; Alex Baden; J. Vogelstein; R. Burns

ocar.opportunity: Resurgent interest in synaptic circuitry and plasticity needs densely reconstructed hippocampal neuropil that can train people, constrain biophysical models, and test reconstruction algorithms.
ocar.challenge: Prior 3DEM of hippocampus had not provided densely reconstructed public volumes with all axons, dendrites, glia, and synapses, plus traces and software, at a resolution that also captures subcellular organelles.
ocar.action: In Scientific Data (2015), Harris, Spacek, Bell, Parker, Lindsey, Baden, Vogelstein, and Burns release three adult-rat CA1 neuropil volumes imaged at about 2 nm in X–Y on 50–60 nm serial sections, densely reconstructed in a cube (~10 µm³) around a large spine, a cylinder (~43 µm³) around a 3.4 µm oblique dendrite, and a parallelepiped (~178 µm³) around a 4.9 µm apical dendrite, hosted with Reconstruct files at the Open Connectome Project.
ocar.resolution: These are presented as the first densely reconstructed hippocampal volumes, with quantified synapses from varying section planes and reconstructions of microtubules, polyribosomes, SER, and endosomes in a subset of dendrites, intended as ultrastructural standards, modeling geometry, and a segmentation test bed.
ocar.future_work: They flag extracellular-space underestimation from oblique membranes and chemical fixation, alignment scaling of about 10–15% on average in Reconstruct for the apical and oblique volumes, and they hope the data seed machine-learning detection of rare objects such as the spine apparatus and studies of learning and disease.

plain_language_summary: This paper shares three tiny but complete 3D electron-microscope maps of rat hippocampus, with every axon, dendrite, glial bit, and synapse traced. Students and computer programs can use them as a practice set for reading brain ultrastructure.

summaries.beginner: This paper shares three tiny but complete 3D electron-microscope maps of rat hippocampus, with every axon, dendrite, glial bit, and synapse traced. Students and computer programs can use them as a practice set for reading brain ultrastructure.
summaries.intermediate: In Scientific Data (2015), Harris and colleagues publish three densely reconstructed adult-rat CA1 volumes at ~2 nm X–Y and ~50–60 nm section thickness: ~10, ~43, and ~178 µm³ around a large spine, an oblique dendrite, and an apical dendrite. Images, traces, and Reconstruct software are freely available via the Open Connectome Project. Alignment in Reconstruct required on average ~10–15% overall scaling for the apical and oblique volumes, concentrated away from the densely reconstructed centers.

ECS measurements are qualified by oblique-section occlusion and fixation/dehydration effects versus cryo-EM. Scaling artifacts are largest at image edges; dense reconstructions were kept near center. Organism is Rattus norvegicus hippocampal formation.

title: The Open Connectome Project Data Cluster: Scalable Analysis and Vision for High-Throughput Neuroscience
authors: R. Burns; N. Kasthuri; M. Kazhdan; Stephen J. Smith; D. Kleissas; E. Perlman; Kwanghun Chung; Nicholas C Weiler; J. Lichtman; Alex Szalay; Joshua T. Vogelstein; Kunal Lillaney; R. J. title: Highly Nonrandom Features of Synaptic Connectivity in Local Cortical Circuits
authors: Sen Song; P. J. Sjöström; Markus Reigl; S. Nelson; D. Chklovskii

ocar.opportunity: Cortical function depends on synaptic wiring diagrams, but a full EM reconstruction of a cortical column was then impossible, so connectivity has to be described statistically from sampled recordings.
ocar.challenge: Pair recordings had shown sparse, often bidirectional-overrepresented connectivity and broad strength distributions, yet motifs beyond two neurons, the shape of the strength distribution, and correlations among strengths sharing a cell were open.
ocar.action: In PLoS Biology (2005), Song, Sjöström, Reigl, Nelson, and Chklovskii analyze several hundred simultaneous quadruple whole-cell recordings from layer 5 pyramidal neurons in rat visual cortex, counting two- and three-neuron motifs and measuring peak EPSP amplitudes.
ocar.resolution: Bidirectional connections are overrepresented versus random; several clustered three-neuron patterns are overrepresented. Connection strengths differ from Poisson and fit a lognormal, concentrating weight in a heavy tail; strengths sharing pre- or postsynaptic neurons are correlated, so strong connections cluster even more. They summarize the local network as a skeleton of stronger connections in a sea of weaker ones.
ocar.future_work: They argue that skeleton is likely important for network dynamics and should be investigated further; existing data were still insufficient for scale-free or small-world tests they discuss in the introduction.

plain_language_summary: Are local brain circuits just random spaghetti, or do they have a hidden pattern? Recordings from groups of rat visual-cortex cells show extra two-way links, extra triangles, and a few very strong contacts that tend to hang together—more like a sturdy skeleton than a uniform mesh.

summaries.beginner: Are local brain circuits just random spaghetti, or do they have a hidden pattern? Recordings from groups of rat visual-cortex cells show extra two-way links, extra triangles, and a few very strong contacts that tend to hang together—more like a sturdy skeleton than a uniform mesh.

title: FEABAS: A Stitching and Alignment Tool for Serial EM Data
authors: Yuelong Wu; J. Lichtman

title: Long-range axon branching: contributions to brain network plasticity and repair
authors: L. J. Richards; Cheng Huang; A. Bauer; Jin-Moo Lee

title: Synapse Detection Efficiency in EM Drosophila Connectomics
authors: Louis K. Scheffer

ocar.opportunity: Different Drosophila EM reconstructions of similar circuitry report different synapse counts, which matters for comparing connectomes across labs and techniques.
ocar.challenge: Sample size, software detectors, proofreading, sex, age, and imaging modality (ssTEM versus FIB-SEM) are confounded; raw counts cannot be compared naively.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv (2025), Scheffer estimates human-visible synapse numbers from raw detections in FANC, MANC, FAFB (original and FAFB2), male CNS, BANC, hemibrain, and smaller optic-lobe volumes, compensating where possible for volume and detector efficiency, then compares overlapping compartments pairwise.
ocar.resolution: In almost all known cases reconstructed by both techniques, isotropic FIB-SEM volumes show more human-visible synapses than microtome-sliced ssTEM, typically by more than 40%. He interprets this as strong but not conclusive evidence that synapses are easier to see in isotropic FIB-SEM.
ocar.future_work: If anisotropy is the issue, better human ground truth and possibly machine detection of subtle cues (by analogy to neurotransmitter prediction) are suggested. Tables of path-strength reporting (for example ≥5-synapse “strong” paths) illustrate how count differences propagate into graph statistics.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly wiring maps from different microscopes do not agree on how many synapses they see. This comparison finds that 3D ion-beam microscopes usually show over 40% more human-visible synapses than sliced transmission-EM volumes of matching regions.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly wiring maps from different microscopes do not agree on how many synapses they see. This comparison finds that 3D ion-beam microscopes usually show over 40% more human-visible synapses than sliced transmission-EM volumes of matching regions.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2025 bioRxiv preprint, Louis Scheffer compares synapse detection across major Drosophila reconstructions (1C, 7C, FIB19, hemibrain, FANC, FAFB/FAFB2, MANC, male CNS, BANC, and others). Analyses use raw synapse counts to avoid proofreading dependence and attempt to correct for sample size and software efficiency, estimating synapses a skilled human would see. Pairwise comparison of overlapping regions finds FIB-SEM typically exceeding ssTEM by more than 40% in human-visible synapses. The conclusion is carefully hedged: strongly suggestive, not proven.
summaries.advanced: “Typically by more than 40%” is the headline comparison, not a single universal factor. Confounds of genotype, age, and true biological variation remain. FAFB2 is a new synapse set on ssTEM, not a new volume. Table 8 in the extract reports odds that paths of given biological strength are called strong (≥5 synapses) across BANC, FAFB, hemibrain, CNS, and MANC—those percentages are graph-threshold statistics, not the 40% imaging result.

title: Cell nuclei segmentation in mm-scale x-ray holographic nanotomography images of mouse brain tissue
authors: Andrea Nathansen; Matthis Clausen; Manuel Berning; E. MacKenzie; Yuxin Zhang; A. Pacureanu; Andreas T. Schaefer; Norman Rzepka; Carles Bosch

ocar.opportunity: X-ray holographic nanotomography can resolve subcellular detail across ~mm³ landscapes of intact tissue and is compatible with follow-up volume EM, offering cell-density and spatial-distribution maps that histology needs for circuit and tissue mechanics.
ocar.challenge: Manual annotation of nuclei in terabyte-scale ~mm³ volumes is unrealistic; classifiers must generalize across biological replicates with little extra ground truth and support multi-user proofreading.
ocar.action: In SPIE Optical Engineering + Applications (2024), Nathansen, Clausen, Berning, Bosch, Rzepka and colleagues train an automated nuclei segmenter for mouse-brain XNH, run it on HPC, and export a data table plus browser-explorable segmentations and meshes (WEBKNOSSOS) for collaborative proofreading.
ocar.resolution: The classifier reports spatial locations and morphologies of about 80,000 nuclei per dataset with high recall, generalizes to similar replicate datasets with minimal added ground truth, and is positioned for automated histological pipelines in systems neuroscience and broader tissue biology. Meshes larger than 10× mean nuclear volume were treated as conversion artefacts and masked.
ocar.future_work: Code and training data are on GitHub (cboschp/segVolData). Conflicts: several authors are at scalable minds, which sells related software. Broader tissue types beyond mouse brain XNH are a stated use, not the training domain.

plain_language_summary: A new X-ray microscope can photograph a cubic millimetre of mouse brain in enough detail to see cell nuclei, but there are tens of thousands of them. This paper trains a computer to find those nuclei and puts the results in a browser so people can check the work.

title: Comprehensive analysis of the C. elegans connectome reveals novel circuits and functions of previously unstudied neurons
authors: Scott W. Emmons

ocar.opportunity: Updated chemical and gap-junction connectomes of both adult C. elegans sexes now cover the whole animal including muscle and other end organs, so neuron functions and overall architecture can be read from connectivity rather than from the classic partial diagrams alone.
ocar.challenge: Despite decades of anatomy, circuits for behavior remain incomplete and many neuron classes still have unknown function; modular structure and the role of muscle as both sink and sensory source were under-emphasized.
ocar.action: In PLoS Biology (2024), Emmons applies modularity analysis and degree-based inspection to these whole-animal connectomes to partition communities, highlight end-organ convergence/feedback, and propose functions for previously unstudied neurons.
ocar.resolution: Ten communities map onto broad behavioral categories. Body-wall muscle is both a major convergence site and, via a body-wide mechanosensory field onto DVA and PVR, a feedback source; most interneurons have similar in- and out-degree, dispersing information as much as they aggregate it. Newly emphasized features include high-degree gap-junction interneurons in the ventral cord and hub-and-spoke cells such as RIG and RMG.
ocar.future_work: The paper is offered as a guide for theory and for experiments on individual classes and circuits, not as a substitute for those experiments.

plain_language_summary: The worm’s complete wiring list has been updated to include muscles and both sexes, but many cells still had no known job. This analysis splits the network into ten behavior-related groups and points to overlooked cells—including two that collect touch from the whole body.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s complete wiring list has been updated to include muscles and both sexes, but many cells still had no known job. This analysis splits the network into ten behavior-related groups and points to overlooked cells—including two that collect touch from the whole body.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Biology (2024), Scott Emmons analyzes recently completed hermaphrodite and male C. elegans chemical and gap-junction connectomes including end organs. Modularity yields 10 communities correlated with behavioral categories. Muscle is both a hierarchical sink and, through a body-wide mechanosensory field onto DVA and PVR, a source of feedback. Multisensory integration is distributed: interneurons typically have matched in- and out-degree. Newly emphasized features include ventral-cord high-degree gap-junction interneurons and hub-and-spoke cells RIG and RMG. Several pathways involve previously unstudied neurons.

DVA/PVR as a body-wide field is an anatomical claim from convergence patterns. Analysis uses previously published connectome tables (author’s and others’); no new EM is reported. Sex differences are in the data but the abstract emphasizes shared architectural themes.

title: Mapping of Multiple Neurotransmitter Receptor Subtypes and Distinct Protein Complexes to the Connectome
authors: Piero Sanfilippo; Alexander J. Kim; Anuradha Bhukel; Juyoun Yoo; Pegah S. Mirshahidi; V. Pandey; Harry Bevir; Ashley Yuen; Parmis S. Mirshahidi; Peiyi Guo; Hong-Sheng Li; James A. Wohlschlegel; Yoshinori Aso; S. Zipursky

ocar.opportunity: Neurons mix receptor subtypes and receive mixed transmitters, so a connectome of partners is incomplete without knowing which neurotransmitter receptors sit at which identified synapses.
ocar.challenge: Localizing endogenous receptor subunits to specific inputs in single cells has been difficult without destroying native expression timing or lacking EM-identified partners.
ocar.action: In Neuron (2024), Sanfilippo, Kim, Bhukel, Aso, Zipursky and colleagues conditionally epitope-tag endogenous Drosophila neurotransmitter-receptor subunits, image them with expansion light-sheet microscopy, match synapses to EM connectomes, and immunopurify associated proteins, focusing on direction-selective T4/T5 motion-sensitive neurons.
ocar.resolution: Different receptor subunits occupy a stereotyped molecular topography aligned with cell-type-specific input domains, and developmental observations suggest receptors or receptor–membrane-protein complexes help determine input patterns. They identify a transmembrane protein restricted to a subset of spatially confined synapses and show genetically that it is required for synapse formation. They propose receptor spatial distribution as molecular cartography for dendritic connection patterns.
ocar.future_work: Tagged receptors are offered as a resource for localization, assembly, and plasticity studies. Concordance with EM is receptor-dependent (GluClα matches well; Rdl and nAChR subunits vary, possibly extrasynaptic or trafficking pools). Tagging other receptor classes will need structure-guided insertion sites.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram says who talks to whom, but not which molecular “mailbox” sits at each contact. This fly study tags native transmitter receptors, looks at them in super-resolution, and shows that different mailboxes sit in different neighborhoods on motion-detecting cells.

Requirement of the identified transmembrane protein is genetic evidence for a subset of synapses, not all inputs. Catalog method lists light-sheet; EM is used for partner identity. This is fly visual motion circuitry, not a brain-wide receptor atlas.

title: Neuropeptide signaling network of Caenorhabditis elegans: from structure to behavior
authors: Jan Watteyne; A. Chudinova; Lidia Ripoll-Sánchez; William R. Schafer; Isabel Beets

ocar.opportunity: Neuropeptides are abundant, diverse modulators of physiology and behavior; C. elegans, with a compact nervous system and a mapped synaptic connectome, is a prototype for organism-wide peptide networks.
ocar.challenge: Organization of peptide–receptor pathways, circuit motifs, and the spatial/temporal range of extrasynaptic transmission needed a synthesis spanning conservation, expression, ligand–receptor maps, and in vivo function.
ocar.action: In a Genetics (2024) WormBook-style review, Watteyne, Chudinova, Ripoll-Sánchez, Schafer, and Beets survey evolutionary conservation, molecular expression, receptor–ligand pairing, and system-wide architecture of C. elegans neuropeptide signaling, plus motifs and timescales from in vivo studies.
ocar.resolution: They describe an extensive extrasynaptic network whose structure differs from synaptic and monoamine graphs, with combinatorial convergent, antagonistic, feedforward, and feedback peptide actions spanning seconds (NLP-40 on DVB/defecation) to minutes (PDF-1 versus serotonin roaming/dwelling) to hours (FLP-1 pathogen avoidance). Whole-brain imaging (Randi et al. 2023) indicates extrasynaptic signaling also shapes short-timescale dynamics. They position the worm peptidergic connectome as a prototype for other species.
ocar.future_work: How coexpression fingerprints translate into addressed communication in pervasive peptide networks remains open, as does transferring motifs to vertebrates even though broad peptide/receptor coexpression is already reported there.

plain_language_summary: Besides wired synapses, worm neurons broadcast many small peptides that change behavior over seconds to hours. This review maps that chemical network and explains the repeating circuit tricks—push, pull, loops—that peptides use.

summaries.beginner: Besides wired synapses, worm neurons broadcast many small peptides that change behavior over seconds to hours. This review maps that chemical network and explains the repeating circuit tricks—push, pull, loops—that peptides use.

Functional-connectivity imaging suggests broad short-timescale extrasynaptic impact. The worm is offered as a prototype while peptide mapping proceeds in other animals.

title: Systematic annotation of a complete adult male Drosophila nerve cord connectome reveals principles of functional organisation
authors: E. Marin; Billy J. Morris; T. Stürner; A. Champion; D. Krzemiński; Griffin Badalamente; Marina Gkantia; Christopher R. Dunne; K. Eichler; Shin-ya Takemura; Imaan F. M. ocar.opportunity: A complete adult male Drosophila ventral-nerve-cord connectome (MANC; companion Takemura et al., 2023) is the first synaptic-resolution nerve cord of an animal that walks and flies, but it is unusable without systematic names linking cells to the experimental literature.
ocar.challenge: A century of VNC work focused on accessible neurons, leaving most interneurons a black box; hemilineage studies helped, but a full inventory, serial homology, sensory modalities, and programmatic types were missing.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv (2024 posting of a 2023 manuscript), Marin, Morris, Stürner, Jefferis and colleagues apply hierarchical annotations, group neurons across midline and segments, define systematic types for sensory, intrinsic, ascending, and non-motor efferent neurons, assign hemilineages and neurotransmitters, and release annotations in neuPrint and Clio.
ocar.resolution: They classify 13,060 VNC intrinsics, 185 ascending, 1,328 descending, 737 motor, about 100 other efferent, and nearly 6,500 sensory neurons, assigning hemilineages to 88% of VNC neurons (97% of thoracic-origin cells). Over 35% of intrinsic, ascending, and non-motor efferent neurons match across segments, and sensory modality is assigned to over 5,000 sensory neurons, revealing serial types and a layered organization likely matching the periphery. Larval-born neurons in a hemilineage usually share a transmitter, though earlier-born neurons often differ; the annotations underpin descending-input and motor-output analyses in a companion paper (Cheong et al., 2023).
ocar.future_work: They did not match every published light-level type; experts must still bridge most cells to images. Serial homology covers over a third of non-descending, non-sensory neurons, not all. Primary-neuron counts slightly exceed some larval estimates, pending a complete larval VNC tabulation.

plain_language_summary: A complete wiring diagram of a male fruit-fly nerve cord is only useful if every cell has a name and a job description. This companion paper labels tens of thousands of neurons, matches many of them across body segments, and posts the phone book next to the map.

title: Brain wiring determinants uncovered by integrating connectomes and transcriptomes.
authors: Juyoun Yoo; Mark Dombrovski; Parmis S. Mirshahidi; Aljoscha Nern; S. LoCascio; S. Zipursky; Y. Kurmangaliyev

ocar.opportunity: Synapse-level connectomes show that developing neurons contact many cell types yet synapse with only a subset. Pairing those maps with cell-type transcriptomes and cell-adhesion-molecule binding tables could identify receptor–ligand pairs that match synaptic partners.
ocar.challenge: Many CAM families contribute to wiring, but it has been hard to name receptor–ligand pairs that directly match neurons to their synaptic targets amid circuit complexity.
ocar.action: Yoo, Dombrovski, Zipursky, Kurmangaliyev and colleagues, in Current Biology (2023), integrate a Drosophila visual-system synapse-level connectome with developmental CAM expression and binding specificities, focusing on genetically related T4/T5 subtypes that choose alternative targets in adjacent neuropil layers.
ocar.resolution: Layer choice correlates with matching Beat and Side family receptor–ligand pairs on synaptic partners. Genetic analysis shows that presynaptic Side-II and postsynaptic Beat-VI restrict partners to the same layer; removing the pair disrupts layers and causes inappropriate targeting of presynaptic sites and postsynaptic dendrites.
ocar.future_work: The authors propose that different Side/Beat pairs collaborate with other recognition molecules, and that combining transcriptomes, connectomes, and protein interactomes can identify wiring determinants more generally.

title: Chemical cognition: chemoconnectomics and convergent evolution of integrative systems in animals
authors: Leonid L. Moroz; D. Y. Romanova

ocar.opportunity: Neurons underpin animal cognition, but the evolutionary and mechanistic roots of even elementary cognition remain unclear. Independent origins of neural and neuroid systems, plus a chemical connectome of volume transmission, offer comparative experiments that synaptic wiring diagrams alone do not.
ocar.challenge: How neurons originated, and how ensembles generate stereotyped and learned behavior, is unknown. Dynamic chemical micro-environments and cell-specific volume transmission are poorly measured, so links from chemistry to behavior are missing.
ocar.action: Moroz and Romanova, in Animal Cognition (2023), review evidence that neural and other integrative systems evolved more than once among basal metazoans, and they introduce chemoconnectomics as the study of hundreds of signal molecules operating in tandem with classical synapses.
ocar.resolution: They highlight ctenophore nervous systems and neuroid-like systems in placozoans and sponges as independent experiments. They argue that roughly 20 classical transmitters plus 100+ peptides and hundreds of receptors expand information capacity, with nitric oxide as a shared non-synaptic integrator across basal metazoans and choanoflagellates, and that ctenophores use a largely different transmitter set than cnidarians and bilaterians.
ocar.future_work: They call for new tools linking orchestrated volume transmission to behavior, and for studying early-branching lineages as alternative integrative systems to decipher chemical syntaxes of cognition.

plain_language_summary: Animal thinking is often treated as a product of wired nerve cells, but much signaling is chemical and may have evolved more than once. This review argues we should map those chemical conversations, especially in comb jellies, placozoans, and sponges.

summaries.beginner: Animal thinking is often treated as a product of wired nerve cells, but much signaling is chemical and may have evolved more than once. This review argues we should map those chemical conversations, especially in comb jellies, placozoans, and sponges.
summaries.intermediate: In Animal Cognition (2023), Moroz and Romanova argue that integrative systems evolved convergently among basal metazoans and that a chemical connectome of volume transmission is the most information-rich source of adaptability. They cite ctenophore neurons versus neuroid systems in placozoans and sponges, and they tally molecular diversity on the order of ~20 classical transmitters, 100+ peptides, and usually several hundred receptors. They frame chemoconnectomics plus cellular behavior in early-branching lineages as a foundation for studying elementary cognition.
summaries.advanced: This is a conceptual review, not a new connectome. Counts of transmitters and peptides are order-of-magnitude statements in the conclusion, not a census of one species. Cognition is used broadly (including non-neural examples such as bacteria and Physarum). Catalog stage is infrastructure; there is no EM reconstruction here.

title: msemalign: a pipeline for serial section multibeam scanning electron microscopy volume alignment
authors: Paul V Watkins; Eric Jelli; K. Briggman

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section multibeam SEM can collect cubic-millimeter-scale neural volumes at synaptic resolution, creating petabyte datasets that can become connectomes. Those volumes exist only after hundreds of millions of image tiles are aligned into a 3D stack.
ocar.challenge: A cubic-millimeter mSEM dataset comprises hundreds of millions of tiles (each 15.5 × 13.5 μm² in the authors’ Zeiss multiSEM setup). Alignment must keep navigation smooth in all directions while minimizing section distortions relative to the original micrographs, including missing sections and thickness variation.
ocar.action: Watkins, Jelli, and Briggman introduce msemalign in Frontiers in Neuroscience (2023): a scalable, relatively simple pipeline for ssmSEM volume alignment, used with customized sectioning and parallel multiSEM acquisition aimed at petabyte-scale datasets.
ocar.resolution: They report that the pipeline can align petabyte-scale data with smooth transitions while limiting overall section distortion versus the acquired micrographs. Contrast correction uses histogram matching to a template rather than CLAHE-style equalization, to avoid flattening real tissue differences such as soma versus neuropil.
ocar.future_work: They suggest richer multi-algorithm keypoint matching for missing sections and multiple template histograms for long z-stacks as practical enhancements.

plain_language_summary: Giant electron-microscope brain volumes are photographed as millions of tiny overlapping tiles that must be stitched into a smooth 3D picture. This paper describes software built to do that stitching at huge scale without warping the original photos more than necessary.

summaries.beginner: Giant electron-microscope brain volumes are photographed as millions of tiny overlapping tiles that must be stitched into a smooth 3D picture. This paper describes software built to do that stitching at huge scale without warping the original photos more than necessary.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroscience (2023), Watkins, Jelli, and Briggman present msemalign for serial-section multibeam SEM alignment. They target ~1 mm³ or larger synaptic-resolution volumes whose acquisition yields hundreds of millions of tiles. Design goals are scalability, simple architecture, smooth 3D navigation, and minimal distortion relative to original micrographs, with template histogram matching to preserve tissue appearance.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods paper; the selected text does not report a completed connectome or numeric alignment-error tables. Tile size 15.5 × 13.5 μm² is specific to their multiSEM configuration. Catalog tags include mouse and DS13 MICrONS, but the paper is a general ssmSEM alignment pipeline rather than a MICrONS data release. Distortion minimization is qualitative in the abstract.

title: Identifying Inputs to Visual Projection Neurons in Drosophila Lobula by Analyzing Connectomic Data
authors: Ryosuke Tanaka (田中涼介); Damon A. Clark

ocar.opportunity: EM connectomes have clarified fly visual computations, but the lobula—thought to detect object-like features and drive behaviors via LC and LPLC outputs—still lacked a map of columnar inputs onto those outputs.
ocar.challenge: Available dense reconstructions often omit upstream visual neuropils that would normally identify lobula inputs, leaving fragmented axon terminals that are hard to type.
ocar.action: Tanaka and Clark, in eNeuro (2022), cluster fragmented lobula terminals in the hemibrain connectome by connectivity and morphology, then match clusters to previously described cell types.
ocar.resolution: They extract 40 clusters with homogeneous connectivity and morphology and morphologically match 24, with highest confidence for T3 (clusters 1–4), T2 (5), TmY29 and/or Tm28 (10), Tm20 (17), Tm9 (30), and TmY11 (35). Other assignments (including TmY5a as cluster 40) are more speculative. They report previously undocumented input–output connectivity usable as hypotheses for feature detection.
ocar.future_work: They state that more complete reconstructions are required to verify the map, and they point to molecular tracing (GRASP, trans-Tango, optogenetics) as complementary tests.

plain_language_summary: A part of the fruit-fly visual brain is thought to spot objects such as other flies, but many of its incoming wires were unnamed fragments. This study groups those fragments by shape and connections and proposes which known cell types they are.

summaries.beginner: A part of the fruit-fly visual brain is thought to spot objects such as other flies, but many of its incoming wires were unnamed fragments. This study groups those fragments by shape and connections and proposes which known cell types they are.
summaries.intermediate: In eNeuro (2022), Tanaka and Clark cluster columnar inputs to Drosophila lobula in the hemibrain EM volume despite missing upstream neuropils. Among 40 clusters, 24 receive morphological matches of varying confidence, with strongest IDs for T3, T2, TmY29/Tm28, Tm20, Tm9, and TmY11. They report previously undocumented synapses onto lobula output neurons (LC/LPLC and related types) as a basis for physiological hypotheses.
summaries.advanced: The hemibrain largely lacks medulla and lobula plate, so input identities are inferred from terminal morphology and local connectivity, not from complete cells. Many type assignments are explicitly speculative. Per-cell synapse counts onto named outputs (e.g., cluster 40 onto LC10 at 4.3 synapses/cell) are cluster means, not circuit proofs. Catalog has no named dataset tag; the volume is hemibrain.

title: A connectome is not enough - what is still needed to understand the brain of Drosophila?
authors: Louis K. Scheffer; I. Meinertzhagen

ocar.opportunity: Drosophila melanogaster offers a near-term path to understanding a whole brain: roughly 200,000 neurons, rich behavior, and many experimental tools. An EM-level list of neurons and chemical synapses is expected within a few years.
ocar.challenge: A wiring diagram alone will not explain how the brain operates. The field still needs to specify what additional data must be collected and organized to build an integrated model.
ocar.action: Scheffer and Meinertzhagen, in Journal of Experimental Biology (2021), itemize the measurements they argue are still required—beyond the coming connectome—to understand structure and operation of the fly brain.
ocar.resolution: The essay is a requirements list for an integrated model rather than a new dataset: it treats the connectome as necessary but not sufficient and enumerates missing physiological, molecular, and behavioral ingredients.
ocar.future_work: Collating and organizing those additional data types is presented as the work still needed once the connectome exists.

plain_language_summary: A complete wiring diagram of a fruit-fly brain is nearly in hand, but wires alone do not explain behavior. This essay asks what else—activity, chemistry, and experiments—still has to be measured to understand that brain.

summaries.beginner: A complete wiring diagram of a fruit-fly brain is nearly in hand, but wires alone do not explain behavior. This essay asks what else—activity, chemistry, and experiments—still has to be measured to understand that brain.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Experimental Biology (2021), Scheffer and Meinertzhagen argue that Drosophila, with on the order of 200,000 neurons, is an enticing whole-brain target. They take an imminent EM connectome of neurons and chemical synapses as given and catalog further data needed for an integrated model of how the brain works.
summaries.advanced: The attached PDF extract is a different paper (Pugliese et al. on a walking CPG); this annotation follows the catalog abstract only. This is a perspective, not new reconstructions. The ~200,000-neuron figure is the authors’ order of magnitude. Chemical synapses are the stated connectome contents; electrical synapses and neuromodulation are among the implied gaps.

title: Circuit motifs and graph properties of connectome development in C. elegans
authors: Jordan K. Matelsky; Raphael Norman-Tenazas; Felicia Davenport; E. Reilly; William Gray-Roncal

ocar.opportunity: Complete C. elegans connectomes now exist at multiple ages, so graph and motif tools can summarize how a whole wiring diagram changes through development instead of inspecting every neuron by hand.
ocar.challenge: Synapse-resolution datasets are already too large to proofread neuron by neuron. The task is to find which network patterns are stable, which grow, and which decay unexpectedly across time points.
ocar.action: Matelsky, Gray-Roncal and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2021), apply graph-analysis and motif-atlas scans (via DotMotif) to C. elegans connectomes at multiple developmental stages, comparing undirected subgraphs of six or fewer neurons.
ocar.resolution: They report changing local structure: the most rapidly growing undirected motif is 353 times more frequent in Dataset 8 than in Dataset 1, whereas triangles and the triangular-prism net grow only about 9.24× and 9.33×. They present these stable and shifting invariants as a substrate for further analysis.
ocar.future_work: Software (dotmotif, grand) is shared; they frame the nematode as a preview of comparative graph analysis in flies, mice, and humans.

plain_language_summary: As a worm grows, its wiring diagram changes in patterned ways. This preprint counts small repeating circuit shapes across ages and shows that some shapes explode in number while others barely keep pace.

summaries.beginner: As a worm grows, its wiring diagram changes in patterned ways. This preprint counts small repeating circuit shapes across ages and shows that some shapes explode in number while others barely keep pace.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2021), Matelsky et al. compare C. elegans connectomes across developmental time points with graph metrics and an undirected motif atlas. Relative to the earliest dataset, one six-or-fewer-neuron motif increases 353-fold by Dataset 8, while triangles and a triangular-prism motif increase only ~9-fold. Tools are released at github.com/aplbrain/dotmotif and grand.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint. Motif fold-changes are ratios to Dataset 1, not absolute synapse counts, and depend on the Witvliet-style multi-age reconstructions cited as (4,5). Analyses are undirected in the highlighted atlas scan. Catalog dataset is DS01 C. elegans (White+).

title: Postnatal connectomic development of inhibition in mouse barrel cortex
authors: Anjali Gour; K. Boergens; Natalie Heike; Yunfeng Hua; Philip Laserstein; Kun Song; M. Helmstaedter

ocar.opportunity: High-throughput 3D electron microscopy now lets the same cortical volume type be mapped at many postnatal ages, so inhibitory circuit formation can be quantified synapse by synapse rather than inferred from single snapshots.
ocar.challenge: A comprehensive map of how cortical inhibitory axons acquire preferences for cell bodies, apical dendrites, and axon initial segments during postnatal development was missing.
ocar.action: Gour, Helmstaedter and colleagues, in Science (2020), analyze 13 three-dimensional EM datasets from mouse somatosensory cortex layers 4 and 2/3 at postnatal days 5, 7, 9, 14, 28, and 56, reconstructing inhibitory innervation of those compartments.
ocar.resolution: Apical-dendrite preference is already near adult levels at P5. Soma-targeting axons acquire specificity mainly between P7 and P9, with cell-body preference increasing almost threefold and synapse density along those axons dropping almost twofold, consistent with removal of off-target synapses. Chandelier axo-axonic preference is first clear by P14 and nearly complete by P28, reaching about 50% of axon-initial-segment synaptic input, with cartridges forming after preference begins.
ocar.future_work: They present connectomic screening across ages as a template for later genetic or environmental perturbations of circuit formation.

plain_language_summary: Inhibitory brain cells must learn which parts of other cells to contact as a mouse grows. Electron-microscope maps at many ages show that some targeting is present from the start, while other targeting is sculpted by removing misplaced contacts.

summaries.beginner: Inhibitory brain cells must learn which parts of other cells to contact as a mouse grows. Electron-microscope maps at many ages show that some targeting is present from the start, while other targeting is sculpted by removing misplaced contacts.
summaries.intermediate: In Science (2020), Gour et al. map inhibitory synaptogenesis in mouse somatosensory cortex with 13 3D EM volumes spanning P5–P56 (focus on the first four postnatal weeks). Apical-dendrite preference is early; soma preference rises sharply from P5 to P9 with synaptic overabundance then removal; chandelier AIS preference develops from P14 to P28. The work is framed as developmental connectomic screening of barrel-related cortex.
summaries.advanced: The attached PDF extract is a different paper (Zhang et al. 2026 ssEM inpainting); this annotation follows the catalog abstract only. Time points include P56 as adult comparison. “Almost threefold” and “almost twofold” are abstract phrasing, not exact ratios. Dataset tag DS12 L4 barrel cortex matches the somatosensory focus; L2/3 is also imaged.
