title: Synaptic architecture of leg and wing premotor control networks in Drosophila
authors: Ellen Lesser; Anthony W. Azevedo; Jasper S. Phelps; L. Elabbady; Andrew P. Cook; Durafshan Sakeena Syed; Brandon Mark; Sumiya Kuroda; Anne Sustar; Anthony J. Moussa; Chris J. Dallmann; S. Agrawal; Su-Yee J. Lee; B. Pratt; K. Skutt-Kakaria; Stephan Gerhard; R. Lu; N. Kemnitz; Kisuk Lee; Akhilesh Halageri; M. Castro; Dodam Ih; Jay Gager; M. Tammam; S. Dorkenwald; F. Collman; C. Schneider-Mizell; D. Brittain; C. Jordan; T. Macrina; Michael H. Dickinson; Wei-Chung Allen Lee; John C. Tuthill

ocar.opportunity: Motor neurons activate muscles, but premotor networks let the same muscles contribute to many behaviors; comparing those networks for different effectors in one animal can reveal shared wiring logic versus biomechanical specializations.
ocar.challenge: It was unknown whether Drosophila leg and wing motor neurons are organized into modules by shared premotor input, and whether synaptic weights onto motor neurons follow size-based hierarchical recruitment as in some vertebrate motor pools.
ocar.action: Lesser, Azevedo, Phelps, and a large consortium use the FANC ventral-nerve-cord connectome to analyze premotor circuits of the Drosophila leg and wing (Nature, 2024), with proofreading in CAVE and community reconstruction.
ocar.resolution: Both premotor networks cluster into modules linking motor neurons of related muscle function. In most leg modules, premotor synaptic weights scale with target motor-neuron size, a circuit basis for hierarchical recruitment. Wing premotor networks lack that proportional connectivity, which may allow more flexible recruitment of steering muscles. A typical fly motor neuron receives thousands of synapses from hundreds of premotor neurons. Most premotor cells prefer one module despite mixed dendritic locations and despite shared developmental lineages.
ocar.future_work: Quantifying how premotor connectivity varies across individual flies is highlighted as the way to test how hard-wired these patterns are. A parallel male VNC reconstruction is cited as showing roughly similar patterns. Some wing steering modules yield new predictions for three-dimensional wing-hinge mechanics.

plain_language_summary: Flies walk and fly with different muscles, but both are driven by networks that sit just upstream of motor neurons. This connectome study finds those networks come in modules, with a size-based recruitment ladder in the leg that the wing steering system does not copy.

summaries.beginner: Flies walk and fly with different muscles, but both are driven by networks that sit just upstream of motor neurons. This connectome study finds those networks come in modules, with a size-based recruitment ladder in the leg that the wing steering system does not copy.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2024), Lesser, Azevedo, Tuthill, Lee, and colleagues compare Drosophila leg and wing premotor connectivity in the female adult nerve cord (FANC). Motor neurons cluster into modules defined by shared premotor partners; leg modules often show synaptic weights proportional to motor-neuron size, whereas wing steering modules do not. Integration scale is compared to other species (on a par with rodent cortical pyramidal cells, an order of magnitude above larval zebrafish motor neurons, about ten times fewer synapses than cat motor neurons). Module preference is not explained by developmental lineage or simple spatial segregation of dendrites.
summaries.advanced: Reconstruction and analysis focus on a single female; male similarity is cited from a parallel project rather than proven identical here. Synapse counts are from a proofread EM segmentation and inherit its thresholds. “Flexible recruitment” of wing muscles is an inference from the lack of size-proportional weights, not a behavioral demonstration in this paper. Some steering-module function predictions (for example module B: i1, i2, b3 decreasing ipsilateral stroke amplitude) rest on prior recordings from a subset of those neurons.

title: Synaptic promiscuity in brain development
authors: Neele Wolterhoff; P. Hiesinger

ocar.opportunity: Precise adult synaptic connectivity is required for circuit function, yet neurons removed from their developmental context readily form unspecific synapses, including autapses, which poses a puzzle for how genomes encode wiring.
ocar.challenge: Most experiments perturb development genetically and score connectivity only in adults, so they cannot tell whether a defect happened before, at, or after the moment of partner choice. The pool of available partners and the degree of promiscuity at that moment are often unknown.
ocar.action: Wolterhoff and Hiesinger review the evidence for promiscuous synapse formation in Current Biology (2024), organizing development into pre-specification (before synapse formation), the moment of choice, and post-specification (stabilization or pruning).
ocar.resolution: They argue that specificity is an outcome of an algorithmic process: neurons capable of promiscuous synaptogenesis are continuously prevented from wrong choices, with no single mechanism or time point sufficient. Promiscuity can be required for plasticity, robustness, and evolutionary adaptation. Many “specificity” genes actually restrict partner availability before synapses form; competency, interaction dynamics, and molecular recognition further restrict choice; later pruning can correct initially exuberant synapses.
ocar.future_work: They speculate that promiscuous synapse formation may be an ancestral state, and that selection on mutations at any pre- to post-specification level enabled more complicated architectures. They caution that specificity studies should not treat adult connectivity as a direct readout of the moment of choice.

plain_language_summary: Brain cells can plug into the wrong partners if you take them out of context, yet adult brains are wired precisely. This review says messy, overlapping synapse formation during growth is often a feature: later steps and earlier positioning keep the wrong connections from lasting.

summaries.beginner: Brain cells can plug into the wrong partners if you take them out of context, yet adult brains are wired precisely. This review says messy, overlapping synapse formation during growth is often a feature: later steps and earlier positioning keep the wrong connections from lasting.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Biology (2024), Wolterhoff and Hiesinger review synaptic promiscuity as a developmental process distinct from adult specificity. They split wiring into growth before synapses, partner choice, and later strengthening or removal, noting feedback among these stages. Experimental designs that assay only adults after genetic perturbation often reveal pre-specification (partner availability) rather than lock-and-key choice. Promiscuity plus continuous restriction is offered as an algorithmic account of precise outcomes, supporting plasticity and robustness.
summaries.advanced: This is a conceptual review, not a new connectomic dataset. Generality claims (“some observations seem to hold with considerable generality”) are argumentative. The authors explicitly did not use AI for text or figures. Competing “chemoaffinity versus Peters’ rule” debates are reframed rather than experimentally decided. Readers should not treat promiscuity as proven to be ancestral; that is labeled speculation.

title: A leaky integrate-and-fire computational model based on the connectome of the entire adult Drosophila brain reveals insights into sensorimotor processing
authors: Philip K. Shiu; Gabriella R. Sterne; N. Spiller; R. Franconville; Andrea Sandoval; Joie Zhou; Neha Simha; C. Kang; Seongbong Yu; Jinseop S. Kim; S. Dorkenwald; Arie Matsliah; P. Schlegel; Szi-chieh Yu; Claire E. McKellar; A. Sterling; Marta Costa; K. Eichler; G. Jefferis; M. Murthy; A. S. Bates; N. Eckstein; Jan Funke; Salil S. Bidaye; Stefanie Hampel; A. Seeds; Kristin Scott

ocar.opportunity: The adult Drosophila central brain connectome—over 125,000 neurons and 50 million synapses—offers a template for asking how sensory signals become actions across an entire brain.
ocar.challenge: Connectivity lists paths, not whether those paths transform taste or touch into motor output. Building a whole-brain dynamical model requires neurotransmitter signs and synaptic weights, most of which are predicted or standardized rather than measured cell by cell.
ocar.action: Shiu, Sterne, Scott, and a large consortium build a leaky integrate-and-fire model of the entire fly brain from FlyWire connectivity and predicted neurotransmitter identity, with a single free synaptic-weight parameter, and they test feeding and grooming circuit predictions with optogenetics, calcium imaging, and behavior (bioRxiv, 2023).
ocar.resolution: Activating sugar- or water-sensing gustatory neurons in the model predicts taste-responsive cells required for feeding initiation. Predicted feeding-region neurons that drive motor-neuron firing are validated optogenetically. Sugar and water are predicted to share a partial appetitive pathway, confirmed by imaging and behavior. Mechanosensory activation predicts a small antennal-grooming set that does not overlap gustatory circuits. Across 164 empirically tested predictions, 91% were consistent (84% after excluding split-GAL4 experiments in which most types did not elicit MN9 activation).
ocar.future_work: The authors suggest that more complete transmitter and receptor information and more morphological realism may improve future models, and they conclude that a simple model can describe complete sensorimotor transformations at the complexity of the whole Drosophila brain.

plain_language_summary: If you know who is connected to whom in a fly brain, can you guess how tasting sugar leads to eating? This team builds a simple whole-brain spiking model from the wiring diagram, then checks many of its guesses with real fly experiments and reports that most of them hold.

summaries.beginner: If you know who is connected to whom in a fly brain, can you guess how tasting sugar leads to eating? This team builds a simple whole-brain spiking model from the wiring diagram, then checks many of its guesses with real fly experiments and reports that most of them hold.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2023), Shiu and colleagues implement a leaky integrate-and-fire whole-brain model using FlyWire synapse counts and predicted transmitters. Membrane parameters are taken from prior Drosophila modeling (for example V_resting = −52 mV, V_threshold = −45 mV); the sole free parameter W_syn = 0.275 mV is set so 100 Hz sugar GRN drive yields about 80% of maximal MN9 firing. The model is applied to gustatory feeding initiation and antennal grooming, with optogenetic and imaging tests. Reported empirical consistency is 91% of 164 predictions (84% in a restricted subset).
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint of a whole-brain model, not a claim that all FlyWire transmitters are ground truth. W_syn is globally shared, so cell-type differences in synaptic strength are not represented. Accuracy percentages mix many negative “does not activate MN9” results with positive circuit predictions. Morphology is collapsed to point neurons. Overlap of sugar and water pathways is a model prediction confirmed in the authors’ assays, not a unique circuit proof against other formulations. Later published versions may differ in numbers; these figures are from the 2 May 2023 preprint text.

title: Diversity of visual inputs to Kenyon cells of the Drosophila mushroom body
authors: Ishani Ganguly; Emily L. Heckman; Ashok Litwin-Kumar; E. Josephine Clowney; Rudy Behnia

ocar.opportunity: The mushroom body is a classic expansion layer for olfaction, but 8% of Drosophila Kenyon cells receive predominantly visual input, and their tuning and function are poorly understood.
ocar.challenge: Prior work identified a few visual routes into Kenyon cells, yet a systematic inventory of visual projection neurons and local visual interneurons, and whether individual visual Kenyon cells sample those channels randomly, was lacking.
ocar.action: Ganguly, Heckman, Litwin-Kumar, Clowney, and Behnia use the FlyWire adult whole-brain connectome to identify inputs to visual Kenyon cells (Nature Communications, 2024).
ocar.resolution: Input types are similar across hemispheres and connectomes, with certain inputs highly overrepresented. Many visual projection neurons presynaptic to Kenyon cells sample large swathes of visual space, while local visual interneurons provide smaller, more spatially restricted, possibly feature-tuned input. Individual visual Kenyon cells receive sparse combinations from multiple optic-lobe neuropils, consistent with random sampling of available inputs. Expansion-coding properties differ from olfaction because a specific visual repertoire projects onto a relatively small Kenyon-cell population.
ocar.future_work: The authors conclude that visual mushroom-body coding is sparse, distributed, and combinatorial like olfaction, but more constrained by a limited input menu and a smaller intrinsic population.

plain_language_summary: Most of the fly’s learning center cells smell the world; a minority mostly see it. Mapping who talks to those visual cells shows they mix a small set of visual channels at random, more like a constrained code than the huge combinatorial smell code.

summaries.beginner: Most of the fly’s learning center cells smell the world; a minority mostly see it. Mapping who talks to those visual cells shows they mix a small set of visual channels at random, more like a constrained code than the huge combinatorial smell code.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (2024), Ganguly and colleagues catalog synaptic inputs to visual Kenyon cells in FlyWire. Repertoires match across hemispheres and connectomes, with overrepresented types. Wide-field visual projection neurons dominate some input, while local visual interneurons contribute spatially restricted signals. Sparse, combinatorial, apparently random sampling across optic-lobe neuropils is reported, contrasting with olfactory expansion because fewer visual Kenyon cells (8% of the population) receive a specific input set. Cell classes discussed include KCαβ-p innervating the dorsal accessory calyx and previously described VPN-MB and aMe pathways.
summaries.advanced: “Random sampling” is a connectivity-statistical description, not proof of a developmental random-wiring mechanism. Visual function of these Kenyon cells is not measured here. Overrepresentation of inputs could reflect reconstruction or proofreading bias as well as biology. Comparison of expansion-coding properties is qualitative (repertoire size versus Kenyon-cell number). The catalog year on some records is 2023 (preprint); the PDF is the 2024 journal article.

title: Efficient Search for Circuit Structure by ‘Smooth-Index’ Matrix-Reordering
authors: Alexander Borst; Winfried Denk

ocar.opportunity: Volume EM is producing ever-larger cell-to-cell connectivity matrices that hide circuit motifs such as assemblies and feedback unless rows and columns are ordered well.
ocar.challenge: Discrete matrix-reordering algorithms either degrade as circuits grow or scale poorly in CPU time. Topological sorting is a common alternative but is not always best at exposing feedforward versus feedback structure.
ocar.action: Borst and Denk (bioRxiv, 2023) assign each cell a real-valued “smooth-index” position, minimize a differentiable cost (for example recurrent connections above the diagonal) by gradient descent, then re-discretize ranks to permute the matrix.
ocar.resolution: They report that the method outperforms compared algorithms, including topological sorting, and scales favorably with neuron number. Applications include recovering recurrent synapses from scrambled matrices (with probabilities over many runs) and reordering bandwidth-limited and block-diagonal matrices, with performance summarized as relative upper-triangle mass or recovered bandwidth versus the original.
ocar.future_work: The algorithm is offered as a practical way to make feedback, feedforward, and modular structure visible in large connectomic matrices so theories of computation in a region can be tested against motif layout.

plain_language_summary: A huge table of who connects to whom is hard to read until the cells are lined up in a sensible order. This paper treats each cell’s place in line as a sliding number, slides those numbers to reduce messy loops, then snaps them back to a ranking that reveals feedforward versus feedback.

summaries.beginner: A huge table of who connects to whom is hard to read until the cells are lined up in a sensible order. This paper treats each cell’s place in line as a sliding number, slides those numbers to reduce messy loops, then snaps them back to a ranking that reveals feedforward versus feedback.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2023), Borst and Denk introduce smooth-index matrix reordering: continuous vertex positions, a differentiable cost, gradient-based minimization, then ranking. They contrast it with discrete reordering and topological sorting on both synthetic circuits (scrambled matrices with a few recurrent connections; bandwidth-limited and block-diagonal structure) and report favorable scaling of CPU time versus out-degree sorting. Recurrence can be scored as a probability across many sorting runs rather than a single binary label.
summaries.advanced: “Outperforms all algorithms we compared it to” is relative to the authors’ chosen baselines, not a comprehensive bakeoff. Cost functions (recurrence, bandwidth) encode what structure you want to see; a different scientific question needs a different cost. Gradient descent can have local minima; they inspect multiple runs. No specific biological connectome is required as the main result—the paper is a methods preprint. Re-discretization after a continuous relaxation can in principle miss combinatorial optima.

title: From connectome to effectome: learning the causal interaction map of the fly brain
authors: Dean A. Pospisil; Max J Aragon; S. Dorkenwald; Arie Matsliah; A. Sterling; Philipp Schlegel; Szi-chieh Yu; Claire E. McKellar; Marta Costa; K. Eichler; G. Jefferis; M. Murthy; Jonathan W. Pillow

ocar.opportunity: A causal model of a nervous system would explain behavior from dynamic interactions among neurons, but a connectome specifies possible synaptic paths, not whether or how neurons affect each other in vivo.
ocar.challenge: Estimating a whole-brain dynamical system has a huge number of parameters, so perturbation experiments alone are infeasible. Synapse counts also need not equal functional effect sizes.
ocar.action: Pospisil, Aragon, Pillow, Murthy, and colleagues propose an “effectome”: an estimator that uses stochastic optogenetic perturbation as instrumental variables and the fly connectome as a Bayesian prior on a linear dynamical model (bioRxiv, 2023/2024). They then analyze the connectome prior to find circuits with the greatest total effect on brain dynamics.
ocar.resolution: In simulation the estimator is consistent; the connectome prior makes estimation efficient. Dominant circuits involve relatively small, often anatomically localized neuron populations, implying imaging and stimulation are feasible. The approach re-discovers known circuits (including opponent motion and a mechanism for visual spatial selectivity in the ellipsoid body) and supports the view that global fly-brain dynamics are generated by many small circuits operating largely independently.
ocar.future_work: The authors argue that even a partial effectome can improve anatomy-to-physiology models, for example by testing the assumption that effect magnitude is linear in synapse number with a global scale, and they discuss extending lags using axon length. They note the estimator captures linear (locally approximate) effects in a nonlinear brain.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram shows possible routes, not which routes actually change activity. This paper proposes combining random optogenetic pokes with the fly connectome as a statistical prior so that a causal “effect map” of the brain might be learned from many small circuits rather than one impossible whole-brain recording.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram shows possible routes, not which routes actually change activity. This paper proposes combining random optogenetic pokes with the fly connectome as a statistical prior so that a causal “effect map” of the brain might be learned from many small circuits rather than one impossible whole-brain recording.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2023; version February 2024), Pospisil, Aragon, and colleagues introduce a combined experimental–statistical strategy for a fly “effectome.” Stochastic optogenetic perturbations identify causal effects; synapse counts regularize a dynamical-system estimator. Connectome analysis is used to prioritize small, high-total-effect circuits. They report that whole-brain dynamics may be a collection of largely independent local circuits, making a causal brain model feasible in Drosophila. Related-work discussion ties the method to instrumental-variable optogenetics and linear dynamical systems.
summaries.advanced: The empirical effectome is a proposed strategy plus connectome-prior analysis and simulation, not a completed whole-brain causal map. The prior assumes effects scale with synapse number (optionally with later hierarchical variation). Linear local approximation is explicitly a limitation in a nonlinear nervous system. “Re-discovers known circuits” is a sanity check on the prior, not independent causal proof. Feasibility of small-population imaging does not by itself deliver cell identification in every prioritized circuit.

title: Deep residual contextual and subpixel convolution network for automated neuronal structure segmentation in micro-connectomics
authors: Chi Xiao; Bei Hong; Jing Liu; Yuanyan Tang; Qiwei Xie; Hua Han

ocar.opportunity: Micro-connectomics aims to reconstruct nervous-system wiring from electron microscopy, but the variety of neuronal structures makes segmentation one of the hardest steps and a bottleneck for manual labeling.
ocar.challenge: Anisotropic EM stacks are difficult for 3D networks that must recover fine processes; naive upsampling can lose localization, and raw network predictions need a grouping stage to become instance reconstructions.
ocar.action: Xiao, Hong, Liu, Tang, Xie, and Han propose a deep residual contextual and subpixel-convolution network for neuronal structure segmentation in anisotropic EM, with lifted multicut post-processing (Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine, 2022).
ocar.resolution: On the ISBI EM segmentation challenge they report a Rand score of 0.98788, ranking among the top of the leaderboard. On public mouse piriform-cortex stacks they report Rand scores of 0.9562 and 0.9318, described as significant improvements over compared state-of-the-art methods.
ocar.future_work: They present the pipeline as a practical automatic aid for neuroanatomists to obtain segmentation and reconstruction of neurons in micro-connectomic volumes.

plain_language_summary: Tracing every neuron in electron-microscope pictures is exhausting. This paper trains a deep network, then tidies its predictions with a grouping algorithm, and reports high scores on a public EM challenge and on mouse cortex stacks.

summaries.beginner: Tracing every neuron in electron-microscope pictures is exhausting. This paper trains a deep network, then tidies its predictions with a grouping algorithm, and reports high scores on a public EM challenge and on mouse cortex stacks.
summaries.intermediate: In Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine (2022), Xiao and colleagues combine a residual contextual architecture with subpixel convolution for anisotropic EM neuron segmentation, followed by lifted multicut. They report Rand 0.98788 on the ISBI EM segmentation challenge and Rand 0.9562 and 0.9318 on two mouse piriform-cortex testing stacks, stating improvement versus compared methods. The intended application is micro-connectome reconstruction from ssTEM-like anisotropic volumes.
summaries.advanced: Leaderboard rank is described as “among the top,” not a named first-place snapshot with date. Rand scores are dataset-specific; piriform results are two stacks, not a whole-brain mouse connectome. Lifted multicut quality depends on the predicted affinities. The paper does not, in the extracted text, report path-length split/merge metrics used in some later connectomics bakeoffs. Organism for ISBI challenge data is the standard ssTEM challenge volume, distinct from the mouse piriform tests.

title: Neuronal contact predicts connectivity in the C. elegans brain
authors: Steven J. Cook; Cristine Kalinski; O. Hobert

ocar.opportunity: Building a nervous system requires axons to reach a region, contact neighbors, and choose synaptic partners. Two classical ideas compete: Sperry-style molecular lock-and-key among adjacent cells versus Peters’ rule that proximity is the main predictor of synapses.
ocar.challenge: Whether Peters’ rule organizes C. elegans brain wiring was unresolved. Older estimates (White: synapses with about 45% of neighbors; later work claiming synapse probability nearly independent of adjacency weight) seemed to argue against it, but new whole-brain contactomes and connectomes allow a nanoscale re-test.
ocar.action: Cook, Kalinski, and Hobert evaluate the set of available C. elegans connectomes and contactomes, modeling chemical synaptic connectivity as a path-length-dependent process of neuronal adjacency plus nerve-ring strata (bioRxiv, 2022).
ocar.resolution: They conclude that adjacency plus strata accurately model synapses, supporting Peters’ rule as an organizational principle of the C. elegans brain. Neurites occupy minimally overlapping functional strata; after cells are directed into a stratum, a contact-length threshold predicts connections. They argue this matches the historical yield of axon-guidance genetics versus the scarcity of lock-and-key specificity molecules.
ocar.future_work: They call for replicate wiring diagrams of more complex brains to test whether Peters’ rule remains primary as neuron number and type diversity increase, when molecular “rulemaking” might become more important. Population variability is treated as something new diagrams will quantify rather than a refutation of the aggregate model.

plain_language_summary: Do worm neurons pick partners with a molecular lock, or do they mostly synapse on whoever they physically touch? Using many wiring and contact maps, this paper argues that how much two cells touch—and which bundle they travel in—goes a long way toward predicting connections.

summaries.beginner: Do worm neurons pick partners with a molecular lock, or do they mostly synapse on whoever they physically touch? Using many wiring and contact maps, this paper argues that how much two cells touch—and which bundle they travel in—goes a long way toward predicting connections.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2022), Cook, Kalinski, and Hobert revisit Peters’ rule in the C. elegans nerve ring using multiple published connectomes and adjacency (“contactome”) datasets. They model chemical synapses as path-length-dependent on physical contact within brain strata defined by neurite adjacency bundles. Despite inter-individual variability, an aggregate model is reported to explain connectivity. They contrast productive genetic work on guidance and fasciculation with the relative lack of Sperry-style partner-choice molecules in worms.
summaries.advanced: Support for Peters’ rule is a statistical model of chemical synapses, not a proof that molecular recognition is absent. Gap junctions are outside the main claim. Strata themselves are derived from adjacency, so some circularity between neighborhood definition and predicted synapses should be kept in mind. “Accurately modeled” is not given as a single R² in the extracted text. Generalization to vertebrate brains is explicitly left open and may fail as cell-type diversity grows. This 2022 preprint should not be conflated with the authors’ later P. pacificus Science comparison.

title: Rewarding Capacity of Optogenetically Activating a Giant GABAergic Central-Brain Interneuron in Larval Drosophila
authors: Nino Mancini; Juliane Thoener; Esmeralda Tafani; D. Pauls; O. Mayseless; M. Strauch; K. Eichler; A. Champion; O. Kobler; Denise Weber; Edanur Sen; Aliće Weiglein; V. Hartenstein; Charalampos-Chrysovalantis Chytoudis-Peroudis; T. Jovanic; Andreas S. Thum; Astrid Rohwedder; M. Schleyer; B. Gerber

ocar.opportunity: Larval Drosophila offers a synaptic connectome plus single-cell genetic tools, making it possible to study how a numerically simple brain implements complex circuit functions. The GABAergic anterior paired lateral (APL) neuron is among the most complex cells in that brain.
ocar.challenge: APL is known to inhibit mushroom-body Kenyon cells and to sparsen sensory representations, so experimental activation would be expected to suppress, not substitute for, reward. Whether that giant interneuron can itself instruct associative memory was unclear.
ocar.action: Mancini, Gerber, and colleagues combine behavioral assays, connectomics, optogenetics, calcium imaging, and pharmacology to study APL in larval Drosophila of either sex (bioRxiv 2022; Journal of Neuroscience catalog venue).
ocar.resolution: They provide a detailed account of APL structure, regional polarity, connectivity, and metamorphic development, and confirm that optogenetic APL activation inhibits Kenyon cells. Unexpectedly, pairing APL activation with an odor establishes an odor-specific appetitive short-term memory without changing naive olfactory behavior. Acute systemic blockade of dopamine synthesis and ablation of dopaminergic pPAM neurons impair that APL-driven reward learning.
ocar.future_work: The findings are offered as a case study of complex function in a simple brain and as evidence that central-brain GABAergic neurons can engage dopaminergic reinforcement pathways.

plain_language_summary: A huge inhibitory cell in the larval fly brain is known for quieting the learning center so smells stay sparse. Turning that cell on together with an odor can nonetheless teach the larva to like the odor, and that teaching seems to need dopamine neurons.

summaries.beginner: A huge inhibitory cell in the larval fly brain is known for quieting the learning center so smells stay sparse. Turning that cell on together with an odor can nonetheless teach the larva to like the odor, and that teaching seems to need dopamine neurons.
summaries.intermediate: In work posted on bioRxiv (2022) and catalogued as Journal of Neuroscience, Mancini and colleagues characterize larval APL anatomy and show optogenetic activation inhibits mushroom-body Kenyon cells, consistent with sparsening. The same activation, paired with odor, creates an appetitive short-term odor memory; unpaired controls and naive olfactory behavior argue against a nonspecific sensory change. Dopamine-synthesis inhibition and pPAM ablation impair the APL-activation reward effect, suggesting APL taps dopaminergic reinforcement rather than replacing it.
summaries.advanced: The extracted PDF is the 19 December 2022 preprint; later journal copy-editing may differ. “Strong rewarding effect” is behavioral, not a direct APL-to-Kenyon-cell excitatory synapse. Dependence on pPAM and dopamine synthesis implies an indirect route; the exact synaptic path is not fully reduced in the abstract. Memory is short-term and odor-specific under the reported protocol. Connectomic description of APL is larval and should not be assumed identical to adult APL without the paper’s metamorphic analysis.

title: Bayesian reconstruction of memories stored in neural networks from their connectivity
authors: Sebastian Goldt; Florent Krzakala; Lenka Zdeborov'a; N. Brunel

ocar.opportunity: Connectomes map synaptic weights in large recurrent circuits, raising the question of whether information stored in those weights—the memories of an attractor network—can be read back from connectivity alone.
ocar.challenge: Inference of stored patterns from a connectivity matrix is not always theoretically possible, depends on the learning model, and standard tools such as PCA may miss structure that a Bayesian treatment of the generative model could recover.
ocar.action: Goldt, Krzakala, Zdeborová, and Brunel determine when reconstruction is theoretically possible in specific attractor models, then give a statistical-physics-inspired approximate Bayesian algorithm that is amenable to exact analysis (PLoS Computational Biology, 2021; arXiv:2105.07416).
ocar.resolution: They study performance on three models, compare with PCA, and map limitations. The core setting is a symmetric learned connectivity with a truncated-Gaussian non-negative weight model and inhibition treated as uniform thresholding. They discuss why cortical and hippocampal data often show excess bidirectional connections and temporally symmetric plasticity, which motivates the symmetric case.
ocar.future_work: Flagged extensions include asymmetric matrices (for sequence storage), inhibitory plasticity, palimpsest memories of unequal strength (likely recovering only strongly embedded patterns), and arbitrary non-negative weight distributions via a changed nonlinearity. Practically, they say the method only makes sense when reconstructed matrices show substantial symmetry.

plain_language_summary: If a network stores memories in its connection strengths, can you read those memories from a wiring diagram? This theory paper gives conditions and an algorithm for attractor networks, and explains when ordinary tricks like PCA are not enough.

summaries.beginner: If a network stores memories in its connection strengths, can you read those memories from a wiring diagram? This theory paper gives conditions and an algorithm for attractor networks, and explains when ordinary tricks like PCA are not enough.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Computational Biology (2021), Goldt and colleagues frame memory retrieval from a recurrent connectivity matrix as Bayesian inference in attractor-network generative models. A message-passing algorithm from statistical physics is analyzed exactly and tested on three models versus PCA. The default learned component is symmetric; inhibition is a uniform threshold, not a plastic inhibitory population. Limitations and biologically motivated extensions (asymmetry, inhibitory learning, heterogeneous embedding strengths, log-normal-like weights) occupy a substantial discussion.
summaries.advanced: This is a theoretical/algorithmic paper on models, not a reconstruction of a biological connectome’s memories. Applicability hinges on a strong symmetric Hebbian component; the authors warn against use when that is absent (for example sequence-coding nets). Experimental citations on bidirectional excess and persistent activity motivate the model but do not validate recovery on EM data. Palimpsest and inhibitory-plasticity regimes are discussed as likely failure or extension cases, not as solved. “Three models” performance details are in figures not fully captured in the selected extract.

title: Dopamine modulation of sensory processing and adaptive behavior in flies
authors: K. Siju; Jean‐François De Backer; Ilona C. Grunwald Kadow

ocar.opportunity: Animals must integrate external cues, internal state, and past experience to make survival decisions, and neuromodulators are a conserved way to reconfigure circuits across timescales.
ocar.challenge: Dopamine is classically tied to reward-based associative learning, but dopaminergic neurons are heterogeneous and participate in many adaptive behaviors. How they inject state and context into decision circuits, and how to study that at synaptic resolution, remained poorly synthesized for flies.
ocar.action: Siju, De Backer, and Grunwald Kadow review dopamine modulation of sensory processing and adaptive behavior in Drosophila (Cell and Tissue Research, 2021), emphasizing the mushroom body as a structure richly innervated by dopaminergic neurons that can integrate multimodal, state, and contextual signals.
ocar.resolution: They argue that dopaminergic neuron populations are highly heterogeneous and involved in nearly all processes that increase success at survival and reproduction, not only reinforcement learning. The combination of genetics, connectomics, physiology, and quantitative behavior in the fly, including a whole-brain synaptic connectome, is presented as making state-dependent decision making tractable.
ocar.future_work: The review closes by noting that this toolkit has already shifted the view of dopamine, and that remaining questions concern how diverse dopaminergic neurons implement flexible, state-dependent action selection across sensory modalities.

plain_language_summary: Dopamine is famous as a reward chemical, but in flies it also helps the brain mix what is happening now with hunger, memory, and context. This review explains how dopamine cells feeding the mushroom body give the fly a flexible decision switch, and why fly wiring diagrams make that switch studyable.

summaries.beginner: Dopamine is famous as a reward chemical, but in flies it also helps the brain mix what is happening now with hunger, memory, and context. This review explains how dopamine cells feeding the mushroom body give the fly a flexible decision switch, and why fly wiring diagrams make that switch studyable.
summaries.intermediate: In Cell and Tissue Research (2021), Siju, De Backer, and Grunwald Kadow review Drosophila dopamine as a neuromodulator of sensory processing and adaptive behavior. Beyond reward learning, they highlight heterogeneous dopaminergic populations that integrate external, internal, and learned signals, especially via mushroom-body innervation. They position the fly whole-brain connectome plus genetics and physiology as a practical system for decision-making research.

Heterogeneity and “nearly all” survival-related processes are synthesis claims over a literature, not a quantified census. Connectome availability is a motivating context; specific synapse counts are not the paper’s result. Cross-species comparisons to vertebrates are conceptual. Readers looking for a single canonical mushroom-body dopamine wiring diagram will need the primary studies cited therein.

title: Large-scale image segmentation based on distributed clustering algorithms
authors: R. Lu; A. Zlateski; H. Seung

ocar.opportunity: Many 3D EM segmentation pipelines hierarchically cluster supervoxels into regions, but production connectomics graphs are too large to agglomerate in one machine’s memory.
ocar.challenge: Iterative agglomeration scores a pair of regions by a statistic (mean or median) of affinities on their interface, and that interface can span arbitrarily many chunks, so naive chunking would make results depend on the cut and could cascade local errors globally.
ocar.action: Lu, Zlateski, and Seung describe a recursive distributed clustering algorithm (arXiv, 2021): the volume is processed in chunks that double in all dimensions each round until one chunk covers the image. Merge decisions for regions that touch chunk boundaries are delayed until a later round when those regions lie fully inside a chunk.
ocar.resolution: The final clustering is provably independent of the chunking scheme and identical to processing the whole image at once. They demonstrate clustering of an affinity graph with over 1.5 trillion edges between 135 billion supervoxels from a 3D electron-microscopic brain image.
ocar.future_work: The algorithm is offered for production-scale hierarchical agglomeration where convolutional affinity prediction is imperfect and statistical grouping must still be global.

plain_language_summary: Stitching tiny pieces of a brain image into neurons usually requires looking at the whole volume at once, which will not fit in memory. This paper splits the job across computers but postpones glue decisions at the edges until the pieces are large enough, so the answer matches doing it all in one step.

summaries.beginner: Stitching tiny pieces of a brain image into neurons usually requires looking at the whole volume at once, which will not fit in memory. This paper splits the job across computers but postpones glue decisions at the edges until the pieces are large enough, so the answer matches doing it all in one step.
summaries.intermediate: In an arXiv preprint (2021), Lu, Zlateski, and Seung present distributed hierarchical clustering for supervoxel agglomeration. Chunk size doubles each recursive round; boundary-touching merges are deferred so interface statistics remain correct. They prove chunk-independence and apply the method to a graph of more than 1.5 trillion edges and 135 billion supervoxels from 3D EM. The setting is residual error in convolutional affinities that makes connected components insufficient and motivates statistical agglomeration.

The demonstration is scale and correctness relative to single-machine agglomeration, not a claim of superior biological accuracy versus other segmenters. Affinity quality still limits splits and merges. “Brain image” is not named as a public dataset in the extracted abstract. Supervoxel count (135 billion) is the clustering input size, not a count of neurons.

title: Neuronal circuits integrating visual motion information in Drosophila
authors: Kazunori Shinomiya; Aljoscha Nern; I. Meinertzhagen; Stephen M. Plaza; Michael B. Reiser

ocar.opportunity: Directionally selective T4 and T5 neurons encode ON and OFF motion and terminate in four lobula-plate layers, each for a cardinal direction, but how those signals are integrated downstream was largely unknown at synaptic resolution.
ocar.challenge: Input circuits onto T4/T5 had been reconstructed, yet partners in the lobula plate—including how ON and OFF pathways converge, how motion opponency is implemented, and whether new motion directions are synthesized—had not been comprehensively identified.
ocar.action: Shinomiya, Nern, Meinertzhagen, Plaza, and Reiser report a 3D electron-microscopy reconstruction that comprehensively identifies T4/T5 synaptic partners in the Drosophila lobula plate (bioRxiv, 2021), combining EM with genetic driver lines to visualize cell types.
ocar.resolution: T4 and T5 cells projecting to the same layer connect to common partners with similar weights, explaining ON/OFF convergence, and form a core motif with bilayer interneurons that details motion opponency. Additional pathways appear to combine vertical and horizontal T4/T5 signals into new directions. Substantial projections into the lobula suggest directionally selective signals shape feature detection there. New cell types are described and known types receive revised connectivity.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the circuits as anatomical substrate for experimental and computational analyses of motion vision and as a step toward complete sensory-motor pathways.

plain_language_summary: Flies see motion with cells that prefer bright or dark edges moving in four main directions. This reconstruction maps who those cells talk to next, showing how bright and dark paths join, how opposite directions cancel, and how new directions and messages into another visual area may be built.

summaries.beginner: Flies see motion with cells that prefer bright or dark edges moving in four main directions. This reconstruction maps who those cells talk to next, showing how bright and dark paths join, how opposite directions cancel, and how new directions and messages into another visual area may be built.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2021), Shinomiya and colleagues reconstruct T4/T5 partners in the Drosophila lobula plate. Same-layer T4 and T5 share partners symmetrically; bilayer LPi interneurons complete an opponency motif. Pathways that mix vertical and horizontal cardinal channels are proposed to encode intermediate directions. Outputs into the lobula extend classical lobula-plate motion pathways. Driver-line anatomy complements but does not replace EM synapse counts. Symmetric ON/OFF weights are anatomical similarity, not matched gain in vivo.

title: Capillary-Based and Stokes-Based Trapping of Serial Sections for Scalable 3D-EM Connectomics
authors: Timothy J. Lee; Mighten C. Yip; Aditi Kumar; Colby F. Lewallen; D. Bumbarger; R. Reid; C. Forest

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section electron microscopy reconstructs tissue by imaging consecutive slices, but handling 10^0–10^6 delicate sections between the knife and the imaging substrate remains a bottleneck, especially in the mesoscale 10^2–10^3-section regime.
ocar.challenge: Manual pickup of ribbons demands skilled users and does not scale. Fully automated tape collection (ATUM) is powerful but can constrain substrate choice (for example immunolabeling needs). A device that fits a conventional diamond-knife boat and places sections repeatably for robotic pickup was needed.
ocar.action: Lee, Yip, Kumar, Lewallen, Bumbarger, Reid, and Forest present a section-handling trap that uses curvature-induced capillary forces and Stokes drag, with a mathematical model of water–air interface forces, interfacing with a standard ultramicrotome knife (eNeuro, 2020).
ocar.resolution: They report in-line exact-constraint trapping with 100 μm RMS repeatability, enabling open-loop collection. Across n=8 datasets of 126 serial sections, average loss rate was 0.50% and throughput 63 s/section, onto a variety of electron- and light-microscopy substrates without significant defects. The model predicts trapping position over a parameter range with RMSE=0.27 mm.
ocar.future_work: For more than about 10^3 sections they suggest tighter environmental control or ATUM as alternatives if a 1% loss ceiling is required. Piecewise adoption (trap without robot; mixed substrates) is offered for labs that already have an ultramicrotome.

plain_language_summary: Cutting thousands of ultras-thin brain slices is one thing; picking them up without wrecking them is another. This paper describes a water-boat trap that parks each slice in the same spot so a robot can lift it, with only a small fraction lost in tests of a hundred-plus sections.

summaries.beginner: Cutting thousands of ultras-thin brain slices is one thing; picking them up without wrecking them is another. This paper describes a water-boat trap that parks each slice in the same spot so a robot can lift it, with only a small fraction lost in tests of a hundred-plus sections.
summaries.intermediate: In eNeuro (2020), Lee and colleagues describe capillary- and Stokes-based trapping of serial sections for mesoscale ssEM. A device on a conventional diamond knife achieves 100 μm repeatability. Automated collection of 126-section series (n=8) yielded 0.50% average loss and 63 s/section. Modeling of interface forces is presented as an extension of water–air interaction theory (position RMSE 0.27 mm). Humidity 41–42% and 21–22°C with water-level control within 65 μl are the reported experimental envelope.
summaries.advanced: Demonstrations are mesoscale (~10^2 sections), not 10^6-section production. Loss rate <1% is tied to tightly controlled conditions on one tissue block; the authors say longer runs likely need more precise control. 63 s/section is slower than some tape methods. Substrate flexibility is an advantage versus Kapton-only ATUM, not a claim of superior ultrastructure. Repeatability of 100 μm is positioning for pickup, not cutting-thickness precision.

title: Cell-type specific innervation of cortical pyramidal cells at their apical dendrites
authors: Ali Karimi; Jan Odenthal; F. Drawitsch; K. Boergens; M. Helmstaedter

ocar.opportunity: Apical dendrites of pyramidal cells converge near the layer 1/2 border, a site implicated in coupling layer-1 top-down input with basal dendritic drive and in regenerative dendritic events, so their inhibitory/excitatory innervation is a key cortical computation parameter.
ocar.challenge: Whether that innervation is the same for layer 2, 3, and 5 pyramids, and whether inhibitory axons mix targets or prefer one class, was unknown; light microscopy cannot resolve synapse type on identified apical trunks across multiple cortical areas.
ocar.action: Karimi, Odenthal, Drawitsch, Boergens, and Helmstaedter acquire four serial block-face EM volumes at the L1/L2 border in mouse S1, V2, posterior parietal, and anterior cingulate cortex (volumes between 72×93×141 μm³ and 66×89×202 μm³; voxels about 11–12 × 11–12 × 28–30 nm³) and reconstruct apical-dendrite synapses (eLife, 2020).
ocar.resolution: Relative inhibitory input at the main bifurcation is more than 2-fold larger for L2 than for L3 and L5 thick-tufted pyramids. Toward distal tufts in upper L1, relative inhibitory input is at least about 2-fold larger for L5 pyramids than for others. Only L3 cells show a homogeneous inhibitory fraction. Inhibitory axons preferentially innervate either L2 or L3/5 apical dendrites, not both. Innervation is therefore cell-type specific rather than a generic layer-1 rule.
ocar.future_work: The authors interpret these connectomic principles as evidence for differential computation in L2 versus L3 versus L5 (and L5 subtype) pyramids at their apical tufts.

plain_language_summary: The treetops of cortical neurons meet in the upper layers, where they receive a mix of go and stop synapses. Mapping those contacts in mouse cortex shows layer-2, layer-3, and layer-5 cells are not wired the same: inhibition is aimed differently depending on cell type and on whether you look at the main fork or the fine tips.

summaries.beginner: The treetops of cortical neurons meet in the upper layers, where they receive a mix of go and stop synapses. Mapping those contacts in mouse cortex shows layer-2, layer-3, and layer-5 cells are not wired the same: inhibition is aimed differently depending on cell type and on whether you look at the main fork or the fine tips.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2020), Karimi and colleagues use SBEM at the layer 1/2 border in four mouse cortical areas to quantify inhibitory versus excitatory synapses on apical dendrites. L2 main bifurcations are more inhibition-rich (more than 2-fold versus L3 and L5 thick-tufted cells); L5 distal tufts in upper L1 are at least about 2-fold more inhibition-rich than other types; L3 is comparatively homogeneous. Inhibitory axons tend not to mix L2 with L3/5 targets. Layer origin of each apical dendrite is assigned within the volumes.
summaries.advanced: The catalog abstract states a “more than 3-fold” L2 effect; the published eLife abstract in the PDF uses “more than 2-fold.” This card follows the PDF. Volumes are local L1/2 blocks, not full-depth reconstructions of every pyramid. L5 sample is thick-tufted-focused in the comparison quoted. Inhibitory-axon preference is from reconstructed axons in these volumes, not a complete inhibitory-neuron census. Four areas support a general cortical claim but still all mouse. Computational implications are inferred from synapse ratios, not from physiology in this paper.

title: Computing Temporal Sequences Associated With Dynamic Patterns on the C. elegans Connectome
authors: V. George; F. Puppo; G. Silva

ocar.opportunity: How a network’s wiring and geometry constrain the dynamics it can support is still poorly understood, even in the fully mapped C. elegans nervous system.
ocar.challenge: Computational studies often simulate a named circuit in isolation, so it is unclear whether the signaling paths that appear in that reduced network still exist once the same cells sit inside the full connectome.
ocar.action: In Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience (2021), George, Puppo, and Silva simulate emergent dynamics on the known C. elegans connectome with a local-interaction model that does not depend on cell-intrinsic biophysics, stimulating the chemosensory neuron ASEL in a feeding circuit both in isolation and embedded in the whole worm.
ocar.resolution: Contralateral ventral (VB) and dorsal (DB) motor-neuron activations emerge that are qualitatively similar to rhythmic firing associated with locomotion. Using Temporal Sequences (TSeq)—time-ordered walks of signals on the graph—they find that only 5% of TSeq are preserved between the isolated feeding network and its embedded counterpart; 95% of isolated-network pathways are absent when the circuit is embedded.
ocar.future_work: The authors treat the result as a caution for computational studies of isolated neurobiological circuits. They also define Basis TSeqs (repeating versus one-time sequences) as a way to compress cyclic walks, but they do not claim a unique extraction algorithm.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram can be run as a simple simulation to see what activity patterns it can produce. This team finds that a feeding-circuit simulation in the worm looks locomotion-like, but almost all of the signaling paths change once that circuit is placed back inside the full nervous system.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram can be run as a simple simulation to see what activity patterns it can produce. This team finds that a feeding-circuit simulation in the worm looks locomotion-like, but almost all of the signaling paths change once that circuit is placed back inside the full nervous system.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience (2021), George, Puppo, and Silva stimulate ASEL in a known C. elegans feeding circuit both in isolation and embedded in the full connectome, using a model in which local interactions among connected neurons generate global dynamics without cell-intrinsic biophysical detail. Contralateral VB and DB motor-neuron activations emerge that they interpret as qualitatively similar to rhythmic locomotion patterns, which they take as evidence of purposeful structural wiring. An analytic framework of Temporal Sequences (TSeq) shows that only 5% of isolated-network signaling paths survive embedding; 95% do not. Code-level Basis TSeqs split repeating (cycle-derived) from one-time walks.
summaries.advanced: The catalog lists a 2020 bioRxiv record; the extract is the March 2021 Frontiers article (doi 10.3389/fnsys.2021.564124). Dynamics are “plausible” simulations, not electrophysiology. Similarity to locomotion is qualitative. The 5%/95% TSeq comparison is between one isolated feeding network and its embedded counterpart under this model, not a general theorem about all reduced circuits. “Purposeful wiring” is the authors’ interpretation.

title: Graph Properties of the Adult Drosophila Central Brain
authors: Louis K. Scheffer

ocar.opportunity: A dense reconstruction of the adult Drosophila central brain makes it possible to treat a real insect brain as a directed, synapse-weighted graph rather than a sparse sample of connections.
ocar.challenge: Even with a dense connectome it is unclear which graph statistics are like human-designed logic, which differ across compartments, and which depend on unreconstructed biology such as gap junctions and neuromodulators.
ocar.action: In a May 2020 bioRxiv preprint, Scheffer analyzes the hemibrain as a directed graph with edge weights equal to synapse counts, reporting metrics for the sample as a whole and for computational compartments.
ocar.resolution: The volume contains around 25,000 neurons and about 20 million chemical synapses (21,662 uncropped traced neurons; 4,495 large but cropped). Neurons average 153 inputs and 153 outputs. Wiring is not random; compartments differ in all measured characteristics; paths are short compared with man-made circuits; connection strengths look like a power law with an exponential tail, unlike measured mammalian connections; cliques and many-to-one motifs are present; electrical response is strongly determined by compartment structure; and there is evidence for efficient packing.
ocar.future_work: Scheffer calls for whole-brain and ventral-nerve-cord analyses, additional specimens and species, and inclusion of neuromodulators, receptors, gap junctions, glia, and cell biology that this connectome omits.

plain_language_summary: A nearly complete wiring diagram of part of a fruit-fly’s central brain can be treated like a directed map of who talks to whom. This preprint reports that fly neurons have many inputs and outputs, paths are short, compartments differ, and the wiring is not random.

summaries.beginner: A nearly complete wiring diagram of part of a fruit-fly’s central brain can be treated like a directed map of who talks to whom. This preprint reports that fly neurons have many inputs and outputs, paths are short, compartments differ, and the wiring is not random.
summaries.intermediate: In a bioRxiv preprint posted 20 May 2020, Scheffer treats the Drosophila hemibrain as a directed, synapse-count-weighted graph. The reconstruction comprises about 25,000 neurons and about 20 million chemical synapses, including 21,662 uncropped traced neurons and 4,495 large (≥1000 connections) cropped cells. Reported conclusions include an average of 153 inputs and outputs, non-random wiring, compartment differences, short paths, a power-law-like strength distribution with an exponential tail, non-uniform strong connections, cliques and many-to-one motifs, compartment-determined electrical response, and evidence for efficient packing.
summaries.advanced: This is an unreviewed preprint that consolidates some analyses already in the hemibrain paper with new ones. Synapse count is treated as connection strength, which the author flags as an approximation. Cropped neurons and the volume boundary bias degree and path statistics. Gap junctions, neuromodulators, and glia are absent. “Electrical response” here is a graph-derived claim, not a new physiology experiment in this extract.

title: The growing topology of the C. elegans connectome
authors: Alexander Helm; A. Blevins; D. Bassett

ocar.opportunity: The developing C. elegans connectome has a rich club in a small-world architecture, but standard network statistics miss weakly connected motifs such as topological cavities that may support segregated computation.
ocar.challenge: It is unclear whether the growing connectome’s topology is a robust developmental feature, whether it is explained by simple growth models, and how sensitive it is to errors in birth times and missing synapses.
ocar.action: Helm, Blevins, and Bassett (bioRxiv/arXiv, 2020–2021) use persistent homology to track topological cavities as neurons are added in developmental birth order, and they test robustness with surrogate connectomes that add edges and jitter birth times.
ocar.resolution: Growing topology is relatively robust to birth-time noise and is not captured by similar growth models. In the PDF abstract, the growing topology is particularly insensitive to exact motor-neuron birth times. Sensitivity analyses (1,000 surrogates adding 800 connections and reassigning birth times within reported error: 10% embryonic, 2% later; about 10% of connections presumed missing) yield qualitatively similar Betti curves that remain statistically distinct from the reported connectome (p < 0.001).
ocar.future_work: The authors anticipate that cavity-tracking measurements will help build more accurate models of neuronal development. Wiring-cost-constrained surrogates shrink quantitative gaps but still differ from the reported curve.

plain_language_summary: As a worm’s neurons are born, the wiring diagram grows a shape that ordinary network scores can miss. This study tracks holes in that growing graph and finds the shape is fairly robust to noisy birth times and is not explained by simple growth models.

summaries.beginner: As a worm’s neurons are born, the wiring diagram grows a shape that ordinary network scores can miss. This study tracks holes in that growing graph and finds the shape is fairly robust to noisy birth times and is not explained by simple growth models.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (doi 10.1101/2020.12.31.424985; arXiv:2101.00065v2, August 2021), Helm, Blevins, and Bassett apply persistent homology to the C. elegans connectome grown in neuron birth order. They report that developing topology is robust to birth-time perturbation, is not captured by standard growth models, and—in this PDF version—is particularly insensitive to exact motor-neuron birth times. One thousand surrogates that add 800 edges and jitter birth times within published margins (10% embryonic, 2% later) keep the qualitative Betti-curve shape, with more cavities but p < 0.001 distance from the original curves; a wiring-cost-constrained variant reduces the quantitative gap.
summaries.advanced: The catalog abstract says topology is particularly sensitive to a small set of predominantly motor neurons; the PDF abstract says particularly insensitive to motor-neuron birth times—this card follows the PDF. Surrogate tests reject a “trivial perturbation” null but do not prove biological robustness of every cavity. Birth times and the connectome inherit White/Varshney-era incompleteness (about 10% missing connections assumed). Persistent homology of a growing graph depends on node order and edge set.

title: The hourglass organization of the Caenorhabditis elegans connectome
authors: K. M. Sabrin; Yongbin Wei; M. P. Heuvel; C. Dovrolis

ocar.opportunity: The complete C. elegans wiring diagram can be read as an information-processing network from roughly 90 sensory neurons through about 80 interneurons to about 120 motor neurons.
ocar.challenge: Highly recurrent interneuron connectivity hides whether feedforward sensory-to-motor flow actually bottlenecks through a small core, and whether that core matches other notions of hub neurons such as the rich club.
ocar.action: In PLoS Computational Biology (2020), Sabrin, Wei, van den Heuvel, and Dovrolis apply an “hourglass effect” analysis to the feedforward flow from sensory to motor neurons, separating feedforward from feedback paths.
ocar.resolution: Feedforward flow traverses a waist of 10–15 interneurons that largely overlap the previously identified rich club. The core is mostly stable whether chemical synapses are used alone or with gap junctions, and for the complete network they list 12 core cells (AVAL/R, AVBL/R, AVEL/R, PVCL/R, AIBR, AVDR, DVA, VD01), 10 of which were also synaptic-network cores. They analogize the waist to an encoder–decoder information bottleneck.
ocar.future_work: The authors frame the core as integrating sensory modalities before driving higher circuits; relating hourglass membership to physiology remains an experimental task. Data and code are at github.com/kmsabrin/hourglass-celegans.

plain_language_summary: Information entering a worm’s sensors has to reach muscles through a tangle of interneurons. This paper finds that the useful forward paths squeeze through a small set of about a dozen cells that were already known as a densely linked “rich club.”

summaries.beginner: Information entering a worm’s sensors has to reach muscles through a tangle of interneurons. This paper finds that the useful forward paths squeeze through a small set of about a dozen cells that were already known as a densely linked “rich club.”
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Computational Biology (2020), Sabrin and colleagues treat the C. elegans connectome as an information-processing network (~90 sensory, ~80 inter, ~120 motor neurons) and apply hourglass analysis to feedforward sensory-to-motor paths. They report a waist of 10–15 interneurons overlapping the rich club, robust to how feedforward versus feedback is separated and largely unchanged when gap junctions are added. Table 3 lists 12 core neurons in the complete network (AVAL covering 0.29 of new paths, then AVAR 0.23, AVBL 0.16, AVBR 0.11, and others). They compare this bottleneck to encoder–decoder artificial nets.
summaries.advanced: Hourglass membership is a path-coverage statistic on an abstracted feedforward graph, not a measured information bottleneck in living worms. Overlap with rich-club, closeness-centrality, and connector-hub lists is correlative. Core lists depend on the path set (e.g., SP+2). Encoder–decoder language is an analogy. Results inherit connectome polarity and completeness conventions.

title: The Wiring Logic of an Identified Serotonergic Neuron That Spans Sensory Networks
authors: Kaylynn E. Coates; Steven A. Calle-Schuler; Levi M. Helmick; Victoria L. Knotts; Brennah N. Martik; Farzaan Salman; Lauren Warner; Sophia V. Valla; D. Bock; A. Dacks

ocar.opportunity: Serotonergic neurons project widely and modulate many behaviors, but their connectivity has not been mapped at single-cell resolution through a whole brain.
ocar.challenge: A single identified serotonergic cell (the CSDn) spans several olfactory regions, so glomerulus-to-glomerulus differences, local versus projection targets, and non-olfactory inputs cannot be read from light-level anatomy alone.
ocar.action: In a February 2020 bioRxiv preprint (cataloged as Journal of Neuroscience), Coates, Calle-Schuler, Helmick, Knotts, Martik, Salman, Warner, Valla, Bock, and Dacks reconstruct CSDn synapses in a whole-brain EM volume of a female Drosophila.
ocar.resolution: In the antennal lobe the CSDn receives glomerulus-specific input and preferentially targets distinct local-interneuron subtypes rather than matching output to each glomerulus. Wiring logic differs in the lateral horn, where connectivity is more distributed and aligned with presumptive transmitter content of principal cells; the CSDn does not keep the same synaptic relationship with individual projection neurons that span AL and LH. Protocerebral neurons provide abundant non-olfactory synaptic input.
ocar.future_work: The study is offered as a ground plan for heterogeneous modulatory effects; physiology of the identified partners and generalization beyond this single neuron and specimen are left open.

plain_language_summary: A serotonin cell can wander through many smell-processing areas, so it is hard to know whom it actually talks to. This EM reconstruction of one identified fly neuron shows different wiring rules in different regions and strong input from outside olfaction.

summaries.beginner: A serotonin cell can wander through many smell-processing areas, so it is hard to know whom it actually talks to. This EM reconstruction of one identified fly neuron shows different wiring rules in different regions and strong input from outside olfaction.
summaries.intermediate: In a bioRxiv preprint posted 25 February 2020 (catalog journal: Journal of Neuroscience), Coates and colleagues map the CSDn in a female Drosophila whole-brain EM volume. Within the antennal lobe they report glomerulus-specific input and preferential targeting of local interneuron subtypes; across the AL and lateral horn the same CSDn does not preserve its relationship with individual spanning projection neurons, and LH connectivity is more distributed by transmitter class. They also identify protocerebral neurons that provide abundant synaptic input. The significance framing is a single-cell account of serotonergic modulation in olfaction plus novel extrinsic drive.
summaries.advanced: The extract is the bioRxiv version of a paper cataloged as Journal of Neuroscience. Results are from one female brain and one identified neuron. Transmitter assignments for LH partners are presumptive. Connectivity is not a functional map of serotonin release or receptors. Polyadic insect synapses and proofreading completeness of the volume limit partner lists.

title: Two Stream Active Query Suggestion for Active Learning in Connectomics
authors: Zudi Lin; D. Wei; Won-Dong Jang; Siyan Zhou; Xupeng Chen; Xueying Wang; R. Schalek; D. Berger; Brian Matejek; Lee; Kamentsky; A. Peleg; Daniel Haehn; T. Jones; T. Parag; J. Lichtman; H. Pfister

ocar.opportunity: Large biomedical volumes have too little expert label to train strong deep models, so active learning that picks the next images to annotate is a practical way to stretch a limited budget.
ocar.challenge: Query-suggestion networks trained only on the small labeled set become poorly matched to the harder unlabeled volume, so they stop choosing representative examples.
ocar.action: In ECCV (2020), Lin, Wei, Jang, Zhou, Chen, Wang, Schalek, Berger, Matejek, Kamentsky, Peleg, Haehn, Jones, Parag, Lichtman, and Pfister add an unsupervised feature stream trained on all raw images to a supervised stream, and they wrap the method in an end-to-end active-learning loop for 3D synapse detection and mitochondria segmentation.
ocar.resolution: They curate what they describe as the largest connectomics dataset with dense synapse and mitochondria annotation. On that set the method outperforms previous state-of-the-art by 3.1% (synapse) and 3.8% (mitochondria) in region-of-interest proposal accuracy, and it also outperforms prior approaches on CIFAR-10 under the same limited annotation budget. In a synapse ablation, initial ROI accuracy is 0.762; annotating 4.46% of instances at random would add about 0.01, while their clustering module adds about 0.08.
ocar.future_work: They note that core-set and learning-loss methods, tuned on natural-image benchmarks, capture unlabeled connectomics appearance poorly and that global-average-pooling loss estimators discard object structure. Project page: https://zudi-lin.github.io/projects/#two_stream_active.

plain_language_summary: Experts cannot label every synapse and mitochondrion in a huge electron-microscope volume. This paper picks which examples to label next by combining a network trained on labels with another trained on all the raw pictures, and it reports better proposals than earlier active-learning methods.

summaries.beginner: Experts cannot label every synapse and mitochondrion in a huge electron-microscope volume. This paper picks which examples to label next by combining a network trained on labels with another trained on all the raw pictures, and it reports better proposals than earlier active-learning methods.
summaries.intermediate: In ECCV 2020 (Comput Vis ECCV 12363:103–120), Lin and colleagues propose two-stream active query suggestion: a supervised feature extractor plus an unsupervised extractor trained on all raw images and later fine-tuned on new labels. Applied to 3D synapse detection and mitochondria segmentation in connectomics, they report a densely annotated dataset and gains of 3.1% (synapses) and 3.8% (mitochondria) in ROI-proposal accuracy over prior state of the art, plus a CIFAR-10 comparison under a matched annotation budget. An ablation starts from 0.762 instance-proposal accuracy; 4.46% random labels add ~0.01, versus ~0.08 from their clustering with Q = 5 representatives.
summaries.advanced: “Largest” is the authors’ claim, not independently audited here. The 3.1% and 3.8% figures are ROI-proposal accuracy, not final instance segmentation. Ablation numbers are on their synapse benchmark with a fixed annotation budget and cluster count. CIFAR-10 is a natural-image check, not connectomics. Late fusion of streams can be dominated by a 1,000-d image embedding versus a 20-d mask embedding.

title: Useful road maps: studying Drosophila larva’s central nervous system with the help of connectomics
authors: Claire Eschbach; Marta Zlatic

ocar.opportunity: The Drosophila larva is small enough that synapse-resolution wiring, cellular-resolution activity, and behavior can in principle be combined for the same circuits.
ocar.challenge: Even with those tools, it is still hard to state which circuit motifs implement multisensory integration, learning, and action selection, and how brain, subesophageal zone, and ventral nerve cord divide those jobs.
ocar.action: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2020), Eschbach and Zlatic review recently reconstructed larval CNS circuits, emphasizing first-instar EM, genetic single-cell targeting, and whole-brain imaging.
ocar.resolution: They note an early larval CNS of about 15,000 neurons, with somatosensory and motor circuits in the VNC, feeding and neuromodulation in the SEZ, and first- and higher-order sensory centers in the brain reconstructed in the same EM volume; comprehensive CNS reconstruction is described as within reach. Gerhard et al. are cited for synaptic-input fractions that remain similar despite a five-fold size change from first to third instar. Themes include early multisensory loops for specific actions versus more centralized valence-like signals in higher areas.
ocar.future_work: Open questions include how descending brain/SEZ neurons bias VNC somatosensory choices, and using multi-individual connectomes to study memory traces, individuality, and mutants.

plain_language_summary: The fruit-fly maggot has a small nervous system, so wiring, activity, and behavior can be studied together. This review gathers recent maps of how the larva combines senses, learns, and chooses actions.

summaries.beginner: The fruit-fly maggot has a small nervous system, so wiring, activity, and behavior can be studied together. This review gathers recent maps of how the larva combines senses, learns, and chooses actions.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2020, 65:129–137), Eschbach and Zlatic review Drosophila larva CNS connectomics. They contrast the early larva’s roughly 15,000 smaller neurons with the adult, and they summarize synaptic-resolution reconstructions in one first-instar EM volume covering VNC somatosensory and motor programs, SEZ feeding and neuromodulation, and brain sensory and associative centers. They highlight Gerhard et al. on conserved synaptic-input fractions despite five-fold growth, and they organize recent results around multisensory integration, mushroom-body learning (including recurrent dopaminergic motifs), and action selection such as crawl-versus-turn.

Neuron counts, circuit lists, and the five-fold size comparison are cited from other papers. “Comprehensive reconstruction within reach” was a 2020 outlook. Functional claims (valence-like signals, specific sensorimotor loops) synthesize physiology plus anatomy from the cited studies. The tripartite insect/vertebrate analogy is organizational, not a homology proof.

title: What would a synthetic connectome look like?
authors: I. Rabinowitch

ocar.opportunity: Connectomics usually reverse-engineers existing brains, while synthetic biology forward-engineers living systems from parts; combining them could let researchers build and test wiring diagrams in behaving animals.
ocar.challenge: It is unclear what a designed, constructed connectome would look like, what scientific or societal purposes it would serve, and how it could be built.
ocar.action: Rabinowitch, in Physics of Life Reviews (2020), reviews the idea of synthetic connectomics: artificially designing and constructing connectomes of live behaving organisms as a platform to test theories of network function and possibly new forms of artificial life.
ocar.resolution: The article is a conceptual review rather than a constructed organism: it argues that building a system is a powerful way to understand it, sketches purposes (unifying brain-operation questions; exploring theoretical network predictions empirically), and aims to lay initial implementation steps and contemplate scientific and social impact.
ocar.future_work: The review itself is the proposed research program: methods of construction, design goals, and impact remain prospective.

plain_language_summary: Most brain-wiring research takes animals apart; a complementary idea is to design and build wiring on purpose. This review asks what a synthetic connectome would be for and how one might start making one.

summaries.beginner: Most brain-wiring research takes animals apart; a complementary idea is to design and build wiring on purpose. This review asks what a synthetic connectome would be for and how one might start making one.
summaries.intermediate: In Physics of Life Reviews (2020), Rabinowitch proposes synthetic connectomics as a meeting point of connectomics and synthetic biology: the artificial design and construction of connectomes in live behaving organisms. The piece contrasts reverse-engineering of existing brains with construction-based forward-engineering, and it frames synthetic connectomes as a way to test theoretical predictions about network function and, more speculatively, to generate new forms of artificial life. It is organized around three questions—what such a connectome would look like, what it would be for, and how it could be constructed—and is explicitly a conceptual outline rather than a methods paper with results.
