title: An effective AI integrated system for neuron tracing on anisotropic electron microscopy volume
authors: Jing Liu; Bei Hong; Xi Chen; Qiwei Xie; Yuanyan Tang; Hua Han

ocar.opportunity: Dense EM reconstruction is extremely laborious; sparse neuron tracing from seed masks could recover specific morphologies with less manual work.
ocar.challenge: Sparse reconstruction on highly anisotropic EM volumes is understudied, interlayer context is weak, and misalignment breaks traces in large-scale data.
ocar.action: Liu, Hong, Chen, Xie, Tang, and Han in Biomedical Signal Processing and Control (2021) combine convolutional LSTMs for inter-slice spatial context, a lightweight U-Net for intra-slice cues, recursive training, and a shift-estimation and correction module.
ocar.resolution: They report better performance than other methods on two highly anisotropic datasets, claim a first application of a recurrent network to neuron tracing, and state that shift correction increased traced neuron length.
ocar.future_work: The selected extract does not name the two datasets or quote numeric scores. Dense voxel morphology is not the goal; the system traces from seeds. Recursive training and alignment correction remain engineering choices whose failure modes are not fully described in the truncated PDF text.

plain_language_summary: Following one neuron through a stack of stretched electron-microscope slices is hard when the slices do not line up. This system uses a memory network plus a U-Net, starting from a seed, to keep tracing despite those jumps.

summaries.beginner: Following one neuron through a stack of stretched electron-microscope slices is hard when the slices do not line up. This system uses a memory network plus a U-Net, starting from a seed, to keep tracing despite those jumps.
summaries.intermediate: In Biomedical Signal Processing and Control (2021), Liu, Han and colleagues present an AI system for sparse neuron tracing on anisotropic EM. ConvLSTMs estimate context between adjacent sections, a lightweight U-Net supplies in-plane information, recursive training is used to boost performance, and a shift-estimation module targets misalignment. title: Drosophila gustatory projections are segregated by taste modality and connectivity
authors: S. Engert; Gabriella R. Sterne; D. Bock; Kristin Scott

ocar.opportunity: Gustatory receptor neurons report caloric versus harmful compounds and thereby bound what the brain can use for feeding decisions; their synaptic transmit-and-receive pattern in the adult fly brain was unmapped.
ocar.challenge: Whether labellar axons are organized by taste modality and whether they synapse on one another—as other sensory axons do—was unknown at EM resolution.
ocar.action: Engert, Sterne, Bock, and Scott in eLife (2022) reconstructed 87 gustatory projections from the proboscis labellum in the right hemisphere and 57 in the left of a whole-brain EM volume, clustering them by morphology and connectivity.
ocar.resolution: GRNs have nearly equal interspersed pre- and postsynaptic sites and extensive axon–axon connectivity. Clustering yielded six groups likely corresponding to taste modalities, with the vast majority of synapses within groups. About 39% of GRN input comes from other GRNs, paralleling ORN–ORN connectivity in olfaction.
ocar.future_work: Modality assignments (bitter, candidate low-salt Ir94e, high salt, sugar, water) are anatomical correlations with light-level maps and remain tentative until second-order neurons are identified and physiologically tested. Left and right counts differ; not all labellar axons were reconstructed.

plain_language_summary: Taste cells from the fly’s mouthparts send axons into the brain that talk not only to other cells but also to each other. This reconstruction shows those axons cluster by taste type and mostly synapse within their own group.

summaries.beginner: Taste cells from the fly’s mouthparts send axons into the brain that talk not only to other cells but also to each other. This reconstruction shows those axons cluster by taste type and mostly synapse within their own group.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2022), Engert, Sterne, Bock, and Scott reconstruct the majority of labellar gustatory axons in a whole adult Drosophila EM volume (87 right, 57 left). The editor’s evaluation highlights the match to published functional taste classes via light-level anatomy.

Hemisphere imbalance (87 vs 57) means the map is not fully bilateral. “Majority of labellar gustatory axons” is the authors’ completeness claim. Functional roles of axon–axon synapses (signal enhancement versus dynamic range) are suggested, not measured here.

title: Establishment and Maintenance of Neural Circuit Architecture
authors: Emily L. Heckman; C. Doe

ocar.opportunity: New EM reconstructions, live imaging, omics, and genetics have expanded how we can study both the wiring of circuits and their long-term maintenance.
ocar.challenge: Cellular and subcellular synaptic specificity must be established and then maintained for years while remaining plastic enough for learning, and the molecular rules are still incomplete.
ocar.action: Heckman and Doe review in Journal of Neuroscience (2021) mechanisms of synaptic specificity—chemoaffinity and cell-surface cues, secreted signals, neuron–glia interactions, and activity—and mechanisms of maintenance via ECM, adhesion molecules, scaffolds, and the cytoskeleton.
ocar.resolution: They synthesize how a rigid support network allows synapses to persist, while opposing processes in regions such as hippocampus permit structural modification. Connectomes supply maps of stereotyped and variable connections that ground these principles.
ocar.future_work: The review flags stochastic versus deterministic wiring as an open contrast and asks how establishment/maintenance principles could prevent or restore synapse loss in disease. Those applications are not demonstrated here.

plain_language_summary: Brains must wire the right partners together and then keep those contacts for years without freezing all change. This review walks through the molecular and cellular rules that build and maintain circuits, using connectomes as maps.

summaries.beginner: Brains must wire the right partners together and then keep those contacts for years without freezing all change. This review walks through the molecular and cellular rules that build and maintain circuits, using connectomes as maps.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Neuroscience (February 2021), Heckman and Doe review circuit establishment and maintenance. They start from partner-derived cues for cellular synaptic specificity, revisit chemoaffinity from Langley and Sperry, and incorporate secreted cues, glia, and activity. Maintenance is attributed to ECM, CAMs, intracellular scaffolds, and cytoskeleton, with hippocampal dynamism as a counterexample. EM connectomes of model organisms are cited as providing stereotyped and variable connection maps that let these hypotheses be tested.

title: Neuromuscular connectomes across development reveal synaptic ordering rules
authors: Y. Meirovitch; Kai Kang; R. W. Draft; Elisa C. Pavarino; Maria Fernanda Henao Echeverri; Fuming Yang; Stephen G. Turney; D. Berger; A. Peleg; M. Montero-Crespo; R. Schalek; Ju Lu; J. Livet; J. Tapia; J. Lichtman

ocar.opportunity: Mammalian neuromuscular junctions reorganize after birth from poly-innervation toward Henneman’s size-principle recruitment; a complete wiring view across ages could reveal the ordering rule.
ocar.challenge: Neonatal motor units are large and overlapping, NMJs can be co-innervated by many axons, and some fibers have multiple endplates, so how non-overlapping adult motor units emerge was unclear.
ocar.action: Meirovitch, Kang, Draft, Pavarino, Henao Echeverri, Yang, Turney, Berger, Peleg, Montero-Crespo, Schalek, Lu, Livet, Tapia, and Lichtman post on bioRxiv (2021; this version 10 January 2023) serial-section SEM at birth plus Brainbow and XFP fluorescent reconstructions at later ages.
ocar.resolution: Axons prune about 85% of branches in the first two postnatal weeks, with an about 8-fold reduction in multi-axon NMJs and an about 6-fold reduction in fibers with more than one NMJ. Co-innervation persists longest among neurons nearby in an abstract rank order, likely reflecting activity similarity, and the same ranking governs both local NMJ competition and millimeter-scale contests. At birth no axon was the sole input to any fiber, and >30% of fibers had two or rarely three endplates in this neck muscle.
ocar.future_work: The activity-ranking link is inferred from fiber properties and NMJ distances, not simultaneous motor-unit recordings. Interscutularis is a neck muscle with many dual-endplate fibers; generality to other muscles is not proven in the extract. Ranking at birth is described as subtle because overlap is still high.

plain_language_summary: Baby muscles are wired in a messy many-to-many pattern that later becomes one axon per muscle fiber, recruited from small to large. This team maps that cleanup and finds axons stay partners longest with others that rank near them, probably because they fire similarly.

summaries.beginner: Baby muscles are wired in a messy many-to-many pattern that later becomes one axon per muscle fiber, recruited from small to large. This team maps that cleanup and finds axons stay partners longest with others that rank near them, probably because they fire similarly.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (this extract 10 January 2023), Meirovitch, Lichtman and colleagues reconstruct mouse neuromuscular connectomes at birth (ssSEM), one week, and adult (Brainbow/XFP). They report ~85% axonal branch pruning in two weeks, ~8-fold drop in poly-innervated NMJs, and ~6-fold drop in multi-endplate fibers. Simplification follows a global rank-order co-innervation rule rather than haphazard loss, which they relate to Henneman recruitment. Discussion adds that all motor-unit classes prune, size is already broadly distributed at birth, and co-innervation is graded by motor-unit size rather than a strict fiber-type binary.
summaries.advanced: Percentages in the abstract are the authors’ summary of their reconstructions; the extract does not restate raw axon counts. Rank order is an inferred embedding, not a measured firing-rate sequence. Dual endplates are common in this neck muscle historically; other muscles may differ. Catalog dimension is image-acquisition because of ssSEM, but the scientific payload is developmental graph analysis of connectivity.

title: Leveraging Tools from Autonomous Navigation for Rapid, Robust Neuron Connectivity
authors: Nathan Drenkow; Justin Joyce; Jordan K. Matelsky; Jennifer Heiko; Reem Larabi; Brock Andrew Wester; D. Kleissas; William R. Gray Roncal

ocar.opportunity: Voxel-wise CNN segmentation of terabyte-to-petabyte EM is costly and accumulates merge errors; a cheaper route to the connectivity graph would help labs under schedule and resource limits.
ocar.challenge: Conventional methods label every voxel, are not optimized for graph generation, and are sensitive to alignment and noise when scaled.
ocar.action: Drenkow, Joyce, Matelsky, Heiko, Larabi, Wester, Kleissas, Johnson, and Gray-Roncal post on bioRxiv (2020) a multi-agent path-finding approach: virtual agents with cheap potential-field sensors avoid membranes, find synapses, and share information while traversing 3D volumes.
ocar.resolution: The swarm produces a sparse segmentation of pathways plus connectivity, skeleton similarity, and path length. The authors report meeting or exceeding state-of-the-art performance at substantially lower computational cost, and note CPU parallelizability.
ocar.future_work: Agents miss some small processes and tortuous spine necks; processes that appear disconnected across slices remain hard. Dense morphology needs post-processing. More powerful sensing, learned policies, and transfer to other datasets are proposed. The method is also suggested for bronchial trees or road networks.

plain_language_summary: Instead of painting every pixel as a neuron, this method sends software “robots” through electron-microscope volumes to walk along cells and note synapses, aiming for a wiring graph at lower computer cost.

summaries.beginner: Instead of painting every pixel as a neuron, this method sends software “robots” through electron-microscope volumes to walk along cells and note synapses, aiming for a wiring graph at lower computer cost.

Virtual agents follow local rules on potential fields to avoid membranes and locate synapses, yielding a sparse pathway map and a connectivity graph rather than a dense voxel labeling. title: Multilayer network analysis of C. elegans: Looking into the locomotory circuitry
authors: T. Maertens; E. Schöll; Jorge Ruiz; P. Hövel

ocar.opportunity: Forward locomotion in C. elegans is a tractable behavior whose generating circuit can be studied on a mapped connectome that includes chemical synapses, gap junctions, and peptides.
ocar.challenge: Which neurons belong to the locomotory subnetwork, how their activity becomes traveling muscle waves, and which cells are necessary for coordination were not identified in a multilayer-network plus control-theoretic setting.
ocar.action: Maertens, Schöll, Ruiz, and Hövel (Neurocomputing 2020; this extract is arXiv:2006.08771) build a multilayer network over transmitters and peptides, predict locomotory neurons by logistic regression, simulate Hindmarsh–Rose neurons with leaky-integrator muscles, and apply time-delayed feedback.
ocar.resolution: They predict a locomotory subnetwork, model forward motion as harmonic waves, report a network-based central pattern generator, and show that feedback increases synchronicity. Silencing analyses identify high-impact motor neurons; without silencing, a time-averaged order parameter of 70.1% is the reference, with lower values after silencing groups such as VA12 (60.6% in the figure).
ocar.future_work: Locomotion is simulated, not measured on worms in this extract. The claim that information processing is the same in humans and C. elegans is analogical. Catalog pdf_chars_body is abnormally large, suggesting a messy extract; numbers used here are those visible in the selected text only.

plain_language_summary: The worm’s walking circuit can be drawn as stacked networks of different chemical signals. This modeling paper picks likely walking neurons, simulates their rhythms, and tests which cells, when silenced in the model, break coordinated muscle waves.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s walking circuit can be drawn as stacked networks of different chemical signals. This modeling paper picks likely walking neurons, simulates their rhythms, and tests which cells, when silenced in the model, break coordinated muscle waves.

title: Uncovering the genetic blueprint of the C. elegans nervous system
authors: István A. Kovács; Dániel L. Barabási; A. Barabási
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

ocar.opportunity: Connectomes appear genetically encoded, but a general, experimentally testable map from neuronal expression patterns to wiring rules was missing.
ocar.challenge: Measurement noise, spatial constraints, and combinatorial gene interactions make it hard to invert adjacency matrices into molecular interaction rules.
ocar.action: Kovács, Barabási, and Barabási post on bioRxiv (2020) a connectome model linking the adjacency matrix to neuronal expression, applied first to C. elegans gap junctions.
ocar.resolution: They infer a network of 19 innexin interactions governing gap-junction formation, five of which are already supported by experimental data. The framework is set up to extend to chemical synapses via a directed model B = X O Y and a geometric reading of the wiring-rule matrix O.
ocar.future_work: Chemical-synapse search currently spans the genome; adult transcription-factor expression may not reflect developmental history. plain_language_summary: If each neuron’s gene list is its identity card, there should be rules for which cards are allowed to form a connection. This paper infers such rules for worm gap junctions from wiring plus innexin expression.

title: A developmental framework linking neurogenesis and circuit formation in the Drosophila CNS
authors: Brandon Mark; Sen-Lin Lai; A. Zarin; Laurina Manning; Heather Q. Pollington; Ashok Litwin-Kumar; Albert Cardona; J. Truman; C. Doe

ocar.opportunity: Mechanisms that specify neuronal diversity are well known; whether those same spatial, temporal, and hemilineage programs also specify circuit assembly was unclear.
ocar.challenge: Linking developmental origin to synapse-level connectivity required identifying the same cells in a TEM volume without biasing toward a particular projection pattern.
ocar.action: Mark, Lai, Zarin, Manning, Pollington, Litwin-Kumar, Cardona, Truman, and Doe in eLife (2021) map 160 interneurons from seven bilateral neuroblasts into a synapse-scale TEM reconstruction of the Drosophila larval CNS.

Hemilineage-temporal cohorts share connectivity beyond what proximity predicts. In all lineages examined, NotchON hemilineages projected to dorsal/motor neuropil and NotchOFF to ventral/sensory neuropil.

Testing spatial identity would require duplicating a neuroblast and comparing projections. Catalog year 2019 is the project era; the PDF is eLife 2021.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly nerve-cord cells remember which stem cell they came from, which sister they are, and when they were born. This paper finds those developmental labels still show up in where synapses sit and who talks to whom.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly nerve-cord cells remember which stem cell they came from, which sister they are, and when they were born. This paper finds those developmental labels still show up in where synapses sit and who talks to whom.

Notch-dependent hemilineages split motor versus sensory neuropil targeting; temporal identity refines synapse localization; connectome analysis shows shared connectivity in hemilineage-temporal cohorts that proximity cannot explain. NotchON consistently went dorsal/motor and NotchOFF ventral/sensory in every lineage tested here.

Proximity controls are reported as insufficient; the extract does not quote the statistical test. Catalog year 2019 disagrees with the 2021 publication date on the PDF.

title: GCIB-SEM: A path to 10 nm isotropic imaging of cubic millimeter volumes
authors: K. Hayworth; D. Peale; Michał Januszewski; G. Knott; Z. Lu; C. Xu; H. Hess

ocar.opportunity: Imaging tissue at about 10 nm isotropic voxels over cubic-millimeter scales would let researchers automatically trace whole invertebrate nervous systems and substantial vertebrate regions, including tests of whether memories are stored in structural connectivity.
ocar.challenge: FIB-SEM has the z-resolution needed for automated tracing but a small field of view and is incompatible with ultrafast multibeam SEMs. Diamond-knife section methods can use MultiSEM but struggle to cut tens of thousands of artifact-free thin sections.
ocar.action: Hayworth, Peale, Januszewski, Knott, Lu, Xu, and Hess, on bioRxiv (2019), demonstrate gas cluster ion beam SEM (GCIB-SEM): fewer, much thicker sections are collected, then milled top-down in <10 nm steps and volume-imaged.
ocar.resolution: They acquire <10 nm isotropic stacks of each thick section and stitch them, arguing the method should raise reliability and improve z-resolution by a factor of 3 or more while remaining MultiSEM-compatible. GCIB milling is reported as wide-area and fast (up to 450 µm³/s, 1 mm³/month). MultiSEM images of a GCIB-milled mouse-cortex surface were essentially identical to InLens-SE images of the same surface.
ocar.future_work: InLens-SE membrane contrast drops slightly over the first ~500 nm of milling. The industrial-scale vision of wafers shuttled among GCIB mills and MultiSEM stations is prospective rather than a completed facility.

plain_language_summary: Brain maps at synapse resolution usually force a choice between a tiny, very sharp 3D stack and a large stack that is too coarse in depth. This method mills thick slices in tiny steps so both large area and fine depth become possible.

summaries.beginner: Brain maps at synapse resolution usually force a choice between a tiny, very sharp 3D stack and a large stack that is too coarse in depth. This method mills thick slices in tiny steps so both large area and fine depth become possible.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2019), Hayworth and colleagues introduce GCIB-SEM as a path to <10 nm isotropic imaging of cubic-millimeter volumes. Thick sections are ion-milled top-down and imaged, then stitched, aiming to keep MultiSEM compatibility while avoiding FIB-SEM’s limited field of view. title: Estimating the impact of structural directionality: How reliable are undirected connectomes?
authors: Penelope J. Kale; A. Zalesky; Leonardo L. Gollo

ocar.opportunity: Most chemical synapses are directed, so graph measures of brain networks should in principle respect afferent versus efferent polarity.
ocar.challenge: Human MRI tractography cannot resolve direction, so human connectomes are stored as undirected graphs. It was unclear how that approximation distorts topology.
ocar.action: Kale, Zalesky, and Gollo, in Network Neuroscience (2018), take six directed connectomes (cat, mouse, C. elegans, and three macaque parcellations) and render them undirected by removing unidirectional edges, adding reciprocal edges, or mixing equal numbers of each.
ocar.resolution: Coarse core–periphery assignment remains accurate without direction, but hub identity changes considerably. Adding reciprocal connections (false positives) generally causes larger errors in graph measures than removing the same number of directed connections (false negatives).
ocar.future_work: They argue non-invasive methods should estimate directionality and prefer sparse maps that favor false negatives over false positives. Qualitatively similar topology across directed macaque and undirected human maps suggests resolving human directionality would refine characterization rather than overturn organization.

plain_language_summary: Human brain scans cannot tell which way a fiber points, so maps treat every link as two-way. This paper asks how much that guess scrambles who the hubs are, using animal maps where direction is known.

title: Optimal degrees of synaptic connectivity

ocar.opportunity: Input counts per neuron vary enormously: cerebellar granule cells receive far fewer synapses than Purkinje cells, and insect mushroom bodies show similar divergence, whereas cortex is more uniformly dense.

authors: Xiaolong Jiang; Shan Shen; C. Cadwell; Philipp Berens; Fabian H Sinz; Alexander S. Ecker; Saumil S. Patel; A. Tolias

ocar.action: Jiang, Shen, Cadwell, Berens, Sinz, Ecker, Patel, and Tolias, in Science (2015), combine high-quality adult slices, octuple whole-cell recording, and improved avidin–biotin–peroxidase staining to classify neurons in mouse visual cortex layers 1, 2/3, and 5 and to map connectivity.

title: Focused Proofreading: Efficiently Extracting Connectomes from Segmented EM Images
authors: Stephen M. Plaza

ocar.opportunity: Automatic EM segmentation plus crowd labor could scale connectome tracing beyond tiny brain regions if proofreading were aimed at circuit-critical errors.
ocar.challenge: Unguided manual tracing demands expertise that crowds lack, and automatic segmentation still needs correction. Prior efforts had limited success at scale.
ocar.action: Plaza, on arXiv (2014), proposes focused proofreading: restrict human effort to regions most impactful to the resulting circuit, using biological priors such as synapses, and applies the workflow to a large fly optic-lobe dataset.
ocar.resolution: Reported tracing speedups are 3–5× without sacrificing circuit quality. The task is decomposed into more accessible decisions, argued to improve crowd-sourcing. A figure contrasts expert unguided tracing with novice-focused proofreading plus quality control.
ocar.future_work: Future work should optimize confident intervals, exploit more biological rules, and improve visualization so still more of the workforce can participate.

title: Generation of dense statistical connectomes from sparse morphological data
authors: R. Egger; V. J. Dercksen; D. Udvary; H. Hege; M. Oberlaender

ocar.opportunity: Sensory-evoked flow depends on synaptic innervation probabilities and subcellular input maps, quantities that electrophysiology, light-level overlap, and small EM volumes each capture only in part.
ocar.challenge: Complete local and long-range synaptic in/outputs for every neuron in an entire brain region at subcellular resolution exceed present measurement limits.
ocar.action: Egger, Dercksen, Udvary, Hege, and Oberlaender, in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy (2014), present NeuroNet: integrate sparsely sampled morphologies into an anatomical reference frame, up-scale to an average dense circuit, and measure statistical innervation among all model neurons, illustrated on rat vibrissal cortex.
ocar.resolution: In silico innervation measurements aligned with paired recordings in vitro and in vivo and with light- and electron-microscopic contact reconstructions. The approach implements Peters’ rule in a standardized barrel-cortex geometry without assuming homogeneity at meso/microscopic scales.
ocar.future_work: They consider the method generalizable when the required anatomical data exist, setting the stage for constrained network simulations of sensory-evoked flow. It remains an average statistical connectome, not an instance-specific EM wiring diagram.

title: The Viking viewer for connectomics: scalable multi-user annotation and summarization of large volume data sets
authors: James R. Anderson; Shoeb Mohammed; B. Grimm; Bryan William Jones; Pavel A. Koshevoy; T. Tasdizen; T. Tasdizen; R. Whitaker; R. E. Marc

ocar.opportunity: Automated microscopy now yields terabyte-scale anatomical volumes that must be viewed, annotated, and summarized by many people if connectomes are to be mined.
ocar.challenge: Storage, access, concurrent annotation, and on-the-fly transforms exceed single-user desktop tools. Annotated volumes are expensive and should be community-accessible.
ocar.action: Anderson, Mohammed, Grimm, Jones, Koshevoy, Tasdizen, Whitaker, and Marc, in Journal of Microscopy (2011), present Viking, an HTTP multi-user viewer/annotator built for a 16.5 TB ultrastructural retinal connectome (RC1; about 341,000 images at 16 megapixels) and demonstrated on AII amacrine networks.
ocar.resolution: Viking supports many concurrent users over HTTP, collaborative annotation, separation of viewing from hosting, real-time transforms, and an extensible UI. ocar.future_work: They deferred dependence on automated tracing because generating the primary dataset was already hard; proofreading semi-automated markup can be nearly as slow as manual markup. Fine oblique amacrine processes and synapse orientations remain hard for automation.

title: Connectome-seq: high-throughput mapping of neuronal connectivity at single-synapse resolution via barcode sequencing.
authors: Danping Chen; Alina Isakova; Zhou Wan; M. Wagner; Yunming Wu; B. Zhao

ocar.opportunity: Sequencing-based connectivity mapping could scale to long-distance mammalian circuits while keeping cell-type gene expression, a combination electron microscopy struggles to provide across regions.
ocar.challenge: ssEM does not easily span distant regions with molecular identity. Prior barcode methods (SYNseq, Sindbis, rabies) faced joining failures, missing postsynaptic partners, barcode mixing, or toxicity.

title: From the fly connectome to exact ring attractor dynamics
authors: Tirthabir Biswas; Angel Stanoev; S. Romani; James E. Fitzgerald

ocar.opportunity: Fly head-direction connectomes now constrain models of the cognitive compass, so theory can be required to match both architecture and continuous attractor function.
ocar.challenge: Canonical ring attractors assume idealized symmetry and hand-set weights that conflict with biological variability and multiple cell types in real connectomes.
ocar.action: Biswas, Stanoev, Romani, and Fitzgerald, on bioRxiv (posted 2026; DOI 10.1101/2024.11.01.621596), build multipopulation continuous-attractor models in which compass neurons with local mutual excitation couple to inhibitory neurons, then match four available fly connectomes.
ocar.resolution: They describe a ring-attractor class with weaker symmetry than usual. For each of four fly connectomes they find three distinct realizations. Synaptic variation among and around those connectomes can be compensated by cell-type-specific weight rescaling, possibly via neuromodulation. Velocity-drive analysis in the supplement relates encoded angular speed to drive, noting flies in darkness track head direction only proportionally.
ocar.future_work: Additional sensory cues may be needed to calibrate the proportionality factor for precise angular tracking. The design principle linking synapse-resolution connectivity to computation is proposed rather than proven in behaving animals in this extract.

title: Volumetric denoising enables high-throughput volume electron microscopy and efficient downstream analysis.
authors: Bohao Chen; Fangfang Wang; Haoyu Wang; Yanchao Zhang; Zhuangzhuang Zhao; Haoran Chen; Hua Han; Xi Chen; Yunfeng Hua

ocar.opportunity: Volume EM throughput is set by voxel size and dwell time. If noise can be removed after fast imaging, microscopes could cut thinner and finish larger volumes.
ocar.challenge: Datasets are often acquired slowly at high dose because downstream analysis needs clean images. Axial undersampling from thick cuts hurts 3D structure more than many realize.
ocar.action: Chen, Wang, Han, Chen, Hua and colleagues, in Cell Reports Methods (2026), search acquisition conditions, compare restoration methods including a new 3D context-based self-supervised denoiser, and test serial block-face cutting.
ocar.resolution: Sufficient spatial sampling outweighed high SNR for preserving 3D information. Volumetric denoising beat axial interpolation and 2D denoising for faithful recovery, improved organelle and synapse segmentation, and enabled SBF cutting down to 20 nm (they cite a prior practical limit of 25 nm). Effective XZ resolution after denoising scaled linearly with cutting thickness (R² = 0.994). Volumetric versus 2D continuity gains appeared only for slice thickness under 75 nm.
ocar.future_work: Tissue-specific calibration of the “comfort zone” of acquisition parameters may be required. They frame the work as optimizing acquisition with AI, not only post hoc beautification. Hybrid snapshot/reference-frame routines are proposed.

plain_language_summary: Taking electron-microscope pictures slowly makes them look cleaner but limits how much brain you can image. This team shows that keeping thin slices and then denoising the 3D stack can be better than shooting slowly.

title: Biological Processing Units: Leveraging an Insect Connectome to Pioneer Biofidelic Neural Architectures
authors: Siyu Yu; Zihan Qin; Tingshan Liu; Beiya Xu; R. J. Vogelstein; Jason Brown; J. Vogelstein

ocar.opportunity: A complete Drosophila larval connectome is a compact, evolutionarily selected circuit that might serve as a fixed recurrent substrate for machine-learning tasks.
ocar.challenge: Artificial models often need heavy compute and tuning. It was unknown whether an unmodified biological wiring diagram could support vision-like and strategic tasks.
ocar.action: Yu, Qin, Liu, Xu, Vogelstein, Brown, and Vogelstein, on arXiv (2025), convert the larval wiring diagram into a Biological Processing Unit (BPU)—a fixed recurrent network from synaptic connectivity—and test MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ChessBench, including GNN-BPU and CNN-BPU variants.
ocar.resolution: With about 3,000 neurons and 65,000 weights, the unmodified BPU reached 98% on MNIST and 58% on CIFAR-10, beating size-matched MLPs. A GNN-BPU trained on 10,000 chess games reached 60% move accuracy, described as nearly 10× better than any-size transformer in their comparison. CNN-BPU models with ~2M parameters beat parameter-matched transformers; with depth-6 minimax search, puzzle accuracy reached 91.7% (91.71% in the figure discussion), exceeding a 9M-parameter transformer baseline.
ocar.future_work: They avoided rewiring to isolate intrinsic capacity; task-specific rescaling or constrained plasticity is proposed. Sensory ablations are incomplete as motif-level explanations. The larva is only hours post-hatching; scaling to adult fly or human connectomes is left open.

plain_language_summary: A baby fruit fly’s complete wiring diagram is small but evolved. This team freezes that wiring as a computer network and finds it can classify pictures and help solve chess puzzles surprisingly well.

ocar.challenge: Without a shared morphological bridge, synaptic rules of transcriptomic Sst types cannot be read out in EM volumes.

ocar.resolution: Martinotti cells classified into Sst MET-types with distinct myelination and synaptic output patterns. Predicted MET-8, MET-4, and MET-6 use different inhibition motifs (near-complete targeting of a preferred neighbor type; sparse targeting of all types; sparse targeting except a preferred local type). Findings align with paired-recording connection probabilities and with most Sst connections onto excitatory targets within a 200 µm lateral distance. Blanket inhibition of L4 pyramids is seen from MET-8, not as a universal Sst rule.
ocar.future_work: Differentially expressed adhesion genes (e.g. Cdh12, Pcdh8) are hypothesized to help set morphology and connectivity. Synapse size versus number differences (MET-8 versus MET-6) invite homeostatic interpretations that are not proven here.

plain_language_summary: Gene labels and electron-microscope wiring usually live in different experiments. This study matches cell shapes so somatostatin inhibitory types from Patch-seq can be found in a huge EM volume, revealing that they do not all inhibit the same way.

summaries.advanced: MET-type assignment is morphological prediction, not in-EM transcriptomics. “Nearly 100% of the neighbouring preferred cell type” for MET-8 is the authors’ summary of a motif, not a tabled percentage in the selected extract. title: Reconstruction of a connectome of single neurons in mouse brains by cross-validating multi-scale multi-modality data
authors: Feng Xiong; Lijuan Liu; Hanchuan Peng

ocar.opportunity: Single-cell morphometry now covers tens of thousands of mouse neurons registered to a common atlas, inviting whole-brain connection maps of individual projection cells rather than only regional projectomes.
ocar.challenge: EM synapses are local; mesoscale viral tracing averages populations. Inferring brain-wide single-neuron connectivity from morphology requires complementary, cross-validated pairing rules.
ocar.action: Xiong, Liu, and Peng, in Nature Methods (2025), build an arbor-net by probabilistically pairing dendritic and axonal arbors of 20,247 atlas-registered neurons and a bouton-net from 2.57 million putative boutons on 1,877 fully reconstructed neurons, then cross-validate and assemble SEU-net.
ocar.resolution: Arbor-net and bouton-net agreed on spatially and anatomically modular connection distributions matching functional modules. Single-neuron connections correlated more strongly with gene co-expression than a prior mesoscale mouse connectome. Network analysis found non-random triad motifs. Results were also checked against viral-tracing and barcoding connectomes and a synaptome of relative synapse density.
ocar.future_work: They acknowledge EM of specific regions would further verify predicted synapses. Building mammalian EM connectomes from scratch is treated as impractical relative to this verification path. Axonal varicosities are argued to complement spatial adjacency.

plain_language_summary: Most “whole-brain” mouse maps average many cells in a region. This resource estimates which individual reconstructed neurons could connect across the brain by pairing axons with dendrites and with axonal boutons.

summaries.beginner: Most “whole-brain” mouse maps average many cells in a region. This resource estimates which individual reconstructed neurons could connect across the brain by pairing axons with dendrites and with axonal boutons.

summaries.advanced: Connections are probabilistic pairings, not EM-confirmed synapses. Boutons are putative. Correlation with gene co-expression is reported as stronger than a prior mesoscale connectome without a coefficient in the selected extract. Catalog dimension is graph-analysis.

title: A generative model of the connectome with dynamic axon growth
authors: Yuanzhe Liu; Caio Seguin; Richard F. Betzel; Danyal Akarca; M. D. Di Biase; Andrew Zalesky

ocar.opportunity: Generative network models of the human connectome can encode wiring principles, but they usually skip the physical process of axonal growth.
ocar.challenge: Without explicit growth cones, models cannot speak to axon guidance or fascicle geometry even when they match graph statistics.
ocar.action: Liu, Seguin, Betzel, Akarca, Di Biase, and Zalesky, on bioRxiv (2024), introduce a geometry-only generative model in which axons steer by distance-dependent chemoattractive forces on growth cones, then fit parameters to individual connectomes.
ocar.resolution: The mechanism produced axonal bundles with brain-like geometry and human-like complex-network features: lognormal weights, scale-free degrees, small-worldness, and modularity. Parameters support dimensionality reduction and group comparison; the author summary states sensitivity to subtle interindividual differences among healthy adults.
ocar.future_work: The selected extract’s latter portion is references rather than a limitations paragraph. Bridging axon-guidance experiments and macroscopic connectomes is presented as an opportunity, not a completed multiscale validation.

plain_language_summary: Most computer models of brain networks add links by abstract rules, not by growing axons. This model lets simulated growth cones follow chemical attraction and still ends up with brain-like bundles and network statistics.

summaries.beginner: Most computer models of brain networks add links by abstract rules, not by growing axons. This model lets simulated growth cones follow chemical attraction and still ends up with brain-like bundles and network statistics.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2024), Liu, Zalesky and colleagues emulate chemoaffinity-guided axonal growth in a generative connectome model. Despite depending only on geometry, it yields brain-like fascicles and topological features (lognormal weights, scale-free degrees, small-worldness, modularity) and can be fitted to individual human connectomes.
summaries.advanced: “Scale-free” and related features are claimed as consistent with the human brain; the extract does not quote fitted exponents. The PDF body after the author summary is largely bibliography, so quantitative fit errors are not available here. This is a diffusion/tractography-scale generative model, not EM growth reconstruction.

title: Asymmetry in synaptic connectivity balances redundancy and reachability in the Caenorhabditis elegans connectome
authors: Varun Sanjay Birari; I. Rabinowitch

ocar.opportunity: Bilateral symmetry can add robustness, while asymmetry can allow parallel processing and specialization; a complete pair-wise neuron-class connectome lets that tradeoff be measured.
ocar.challenge: How nervous systems balance symmetry and asymmetry at the level of synaptic partners was unclear even in C. elegans.
ocar.action: Birari and Rabinowitch, in iScience (2024), analyze the C. elegans connectome’s 99 bilaterally symmetrical neuron classes, comparing partner counts versus partner identities, and define graph metrics of Redundancy (multiple alternative synapses reinforcing a path) and Reachability (extent and diversity of each class’s connectivity).
ocar.resolution: Partner numbers are symmetric between left–right class members, but partner identities are markedly asymmetric. Redundancy and Reachability are stochastically tunable by asymmetry level; the worm connectome favors Redundancy over Reachability.
ocar.future_work: Weights (count or efficacy) and signs (E/I) were not included, because pairing and weighted redundancy are ill-defined until those data are complete.

plain_language_summary: Worms look left–right symmetric, but their synaptic partners often are not the same cells on each side. This paper shows that leftover asymmetry can be tuned so backup paths win out over reaching as many different partners as possible.

summaries.beginner: Worms look left–right symmetric, but their synaptic partners often are not the same cells on each side. This paper shows that leftover asymmetry can be tuned so backup paths win out over reaching as many different partners as possible.
summaries.intermediate: In iScience (2024), Birari and Rabinowitch study 99 bilateral neuron classes in the C. elegans connectome. Synapse counts match across the midline, but partner identity does not. Graph metrics show redundancy versus reachability trade off with asymmetry; the empirical connectome prefers redundancy.
summaries.advanced: Redundancy and Reachability are author-defined metrics. The study uses unweighted, unsigned chemical-synapse graphs as stated in Limitations. Stochastic tunability is from symmetrized/desymmetrized simulations described in STAR Methods, not fully numeric in the selected extract.

title: Comparative connectomics of dauer reveals developmental plasticity
authors: Hyunsoo Yim; Daniel T. Choe; J. Bae; Myung-Kyu Choi; Hae-Mook Kang; Ken C. Q. Nguyen; Soungyub Ahn; Sang-kyu Bahn; Heeseung Yang; David H. Hall; Jinseop S. Kim; Junho Lee

ocar.opportunity: Dauer is an alternative C. elegans life stage with distinct behaviors (including nictation), so its chemical connectome can show how far a nervous system rewires under harsh conditions.
ocar.challenge: How flexibly neuronal connections change across development, and specifically in dauer versus other stages, was unknown at synapse resolution.
ocar.action: Yim, Choe, Bae, Kim, Lee and colleagues, in Nature Communications (2024), volumetrically reconstruct the dauer chemical connectome and detect synapses with a deep-learning pipeline (Cnapse), then compare graph structure with other stages.
ocar.resolution: Overall architecture is preserved, but structural changes track connectivity changes tied to dauer behaviors such as nictation (previously linked to IL2). Graph analyses show dauer-specific sensory rewiring and increased clustering among motor neurons. EM, segmentation, and synapses are in BossDB (yim_choe_bae2023); code on GitHub.
ocar.future_work: Connection similarity and conserved-edge analyses average across adult specimens versus dauer. The extract’s later pages are methods for those metrics rather than additional biological claims.

plain_language_summary: When food is scarce, a worm can pause as a hardy dauer larva with special behaviors. This team mapped that stage’s synapses and found the same overall nerve plan with important local rewiring.

summaries.beginner: When food is scarce, a worm can pause as a hardy dauer larva with special behaviors. This team mapped that stage’s synapses and found the same overall nerve plan with important local rewiring.

title: Discovering motifs to fingerprint multi-layer networks: a case study on the connectome of C. Elegans
authors: D. Sharma; Matthias Renz; Philipp Hövel
journal: European Physical Journal B : Condensed Matter Physics

ocar.opportunity: Small recurrent subgraphs (motifs) can fingerprint how a nervous system is organized, including when connections sit in separate molecular layers rather than a single mixed graph.
ocar.challenge: The C. elegans connectome is multi-layer (gap junctions plus chemically distinct synapses), so motif counts on an aggregated graph can hide layer-specific structure, and random graphs of the same size and density are needed as a null.
ocar.action: Sharma, Renz, and Hövel, in European Physical Journal B (2024), apply the ESCAPE subgraph-counting algorithm to 3-, 4-, and 5-node motifs in individual layers, the aggregated network, and the locomotory circuit, comparing counts to an ensemble of 1000 random networks with matched node and link counts.
ocar.resolution: For almost all layers and motif types, motif occurrence cannot be explained by the random model. Wedges, closed-path motifs (triangles, 4- and 5-cycles), and hub-and-spoke stars are abundant; 4-cycles and diamonds recur across layers. 3-path and 4-path motifs are insignificant in the electrical and GABA layers, and 4- and 5-cliques are less prominent.
ocar.future_work: The authors propose fingerprinting other empirical networks, swapping in different null models, using motif composition to inform generative simulations, and counting motifs whose links sit in different layers so cross-layer pathways become visible.

plain_language_summary: The worm C. elegans has a complete wiring diagram that can be split by synapse type. This paper counts small repeating wiring patterns in each layer and shows that most of those patterns are not what you would get from a random network of the same size.

summaries.beginner: The worm C. elegans has a complete wiring diagram that can be split by synapse type. This paper counts small repeating wiring patterns in each layer and shows that most of those patterns are not what you would get from a random network of the same size.
summaries.intermediate: In European Physical Journal B (2024), Sharma, Renz, and Hövel use ESCAPE to count 3-, 4-, and 5-node motifs in the multi-layer C. elegans connectome, including electrical and transmitter-specific synaptic layers, the aggregated graph, and the locomotory circuit. Significance is judged against 1000 density-matched random networks. They report conserved wedge motifs (shared regulators), closed-path motifs consistent with feedback, and hub-and-spoke stars, while 3-path and 4-path motifs fail to characterize the electrical and GABA layers and fully connected 4- and 5-cliques are relatively rare.
summaries.advanced: Significance is relative to Erdős–Rényi-style random graphs of matched size and density, not degree-preserving or spatial nulls; the authors themselves flag other null classes as future work. Motif names (wedge, diamond, clique) are graph-theoretic, not physiological identifications. Counts of more complex 5-node motifs drop in small layers, so absence can reflect size. The extract’s discussion does not report a single numeric enrichment score for the whole connectome.

title: EM-Compressor: Electron Microscopy Image Compression in Connectomics with Variational Autoencoders
authors: Yicong Li; C. Park; Daniel Xenes; Caitlyn Bishop; Daniel R. Berger; A. Samuel; Brock Andrew Wester; J. Lichtman; Hanspeter Pfister; Wanhua Li; Y. Meirovitch

ocar.opportunity: Connectomic EM volumes are already petabyte-scale and heading toward exascale whole-mouse collections, so storage and transfer are becoming a bottleneck even as imaging and analysis improve.
ocar.challenge: Standard codecs such as AVIF and JPEG2000 introduce merge and split errors in membrane and instance segmentation as compression increases, so a method must shrink data without destroying features used for tracing.
ocar.action: Li, Park, Xenes, Bishop, Berger, Samuel, Wester, Lichtman, Pfister, Li, and Meirovitch present EM-Compressor on bioRxiv (2024): variational autoencoders trained on human cortical EM (H01) plus a cloud visualization app.
ocar.resolution: On H01 they report compression to as little as 1/128th of the original size without significantly compromising subsequent segmentation, outperforming standard size-reduction methods at 16×, 32×, and 64× in qualitative membrane and instance tests. In VAE feature space, larger spatial resolution is generally more favorable than more channels for high-fidelity neural segmentation.
ocar.future_work: They suggest 3D VAEs or segmentation-optimized models for still higher rates, but warn that volumetric VAEs may not suit all connectomics applications because of the need for near-perfect 3D alignment.

plain_language_summary: Brain electron-microscope movies are so large that storing them is becoming a problem. This team trains a neural compressor that can shrink human cortex images to as little as one 128th of the original size while still allowing computers to find cell membranes.

summaries.beginner: Brain electron-microscope movies are so large that storing them is becoming a problem. This team trains a neural compressor that can shrink human cortex images to as little as one 128th of the original size while still allowing computers to find cell membranes.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2024), Li and colleagues introduce EM-Compressor, a VAE-based codec evaluated on the H01 human EM volume. They report reduction to as little as 1/128th of original size without significantly harming later segmentation, and qualitative comparisons at 16×, 32×, and 64× against AVIF and JPEG2000, which increasingly produce merge and split errors. A cloud app supports on-the-fly visualization. They also report that, in VAE feature space, larger spatial resolution tends to beat more channels for segmentation fidelity.
summaries.advanced: The 1/128 figure is the most aggressive rate claimed; the extract’s qualitative figure uses 16×–64×. Segmentation quality is described as not significantly compromised rather than as a single F-score. Evaluation is on H01 human cortex, not whole-mouse or fly volumes. Volumetric extension is explicitly cautioned against where 3D alignment must stay near-perfect. The work is a preprint.

title: Nanoscale Connectomics Annotation Standards Framework
authors: Nicole K. Guittari; Miguel E. Wimbish; Patricia K. Rivlin; Mark A. Hinton; Jordan K. Matelsky; Victoria A. Rose; Jorge L. Rivera; Nicole Stock; Brock Andrew Wester; Erik C. Johnson; William Gray-Roncal

ocar.challenge: Without community standards that make volumetric annotations FAIR, costly datasets risk being underused as they grow past petascale and pipelines remain siloed.

ocar.resolution: The stated goal is interoperable annotation management that supports collaboration, more reliable findings, and comparative analysis across species and modalities, considering existing community approaches to neuronal entities, biological components, and metadata.
ocar.future_work: The abstract frames the working group as identifying gaps and refining platforms; it does not report an adopted schema or a completed standard.

plain_language_summary: Huge electron-microscope and X-ray brain maps are expensive to make, and they are hard to reuse if every lab stores labels differently. This paper sketches a shared standards plan so those labels can be found, shared, and compared across tools and species.

title: Recurrent connections enable point attractor dynamics and dimensionality reduction in a connectome-constrained model of the insect learning center
authors: Justin Joyce; Raphael Norman-Tenazas; Patricia K. Rivlin; Grace M. Hwang; Isaac Western; Kechen Zhang; William Gray-Roncal; Brian S. Robinson

ocar.opportunity: The fly mushroom body’s Kenyon cells now have a complete synapse-level wiring map, so theoretical point-attractor models of recurrent memory can be tested on real recurrent excitation rather than invented weights.
ocar.challenge: The computational role of Kenyon-cell to Kenyon-cell recurrence has been unclear, and detailed recurrent connectivity in biological populations is usually unknown, so it has been hard to say whether attractor theory maps onto this circuit.
ocar.action: Joyce, Norman-Tenazas, Rivlin, Hwang, Western, Zhang, Gray-Roncal, and Robinson, on bioRxiv (2024), build a connectome-constrained rate model of the mushroom body (ORN→PN→KC, APL, MBON, and KC→KC) from a public hemibrain-style connectome via neuPrint, keeping only connections with more than five synapses inside the mushroom body.
ocar.resolution: Recurrent excitation is highly symmetric and balanced with feedforward input. In simulations it facilitates dimensionality reduction and allows a small set of self-sustaining point-attractor states. The authors sweep recurrent strength to map dynamical regimes and discuss possible functional implications.
ocar.future_work: They suggest the observed relationship between mushroom-body recurrence and point-attractor properties as a base model for comparison with recurrent circuits in other organisms. Reciprocal KC contacts at convergent/rosette synapses were omitted because it is unknown whether activation can propagate there; PN→ORN and MBON→KC feedback were omitted as 1.3% and 1.5% of feedforward synapse counts.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly learning cells talk to each other as well as to the next layer. This team builds a computer model from the real wiring map and finds that those extra loops can shrink the activity pattern and hold a few stable “memories.”

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly learning cells talk to each other as well as to the next layer. This team builds a computer model from the real wiring map and finds that those extra loops can shrink the activity pattern and hold a few stable “memories.”
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2024), Joyce and colleagues constrain a mushroom-body network model with synapse counts among ORNs, PNs, Kenyon cells, APL, and MBONs from a public connectome (neuPrint), excluding connections with five or fewer synapses in the mushroom body. They report that Kenyon-cell recurrent excitation is highly symmetric and balanced with feedforward input, that it enables dimensionality reduction and a compact set of self-sustaining point attractors, and that varying recurrent strength explores a range of dynamical regimes.

Rosette reciprocal KC synapses and weak PN→ORN / MBON→KC feedback are omitted by design. The extract’s selected text cuts into methods, so quantitative attractor counts and dimensionality numbers are those stated in the abstract rather than tabulated here. The work is a preprint.

title: Social state alters vision using three circuit mechanisms in Drosophila
authors: Catherine E. Schretter; Tom Hindmarsh Sten; Nathan C Klapoetke; M. Shao; Aljoscha Nern; M. Dreher; Daniel Bushey; A. Robie; Adam L. Taylor; Kristin M. Branson; Adriane G. Otopalik; Vanessa Ruta; G. Rubin

ocar.opportunity: Flies must prioritize nearby flies during social behavior, and a connectome can nominate circuit motifs that retune vision when internal state changes.
ocar.challenge: Feature-detecting visual neurons are well mapped, but how attention shifts with goals is much less known, and candidate state-dependent motifs need causal tests.
ocar.action: Schretter, Hindmarsh Sten, Klapoetke, Shao, Nern, Dreher, Bushey, Robie, Taylor, Branson, Otopalik, Ruta, and Rubin, in Nature (2024), use the connectome to identify three motifs poised to change an aggressive female’s response to fly-sized objects, then test them with cell-type-specific genetics, behavior, and physiology; they also examine related circuitry in courting males.
ocar.resolution: The three motifs—convergence of excitatory visual-feature and internal-state inputs, dendritic disinhibition of select feature detectors, and a switch that toggles between two feature detectors—are each used during female aggression. aIPg is the primary sexually dimorphic neuron in the described circuits; LC, lobula interneurons, IB112, and TuTuA are morphologically similar in both sexes. TuTuA activity in males tracking a fictive female, plus the male optic-lobe connectome, suggest the same toggle operates across sexes.
ocar.future_work: The authors argue that multiple motifs give more degrees of freedom for attending to different visual features; mapping how each motif gates distinct motor programs is the implied next step.

plain_language_summary: When a fruit fly is aggressive or courting, it needs to pay extra attention to other flies. This Nature paper uses the wiring diagram to find three circuit tricks that retune vision, then shows they actually work in behaving flies.

summaries.beginner: When a fruit fly is aggressive or courting, it needs to pay extra attention to other flies. This Nature paper uses the wiring diagram to find three circuit tricks that retune vision, then shows they actually work in behaving flies.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2024), Schretter and colleagues start from the Drosophila connectome and identify three state-dependent motifs that could modify responses to fly-sized visual objects: excitatory convergence of visual and internal-state inputs, dendritic disinhibition of feature detectors, and a toggle between two feature detectors. Cell-type-specific tools, behavior, and physiology show each motif is used in female aggression, and features of the toggle also operate in male courtship pursuit. They highlight aIPg as the main sexually dimorphic cell in these circuits.
summaries.advanced: The claim that the same toggle operates across sexes rests on male TuTuA recordings during fictive tracking plus male optic-lobe connectome analysis, not a full repeat of the female aggression suite in males. Motif “use” is demonstrated for identified cell types in the extract, not as a brain-wide attention census. The paper is a compelling example of connectome-guided circuit breaking; quantitative synaptic weights and full stimulus sets live in figures not fully captured here.

title: Tango-seq: overlaying transcriptomics on connectomics to identify neurons downstream of Drosophila clock neurons
authors: Alison Ehrlich; Angelina A. Xu; S. Luminari; S. Kidd; C. Treiber; Jordan Russo; Justin Blau

ocar.opportunity: Genetic circuit tracing could overlay cell identity from single-cell sequencing onto synaptic partners, at throughput that electron microscopy cannot match for plasticity or mutants.
ocar.challenge: EM connectomes are snapshots of one brain, undercount fine neurites, and omit gap junctions and neuromodulation, so they are impractical for asking how connections change over 24 hours or across individuals.
ocar.action: Ehrlich, Xu, Luminari, Kidd, Treiber, Russo, and Blau, on bioRxiv (2024), modify trans-Tango with adult-restricted nuclear reporters so neurons downstream of Drosophila s-LNv clock cells can be purified and sequenced (Tango-seq).
ocar.resolution: s-LNvs preferentially synapse onto a subset of CNMa+ DN1p clock neurons, connections they interpret as likely plastic, and they also find synapses onto mushroom-body Kenyon cells, including a discussion of γ-KC links. The combination supports prior s-LNv→DN2 and s-LNv→DN1p anatomy while adding target specificity.
ocar.future_work: Open questions include the molecular code for choosing CNMa+ DN1ps if the connection is made and broken daily, and whether s-LNv→γ-KC synapses explain circadian rhythms in memory. They recommend adult-restricted trans-Tango ligand expression as part of the toolkit.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope wiring maps cannot easily show how a fly’s connections change from day to night. This team tags cells downstream of clock neurons, sequences them, and finds preferred partners among other clock cells and learning-center cells.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope wiring maps cannot easily show how a fly’s connections change from day to night. This team tags cells downstream of clock neurons, sequences them, and finds preferred partners among other clock cells and learning-center cells.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2024), Ehrlich and colleagues introduce Tango-seq: adult-restricted trans-Tango labeling of neurons synaptically downstream of Drosophila s-LNv clock neurons, followed by nuclear-reporter purification and single-cell sequencing. They report preferential connections to a subset of CNMa+ DN1p neurons, interpreted as likely plastic, and connections to mushroom-body Kenyon cells. They contrast genetic tracing with EM’s single-brain snapshot, synapse undercounting, and lack of gap-junction or neuromodulatory links.
summaries.advanced: Trans-Tango reports proximity/ligand-dependent labeling, not a complete EM-grade synapse census; false partners and missed partners remain possible. “Likely plastic” is an interpretation tied to known s-LNv rhythms, not a time-series connectome in this extract. Sequencing identifies transcriptomic types among labeled cells; quantitative synapse counts versus hemibrain are not given here. The work is a preprint. Flies were raised at 25°C rather than the 18°C sometimes used for strongest trans-Tango, a methods choice noted by the authors.

title: Tracing nerve fibers with volume electron microscopy to quantitatively analyze brain connectivity
authors: M. Turégano-Lopez; Félix de las Pozas; Andrea Santuy; José-Rodrigo Rodríguez; Javier DeFelipe; Á. Merchán-Pérez

title: Mechanosensory and command contributions to the Drosophila grooming sequence
authors: Shingo Yoshikawa; Paul Tang; J. Simpson

ocar.opportunity: A ventral nerve cord connectome can explain why stimulating particular thoracic bristles recruits hind-leg grooming and why the thorax is last in the grooming hierarchy.

ocar.future_work: The full behavioral repertoire of notum bristles remains unknown; linking UMGT1 to specific competing sensory channels in intact flies is the natural next test.

title: A graph network model for neural connection prediction and connection strength estimation
authors: Ye Yuan; Jian Liu; Peng Zhao; Wei Wang; Xiao Gu; Yi Rong; Tinggeng Lai; Yuze Chen; Kuankuan Xin; Xin Niu; Fengtao Xiang; H. Huo; Zhaoyu Li; T. Fang

title: Dynamic Functional Connectivity in the Static Connectome of C. elegans
authors: S. Flavell; A. Gordus

ocar.resolution: They argue that dynamic coupling lets multiple behavioral states live in a physically stereotyped connectome, with serotonin, dopamine, and more than 200 neuropeptides as a large modulatory overlay. title: Scalable Biologically-Aware Skeleton Generation for Connectomic Volumes
authors: Brian Matejek; Tim Franzmeyer; D. Wei; Xueying Wang; Jinglin Zhao; K. Palágyi; J. Lichtman; H. Pfister

title: The synaptic organization in the C. elegans neural network suggests significant local compartmentalized computations
authors: Rotem Ruach; Nir Ratner; S. W. Emmons; Alon Zaslaver

Interneurons are the primary cells implementing local compartmentalized activity, consistent with prior imaging.
ocar.future_work: Functional tests of the proposed local computations remain to be done at the scale of the statistical motifs; several cited studies already show compartmentalized activity in identified interneurons.

ocar.opportunity: Hourglass analysis asks whether a few intermediate nodes mediate paths from many inputs to many outputs; adding synapse weights could change which neurons look like the waist of the C. elegans connectome.
ocar.challenge: Unweighted hourglass methods can miss pathways that are heavily used, and male versus hermaphrodite connectomes plus older versus newer edge sets disagree on core nodes.
ocar.action: Batta, Yao, Sabrin, and Dovrolis, in PLOS ONE (2021), develop a weighted hourglass framework (multi-edge transformation, MET) and apply it to hermaphrodite and male C. elegans structural connectomes, comparing MET with unweighted analysis (UNW) and datasets from White-era maps versus Cook et al. weighted maps.
ocar.resolution: Weighted analysis yields a smaller core and a more visible hourglass than unweighted analysis. Most core nodes in the male concentrate in sex organs, versus the head in the hermaphrodite. Unweighted metrics are higher on the older dataset than on Cook et al.’s unweighted graphs, consistent with added edges being weaker; weighted MET metrics behave differently.
ocar.future_work: They argue that ignoring weights hides network patterns; applying the same weighted hourglass to other connectomes is the natural extension.

plain_language_summary: In a worm, many sensors and muscles might talk through a small set of in-between cells, like sand in an hourglass. This paper counts those paths using synapse size and number, and finds different “waist” cells in males and hermaphrodites.

summaries.beginner: In a worm, many sensors and muscles might talk through a small set of in-between cells, like sand in an hourglass. This paper counts those paths using synapse size and number, and finds different “waist” cells in males and hermaphrodites.
summaries.intermediate: In PLOS ONE (2021), Batta, Yao, Sabrin, and Dovrolis introduce a weighted hourglass-analysis framework and apply it to C. elegans. Compared with unweighted analysis, the weighted (MET) core is smaller and hourglass scores are stronger. Male cores concentrate in sex organs; hermaphrodite cores in the head. Differences versus the White et al. unweighted hermaphrodite map and Cook et al. weighted/unweighted sexed connectomes are discussed, including weaker extra edges reducing unweighted hourglass strength.

Core membership depends on path-weight definitions in MET versus UNW; it is not a unique neuronal “bottleneck” list. Hourglass metrics (H-score, cumulative path coverage) are plotted in figures; exact numeric H-scores are not copied from the extract. Functional use of core neurons is not measured here.

title: Multi-scale light microscopy/electron microscopy neuronal imaging from brain to synapse with a tissue clearing method, ScaleSF
authors: T. Furuta; Kenta Yamauchi; Shinichiro Okamoto; Megumu Takahashi; S. Kakuta; Yoko Ishida; Aya Takenaka; Atsushi Yoshida; Y. Uchiyama; Masato Koike; Kaoru Isa; Tadashi Isa; H. Hioki

ocar.opportunity: A glutaraldehyde-resistant clearing method would let the same labeled neurons be imaged from whole-brain light microscopy down to EM synapses.
ocar.challenge: Standard clearing is poorly compatible with EM fixation, and rare synaptic contacts are hard to find without multi-scale targeting.
ocar.action: Furuta, Yamauchi, Okamoto, Takahashi, Kakuta, Ishida, Takenaka, Yoshida, Uchiyama, Koike, Isa, Isa, and Hioki, in iScience (2021), introduce ScaleSF and successive LM/EM imaging, demonstrated on mouse striatofugal, mouse callosal, and marmoset corticostriatal projections, including APEX2 DAB-Ni²⁺ labeling and FIB-SEM.
ocar.resolution: They report seamless integration of macroscopic, mesoscopic, microscopic, and EM scales, enabling simultaneous interrogation of circuit structure and synaptic connectivity and zooming in on scarce contacts. Highlights list successive LM/EM in optically cleared tissue.
ocar.future_work: The methods section in the extract points to STAR Protocols-style resources; broader cell-type panels and fully automated targeting are implied next steps rather than shown as a production pipeline.

plain_language_summary: Seeing a whole brain and then the same cell’s synapses usually requires different preparations. This paper clears tissue in a way that still works for electron microscopy, so researchers can zoom from brain-wide maps down to individual contacts.

summaries.beginner: Seeing a whole brain and then the same cell’s synapses usually requires different preparations. This paper clears tissue in a way that still works for electron microscopy, so researchers can zoom from brain-wide maps down to individual contacts.

Marmoset inclusion is important for primate translation but is a targeted projection, not cortex-wide mapping.

title: Protocol for preparation of heterogeneous biological samples for 3D electron microscopy: a case study for insects
authors: A. Polilov; A. Makarova; Song Pang; C. Shan Xu; H. Hess

ocar.opportunity: Three-dimensional electron microscopy can map cells and synapses through large volumes, but heterogeneous samples such as whole insect heads stain poorly with existing en-bloc protocols and their hard cuticle chips during serial cutting.
ocar.challenge: Standard TEM staining was designed for post-section contrast, and widely used FIB-SEM and SBF-SEM protocols work well only on homogeneous tissue pieces, so whole heads do not stain uniformly.
ocar.action: Polilov, Makarova, Pang, Xu, and Hess, in Scientific Reports (2021), tested combinations of fixation, staining, dehydration, and infiltration on whole insect heads using only standard EM reagents and equipment, then imaged with FIB-SEM.
ocar.resolution: The resulting protocol produced FIB-SEM series through a whole head of the parasitoid wasp Megaphragma amalphitanum, with usable contrast in peripheral and central neuropil, compound eye, muscle, and fat body. It was also tested on featherwing beetles and Drosophila melanogaster.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the protocol as enabling whole-head or whole-body ultrastructure for connectomics of receptors, central neuropil, and effector pathways; how well it generalizes beyond the tested insects is left as an application rather than a quantified claim.

plain_language_summary: Insect heads mix hard cuticle, brain, eye, and muscle, so they are hard to stain and cut for 3D electron microscopy. This team reports a lab-friendly preparation that lets them image a whole tiny wasp head at cellular and synaptic detail.

summaries.beginner: Insect heads mix hard cuticle, brain, eye, and muscle, so they are hard to stain and cut for 3D electron microscopy. This team reports a lab-friendly preparation that lets them image a whole tiny wasp head at cellular and synaptic detail.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Scientific Reports (2021), Polilov and colleagues describe a sample-preparation protocol for heterogeneous biological material aimed at 3D-EM. Classical TEM stains and existing FIB-SEM/SBF-SEM recipes fail on whole insect heads because cuticle chips and reagents penetrate dissimilar tissues unevenly. Combined with FIB-SEM, the protocol yielded a complete head series of Megaphragma amalphitanum and was also tested on Nephanes titan and Drosophila melanogaster. The authors emphasize that it uses standard EM equipment and reagents rather than specialized connectomics pipelines.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods paper: success is shown as representative sections (brain, eye, muscle, fat body), not as a reconstructed connectome or synapse-detection accuracy. The extract’s conclusions do not quantify staining uniformity, imaging time, or reconstruction completeness. Applicability is claimed for FIB-SEM, SBF-SEM, and TEM without post-section staining; only FIB-SEM of whole heads is illustrated here. Species coverage is three insects, with Megaphragma as the main model.

title: Synaptic inputs to broad thorny ganglion cells in macaque retina
authors: Andrea S Bordt; Sara S. Patterson; Rebecca J Girresch; Diego Perez; Luke Tseng; James R. Anderson; Marcus A. Mazzaferri; J. Kuchenbecker; Rodrigo Gonzales-Rojas; Ashley Roland; C. Tang; C. Puller; A. Chuang; J. Ogilvie; J. Neitz; D. Marshak

ocar.opportunity: Primate broad thorny retinal ganglion cells are highly sensitive to small moving stimuli, but the synaptic circuits that build that motion sensitivity are not well mapped.
ocar.challenge: Their dendrites occupy three contiguous inner-plexiform strata, so both ON and OFF inputs are possible, and it is unclear how much excitation comes from bipolar cells versus amacrine cells.
ocar.action: Bordt, Patterson, and colleagues, in the Journal of Comparative Neurology (2021), reconstructed a broad thorny cell and its presynaptic partners from a serial block-face SEM connectome of central macaque retina, and Puller performed supporting physiology in vitro.
ocar.resolution: Fewer than 2% of inputs were from ON and OFF bipolar cells; the vast majority were from amacrine cells, of which seven morphological types were identified. Physiology confirmed robust excitatory input from both ON and OFF pathways. Identified amacrine cells provided at most six synapses each to this ganglion cell, which received over 1000 amacrine synapses in total.
ocar.future_work: The authors infer that much of the excitatory drive is amacrine-derived and that the same amacrine ensemble likely serves many motion-sensitive ganglion cells; they also predict relatively slow axonal conduction from the cell’s narrow axon diameter.

plain_language_summary: A motion-sensitive cell in the monkey retina gets almost none of its synapses from the usual excitatory bipolar cells. Most of its contacts come from many kinds of amacrine cells, which may help it notice small moving things.

summaries.beginner: A motion-sensitive cell in the monkey retina gets almost none of its synapses from the usual excitatory bipolar cells. Most of its contacts come from many kinds of amacrine cells, which may help it notice small moving things.
summaries.intermediate: Published in the Journal of Comparative Neurology (2021), Bordt and colleagues analyzed synaptic inputs to a reconstructed broad thorny ganglion cell in a central macaque serial block-face SEM volume. Bipolar cells supplied fewer than 2% of synapses; seven amacrine types (narrow-field knotty bistratified Type 1 and wavy multistratified Type 2; medium-field ON starburst and spiny; wide-field wiry Type 2, stellate wavy, and semilunar Type 2) supplied the rest. In vitro physiology confirmed ON and OFF excitatory input. Identified amacrine cells each contributed at most six synapses to this cell, which received over 1000 amacrine synapses overall.
summaries.advanced: The anatomical sample is one reconstructed ganglion cell (cell 103) whose dendrites reached the volume boundary, so input census is incomplete. “Fewer than 2% bipolar” is reported for this cell, not a population mean. Physiology shows ON/OFF excitation but does not, in this extract, quantify how much of that excitation is bipolar versus amacrine. The seven identified types do not account for all amacrine synapses. Annotations used Viking; the volume is available read-only.

title: The Prop1-like homeobox gene unc-42 specifies the identity of synaptically connected neurons
authors: Emily G. Berghoff; Lori Glenwinkel; A. Bhattacharya; Haosheng Sun; E. Varol; Nicki Mohammadi; Amelia Antone; Yi Feng; K. Nguyen; Steven J. Cook; Jordan F. Wood; Neda Masoudi; Cyril C Cros; Yasmin H. Ramadan; D. M. Ferkey; D. Hall; O. Hobert

ocar.opportunity: Many transcription factors are expressed in scattered neuron types, so studying them in one cell class can miss circuit-level roles. A whole-animal view of C. elegans identity genes can test whether shared regulators also assemble those neurons into a network.
ocar.challenge: unc-42 is expressed in 15 sensory, inter-, and motor neuron classes; whether it only sets each cell’s identity or also wires them together is not obvious from single-cell genetics.
ocar.action: Berghoff, Glenwinkel, Bhattacharya, Hobert, and colleagues, in eLife (2021), mapped unc-42 expression, scored neurotransmitter, receptor, neuropeptide, pathfinding, and synapse phenotypes in mutants, and compared collaborating terminal selectors across those 15 classes.
ocar.resolution: All 15 unc-42(+) classes are synaptically interconnected. unc-42 controls communication-route genes and is required for axon pathfinding and synaptic connectivity, acting as a terminal selector rather than for neuron generation. Mutant locomotion phenocopies surgical removal of unc-42(+) neurons. The authors propose that such factors can serve as circuit-organizer transcription factors.
ocar.future_work: They identify additional transcription factors expressed in synaptically connected neurons and hypothesize that these organizational properties may reflect ontogenetic and phylogenetic trajectories of circuit establishment; that claim is interpretive, not a phylogenetic reconstruction.

plain_language_summary: A single gene in the worm is on in 15 neuron types that all connect to each other. When the gene is missing, those cells fail to take on their adult identities and their wiring goes wrong, so the gene looks like a circuit-building switch.

summaries.beginner: A single gene in the worm is on in 15 neuron types that all connect to each other. When the gene is missing, those cells fail to take on their adult identities and their wiring goes wrong, so the gene looks like a circuit-building switch.
summaries.intermediate: Published in eLife (2021), Berghoff and colleagues show that the C. elegans Prop1-like homeobox gene unc-42 is expressed in 15 synaptically interconnected neuron classes. Mutants disrupt neurotransmitter pathway genes, receptors, neuropeptides, axon pathfinding, and synaptic connectivity, while neuron generation and pan-neuronal features are spared. Continuous larval and adult expression suggests a maintenance role as well. The discussion frames UNC-42 as a terminal selector that collaborates with different co-factors (unc-3, ceh-24, lim-4, fax-1) in different cells, and proposes a broader class of circuit-organizer transcription factors.
summaries.advanced: Penetrance and expressivity of marker loss vary by target gene and cell, and mild unc-42 single-mutant effects can be enhanced by removing a co-terminal selector, so “terminal selector” is not an all-or-none claim. Binding-site analysis is used to predict direct regulation. The 15/118 class count and interconnectivity are the paper’s framing; the extract does not tabulate a full synapse census. Phylogenetic interpretation is hypothesis, not evidence from this study.
