title: The cellular architecture of memory modules in Drosophila supports stochastic input integration
authors: Omar A. Hafez; Benjamin Escribano; Rouven L. Ziegler; J. J. Hirtz; E. Niebur; Jan Pielage

ocar.opportunity: Volume EM now gives nanometer morphologies of mushroom-body output neurons; combining that with physiology can test whether synapse location on the dendrite matters for memory readout.
ocar.challenge: Mammalian neurons often need active dendritic strategies for “synaptic democracy”; it was unknown whether a fly MBON integrates its many Kenyon-cell inputs equally.
ocar.action: In eLife (2023), Hafez, Escribano, Ziegler, Hirtz, Niebur, and Pielage build a model of MBON-α3 using EM architecture, 948 presynaptic Kenyon cells, and patch-clamp membrane properties.
ocar.resolution: MBON-α3 is electrotonically compact: simulated odor-like synaptic input robustly drives spiking with little dependence on synapse location, so sparse, stochastic KC connectivity can store many memories without precise anatomical addressing. The editor highlights this as synaptic democracy via passive dendrites.
ocar.future_work: Validity is argued for passive models of fly circuits; it does not claim mammalian pyramidal neurons work the same way.

plain_language_summary: A fly memory-output cell receives almost a thousand input wires. A detailed model says those inputs count roughly equally no matter where they sit on the tree, so the circuit can use messy, random connections and still learn many smells.

summaries.beginner: A fly memory-output cell receives almost a thousand input wires. A detailed model says those inputs count roughly equally no matter where they sit on the tree, so the circuit can use messy, random connections and still learn many smells.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2023; e77578), Hafez and colleagues combine EM morphology of MBON-α3, synapses from 948 Kenyon cells, and patch-clamp parameters in a realistic compartmental model. The neuron is electrotonically compact; sparse KC input drives spiking, and location on the arbor has minimal effect (synaptic democracy). That architecture supports storing many associations with stochastic connectivity. Reviewers contrast this passive strategy with larger mammalian neurons that use active dendritic mechanisms.
summaries.advanced: Results are for one MBON type (α3), not all MBONs. “948 presynaptic KCs” is the reconstructed complement used, not a claim about every fly. Compactness is a modeling conclusion from measured properties plus EM, not in vivo voltage throughout the arbor. Preprint dates to 2020; published 14 March 2023.

title: X-Ray2EM: Uncertainty-Aware Cross-Modality Image Reconstruction from X-Ray to Electron Microscopy in Connectomics
authors: Yicong Li; Y. Meirovitch; Aaron T. Kuan; Jasper S. Phelps; A. Pacureanu; W. Lee; N. Shavit; Lu Mi
journal: IEEE International Symposium on Biomedical Imaging

ocar.opportunity: Hard X-ray holographic nano-tomography (XNH) images thick samples quickly with intrinsic alignment, a potential shortcut around serial-section EM, but resolution is too low for easy membrane segmentation.
ocar.challenge: Cross-modality translation from X-ray to EM-like appearance must preserve membranes and quantify uncertainty if it is to help connectomics pipelines.
ocar.action: At ISBI 2023 (arXiv:2303.00882), Li, Meirovitch, Kuan, Phelps, Pacureanu, Lee, Shavit, and Mi propose X-Ray2EM, an uncertainty-aware 3D cGAN (3D Pix2Pix-style generator plus PatchGAN) with a frozen 2D U-Net segmentation head pretrained on Kasthuri mouse-cortex membranes.
ocar.resolution: They translate XNH to EM-like volumes with improved membrane segmentation quality relative to the X-ray domain, aiming at simpler X-ray-based connectomics. Paired data are ssTEM versus XNH (Kuan–Phelps 2020 Lee lab release).
ocar.future_work: Training details (128×128×64 crops, 100 epochs, loss weights) are methods, not a claim of synapse-resolution X-ray connectomes. Public benchmark EM differs in domain from their X-Ray2EM pair (Figure 5).

plain_language_summary: X-rays can scan thick brain tissue faster than slicing it for electron microscopy, but the pictures are blurrier. This model tries to paint EM-like membranes onto X-ray volumes so computers can trace cells more easily.

summaries.beginner: X-rays can scan thick brain tissue faster than slicing it for electron microscopy, but the pictures are blurrier. This model tries to paint EM-like membranes onto X-ray volumes so computers can trace cells more easily.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE ISBI (2023; DOI 10.1109/ISBI53787.2023.10230759), Li and colleagues present X-Ray2EM, a 3D uncertainty-aware reconstruction network mapping X-ray holographic nano-tomography to EM-like images. A U-Net segmentation network is pretrained on Kasthuri ssSEM membranes, then frozen while a 3D Pix2Pix-style generator is trained with NLL, GAN, and segmentation losses. They visualize membrane probability maps along X–Y and Y–Z. Data: Lee lab XNH/EM pair and a public EM benchmark.
summaries.advanced: The selected extract is heavy on training hyperparameters; headline Dice/F1 scores are not in the captured text. Domain gap between public EM and X-Ray2EM data is explicitly illustrated. XNH is not claimed to replace synaptic-resolution EM. Catalog methods include X-ray microscopy and volume EM as the two domains.

title: Connectomic analysis of thalamus-driven disinhibition in cortical layer 4
authors: Yunfeng Hua; S. Loomba; V. Pawlak; Philip Laserstein; K. Boergens; J. Kerr; M. Helmstaedter

ocar.opportunity: Layer 4 of primary sensory cortex is the main thalamic recipient, but average connectivity has hidden higher-order inhibitory logic.
ocar.challenge: Feedforward inhibition is known functionally, yet a synapse-level picture of which interneurons the thalamus drives, and how they target excitatory subtypes and each other, was missing.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv (1 June 2022), Hua, Loomba, Pawlak, Laserstein, Boergens, Kerr, and Helmstaedter reconstruct about one quarter of the mouse C2 barrel through L4 (and parts of L3/L5A) with SBEM after in vivo two-photon imaging.
ocar.resolution: Thalamic input drives a specific interneuron subset; those cells target spiny stellate versus star pyramidal neurons with subtype specificity and form a directed, thalamus-driven disinhibitory network, creating differential windows of opportunity for excitatory types depending on thalamic timing and strength.
ocar.future_work: They call this a first connectomic description of thalamus-driven L4 inhibition; excitatory intracortical networks are left for future work to test whether equal precision is general in cortex.

plain_language_summary: When a whisker signal hits cortex, it does not only excite cells; it also turns selected inhibitory cells on in a precise pattern. Mapping those connections in a mouse barrel, the authors find a disinhibitory loop that could open different time windows for two kinds of excitatory neurons.

summaries.beginner: When a whisker signal hits cortex, it does not only excite cells; it also turns selected inhibitory cells on in a precise pattern. Mapping those connections in a mouse barrel, the authors find a disinhibitory loop that could open different time windows for two kinds of excitatory neurons.
summaries.intermediate: In a bioRxiv preprint (2022; 10.1101/2022.06.01.494290), Hua, Loomba, and colleagues use SBEM connectomics on ~¼ of the mouse S1 C2 barrel across L4. Thalamic axons preferentially drive a subset of interneurons that inhibit excitatory subtypes differentially and also disinhibit in a directed, thalamus-driven network. The proposed computation is temporal windows for spiny stellates versus star pyramids. Tissue was previously imaged in vivo with two-photon GCaMP in Scnn1a-Cre mice.
summaries.advanced: The extract’s “Outlook” is short; numeric synapse counts and statistical tests are not in the selected text. Volume is a fraction of one barrel, not whole S1. “Unknown degree of specialization” is the authors’ claim relative to prior average connectivity. Methods pages detail virus and imaging but are not results.

title: Connectomics: Relating synaptic connectivity to physiology.
authors: Ishani Ganguly; Ashok Litwin-Kumar

ocar.action: In a Current Biology dispatch (2022), Ganguly and Litwin-Kumar discuss that study’s relationship between synaptic wiring and physiology in a Drosophila pathway.

Drosophila connectome study, implying an intermediate abstraction between point neurons and full multi-compartment models.
ocar.future_work: Understanding how those two input sources interact may reveal new computational principles still amenable to theory.

plain_language_summary: Having a wiring diagram is not the same as knowing how the circuit computes. This short commentary explains a fly study that links synapses to physiology and sketches how modelers might use that link.

title: Instance Segmentation of Unlabeled Modalities via Cyclic Segmentation GAN
authors: Leander Lauenburg; Zudi Lin; Ruihan Zhang; M'arcia dos Santos; Siyu Huang; Ignacio Arganda-Carreras; E. Boyden; H. Pfister; D. Wei

ocar.opportunity: 3D nuclei instance segmentation is routine in annotated EM but costly to label in new modalities such as expansion microscopy (ExM).
ocar.challenge: Generalist pretrained models and two-step translate-then-segment pipelines underuse unlabeled target images and can break instance boundaries.
ocar.action: On arXiv (2022), Lauenburg, Lin, Zhang, dos Santos, Huang, Arganda-Carreras, Boyden, Pfister, and Wei propose CySGAN, jointly training CycleGAN translation and instance segmentation with extra self-supervised and segmentation-adversarial losses, benchmarked on labeled EM to unlabeled ExM nuclei (NucExM dataset released).
ocar.resolution: CySGAN outperforms Cellpose, StarDist, and sequential CycleGAN+segmentation; it beats the second-best (CycleGAN+Segm, IX→IY) by 5.7 percentage points. On the optimized NucExM volume V1, AP-50 is 0.927, dropping to 0.761 without augmentations and 0.878 without semi-supervised losses.
ocar.future_work: They flag target domains whose instance geometry differs strongly from the source as an important open direction.

plain_language_summary: Labeling every nucleus in a new kind of microscope image is slow. This method learns to both paint one image type into another and find each nucleus, using unlabeled examples of the new type, and it beats doing those two steps separately.

summaries.beginner: Labeling every nucleus in a new kind of microscope image is slow. This method learns to both paint one image type into another and find each nucleus, using unlabeled examples of the new type, and it beats doing those two steps separately.
summaries.intermediate: In an arXiv preprint (2022; 2204.03082), Lauenburg and colleagues introduce CySGAN for unlabeled-modality instance segmentation. The benchmark is 3D neuronal nuclei: annotated EM as source, unlabeled ExM as target, with a new densely annotated ExM set (NucExM). Unified translation-plus-segmentation outperforms generalists (Cellpose, StarDist) and sequential translation–segmentation. Ablations show data augmentation and semi-supervised target losses are essential (AP-50 0.927 vs. large drops when removed). Code and data: connectomics-bazaar.github.io/proj/CySGAN/.
summaries.advanced: AP-50 figures are for the stated NucExM splits (train on V1, infer V2 in the sequential/CySGAN comparison). Star-convex priors (StarDist) are said to overlap and miss boundaries. The method assumes source and target instances are similar enough to share a segmentation representation. NSF/NIH funding is acknowledged; Boyden is a coauthor on the ExM side.

title: Neural model generating klinotaxis behavior accompanied by a random walk based on C. elegans connectome
authors: Mohan Chen; Dazheng Feng; Hongtao Su; Tingting Su; Meng Wang

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans klinotaxis (gradual steering up a salt gradient) coexists with a random walk; a connectome-based model that produces both would constrain mechanisms.
ocar.challenge: ASEL/R cannot read a spatial gradient directly (the worm lies on its side); ASEL’s all-or-none depolarization had not been in prior sensory models, and random walking was often added externally rather than generated by synapses.
ocar.action: In Scientific Reports (2022), Chen, Feng, Su, Su, and Wang evolve a connectome-constrained network with a new ASEL all-or-none sensory model, then introduce “liquid synapses” whose stochasticity generates autonomous random walking.
ocar.resolution: Klinotaxis emerges from the evolved network with a plausible steering mechanism; liquid synapses produce random walk from the circuit itself. Simulated ablations are reported as consistent with biological conclusions.
ocar.future_work: Liquid synapses are a modeling hypothesis inspired by biological synaptic stochasticity, not a newly measured synapse class. They analogize to Drosophila larval spontaneous search after sensory block.

plain_language_summary: Worms climb salt gradients while still wandering. This simulation uses the worm’s wiring, a more realistic nose cell, and noisy synapses to get both steering and random walking from the network instead of adding wandering by hand.

summaries.beginner: Worms climb salt gradients while still wandering. This simulation uses the worm’s wiring, a more realistic nose cell, and noisy synapses to get both steering and random walking from the network instead of adding wandering by hand.
summaries.intermediate: In Scientific Reports (2022; 10.1038/s41598-022-06988-w), Chen and colleagues build a C. elegans klinotaxis model with an ASEL all-or-none sensory stage (claimed first) plus ASER, evolve the network, and then add stochastic “liquid synapses” so a random walk is generated internally. They argue the klinotaxis mechanism resembles, but refines, prior minimal models, and that ablation simulations match biology. The paper is positioned as behavioral simulation plus mechanistic hypothesis.
summaries.advanced: “Fairly consistent” ablation results are the authors’ comparison to literature, not a full experimental replication. Liquid synapses are a proposed stochastic synapse model. Connectome completeness cites ~302 neurons and >7000 connections as background, not a new reconstruction. Evolutionary training means the weights are optimized for the task, not taken as measured physiological weights.

title: Reconstructing neural circuits using multiresolution correlated light and electron microscopy
authors: Karl Friedrichsen; Pratyush Ramakrishna; Jen-Chun Hsiang; Katia Valkova; D. Kerschensteiner; Josh L. Morgan

ocar.opportunity: Correlated light and electron microscopy can pair functional and molecular labels with synaptic anatomy, but targeting EM to optically characterized cells without compromising high-throughput reconstruction remains hard.
ocar.challenge: CLEM often trades staining quality or throughput for registration, and thin neurites that are not attached to nearby large processes, myelin, or cell bodies force inefficient leapfrogging through dense optical features.
ocar.action: Friedrichsen, Ramakrishna, Hsiang, Valkova, Kerschensteiner, and Morgan, in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2022), describe mrCLEM: ATUM sections on solid substrate are imaged repeatedly by SEM at multiple scales and matched to multiresolution confocal maps of aldehyde-fixed tissue, from gross anatomy down to subcellular features, to target high-resolution acquisition and annotation.
ocar.resolution: Features visible in lower-resolution EM correspond well to densely labeled optical maps, so iterative matching can aim high-resolution EM at cells of interest. They walk through a mouse retinal light-to-EM experiment and give examples from mouse brain slices. ATUM/SEM is highlighted because sections can be reimaged without distortion and modern SEMs switch between millimeter fields and nanometer resolution.
ocar.future_work: The authors flag that efficiency falls if hundreds of fine neurites must be traced without easy medium-to-high-resolution links; in those cases label-matching CLEM (NIRB or peroxidase) may be cheaper. They argue terabyte-scale volumes should be routinely paired with other modalities rather than waiting only for petabyte complete maps.

plain_language_summary: Light microscopy can show which cells are active or labeled, but electron microscopy is needed to see their synapses. This team images the same mouse tissue at several zoom levels so they only spend high-resolution EM time on the cells they already know from light.

summaries.beginner: Light microscopy can show which cells are active or labeled, but electron microscopy is needed to see their synapses. This team images the same mouse tissue at several zoom levels so they only spend high-resolution EM time on the cells they already know from light.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2022), Friedrichsen and colleagues present mrCLEM, a multiresolution correlated light and electron microscopy pipeline built on ATUM/SEM. Arrays of sections on solid substrate are reimaged at multiple SEM scales and matched to multiresolution confocal maps of aldehyde-fixed tissue, from gross anatomy to subcellular landmarks, to target high-resolution acquisition. A mouse retina light-to-EM walkthrough and mouse brain-slice examples illustrate the link from live optical imaging to EM reconstruction. The discussion stresses that ATUM sections can be reimaged without distortion and that SEM can jump from millimeter overviews (cell bodies resolved) to nanometer fields.
summaries.advanced: The paper is a methods walkthrough rather than a completed dense connectome; imaging parameters are presented as a range of scales, not a single recommended setting. The main stated limit is fine neurites unconnected to nearby large structures, where leapfrogging through dense optical labels reduces the advantage over dense reconstruction. Comparison with NIRB or peroxidase CLEM is qualitative. Discussion does not quantify wall-clock savings, reconstruction completeness, or synapse-detection accuracy.

title: Scale matters: The nested human connectome
authors: M. Axer; K. Amunts

ocar.opportunity: A full description of how neurons and brain regions interconnect is needed for mechanistic accounts of human brain function and dysfunction.
ocar.challenge: Diffusion MRI tractography maps whole-brain pathways at coarse scale, while polarization, fluorescence, and electron microscopy reach axons or synapses but not whole-brain coverage, so the scales are hard to combine.
ocar.action: Axer and Amunts, in Science (2022), review how to constrain whole-brain tractography with regional high-resolution connectivity and local fiber geometry, and they discuss machine learning and simulation where measurements are missing.
ocar.resolution: They argue that future interoperable atlases need high-resolution templates and directionality so that alternative tractography solutions and accuracy estimates can be represented together.
ocar.future_work: The review frames new methods, templates, and uncertainty-aware atlases as mandatory rather than reporting a single completed multi-scale human connectome.

plain_language_summary: Human brain wiring can be mapped with MRI of the whole brain or with microscopes that see single axons, but those views live at very different zoom levels. This Science piece argues we need ways to combine them, and to show how sure we are about each pathway.

summaries.beginner: Human brain wiring can be mapped with MRI of the whole brain or with microscopes that see single axons, but those views live at very different zoom levels. This Science piece argues we need ways to combine them, and to show how sure we are about each pathway.

title: A Novel and Functionally Diverse Class of Acetylcholine-Gated Ion Channels
authors: I. Hardege; J. Morud; Amy Courtney; W. Schafer

ocar.opportunity: Fast cholinergic transmission is well mapped onto excitatory nicotinic receptors, but inhibitory acetylcholine-gated channels in invertebrates, and their circuit roles, are much less understood.
ocar.challenge: C. elegans has a large, partly orphan ligand-gated ion channel repertoire, and a compact nervous system in which the same neuron may mix excitatory and inhibitory receptors for a given transmitter.
ocar.action: Hardege, Morud, Courtney, and Schafer, in Journal of Neuroscience (2023), characterize new inhibitory channels in C. elegans, including choline-preferring LGC-40, LGC-57, and LGC-58 and polymodal LGC-39, then use ligand–receptor pairs to predict synaptic polarity across the hermaphrodite connectome.
ocar.resolution: They report that many neurons express both excitatory and inhibitory channels for acetylcholine and other major transmitters, and they present a polarity model intended to generate circuit hypotheses. GFP tagging of LGC-40, LGC-57, and LGC-58 is stated not to change EC50 in oocyte dose–response curves.
ocar.future_work: The polarity heatmap is a summed-expression model, not a measured sign at each synapse, so circuit tests of predicted excitation versus inhibition remain to be done.

plain_language_summary: In the worm, acetylcholine is not only an on-switch: some newly characterized channels prefer choline and can turn cells down instead of up. The authors use those receptors to guess which connections in the wiring diagram are excitatory or inhibitory.

summaries.beginner: In the worm, acetylcholine is not only an on-switch: some newly characterized channels prefer choline and can turn cells down instead of up. The authors use those receptors to guess which connections in the wiring diagram are excitatory or inhibitory.
summaries.intermediate: Published as an early-release article in Journal of Neuroscience (2023; DOI 10.1523/JNEUROSCI.1516-22.2022), Hardege and colleagues identify inhibitory acetylcholine-gated channels in C. elegans, including choline-preferring LGC-40, LGC-57, and LGC-58 and polymodal LGC-39, activated by cholinergic and aminergic ligands. Using new ligand–receptor pairs they argue that single hermaphrodite neurons often co-express excitatory and inhibitory channels for acetylcholine, glutamate, and GABA. They build a model of synaptic polarity across the connectome as a hypothesis generator. Figure legends in the extract describe oocyte dose–response traces, antagonist applications, and a binary polarity heatmap.

Still-orphan LGICs (LGC-42, -44, -45, -47, -48) appear in co-expression traces with RIC-3 and are not fully deorphanized here.

title: A specialized spinal circuit for command amplification and directionality during escape behavior
authors: Na N. Guan; Lulu Xu; Tianrui Zhang; Chun-Xiao Huang; Zhen Wang; Elin Dahlberg; Haoyu Wang; Fangfang Wang; Irene Pallucchi; Yunfeng Hua; A. El Manira; Jianren Song
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

ocar.opportunity: Urgent actions such as defensive escape must pick a left or right trajectory immediately, so directionality may be implemented in local spinal circuits rather than only in higher cognition.
ocar.challenge: Brainstem Mauthner cells can fire bilaterally, so escape direction may be set downstream in the spinal cord; the identity and role of the relevant descending interneurons had been unclear.
ocar.action: Guan, Xu, Zhang, Huang, Wang, Dahlberg, Wang, Wang, Pallucchi, Hua, El Manira, and Song, in PNAS (2021), combine electrophysiology, serial block-face electron microscopy, and behavior in adult zebrafish to reconstruct a spinal circuit built around segmentally repeating cholinergic V2a (Chx10) interneurons.

title: Architectures of Neuronal Circuits
authors: L. Luo

ocar.opportunity: Individual neurons are well characterized, but brains compute through synaptic patterns; a shared vocabulary of motifs and larger architectures would bridge single cells and whole-brain function.
ocar.challenge: Circuit organization looks heterogeneous across regions and species, and unlike engineered computers, neuronal circuits arise from evolution and development rather than top-down design.
ocar.action: Luo, in Science (2021), reviews core motifs (feedforward and feedback excitation and inhibition, lateral and mutual inhibition) and larger plans (topographic maps, parallel processing, dimensionality expansion, biased neuromodulatory projections, recurrent loops), plus how they assemble in development and evolution.
ocar.resolution: The review treats motifs as “words” and architectural plans as “sentences,” arguing that these patterns implement elementary computations and specialized functions across diverse brains, and that molecular gradients versus combinatorial surface codes can specify maps versus discrete parallel pathways.
ocar.future_work: Luo calls for serial EM and trans-synaptic tracing across species, functional perturbation of key elements, and study of how motifs interact across scales; whether algorithmic changes in wiring explain mammalian complexity remains unknown.

plain_language_summary: Brain cells do not work alone: they are wired into repeating patterns, like feedforward loops and maps of neighboring cells. This review collects those patterns and asks how they are built in development and evolution.

summaries.beginner: Brain cells do not work alone: they are wired into repeating patterns, like feedforward loops and maps of neighboring cells. This review collects those patterns and asks how they are built in development and evolution.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Science (2021), Luo reviews neuronal circuit architectures from microcircuit motifs to larger-scale plans. Motifs include feedforward excitation and inhibition, feedback inhibition, lateral inhibition, and mutual inhibition; larger plans include continuous topographic mapping, discrete parallel processing, dimensionality expansion, biased neuromodulatory projections, and recurrent loops. He discusses conservation versus independent evolution, duplication and divergence, and developmental specification by molecular gradients versus combinatorial cell-surface codes. The outlook urges serial EM, trans-synaptic tracing, and cross-scale functional tests, including inspiration for artificial networks.

The human-brain scale (“about 100 billion neurons”) is background context. Claims about AI inspiration and general-purpose networks are prospective. title: Ascaris suum Informs Extrasynaptic Volume Transmission in Nematodes

title: Conserved Circuits for Direction Selectivity in the Primate Retina
authors: Sara S. Patterson; Briyana N. Bembry; Marcus A. Mazzeferri; M. Neitz; F. Rieke; Robijanto Soetedjo; J. Neitz

ocar.opportunity: Direction selectivity is a classic retinal computation in non-primate mammals, but whether primate retina computes motion direction—or cortex replaced that need—has remained open.
ocar.challenge: Starburst amacrine cells exist in primates, yet their wiring was unknown, primate direction-selective ganglion cells had not been found, and electrophysiology is biased toward the few abundant RGC types.
ocar.action: Patterson, Bembry, Mazzeferri, Neitz, Rieke, Soetedjo, and Neitz, on bioRxiv (2021), reconstruct the ON SAC circuit from a serial EM volume of macaque central retina and ask which ganglion cells SACs target.
ocar.resolution: They report that the structural basis for SAC computation and conferral of directional selectivity is conserved, and that SACs selectively target a single ganglion cell type, a candidate homolog of mammalian ON-sustained dsRGCs that project to the accessory optic system and support gaze-stabilizing reflexes.
ocar.future_work: Physiological confirmation that the targeted RGC type is direction-selective, and how this ancestral circuit sits beside primate cortical motion processing, remain to be shown.

plain_language_summary: Other mammals compute motion direction in the retina; primates were thought to wait until visual cortex. This preprint reconstructs macaque retinal wiring and finds a conserved circuit that could compute direction much earlier than expected.

title: Forward and backward locomotion patterns in C. elegans generated by a connectome-based model simulation
authors: Kazuma Sakamoto; Z. Soh; Michiyo Suzuki; Y. Iino; T. Tsuji

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans produces forward and backward locomotion with only 69 motor neurons and 95 muscle cells, so a connectome-based model could test whether that sparse circuit can generate both gaits.
ocar.challenge: Prior models mapped connectome and cell-class roles but did not analyze the distribution of synaptic and gap-junction weights needed for switching oscillations.
ocar.action: Sakamoto, Soh, Suzuki, Iino, and Tsuji, in Scientific Reports (2021), build a network of A, B, D, and AS motor neurons plus muscle, including chemical and gap junctions, and train connection weights with backpropagation through time on command-neuron input and muscle activation.
ocar.resolution: The circuit generated oscillations with different phase patterns for forward and backward movement and could switch at arbitrary times given binary command-like inputs. Trained synaptic and gap weights followed a Boltzmann-type distribution. The model could be trained to match measured activity in the HRB4 strain. The conclusion stresses that sparse connection strengths suffice for the oscillations.
ocar.future_work: The authors suggest the same supervised approach could analyze more complex measured activity patterns; the extract does not claim a unique biological weight set.

plain_language_summary: The tiny worm walks forward and backward with a small set of motor neurons. This team trains a wiring-based computer model until the virtual muscles oscillate in both directions and can switch when a command-like input flips.

The model is the motor/muscle layer, not the full 302-neuron connectome.

title: Model-based Comparison of Current Flow in Rod Bipolar Cells of Healthy and Early-Stage Degenerated Retina
authors: P. Kosta; E. Iseri; Kyle Loizos; J. Paknahad; Rebecca L. Pfeiffer; C. Sigulinsky; James R. Anderson; Bryan William Jones; G. Lazzi

ocar.opportunity: Retinal prostheses stimulate surviving cells after photoreceptor loss, but current flow in early degenerating retina is poorly quantified, limiting stimulation design.
ocar.challenge: Remodeling can begin before substantial photoreceptor death, so healthy versus early-degenerate rod-to-rod-bipolar pathways may already differ in morphology and input count.
ocar.action: Kosta, Iseri, Loizos, Paknahad, Pfeiffer, Sigulinsky, Anderson, Jones, and Lazzi, in Experimental Eye Research (2021), build conductance-based NEURON models from serial-section TEM connectomes of healthy (RC1) and early-degenerate (RPC1) rabbit retina.
ocar.resolution: Simulated RodBC membrane potential in early degenerate tissue was about 10–20 mV lower than in wild type, attributed primarily to fewer rod inputs rather than intrinsically different RodBC biophysics. Both circuits showed similar low-pass filtering.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the models as tools for later-stage degeneration and prosthesis research; later disease stages are not simulated here.

plain_language_summary: When the retina starts to degenerate, rod bipolar cells still look similar but they receive input from fewer rods. Computer models built from electron-microscope wiring diagrams predict those cells sit at a lower voltage, which matters for designing retinal implants.

title: Promisomics and the Short-Circuiting of Mind
authors: A. Gomez-Marin

ocar.opportunity: Whole-brain synaptic maps are now technically discussed even for a mouse, so the field needs a clear account of what such a map can and cannot explain.
ocar.challenge: Grand projects tend to overpromise: horizontal results (a synapse map) are sold as vertical conclusions (function, behavior, mind), a move Gomez-Marin calls theoretically flawed.
ocar.action: Gomez-Marin, in eNeuro (2021), writes a commentary on Abbott et al. (2020), “The Mind of a Mouse,” contrasting what connectomics measures with what it claims, and criticizing “all details matter” omics as promissory materialism.
ocar.resolution: He argues that suggesting a mouse, human, or fly connectome will “give us the mind” conflates levels of analysis. Maps are useful, but infinite resolution can be worse than the territory, and large projects crowd out other questions. Neural connections are not a replacement for mind.
ocar.future_work: The piece asks for conceptually serious metaphors and hypothesis-led work rather than proposing an alternative mapping project.

plain_language_summary: Some neuroscientists talk as if a complete map of every synapse would explain a mouse’s mind. This commentary says a wiring diagram is still just a map of one level, not a theory of thought or behavior.

title: Geometric framework to predict structure from function in neural networks
authors: Tirthabir Biswas; James E. Fitzgerald

ocar.opportunity: Many networks can produce similar responses, so a method that names which synapses are required by a given function would turn activity into anatomical predictions.
ocar.challenge: Structure–function links are subtle: the same network can compute differently by context, and it is largely unknown which connection patterns are necessary for specific computations.
ocar.action: Biswas and Fitzgerald, in Physical Review Research (catalog year 2020), introduce a geometric framework for threshold-linear recurrent networks that, when the number of specified response patterns does not exceed the number of input synapses, calculates the solution space of feedforward and recurrent matrices consistent with those responses.
ocar.resolution: A noisy generalization shows the solution-space geometry can undergo topological transitions as allowed error grows. Certainty conditions are derived that guarantee a nonzero synapse between neurons, intended for application to neural activity data.
ocar.future_work: The framework is proposed for making rigorous anatomical predictions from activity under the model architecture; empirical tests on recorded circuits are not part of the abstract.

title: Latent Feature Representation via Unsupervised Learning for Pattern Discovery in Massive Electron Microscopy Image Volumes
authors: Gary B. Huang; Huei-Fang Yang; Shin-ya Takemura; P. Rivlin; Stephen M. Plaza

title: Microtubule Tracking in Electron Microscopy Volumes
authors: N. Eckstein; Julia M. Buhmann; Matthew Cook; Jan Funke
journal: International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention

ocar.opportunity: Microtubules follow neuronal morphology and could guide proofreading and subcompartment labels, but they are impractical to trace by hand in large EM volumes.
ocar.challenge: Prior tracking was slow and inaccurate, and a single microtubule can run far in-plane, so naive candidates and orientation priors miss or fragment tracks.
ocar.action: Eckstein, Buhmann, Cook, and Funke, at MICCAI (2020), predict microtubule scores with a 3D UNet, build a candidate graph via strided NMS, and select tracks with a new integer linear program plus block-wise distributed solving, benchmarked on CREMI Drosophila tissue.
ocar.resolution: On three 1.2 × 4 × 4 µm test volumes they report a 53% accuracy increase and three-order-of-magnitude speed-up versus prior art (NMS GRAD averaged over sets A, B, C). They release eight densely annotated 30 × 1000 × 1000 voxel blocks. Block-wise ILP is described as enabling petabyte-scale tracking without a significant accuracy drop.
ocar.future_work: Ablations show connected-component candidates are worse and swapping the UNet for a random forest with NMS causes many false positives; noisy scores still hurt precision when NMS over-extracts candidates.

plain_language_summary: Tiny tubes inside neurons are visible in electron-microscope pictures and can help check whether a cell was traced correctly. This paper teaches a computer to follow those tubes much faster and more accurately than earlier software.

summaries.beginner: Tiny tubes inside neurons are visible in electron-microscope pictures and can help check whether a cell was traced correctly. This paper teaches a computer to follow those tubes much faster and more accurately than earlier software.
summaries.intermediate: Presented at MICCAI (2020; arXiv:2009.08371), Eckstein and colleagues track microtubules in EM by UNet scoring, strided non-maximum suppression candidates, and a new ILP with biological structural priors. They release eight annotated 1.2 × 4 × 4 µm CREMI blocks (github.com/nilsec/micron). Qualitative results include calyx reconstruction in a 76 × 52 × 64 µm Drosophila region in the supplement.
summaries.advanced: The 53% figure is an average over test sets A–B–C for NMS GRAD; NMS SM wins on B and C. Accuracy metric details live in Table 1, not fully reproduced here. CREMI blocks are small relative to whole-brain EM. Microtubule tracks are proposed as proofreading aids, not demonstrated to reduce neuron-split/merge error in this extract.

title: Multiscale ATUM-FIB Microscopy Enables Targeted Ultrastructural Analysis at Isotropic Resolution
authors: Georg Kislinger; H. Gnägi; M. Kerschensteiner; M. Simons; T. Misgeld; Martina Schifferer

ocar.opportunity: Volume EM must choose between large fields of view at limited z-resolution (ATUM/ssTEM) and isotropic FIB-SEM in small volumes; rare events need both context and local isotropic detail.
ocar.challenge: Ultramicrotomy z-thickness and FIB-SEM volume limits are in tension, especially when the target (for example microglia–plaque contacts) is sparse.
ocar.action: Kislinger, Gnägi, Kerschensteiner, Simons, Misgeld, and Schifferer, in iScience (2020), cut 2–10 µm resin sections onto transparent tape, map them by light and EM, then mill selected regions with FIB-SEM (ATUM-FIB), demonstrated on microglia–amyloid contacts in a familial Alzheimer’s mouse model.
ocar.resolution: Serial semithick sections act as a tissue library for on-demand isotropic ultrastructure after relocation of preselected structures. Highlights include fast nanometer-resolution relocation and tape-based multiscale LM/EM.
ocar.future_work: Limitations include sample-specific embedding, fracture risk at contrast transitions, and the method not being optimized to minimize material loss between sections for dense connectomic reconstruction (unlike ultrathick partitioning).

plain_language_summary: Researchers often must choose between seeing a large piece of tissue coarsely or a tiny piece in fine 3D. This hybrid method slices the tissue into thick-ish sheets, finds the rare spot of interest, then zooms in with ion-beam electron microscopy.

summaries.beginner: Researchers often must choose between seeing a large piece of tissue coarsely or a tiny piece in fine 3D. This hybrid method slices the tissue into thick-ish sheets, finds the rare spot of interest, then zooms in with ion-beam electron microscopy.
summaries.intermediate: Published in iScience (2020), Kislinger and colleagues introduce ATUM-FIB: serial 2–10 µm resin sections collected on transparent tape, mapped by serial light and electron microscopy, then targeted with FIB-SEM. title: The connectome
authors: O. Sporns

ocar.opportunity: A connectome is a comprehensive network map of neural elements and their links, and the concept now organizes structural and functional human brain research.
ocar.challenge: Maps can refer to neurons or areas and to synapses or pathways, so definitions, topology, dynamics, and clinical individual differences need a single conceptual frame.
ocar.action: Sporns, in the New Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry (2020), surveys origins and definitions of the connectome, major findings on human connectome topology and how structure shapes dynamics, and themes in development and clinical populations.
ocar.resolution: At a given scale, connectome maps are presented as a complete, systematic account of anatomical or physiological relationships used to study both typical organization and individual differences.
ocar.future_work: The chapter is an overview; it points to ongoing work on individual differences rather than a new dataset.

title: The Mixture Graph-A Data Structure for Compressing, Rendering, and Querying Segmentation Histograms
authors: Khaled A. Althelaya; Marco Agus; J. Schneider
journal: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics

ocar.opportunity: Segmented EM and other volumes store nominal IDs, so ordinary mipmaps and volume rendering alias badly; a compact structure that preserves label mixtures would allow interactive viewing and queries.
ocar.challenge: Each coarse voxel holds a mixture of segment IDs; naively storing and range-querying those histograms is expensive, and transfer functions plus lighting must stay consistent across scales.
ocar.action: Al-Thelaya, Agus, and Schneider, in IEEE TVCG (IEEE Vis 2020), factor mixtures into sequences of two-label interpolations, store them as a pruned DAG (the Mixture Graph), propagate transfer functions from leaves, and support footprint histogram queries.
ocar.resolution: The structure compresses histogram mipmaps, enables pre-filtered rendering at interactive rates, and yields up to 178× speed-up over naive parallelized range queries. Applications include pre-filtered lighting and multi-dimensional transfer functions for shape, geometry, and orientation. Example volumes include hippocampus (1178×1125×789, 353 segments), neocortex (2048×2048×300, 1,182 segments), and a fiber-reinforced polymer (15,917 segments).
ocar.future_work: The extract’s back matter is references; remaining limits on extreme label counts or out-of-core volumes are not detailed in the selected text.

plain_language_summary: When a 3D scan is labeled with many cell IDs, zooming out mixes those labels and the picture can flicker or lie. This data structure stores those mixes compactly so you can still render and ask “what labels are in this box?” quickly.

summaries.beginner: When a 3D scan is labeled with many cell IDs, zooming out mixes those labels and the picture can flicker or lie. This data structure stores those mixes compactly so you can still render and ask “what labels are in this box?” quickly.
summaries.intermediate: To appear in IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (IEEE Vis 2020; arXiv:2009.02702), Al-Thelaya, Agus, and Schneider introduce the Mixture Graph for segmentation-histogram mipmaps. Mixtures are factored into linear interpolations between exactly two IDs and stored as a topologically ordered DAG after pruning. Transfer functions propagate from sources for pre-filtered rendering; footprint queries of partial histograms reach up to 178× versus naive parallel range queries. They also show pre-filtered lighting and interactive exploration with multi-dimensional transfer functions.
summaries.advanced: The 178× figure is an upper bound stated in the abstract, not a per-volume table here. Example volumes mix connectomic (hippocampus, neocortex) and materials data. Novelty is the histogram/DAG factorization, not a new segmentation algorithm. Catalog hyphenation “The Mixture Graph-A Data Structure” matches the title.

title: Towards a functional connectome in Drosophila
authors: K. Vogt

ocar.opportunity: Whole-brain Drosophila connectomes will sit on decades of circuit genetics, offering a path to entire-brain function rather than isolated pathways.
ocar.challenge: In a complete wiring diagram, sensory channels are synaptically interconnected even at early layers, and higher brain regions are densely linked by long-range projections, so contributions of “distinct” circuits are hard to isolate; extrasynaptic communication also matters.
ocar.action: Vogt, in Journal of Neurogenetics (2020), perspectives upcoming larval and adult Drosophila whole-brain reconstructions at Janelia in light of the C. elegans precedent (302 neurons) and argues for combining connectomics with genetic tools and behavior.
ocar.resolution: Connectomes are framed as a scaffold for existing circuit knowledge, while warning that whole-brain context undermines clean isolation of sensory versus higher systems and that modulation beyond direct synapses must be included.
ocar.future_work: The piece looks ahead to using fly genetics and behavioral paradigms on whole-brain maps rather than reporting a finished fly connectome.

plain_language_summary: Complete fruit-fly brain wiring diagrams were on the way, building on the worm’s famous map. This perspective says those maps will help, but they will also show that brain parts are more mixed together than textbook circuits suggest.

summaries.beginner: Complete fruit-fly brain wiring diagrams were on the way, building on the worm’s famous map. This perspective says those maps will help, but they will also show that brain parts are more mixed together than textbook circuits suggest.

It also stresses communication beyond direct synapses. Drosophila genetics and behavior are presented as the way to pursue entire-brain function on that scaffold.

title: Connectome verification: inter-rater and connection reliability of tract-tracing-based intrinsic hypothalamic connectivity
authors: O. Schmitt; Peter Eipert; Sebastian Schwanke; Felix Lessmann; Jennifer Meinhardt; Julia Beier; Kanar Kadir; Adrian Karnitzki; Linda Sellner; Ann-Christin Klünker; Frauke Ruß; Jörg Jenssen

ocar.future_work: The hypothalamus sample is presented as an example; the workflow is meant for broader connectome metastudies.

title: Deciphering neural circuits for Caenorhabditis elegans behavior by computations and perturbations to genome and connectome
authors: J. Karbowski

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans uniquely combines a complete connectome, a well-characterized genome, and quantifiable behavior, so an integrated systems description from genes to locomotion is conceivable.
ocar.challenge: Reverse engineering still requires perturbations and models that cross molecular, circuit, and behavioral scales; even with 302 neurons, structure does not automatically yield function.
ocar.action: Karbowski, in Current Opinion in Systems Biology (2019; arXiv:1910.07451), reviews computational and perturbation work on worm circuits, emphasizing locomotion, and sketches phenomenological multi-state velocity models that can be taken to a Fokker–Planck limit.
ocar.resolution: The review collects successes and challenges of merging genomics, connectomics, behavior, and modeling. An appendix-like derivation relates discrete forward/backward/stop states to continuous noisy velocity dynamics whose drift and diffusion could, in principle, be measured to constrain transition rates.
ocar.future_work: Measuring A(v) and B(v) experimentally is proposed as a way to identify rates in the phenomenological model; it is not carried out here.

plain_language_summary: The worm is the only animal with a full wiring diagram, a mapped genome, and simple measurable behaviors. This review asks how far computer models and genetic or cell perturbations have gone toward explaining how that animal moves.

title: Dynamic Computational Model of the Human Spinal Cord Connectome
authors: J. Arle; Nicolae Iftimia; J. Shils; L. Mei; Kristen W. Carlson

ocar.opportunity: Human brain connectomes are common, but a draft spinal cord connectome could template simulations of pain, stimulation, and other spinal computations.

ocar.resolution: The model includes intra- and interlaminar, intersegmental, and ascending/descending connections, estimated counts per cell type, and highly recurrent local networks. It is offered as a starting point for biomedical hypotheses, each needing extra calibration.
ocar.future_work: The authors call for simulating additional segments and expanding research uses; each application requires further constraints on outputs.

title: MagC, magnetic collection of ultrathin sections for volumetric correlative light and electron microscopy
authors: Thomas Templier

authors: Qiyu Zhang; W. Lee; D. Paul; D. Ginty

title: Novel Technological Advances in Functional Connectomics in C. elegans
authors: Elizabeth M. DiLoreto; Christopher Chute; Samantha Bryce; Jagan Srinivasan

title: Reconstruction of 1,000 projection neurons reveals new cell types and organization of long-range connectivity in the mouse brain
authors: Johan Winnubst; Erhan Bas; Tiago A. Ferreira; Zhuhao Wu; M. Economo; Patrick Edson; B. J. Arthur; Christopher Bruns; Konrad Rokicki; David M. Schauder; D. J. Olbris; S. D. Murphy; David Ackerman; Cameron Arshadi; P. Baldwin; Regina Blake; A. Elsayed; Mashtura Hasan; D. Ramírez; Bruno Paiva dos Santos; Monet Weldon; A. Zafar; J. Dudman; C. Gerfen; A. Hantman; Wyatt L. Korff; S. Sternson; N. Spruston; K. Svoboda; J. Chandrashekar

ocar.opportunity: Axonal arbor shape is a cell-type descriptor and routes long-range information, but few mouse projection neurons had been reconstructed in full.
ocar.challenge: Thin axons (~100 nm) travel centimeters across regions, so serial-section tracing has historically yielded small, often partial samples and bulk tracers average over types.
ocar.action: Winnubst, Bas, Ferreira, Wu, Economo, and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2019), present a MouseLight imaging and reconstruction platform and reconstruct more than 1,000 projection neurons in motor cortex, thalamus, subiculum, and hypothalamus, totaling more than 75 meters of axon, in a searchable database (mouselight.janelia.org).
ocar.resolution: Complete morphologies revealed previously unknown projection subtypes and organizational principles of long-range connectivity, including clustering into putative types, subtypes within known classes, and topographic gradients of single-cell projections.
ocar.future_work: The discussion contrasts this with bulk anterograde studies and combinatorial retrograde labeling whose injection counts scale poorly with target number; expanding coverage beyond the sampled regions is implied.

title: Spectral peculiarity and criticality of a human connectome.
authors: N. Pospelov; S. Nechaev; S. Nechaev; K. Anokhin; K. Anokhin; O. Valba; O. Valba; V. Avetisov; A. Gorsky

ocar.opportunity: Comparing spectral properties of structural connectomes across organisms could show what, if anything, is distinctive about human brain networks and speak to the brain-criticality debate.
ocar.challenge: It is unclear which organizational features matter for cognition and which evolutionary wiring rules produce observed graphs; human networks may not follow the same growth heuristics as other animals.
ocar.action: Anokhin, Avetisov, Gorsky, Nechaev, Pospelov, and Valba (Physics of Life Reviews, 2019; arXiv:1812.06317) perform comparative spectral analysis of open-access structural connectomes and study graph-Laplacian level spacing.
ocar.resolution: Human spectral density showed the largest deviation from a randomized network among organisms studied. Preference for 3-cycle formation reproduced many animal connectomes but fitting the human graph required conserving local clustering. Laplacian level spacing matched a hybrid Wigner–Dyson/Poisson critical regime familiar in condensed-matter physics, taken as support for brain criticality.
ocar.future_work: The work frames spectral criticality as evidence in a debate rather than a mechanistic model of cognition; linking spectra to function is left open.

plain_language_summary: Researchers compared the “sound” of brain-network graphs across animals by looking at their mathematical spectra. The human map stood out, and its spacing of graph frequencies looked like a physical system sitting at a critical point.

title: Neuronal Identity: The neuron types of a simple chordate sibling, the tadpole larva of Ciona intestinalis.
authors: Kerrianne Ryan; I. Meinertzhagen

ocar.opportunity: A complete synaptic-resolution connectome supplies a substrate for hypotheses about circuits and cell identities. For years only C. elegans had such a map; a second, phylogenetically distant species of similar numerical complexity lets those hypotheses be tested in a chordate.
ocar.challenge: Ciona intestinalis is often treated as a chordate C. elegans, but it is a urochordate sibling of vertebrates, not an ecdysozoan. Homologies cannot be cherry-picked, and many larval neurons look idiosyncratic rather than like simplified vertebrate cells.
ocar.action: Ryan and Meinertzhagen, in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (published 2019; DOI 2018), review EM reconstructions of the tadpole-larva central and peripheral nervous systems of Ciona intestinalis and the neuron types those maps define.
ocar.resolution: About 330 CNS cells are mostly ciliated ependymal cells, with ~180 neurons in about 50 morphological types. Most neurons are ciliated and lack dendrites; some lack an axon. Synapses are mostly en passant, some dyads, with heterogeneous vesicles, averaging 49 synapses per neuron, forming a network of unpredicted complexity.
ocar.future_work: Priorities named in the conclusions are whether a second larva would show identical types, cell-by-cell transmitters and receptors (single-cell transcriptomics were underway), and resisting the assumption that tunicate neurons are simply miniature vertebrate homologs.

plain_language_summary: A tiny sea-squirt larva has a complete wiring diagram of its small nervous system. This review catalogs the cell types in that map and warns that they are not just miniature vertebrate neurons.

title: Rewiring the connectome: Evidence and effects
authors: Sophie Bennett; Alastair J. Kirby; G. Finnerty

ocar.opportunity: Connectome mapping has mostly treated connections as stable once formed. If local circuitry rewires during learning, the physical graph is a moving target and a possible therapeutic handle.
ocar.challenge: Evidence for rewiring has been hard to obtain, and structural change must be disentangled from synaptic-strength and excitability plasticity. Long-range tracts are unlikely to rewire extensively in the healthy adult brain.
ocar.action: Bennett, Kirby, and Finnerty, in Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews (2018), review evidence for rewiring at synaptic, microcircuit, and long-range scales and its role in learning.
ocar.resolution: They conclude there is growing evidence that the micro- and meso-connectome rewire during experience-dependent plasticity and learning, whereas long-range rewiring in healthy adults is limited to terminal arbours of projecting axons. Rewiring is argued to be especially useful where connection probability is already low, as among neocortical pyramids.
ocar.future_work: The authors list open questions on how rewiring affects function, how it is coordinated with other plasticity mechanisms, and how to control it therapeutically without causing aberrant wiring in psychiatric or neurological disease.

plain_language_summary: Brain maps often assume the wires stay put after they form. This review argues that local circuits do rewire during learning, which could matter for treating brain disease.

summaries.beginner: Brain maps often assume the wires stay put after they form. This review argues that local circuits do rewire during learning, which could matter for treating brain disease.
summaries.intermediate: Bennett, Kirby, and Finnerty (Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews, 2018) survey evidence that mammalian connectivity is not fixed. They examine rewiring from synapses and microcircuits up to long-range tracts, and they conclude that local circuitry rewires during learning while long-range axons in healthy adults mainly remodel terminal arbours. They argue that forming and losing entire connections expands learning capacity in sparsely connected cortex, and they discuss therapeutic use after injury and in neuropsychiatric disorders.
summaries.advanced: This is a narrative review, not a new reconstruction or a single experiment. The extract’s conclusion distinguishes micro/meso rewiring from limited long-range change but does not quantify rates. Disease-treatment claims are prospective. title: Schaffer Collateral Inputs to CA1 Excitatory and Inhibitory Neurons Follow Different Connectivity Rules
authors: Osung Kwon; Linqing Feng; S. Druckmann; Jinhyung Kim

ocar.opportunity: Fine-scale synaptic maps of identified cell classes can show whether excitatory and inhibitory neurons obey the same spatial wiring rules when they share a presynaptic pathway.
ocar.challenge: Peters’ rule predicts synapses from axonal–dendritic overlap, but prior work showed structured CA3–CA1 pyramidal connectivity, leaving open whether CA1 interneurons follow the same pattern.
ocar.action: Kwon, Feng, Druckmann, and Kim, in Journal of Neuroscience (2018), use mGRASP and neuTube in male mice to map Schaffer-collateral synapses onto CA1 pyramidal cells and parvalbumin-positive interneurons.
ocar.resolution: Pyramidal connectivity strongly departed from randomness, and applying Peters’ rule enhanced that structure, whereas PV cells were more random and became more so under Peters’ rule. Deep-versus-superficial sublayer structure was present for pyramids and little or none for PVs. The same SC axons therefore follow different rules onto the two targets.
ocar.future_work: The discussion links structured pyramidal input to branch-level nonlinear processing and more random PV input to broad winner-take-all inhibition; those functional interpretations are hypotheses for physiology, not tested here.

plain_language_summary: The same incoming axons in mouse hippocampus wire onto excitatory and inhibitory cells in different ways. Excitatory cells get a patterned map; a major inhibitory class looks more random.

summaries.beginner: The same incoming axons in mouse hippocampus wire onto excitatory and inhibitory cells in different ways. Excitatory cells get a patterned map; a major inhibitory class looks more random.
summaries.intermediate: Kwon, Feng, Druckmann, and Kim (Journal of Neuroscience, 2018) map Schaffer-collateral synapses in male-mouse CA1 with mGRASP. CA3–CA1 pyramidal connectivity is spatially structured and becomes more so when overlap (Peters’ rule) is used to predict synapses, whereas parvalbumin-positive interneurons are closer to random and become more random under the same prediction. Deep pyramidal sublayer cells appear more structured than superficial ones; PVs show little sublayer specificity. The paper treats these as distinct connectivity rules for E versus I cells sharing one input stream.

Numeric R² values appear in figures rather than as a single summary statistic in the extract. Functional arguments about winner-take-all are interpretive.

title: The Worm Connectome: Back to the Future.
authors: W. Schafer

ocar.opportunity: Large-scale connectome projects treat whole-brain wiring diagrams as a genome-like resource. The only complete animal connectome for decades was already in hand: C. elegans.
ocar.challenge: Unlike the genetic code, there is no comparable theory that reads function off connectivity, so even a 302-neuron map has not yielded a complete account of behavior.
ocar.action: Schafer, in Trends in Neurosciences (2018), retells the White et al. (1986) reconstruction and its later influence on behavioral neuroscience and network science.
ocar.resolution: White and colleagues mapped 302 identified hermaphrodite neurons connected by approximately 10,000 chemical synapses and 1,000 gap junctions, by hand, from serial TEM. ocar.future_work: The piece closes by calling for theories that relate network topology to circuit function, with C. elegans as the place to develop and test them before interpreting larger connectomes.

title: Volumetric reconstruction of main Caenorhabditis elegans neuropil at two different time points
authors: C. Brittin; Steven J. Cook; D. Hall; S. W. Emmons; N. Cohen

ocar.opportunity: Synaptic partner choice can be separated from mere spatial adjacency only if both synapses and the 3D occupancy of processes are known in the same volume.
ocar.challenge: Peters’ rule and related spatial models may not explain why homologous C. elegans neurons make reproducible synapses despite variable process placement.
ocar.action: Brittin, Cook, Hall, Emmons, and Cohen, on bioRxiv (2018), volumetrically reconstruct the C. elegans nerve ring from legacy serial-section EM at L4 and young adult and compare spatial, synaptic, and subcellular specificity.

title: Connectomics of synaptic microcircuits: lessons from the outer retina
authors: L. Rogerson; Christian Behrens; Thomas Euler; Philipp Berens; T. Schubert

ocar.opportunity: The outer retina has stereotyped anatomical motifs at the photoreceptor synapse, so a complete 3D EM census can test whether those motifs are as strict as textbooks imply.
ocar.challenge: Classical EM and immunolabelling traded sample size against resolution, limiting quantitative connectivity to a few cells; a published mouse volume also lacked explicit synaptic labels.
ocar.action: Rogerson, Behrens, Euler, Berens, and Schubert, in Journal of Physiology (2017), review a 3D serial-EM analysis of mouse outer retina that infers contacts from invaginating versus basal motifs.
ocar.resolution: The quantitative description recovered unexpected exceptions: substantial rod–cone pathway interaction at the photoreceptor synapse, sparse photoreceptor sampling, and atypical contacts, including many rod-to-OFF cone-bipolar contacts. ocar.future_work: The functional weight of atypical contacts remains unsettled, given conflicting physiology, and the unlabeled-synapse inference is a standing limit of the source dataset.

plain_language_summary: Rod and cone pathways in the eye were thought to meet later in the circuit. This review of a 3D electron-microscope map of mouse outer retina finds they already mix at the first synapse, with several exceptions to the textbook wiring.

title: Deep Learning Improves Template Matching by Normalized Cross Correlation
authors: Davit Buniatyan; T. Macrina; Dodam Ih; J. Zung; H. Seung

ocar.opportunity: Petascale serial-section EM stacks may need huge numbers of template matches to align 2D tiles into 3D; even a small false-match rate would break neurite continuity.
ocar.challenge: Normalized cross-correlation on raw or bandpass-filtered patches still yields false matches when sections are deformed, damaged, or missing, and rejecting suspects also discards true matches.
ocar.action: Buniatyan, Macrina, Ih, Zung, and Seung, on arXiv (2017), preprocess template and source patches with siamese convolutional networks trained to enlarge the NCC gap between true and false matches, tested on serial-section brain EM.
ocar.resolution: Relative to a tuned bandpass baseline, the networks reduce false matches. For adjacent sections with 224-pixel templates, rejecting matches with r_delta below 0.05 removed every error while dropping 0.12% of true matches versus 0.40% for bandpass (about 3.5× more efficient). On a harder across-section 160-pixel task, 0.1% error needed <1% true-match rejection versus 20% for bandpass.
ocar.future_work: The authors want tests of generalization across EM datasets and possible transfer to the segmentation network that follows alignment. Failure modes include templates that lack the keypoints the net has learned (e.g. cell-body interiors).

plain_language_summary: Stitching electron-microscope slices into a 3D brain volume depends on matching image patches. A neural net that pre-cleans those patches makes the classic matching method much less error-prone.

summaries.beginner: Stitching electron-microscope slices into a 3D brain volume depends on matching image patches. A neural net that pre-cleans those patches makes the classic matching method much less error-prone.
summaries.intermediate: Buniatyan, Macrina, Ih, Zung, and Seung (arXiv, 2017) wrap normalized cross-correlation with siamese convnets trained so true matches score higher than false ones, using serial-section brain EM patches. Supervision is weak: a true match exists somewhere in the source, but its location is not given. Versus a parameter-tuned bandpass filter, false matches fall, and NCC scores become easier to threshold. For adjacent 224-pixel templates, an r_delta cutoff of 0.05 eliminated all tested errors at 0.12% true-match loss (0.40% for bandpass). The method is motivated by alignment workloads that could reach on the order of 100 million matches for a teravoxel volume.
summaries.advanced: Results are on the authors’ EM patch set, not a public leaderboard. The 100-million-match figure is an order-of-magnitude motivation, not a measured runtime. Generalization across datasets is proposed, not shown. The convnet can fail on templates without learned keypoints; raw images can still help on corner-like edges. This is an arXiv CS.CV preprint.

authors: D. Ville; Robin Demesmaeker; M. Preti

ocar.opportunity: Graph Fourier methods based on the Laplacian give global embeddings, but an analyst often wants organization inside a chosen subgraph without throwing away the rest of the network.
ocar.challenge: Ordinary Laplacian eigenvectors are not concentrated on an arbitrary node set, so they mix local and global structure in a way that is hard to steer.
ocar.action: Van De Ville, Demesmaeker, and Preti, in SPIE Optical Engineering + Applications (2017), apply graph Slepians—band-limited signals with maximal energy in a subgraph—to the structural C. elegans connectome and propose a visualization of subgraph organization balanced against global topology.
ocar.resolution: Selecting sensory or motor neurons and varying bandwidth revealed embeddings that reorganize lobes (e.g. ventral/neck versus left/right) while remaining consistent as bandwidth increases. Concentration-based and modified-embedded-distance Slepian designs spanned similar subspaces; the latter is preferred when eigenvalues are used as frequencies.
ocar.future_work: Suggested extensions include graph uncertainty principles, resampling, hierarchical subgraph refinement, and directed graphs. Matlab code is released.

plain_language_summary: Network maps can be viewed through a mathematical lens that zooms in on one group of cells while still remembering the whole worm. The authors illustrate that trick on the C. elegans wiring diagram.

summaries.beginner: Network maps can be viewed through a mathematical lens that zooms in on one group of cells while still remembering the whole worm. The authors illustrate that trick on the C. elegans wiring diagram.
summaries.intermediate: Van De Ville, Demesmaeker, and Preti (SPIE, 2017) illustrate graph Slepians on the C. elegans structural connectome. Slepians are band-limited graph signals concentrated on a chosen subgraph, used here to visualize that subgraph’s organization without ignoring global structure. Demonstrations on sensory and motor neuron sets show embeddings that change with bandwidth but keep a stable large-scale layout. Two design criteria (energy concentration versus modified embedded distance) give similar subspaces; eigenvalues of the latter can serve as frequencies for filtering. Code is provided.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods illustration on one worm connectome, not a biological discovery paper. The graph-bandwidth product K = N_W N_S / N is compared to summed concentrations and is not identical on irregular domains. ‘Optical Engineering + Applications’ is the SPIE meeting venue; an arXiv version exists. No claim is made that Slepians recover known cell classes better than standard spectral clustering.

title: Multichannel activity propagation across an engineered axon network
authors: H. I. Chen; John A. Wolf; Douglas H. Smith

ocar.opportunity: Whole-brain connectomes do not isolate how activity is transmitted between two nodes. An engineered two-node cortical culture with a long axon tract would be a controllable ‘connectome unit.’
ocar.challenge: Massive interconnectivity in vivo, and short internodal distances in prior patterned cultures, make it hard to study multichannel transmission without the network collapsing into a uniform sheet.
ocar.action: Chen, Wolf, and Smith, in Journal of Neural Engineering (2017), use axon stretch growth to build paired cortical nodes linked by tracts up to 1 cm, then combine optogenetic stimulation with multi-electrode-array recording.
ocar.resolution: Stimulus representations included direct, synaptic, and multiplexed responses that grew more complex with distance and collapsed at higher stimulation frequencies. Glutamatergic blockade revealed a hierarchy of pathways, some initially latent. Adding stimulus channels had divergent local versus distant effects, and ensembles generally beat single cells at discriminating input patterns. Mean conduction velocity across engineered axons is given as 0.26 m/s.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the preparation as a model for neural-code studies and multichannel stimulation therapies; in vivo translation is not demonstrated.

plain_language_summary: Instead of mapping a whole brain, this team grows two clumps of cortex linked by a long bundle of axons. They then watch how patterns of activity change as they travel from one clump to the other.

summaries.beginner: Instead of mapping a whole brain, this team grows two clumps of cortex linked by a long bundle of axons. They then watch how patterns of activity change as they travel from one clump to the other.
summaries.intermediate: Chen, Wolf, and Smith (Journal of Neural Engineering, 2017) engineer a two-node cortico-cortical culture with stretch-grown axon tracts up to 1 cm—an order of magnitude longer than prior modular cultures—and record with MEAs under optical stimulation. Responses include direct, synaptic, and multiplexed components, simplify at high stimulation rates, and expose latent internodal pathways under glutamate-receptor blockade. Ensemble decoding outperformed single cells. Mean conduction velocity is reported as 0.26 m/s and is described as likely an underestimate. The work is framed as an isolated connectome unit for studying the neural code and stimulation therapies.
summaries.advanced: This is an in vitro tissue-engineering study, not an EM connectome. Conduction velocity 0.26 m/s is a mean that omits synaptic delays in the calculation, as the authors note. ‘Hierarchy of latent circuits’ is pharmacological, not anatomical proofreading. Clinical stimulation guidance is speculative. The PDF is an NIH author manuscript.

title: Semiparametric spectral modeling of the Drosophila connectome
authors: C. Priebe; Youngser Park; M. Tang; A. Athreya; V. Lyzinski; J. Vogelstein; Yichen Qin; Benjamin T. Cocanougher; K. Eichler; Marta Zlatic; Albert Cardona

ocar.opportunity: A complete synaptic-resolution mushroom-body connectome lets statistical network models be tested on a biologically labeled directed graph rather than on MRI-scale matrices.
ocar.challenge: A four-type wiring diagram invites a stochastic block model, but latent structure may be richer than four discrete blocks.
ocar.action: Priebe, Park, Tang, Athreya, Lyzinski, Vogelstein, Qin, Cocanougher, Eichler, Zlatic, and Cardona, on arXiv (2017), embed the larval Drosophila mushroom-body graph with adjacency spectral embedding and fit a latent structure model via semiparametric Gaussian mixtures.
ocar.resolution: After dropping 13 isolated Kenyon cells, the right-hemisphere MB graph has 213 vertices (100 KC, 21 MBIN, 29 MBON, 63 PN) and 7,536 directed edges, occupying only eight of sixteen type-type blocks. The resulting ‘connectome code’ is presented as capturing latent structure beyond a simple four-block SBM and as reflecting biologically relevant neuronal properties.
ocar.future_work: The introduction frames connectome coding as asking which properties are preserved across individuals and species; those comparative tests are not the empirical content of this extract.

plain_language_summary: Statisticians take the wiring diagram of a larval fruit-fly learning center and draw a compact map of each cell. The map is meant to show hidden structure, not just the four textbook cell classes.

summaries.beginner: Statisticians take the wiring diagram of a larval fruit-fly learning center and draw a compact map of each cell. The map is meant to show hidden structure, not just the four textbook cell classes.
summaries.intermediate: Priebe and colleagues (arXiv, 2017) analyze the complete larval Drosophila mushroom-body connectome (Eichler et al.) from serial-section TEM of the whole nervous system. The right-hemisphere graph, after removing 13 isolated Kenyon cells, has 213 neurons (100 KC, 21 MBIN, 29 MBON, 63 PN) and 7,536 directed edges. They motivate a latent structure model nested between a stochastic block model and a random dot product graph, fitted by Gaussian mixtures in adjacency-spectral-embedding space. The paper’s claim is that this semiparametric ‘connectome code’ recovers latent structure tied to neuronal properties.
summaries.advanced: This is a statistics preprint; biological labels (KC/MBIN/MBON/PN) come from the source connectome. Eight of sixteen blocks are empty by construction of the directed type graph. Model-fit metrics and out-of-sample prediction are not in the selected extract (which moves from introduction into spectral clustering). Isolate removal makes the graph weakly but not strongly connected.

title: Synaptic organization of visual space in primary visual cortex
authors: M. Iacaruso; Ioana Gasler; S. Hofer

ocar.opportunity: Contextual visual processing depends on long-range excitatory axons, but the functional logic of those inputs onto individual cortical neurons was unknown.
ocar.challenge: It was unclear what parts of visual space synapse onto a cell, how that relates to the cell’s own receptive field, and whether similar features cluster on neighboring spines.
ocar.action: Iacaruso, Gasler, and Hofer, in Nature (2017), map spatial receptive fields of dendritic spines on mouse primary visual cortex neurons with two-photon calcium imaging.
ocar.resolution: Neurons collect functionally diverse inputs from extended visual space. Similar features from the same location cluster on neighboring spines. Putative long-range inputs often land on higher-order branches and are more frequent, and more co-oriented, when the input receptive field is displaced along the axis of the postsynaptic orientation preference. Connectivity thus prefers co-oriented, co-axially aligned partners, a motif suited to elongated-edge amplification.
ocar.future_work: The authors present this as a candidate substrate for contour integration and object grouping; causal tests of that computation are not in this extract.

plain_language_summary: A visual-cortex cell sees a small patch of the world, but its dendrites also listen to other patches. This study maps those listening posts on individual spines and finds they prefer partners that line up with the cell’s favorite orientation.

summaries.beginner: A visual-cortex cell sees a small patch of the world, but its dendrites also listen to other patches. This study maps those listening posts on individual spines and finds they prefer partners that line up with the cell’s favorite orientation.
summaries.intermediate: Iacaruso, Gasler, and Hofer (Nature, 2017) image GCaMP signals in dendritic spines of mouse V1 to map excitatory input receptive fields. Inputs are functionally diverse and spatially extended; similar features from the same location cluster on neighboring spines. Inputs from beyond the somatic receptive field often target higher-order dendrites. Displaced inputs are more common and more co-oriented when offset along the postsynaptic orientation axis, yielding a co-oriented, co-axial connectivity rule. The authors argue this organization can amplify elongated edges.
summaries.advanced: Inputs are inferred from spine calcium, not EM synapses; ‘putative long-range’ is a spatial-RF criterion. Extended Data in the extract repeat main analyses after dropping spines correlated with the parent dendrite (522 spines remaining after removing 26%). Global dendritic contamination is therefore a recognized artifact. The PDF is a Europe PMC author manuscript of the Nature paper.

title: Reconstruction of Neural Circuits Using Serial Block-Face Scanning Electron Microscopy
authors: Gyu Hyun Kim; Sang-Hoon Lee; Kea-Joo Lee

ocar.opportunity: Serial block-face SEM can collect thousands of aligned images automatically, reducing the distortion and alignment burden of serial-section TEM for hippocampal circuit reconstruction.
ocar.challenge: Large-scale EM reconstruction had been limited by cutting thousands of sections and tracing warped stacks; SB-SEM still faces charging, beam damage, and a segmentation bottleneck.
ocar.action: Kim, Lee, and Lee, in Applied Microscopy (2016), present a technical report of the full reconstruction workflow for synaptic networks in rat hippocampal CA1 using SB-SEM.
ocar.resolution: They report a three-dimensional volume of about 37,000 µm³ with resolution sufficient to identify sub-synaptic structures and trace fine processes, arguing SB-SEM yielded more reliable stacks than ssTEM and sped reconstruction by cutting alignment work. They note tiled imaging can enlarge the field.
ocar.future_work: Electrical charging of non-conductive resin remains a caveat, potentially mitigated by conductive resins. Segmentation, not acquisition, is identified as the remaining bottleneck. The authors intend the method for mapping impaired synapses in neurodegenerative disease.

plain_language_summary: This methods report shows how to reconstruct synapses in a piece of rat hippocampus by shaving the sample inside a scanning electron microscope. The pictures come out already aligned, which saves a lot of stitching work.

summaries.beginner: This methods report shows how to reconstruct synapses in a piece of rat hippocampus by shaving the sample inside a scanning electron microscope. The pictures come out already aligned, which saves a lot of stitching work.
summaries.intermediate: Kim, Sang-Hoon Lee, and Kea-Joo Lee (Applied Microscopy, 2016) describe serial block-face SEM reconstruction of synaptic networks in rat CA1. They report a volume of about 37,000 µm³ acquired automatically and say SB-SEM reduced alignment and distortion relative to serial-section TEM. The discussion flags charging and beam damage as limits on lateral resolution and points to conductive resins. Segmentation is called the major remaining bottleneck. The stated aim is connectomic mapping and eventual study of synaptic disease.
summaries.advanced: This is a technical report from Korea Brain Research Institute, not a full connectome of CA1. The 37,000 µm³ figure is the authors’ stated volume; completeness of tracing is not quantified in the extract. Disease applications are prospective. Image quality caveats (charging) are first-order, not footnotes.
