title: Toward Whole-Body Connectomics
authors: C. Lo; A. Chiang

ocar.opportunity: Large brain-connectome projects map neurons inside the head, but behavior is produced by a nervous system that innervates the whole body.
ocar.challenge: Except for C. elegans, whole-body synaptic maps do not exist, and scaling optical and EM methods to large animals faces imaging, clearing, and reconstruction barriers.
ocar.action: Lo and Chiang, in Journal of Neuroscience (2016), expand a SfN Presidential Lecture into a viewpoint on whole-body connectomics, emphasizing optical methods and the need to map brain–body interactions in situ.
ocar.resolution: They argue that consciousness-level understanding requires jointly mapping circuitry, activity, and behavior beyond isolated brains, using MRI, light microscopy, and EM at their respective scales. C. elegans’ 302-neuron whole-body map is the explicit exception among current projects.
ocar.future_work: The piece is a program for mapping whole-body connectomes in large animals; the selected extract’s later pages are references, so specific technical prescriptions in the discussion are not captured here.

plain_language_summary: Most connectome projects map only the brain. This lecture-based essay says we also need the nerves of the rest of the body if we want to explain real behavior.

summaries.beginner: Most connectome projects map only the brain. This lecture-based essay says we also need the nerves of the rest of the body if we want to explain real behavior.
summaries.intermediate: Lo and Chiang (Journal of Neuroscience, 2016) publish a viewpoints article based on a 2016 SfN Presidential Lecture. They note that contemporary large-scale projects target brain neurons, with C. elegans’ 302-neuron whole-body reconstruction as the main exception, and they argue that complex behavior requires mapping interactions between brain and body. The survey emphasizes optical approaches alongside EM and MRI. The article is programmatic rather than a new dataset.
summaries.advanced: This is an opinion/lecture piece. The selected PDF text runs from the introduction into the reference list, so later technological recommendations are not in the extract. ‘Whole-body connectome’ is a scale argument, not a claim that optical methods already deliver synaptic whole-body maps in large animals.

title: Specification of synaptic connectivity by cell surface interactions
authors: J. Wit; Anirvan Ghosh

ocar.opportunity: If neurons carried unique cell-surface identities, they could select synaptic partners with molecular precision rather than by proximity alone.
ocar.challenge: Surface-molecule repertoires and extracellular interactions have been catalogued, but linking that diversity to the precision of circuit wiring remains difficult.
ocar.action: de Wit and Ghosh, in Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2015), as described in the catalog abstract, review cadherin, neurexin, immunoglobulin, and leucine-rich-repeat superfamilies in the specification of connectivity.
ocar.resolution: The abstract concludes that concerted actions of these protein families may critically contribute to neural-circuit assembly, without claiming that any one family is sufficient.
ocar.future_work: How combinatorial surface codes map onto complete connectomes is left as the outstanding problem.

plain_language_summary: Neurons may choose their partners using families of sticky surface proteins. This review discusses several of those protein families and how they might help build precise circuits.

summaries.beginner: Neurons may choose their partners using families of sticky surface proteins. This review discusses several of those protein families and how they might help build precise circuits.
summaries.intermediate: de Wit and Ghosh (Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 2015) review how cadherins, neurexins, immunoglobulin-superfamily proteins, and leucine-rich-repeat proteins could confer cell-surface identities that specify synapses. The catalog abstract states that concerted actions of these families may be critical for circuit assembly, while noting that connecting molecular diversity to wiring precision has been challenging. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Yang, Song, Lu, and Lin, Chemical Reviews (2026), on in-cellulo fabrication of supramolecular protein assemblies, not the de Wit and Ghosh synapse-specification review. Claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Independent reading of the Nature Reviews Neuroscience paper is required for the primary literature discussed there.

title: Automatic discovery of cell types and microcircuitry from neural connectomics
authors: Eric Jonas; Konrad Paul Kording

ocar.opportunity: High-throughput connectomes will outrun manual cell-typing. Combining connectivity, soma location, and synapse spatial distributions in one probabilistic model could recover types automatically.
ocar.challenge: There is no closed-form optimum for parsing neurons into types and motifs; inference is approximate and slows with data size, and monotonic distance–connectivity likelihoods are too simple for some systems.
ocar.action: Jonas and Kording, in eLife (2014; arXiv preprint in the extract), present a nonparametric Bayesian method and apply it to retina, C. elegans, and the 6502 microprocessor.
ocar.resolution: The model recovers known retinal types better than simpler algorithms and supports connectivity prediction. It also finds structure in C. elegans and automatically discovers spatial/connectivity clusters among MOS transistors in a 6502 reconstruction. Combining data types is presented as the key.
ocar.future_work: MCMC does not guarantee a global optimum; runtime is hours at 1,000 neurons; ~70 retinal types cannot all be distinguished from the available cells. Broader likelihoods and faster inference are proposed.

plain_language_summary: Instead of naming cell types by hand, this method lets a statistical model group neurons from their wiring and positions. It works on retina and worm data, and even on the transistors of an old computer chip.

summaries.beginner: Instead of naming cell types by hand, this method lets a statistical model group neurons from their wiring and positions. It works on retina and worm data, and even on the transistors of an old computer chip.
summaries.intermediate: Jonas and Kording (eLife, 2014) introduce a nonparametric Bayesian clustering of connectome data that jointly uses connectivity, cell-body location, and spatial synapse distributions. They report recovery of known retinal neuron types and better connectivity prediction than simpler algorithms, plus structure in C. elegans and in a 6502 microprocessor graph (gate/C1/C2 terminals). The discussion is frank that inference is approximate (MCMC), that 1,000 neurons took several hours, and that the cells on hand cannot statistically resolve all ~70 anatomical retinal types.
summaries.advanced: The supplied PDF is an arXiv preprint (v1 2014) with a later header date; the catalog DOI is the eLife version—treat page-level details as preprint. The 6502 example is a provocative analogy, not neural tissue. Distance-dependent likelihoods are assumed monotonic. Type discovery is unsupervised relative to some labels but evaluated against known anatomy where available.

title: Motif-Role-Fingerprints: The Building-Blocks of Motifs, Clustering-Coefficients and Transitivities in Directed Networks
authors: M. McDonnell; Ömer Nebil Yaveroğlu; B. Schmerl; Nicolangelo Iannella; L. M. Ward

ocar.opportunity: Directed connectomes are often summarized by motif counts, clustering coefficients, and transitivity, which are not independent statistics.
ocar.challenge: Node-level ‘who participates in which subgraph’ (motif-role fingerprints) had not been shown to convert cleanly between functional (partial) and structural (induced) counts, nor to generate those global metrics.
ocar.action: McDonnell, Yaveroğlu, Schmerl, Iannella, and Ward, in PLoS ONE (2014), derive matrix conversions among functional and structural motif-role fingerprints, motif fingerprints, and global subgraph counts, and illustrate them on C. elegans chemical-synapse graphs.
ocar.resolution: A vector of functional motif-role fingerprints from any directed adjacency matrix maps invertibly to structural fingerprints, so the two descriptions are equivalent. The same logic extends to role-free fingerprints and standard motif totals. Motif-role fingerprints are shown to underlie directed clustering coefficients and transitivities, suggesting new subtypes. Matlab code is provided.
ocar.future_work: Proposed uses include centrality on synaptic networks, anomaly detection, and finding similar nodes or graphs; those applications are not benchmarked as a connectome biology result in the extract.

plain_language_summary: When scientists count little wiring triangles in a brain graph, they are really counting how each cell sits inside those triangles. This math paper shows those cell-level counts are the building blocks of several popular network scores.

summaries.beginner: When scientists count little wiring triangles in a brain graph, they are really counting how each cell sits inside those triangles. This math paper shows those cell-level counts are the building blocks of several popular network scores.
summaries.intermediate: McDonnell et al. (PLoS ONE, 2014) define motif-role fingerprints—per-node counts of participation in directed subgraphs—and prove that functional (partial-subgraph) fingerprints convert to structural (induced-subgraph) fingerprints by an invertible matrix. Analogous results hold without roles and for global motif counts. They emphasize that directed clustering coefficients and transitivities are derived from these fingerprints, and they apply the machinery to public C. elegans hermaphrodite and male chemical-synapse adjacency matrices. Matlab code is included as supporting information.
summaries.advanced: This is a graph-theory methods paper; biological interpretation of C. elegans motifs is not the main result. ‘Functional’ versus ‘structural’ here means partial versus induced subgraphs, not physiology versus anatomy. New clustering-coefficient subtypes are proposed from the algebra, not validated as superior biomarkers.

title: Polarity-specific high-level information propagation in neural networks
authors: Yen-Nan Lin; Po-Yen Chang; Pao-Yueh Hsiao; C. Lo

ocar.opportunity: Standard graph metrics ignore two neural facts: information has a preferred input–interneuron–output polarity, and computation often uses recurrent high-level paths rather than shortest paths.
ocar.challenge: Small-world rewiring improves some mixing measures while harming others, so it is unclear whether real neural graphs avoid that trade-off.
ocar.action: Lin, Chang, Hsiao, and Lo, in Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2014), quantify ‘vertical’ (specific input to specific output) and ‘horizontal’ (one input shared across outputs) high-level propagation in the C. elegans somatic nervous system and a partial Drosophila central-complex network, versus classic small-world graphs.
ocar.resolution: Both biological networks show efficient vertical and horizontal propagation. Small-world graphs trade the two: higher rewiring probability helps horizontal sharing but hurts vertical routing. Reassigning or reversing I/O nodes degrades efficiency even when architecture is unchanged. Direct (level 0) and one-hop (level 1) channel patterns differ, consistent with distinct functions.
ocar.future_work: The discussion links pathway counts to behaviors (head withdrawal versus oxygen-modulated locomotion) as illustrations, not as new causal experiments.

plain_language_summary: Brain networks have an in door, a middle, and an out door. Measuring how signals travel along those directions, not just along shortest shortcuts, shows worm and fly circuits mix and route information more efficiently than simple small-world models.

summaries.beginner: Brain networks have an in door, a middle, and an out door. Measuring how signals travel along those directions, not just along shortest shortcuts, shows worm and fly circuits mix and route information more efficiently than simple small-world models.
summaries.intermediate: Lin, Chang, Hsiao, and Lo (Frontiers in Neuroinformatics, 2014) analyze the C. elegans somatic nervous system and a partial Drosophila central-complex network with polarity-aware, high-level pathway counts. Vertical propagation tracks specific input–output pairs; horizontal propagation tracks sharing of one input across outputs. Both real networks are efficient in both directions, whereas Watts–Strogatz rewiring improves horizontal efficiency at the expense of vertical efficiency. Swapping or randomizing input/output labels reduces performance. Direct versus indirect channel matrices suggest different functional regimes.
summaries.advanced: ‘Efficiency’ is a graph-path construct, not measured spike transmission. The Drosophila network is partial (central complex). Error bars on reassignment plots are from 100 realizations. Behavioral anecdotes (OLQ/IL1–RMD versus AQR/PQR–locomotion) are literature links, not new physiology. Polarity labels are annotations, so they are part of the result rather than a purely topological invariant.

title: The AII amacrine cell connectome: a dense network hub
authors: R. Marc; James R. Anderson; Bryan William Jones; C. Sigulinsky; J. S. Lauritzen

ocar.opportunity: The AII amacrine cell is the textbook hub from rods into cone pathways; a full connectome can test whether it is a simple relay or a multifunctional network node.
ocar.challenge: Physiology and sparse TEM never catalogued its full partner set, and mouse versus rabbit geometry may change apparent synaptic variance.
ocar.action: Marc, Anderson, Jones, Sigulinsky, and Lauritzen, in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2014), analyze AII cells in the rabbit retinal connectome, including complete synaptic counts for five AIIs.
ocar.resolution: AII cells contact at least 28 cell classes, including every bipolar class. Besides distributing rod signals, they are implicated in photopic OFF feedback/feedforward, ON–OFF crossover, and cone-pathway inhibition that may switch rod versus cone vision. Sampling is normalized to encounter rates, targeting appears specific and errorless, and partner cohorts are distinguished by synaptic or coupling weights. Homologs in non-mammals are proposed as glycinergic photopic crossover cells, with mammalian rod bipolar expansion as the evolutionary add-on.
ocar.future_work: A complete physiological model still does not fall out of the anatomy; mouse–rabbit differences in span caution against transferring coefficients of variation across species.

plain_language_summary: A famous retinal cell that helps you see in dim light turns out to talk to at least 28 kinds of partners. Far from a simple relay, it sits at the center of several rod and cone networks.

summaries.beginner: A famous retinal cell that helps you see in dim light turns out to talk to at least 28 kinds of partners. Far from a simple relay, it sits at the center of several rod and cone networks.
summaries.intermediate: Marc and colleagues (Frontiers in Neural Circuits, 2014) use the rabbit RC1 connectome to re-examine AII amacrine cells. AIIs contact at least 28 classes, including every bipolar class, via class-specific rules (e.g. postsynaptic to rod bipolars, coupled to most ON cone bipolars, mixed with OFF cone bipolars). Complete counts from five AIIs indicate encounter-normalized sampling, apparently errorless qualitative targeting, and strong weight differentiation. The cell is framed as a dense hub for scotopic distribution plus photopic crossover and switching. An evolutionary sketch posits non-mammalian glycinergic homologs plus later expansion of pure rod bipolars.
summaries.advanced: ‘Most complex interaction repertoire of any known vertebrate neuron’ is an authorship claim. ‘Errorless’ targeting is reported for this volume and cell sample. Mouse CV comparisons (Tsukamoto and Omi) are attributed to smaller mouse spans (~10 μm versus rabbit AII spans of 70 μm or more). TH1 cells are reidentified as glutamatergic, not dual GABAergic/dopaminergic, in this rabbit profiling. Catalog organism tags include mouse; the paper is rabbit RC1.

title: Deconstructing Complexity: Serial Block-Face Electron Microscopic Analysis of the Hippocampal Mossy Fiber Synapse
authors: Scott A. Wilke; Joseph K. Antonios; E. Bushong; Ali Badkoobehi; Elmar Malek; Minju Hwang; M. Terada; Mark Ellisman; Anirvan Ghosh

ocar.opportunity: The hippocampal mossy-fiber bouton is among the largest synapses in the brain, but its postnatal assembly is hard to reconstruct with serial-section TEM.
ocar.challenge: Standard EM could not quickly capture aligned volumes spanning developing boutons, thorny excrescences, and filopodia together.
ocar.action: Wilke, Antonios, Bushong, Badkoobehi, Malek, Hwang, Terada, Ellisman, and Ghosh, in Journal of Neuroscience (2013), use serial block-face EM to reconstruct mouse mossy-fiber connectivity across postnatal development.
ocar.resolution: Mossy-fiber axons first make bouton-like specializations on dendritic shafts; dendritic protrusions largely arise independently of those contacts; complexity of both sides jumps after bouton–CA3 protrusion association. A transient filopodial exploration period is followed by refinement. Between P14 and adult, many small contacts appear to become fewer, larger synaptic sites. Occasional multi-bouton innervation of one thorny spine and dual-dendrite targeting at P14 were not seen in adult.
ocar.future_work: Whether small sites compete or merge, and how these structural stages map onto detonator-synapse physiology, remains open. The paper presents SBEM as a general developmental-circuit tool.

plain_language_summary: The giant mossy-fiber synapse in hippocampus is built in stages after birth. Volume electron microscopy shows early contacts on the dendritic shaft, a messy exploratory phase, then a cleaned-up adult structure.

summaries.beginner: The giant mossy-fiber synapse in hippocampus is built in stages after birth. Volume electron microscopy shows early contacts on the dendritic shaft, a messy exploratory phase, then a cleaned-up adult structure.
summaries.intermediate: Wilke et al. (Journal of Neuroscience, 2013) apply SBEM to mouse mossy-fiber–CA3 synapses at postnatal ages including P7, P14, and adult. Volume reconstructions indicate initial shaft boutons, largely independent emergence of dendritic protrusions, then a sharp rise in pre- and postsynaptic complexity once boutons associate with CA3 thorny excrescences, followed by filopodial exploration and later refinement. Background anatomy cited includes 10–15 mossy terminals per granule cell, ~50 dentate inputs per CA3 neuron, and up to 37 release sites per bouton. P14 still shows multi-bouton spines and dual-dendrite contacts absent in adult.
summaries.advanced: Developmental claims are from SBEM volumes at sampled ages, not longitudinal imaging of the same synapses. The 10–15, ~50, and 37 figures are cited from prior literature (Amaral, Acsády, Chicurel and Harris), not new counts in the extract. Competitive versus merger models of contact refinement are offered as alternatives. Functional ‘detonator’ language is background, not measured here.

title: ON Cone Bipolar Cell Axonal Synapses in the OFF Inner Plexiform Layer of the Rabbit Retina

title: From functional architecture to functional connectomics
authors: R. Reid

ocar.opportunity: Hubel and Wiesel’s functional architecture still organizes how cortical connectivity is discussed: topography, cell type, and function as separate specificities.
ocar.challenge: Thalamic input to simple cells was verified, but intracortical functional specificity—whether neurons connect by what they encode, not only by where they sit—was only becoming experimentally tractable.
ocar.action: Reid, in Neuron (2012), revisits the 1962 Hubel and Wiesel paper and subsequent slice and in vivo work, including Peters’ rule as a null model of non-specific connectivity.
ocar.resolution: Orientation columns exemplify topographic specificity. Fine-scale functional specificity of thalamic input to simple cells was confirmed in the 1990s. A simplifying assumption that neurons of a class are equivalent, with synapses reflecting availability (Peters’ rule), is contrasted with emerging evidence for more specific intracortical wiring. Cell-type architecture from slices is reviewed as necessary but not sufficient.
ocar.future_work: The essay points to new techniques as the way to settle intracortical functional specificity; it is not itself a connectomic reconstruction.

plain_language_summary: A classic 1962 vision paper taught us that cortex is organized in columns. This essay explains how that idea splits into ‘where a cell sits,’ ‘what type it is,’ and ‘what it encodes,’ and why the last piece was still the hardest to map in 2012.

summaries.beginner: A classic 1962 vision paper taught us that cortex is organized in columns. This essay explains how that idea splits into ‘where a cell sits,’ ‘what type it is,’ and ‘what it encodes,’ and why the last piece was still the hardest to map in 2012.
summaries.intermediate: Reid (Neuron, 2012) commemorates Hubel and Wiesel (1962), extracting topographic specificity (e.g. orientation columns), cell-type specificity, and functional specificity as distinct determinants of cortical connectivity. Thalamic models of simple-cell input are described as verified in the 1990s, while intracortical functional specificity remained the open, harder problem. Slice work on stereotyped connections (e.g. chandelier cells onto axon initial segments) is summarized, and Peters’ rule is presented as the canonical non-specific alternative. The piece is a conceptual review, not new data.
summaries.advanced: This is a historical/theoretical Neuron article. Peters’ rule is discussed as a corollary of class-equivalence, not refuted with a new dataset here. ‘Only now becoming tractable’ is a 2012 claim about methods (two-photon, EM). The PDF is an NIH author manuscript; the citation to Lee and Reid 2011 is the companion Current Opinion review in this shard.

Lesioning three model hindbrain neurons including Mauthner reduced short sensorimotor paths, matching known behavior.

Dedicated and distributed variants in the supplement change >20% of inter-compartment edges yet keep similar degree and small-world scores, so those metrics are coarse. title: Visualizing Neuromodulation In Vivo: TANGO-Mapping of Dopamine Signaling Reveals Appeptite Control of Sugar Sensing
authors: Hidehiko K. Inagaki; S. B. de-Leon; A. Wong; Smitha Jagadish; H. Ishimoto; G. Barnea; T. Kitamoto; R. Axel; D. Anderson

ocar.opportunity: A wiring diagram cannot predict behavior because neuromodulation superimposes a chemical map on synapses. A brain-wide genetic reporter of modulator receptor activation would locate that map in identified cells.
ocar.challenge: Voltammetry and microdialysis are limited in Drosophila and do not identify postsynaptic targets of released modulators.
ocar.action: Inagaki, Ben-Tabou de-Leon, Wong, Jagadish, Ishimoto, Barnea, Kitamoto, Axel, and Anderson, in Cell (2012), introduce TANGO-mapping of dopamine signaling and combine it with genetic perturbations of hunger-dependent sugar sensitivity.
ocar.resolution: Hunger enhances behavioral sensitivity to sugar at least in part via dopamine onto primary gustatory receptor neurons, increasing sugar-evoked calcium influx. DopR-Tango reports starvation-induced dopamine onto GRNs but not, under the same conditions, onto mushroom body or antennal lobe despite L-dopa feeding activating those sites. DopEcR mutation or GRN knockdown blocks the starvation effect at 6 h but not at 24 h of deprivation.
ocar.future_work: The method is offered for other neuromodulators and organisms. Later-stage starvation appears to recruit additional mechanisms beyond DopEcR in GRNs.

plain_language_summary: A connectome list of synapses cannot tell you how a hungry fly will act, because chemicals such as dopamine retune the circuit. This paper introduces a genetic map of where dopamine lands and shows it turns up sugar sensors when the fly is hungry.

summaries.beginner: A connectome list of synapses cannot tell you how a hungry fly will act, because chemicals such as dopamine retune the circuit. This paper introduces a genetic map of where dopamine lands and shows it turns up sugar sensors when the fly is hungry.
summaries.intermediate: Inagaki et al. (Cell, 2012) introduce TANGO-mapping to report sites of neuromodulation brain-wide in Drosophila. Applied to dopamine, the method plus genetics shows hunger increases sugar-evoked calcium in primary gustatory neurons via dopamine release onto those cells, contributing to enhanced PER sugar sensitivity. Starvation raised DopR-Tango in GRNs but not mushroom body or antennal lobe, even though L-dopa feeding could activate the latter. Knockdown or mutation of DopEcR in sugar GRNs removed the 6-hour starvation effect but not the 24-hour effect, implying additional later mechanisms.
summaries.advanced: TANGO is a transcriptional reporter, not a millisecond release assay; spatial resolution is cell class, not synapse. The 6 h versus 24 h split is an important caveat for claiming a single dopaminergic mechanism. The paper’s opening claim that behavior cannot be predicted from a connectome is a framing thesis, not a failed prediction on a specific EM graph. title: The Interscutularis Muscle Connectome
authors: Ju Lu; J. Tapia; Olivia L. White; J. Lichtman

ocar.opportunity: Complete circuit maps had been obtained only in C. elegans. A tractable mammalian circuit would show whether similar organizational principles hold when neurons are not uniquely identified.
ocar.challenge: Mammalian nervous systems are too large to reconstruct wholesale; pooling partial data across animals assumes class-level homogeneity that may be false.
ocar.action: Lu, Tapia, White, and Lichtman, in PLoS Biology (2009), reconstruct the motor-axon innervation of six interscutularis muscles from adult transgenic mice with fluorescent proteins in all motor axons, using automated optical microscopy and computer-assisted analysis.

title: Three-Dimensional Structure and Composition of CA3→CA1 Axons in Rat Hippocampal Slices: Implications for Presynaptic Connectivity and Compartmentalization
authors: G. Shepherd; K. Harris

ocar.opportunity: Whether individual CA3→CA1 axonal boutons can act as local compartments for synaptic efficacy and microconnectivity depends on their 3D shape, vesicle and mitochondrial content, and spacing.
ocar.challenge: Physiology had shown pre- and postsynaptic plasticity at Schaffer synapses, but serial-EM morphology of a nearly homogeneous CA3→CA1 axon population in stratum radiatum was incomplete.
ocar.action: Shepherd and Harris, in Journal of Neuroscience (1998), use serial EM in hippocampal slices to locate PSDs, vesicles, and mitochondria along 75 CA3→CA1 axon segments in mid-CA1 stratum radiatum, fully reconstructing eleven axons.
ocar.resolution: Synapses (PSD plus vesicles) occurred on average every 2.7 μm. Most varicosities (68%) had one PSD, 19% had 2–4, 13% had none; 90% contained vesicles; 53% lacked mitochondria and 8% contained only mitochondria. Varicosities varied greatly in length (1.1 ± 0.7 μm) and volume (0.13 ± 0.14 μm³); shafts were uniformly thin (0.17 ± 0.04 μm). Narrow shafts are argued to promote biochemical compartmentalization. Measurements are presented uncorrected for shrinkage.
ocar.future_work: The discussion flags convergence onto identified CA3–CA1 cell pairs and the heterogeneity of synaptic spacing (edge-to-edge PSD spacing varied more than 20-fold) as next questions; about 40% of PSDs sat on multiple-synapse boutons.

plain_language_summary: In the hippocampus, the axons that carry messages from CA3 to CA1 are not a string of identical beads. Serial electron microscopy shows boutons of many sizes, many without mitochondria, and thin necks that could keep each bouton chemically private.

title: Connectomic analysis reveals the axial circuit for self-righting posture control in Drosophila
authors: J. Picao-Osorio; W. Roseby; C.E. Hancock; A. Cardona; C. Alonso

ocar.opportunity: Self-righting when turned upside-down is a stereotyped postural behavior, but the sensory-to-motor circuit that implements it along the body axis had not been mapped in any animal.
ocar.challenge: Larval Drosophila self-righting depends on segmentally repeated LT1/2 motor neurons and Hox-targeting microRNAs, yet the upstream sensory and interneuron architecture across abdominal segments was unresolved.
ocar.action: Picao-Osorio, Roseby, Hancock, Cardona, and Alonso, in a July 2026 bioRxiv preprint, combine connectomic reconstruction from a first-instar EM volume with thermogenetic silencing to trace and test the self-righting circuit along the antero-posterior axis.
ocar.resolution: Starting from LT1/2 motor neurons they identify premotor interneurons, upstream partners, and class IV multidendritic sensory neurons as core elements; silencing most of these impairs self-righting. The circuit overlaps nociceptive rolling and touch crawling at shared interneurons including DnB, A02o (Wave-1), and TePn05. Network analyses show nested hubs, a few integrator neurons, and declining synapse number and density toward posterior segments.
ocar.future_work: Several elements were reconstructed in only a subset of segments, and analysis is restricted to one first-instar EM volume, so axial trends are a first approximation. They suggest dissecting computations at integrator nodes, linking Hox-regulated microRNAs to this wiring, and informing axial control in soft robotics.

title: Evidence for a Functional Proximity Law in Multilayer Networks

title: Imprecision in Vision: Lessons From Neural Circuits in the Fly
authors: Mathias F. Wernet; Marion Silies

ocar.opportunity: Fly visual-system connectomes now cover whole optic lobes, so one can ask whether ‘the same’ cell type really wires the same way across columns.

Peripheral examples include precise R1–R6 lamina wiring versus more divergent medulla pathways, with only 15 cell types described as truly columnar (once per medulla column) among many more downstream types.
ocar.future_work: The open question is functional: whether imprecise connectivity is noise, feature extraction, or a robustness mechanism. The review points to recently released female and male visual-system connectomes as the data to press that question.

plain_language_summary: Fly eyes look like a repeating grid of identical units, which should make vision the same everywhere. This essay uses wiring diagrams to argue that cells of one named type still differ in who they connect to.

summaries.beginner: Fly eyes look like a repeating grid of identical units, which should make vision the same everywhere. This essay uses wiring diagrams to argue that cells of one named type still differ in who they connect to.
summaries.intermediate: Wernet and Silies (BioEssays, 2026) review heterogeneity in Drosophila visual circuits in light of whole optic-lobe connectomes. They contrast the textbook picture of uniform, translationally invariant columns with connectomic reports that cells of one type vary in partners and synapse numbers. Lamina R1–R6 connectivity is described as extremely precise, while medulla pathways diverge; only 15 types are called truly columnar. The essay asks whether variable connectivity increases functional variability or robustness.
summaries.advanced: Review essay, not a new reconstruction. Columnar-type counts (15 of >50 downstream of L1–L5 in the extract) come from cited connectomes (e.g. recent female/male visual-system maps). Functional interpretations are explicitly open. Figure 1 notes BioRender and ChatGPT assistance for a schematic. Catalog journal spelling is Bioessays.

title: Perfusion quality does not necessarily predict ultrastructural preservation after hyperosmotic brain perfusion
authors: Andria Slaughter; Macy Garrood; Katelyn Hedden; Allison Sowa; William Janssen; E. Thorn; Claudia De Sanctis; Kurt Farrell; John F. Crary; Andrew T. McKenzie

ocar.opportunity: Whole-mammalian-brain connectomics needs perfusion protocols that preserve ultrastructure, not only protocols that look well cleared on the bench or in a scanner.
ocar.challenge: Perfusion quality is often scored by gross appearance and neuroimaging of fixative distribution, which may not predict EM preservation when dehydrating agents are added.
ocar.action: Slaughter, Garrood, Hedden, Sowa, Janssen, Thorn, De Sanctis, Farrell, Crary, and McKenzie, in a July 2026 bioRxiv technical report, compare macroscopic/radiological perfusion metrics with EM in human and canine brains perfused with hyperosmotic additives.
ocar.resolution: In three human donors and one canine donor perfused with 10% mannitol plus 10% PEG 35 kDa, perfusion looked adequate or favorable macroscopically and radiologically, but EM showed expanded extracellular space, shrunken processes, and distorted membranes consistent with osmotic shock. Similar artifacts appeared in a canine brain with 20% mannitol in 20% NBF without PEG. Comparison cases used standard NBF without osmotic additives.
ocar.future_work: The report warns against optimizing connectomics perfusion on macroscopic or CT metrics alone. It does not propose a replacement recipe in the extract beyond that caution.

plain_language_summary: Flushing a brain with fixative can look successful from the outside or on a scan and still ruin the fine structure needed for wiring diagrams. This technical report shows that extra dehydrating chemicals can cause that mismatch.

summaries.beginner: Flushing a brain with fixative can look successful from the outside or on a scan and still ruin the fine structure needed for wiring diagrams. This technical report shows that extra dehydrating chemicals can cause that mismatch.
summaries.intermediate: Slaughter et al. (bioRxiv, posted 30 July 2026) report that hyperosmotic brain perfusion can satisfy gross and radiological quality checks while destroying ultrastructure. Three human brains and one canine brain received 10% mannitol and 10% PEG 35 kDa; EM showed osmotic-shock artifacts. A canine case with 20% mannitol in 20% neutral buffered formalin without PEG was similar. They contrast these with previously reported standard-formalin perfusions. The implied lesson for connectomics is not to tune protocols only on appearance or CT.
summaries.advanced: Unreviewed technical report; n is small (three human, two canine conditions in the abstract). ‘Adequate or favorable’ macroscopic/radiological scores are qualitative. Comparison NBF cases are previously reported, not a fully matched new control series in the truncated extract. No synapse-level connectome is attempted on these samples.

title: Probing molecular diversity and ultrastructure of brain cells with fluorescent aptamers
authors: Xiaotang Lu; Yuelong Wu; Peter H. Li; Tao Fang; R. Schalek; Yaxin Su; Daniel R. Berger; Jeff Carter; S. Lynch; D. Schneider; Shashi Gupta; Viren Jain; N. Janjić; J. Lichtman

ocar.opportunity: Volumetric CLEM can place molecular cell types onto EM-reconstructable circuits, but only if labels enter tissue without detergents that destroy membranes.
ocar.challenge: Suitable small affinity reagents for detergent-free labeling are scarce relative to the biomarker lists coming from single-cell transcriptomics.
ocar.action: Lu, Wu, Li, Fang, Schalek, Su, Carter, Gupta, Jain, Janjic, and Lichtman introduce CAptVE: slow off-rate modified aptamers (SOMAmers) for fluorescent labeling on ultrastructurally reconstructable EM. The catalog paper is Nature Communications (2026); the supplied extract is the 18 September 2023 bioRxiv preprint of the same title and core author list.
ocar.resolution: The preprint reports detergent-free SOMAmer labeling, including Cy5 anti-GFP aptamers in GIN mouse cortex, and argues aptamer size (~16 kDa) is nanobody-like. CAptVE is presented as a path to integrate molecular analysis into volumetric EM and connectomics. A SomaScan comparison in the supplement notes reduced binding after aldehyde fixation for most targets.
ocar.future_work: Expanding the reagent panel after fixation, and applying CAptVE at connectomic scale, remain the stated aims. Readers should check the 2026 journal version for methods that may have changed after the 2023 preprint.

plain_language_summary: Wiring diagrams from electron microscopy usually cannot tell you a cell’s molecular type. This method uses small DNA-like aptamer labels that glow under light microscopy without soap that would wreck the membranes needed for EM.

summaries.beginner: Wiring diagrams from electron microscopy usually cannot tell you a cell’s molecular type. This method uses small DNA-like aptamer labels that glow under light microscopy without soap that would wreck the membranes needed for EM.
summaries.intermediate: Lu et al. present CAptVE, detergent-free labeling with SOMAmer reagents for correlated aptamer-assisted volumetric EM. They motivate the method by the limits of inferring molecular type from EM alone and by the scarcity of small immunoprobes. Demonstrations in the preprint include anti-GFP aptamers in GIN mice. Publisher-style copy in the catalog abstract adds that the technique preserves ultrastructure for large-scale connectomics.
summaries.advanced: The extract is a 2023 preprint, not the 2026 Nature Communications PDF; title and approach match the catalog paper, so summaries use the preprint plus catalog abstract, with the version mismatch noted. Author lists differ slightly (catalog includes Berger, Lynch, Schneider, Lichtman spelling variants). Fixation reduced SOMAmer binding for 95.2% of selected SomaScan targets in a supplementary comparison; 481 targets remained above 3× background. Not a dense connectome release.

title: RAEM: random-access electron microscopy for revisitable 3D imaging
authors: I. Chandok; Milan Patel; Yuelong Wu; Daniel R. Berger; R. Schalek; J. Lichtman; A. Samuel; Y. Meirovitch

ocar.opportunity: Many biological questions need nanometer EM of sparse targets inside specimens too large to image exhaustively at full resolution.
ocar.challenge: Traditional serial-section EM forces a choice between broad context and ultrastructural detail; exhaustive high-resolution acquisition is prohibitive.
ocar.action: Chandok, Patel, Wu, Berger, Schalek, Lichtman, Samuel, and Meirovitch, in a June 2026 bioRxiv preprint, introduce random-access electron microscopy (RAEM): a lower-resolution 3D survey, then physically revisited high-resolution imaging at selected sites by linking reconstructed coordinates to electron-beam positions on the original sections.
ocar.resolution: Demonstrations include vesicle-resolved synaptic boutons in human cortex, targeted imaging of more than one million human cortical mitochondria, hierarchical imaging of a nematode nervous system, and retrospective targeting in a published petabyte-scale human cortical volume. They argue ssEM becomes query-driven and multi-resolution, including on single-beam SEM, building on prior SmartEM work.
ocar.future_work: Discussion proposes registering light microscopy into the RAEM frame for correlative targeting, treating mapped volumes as shared resources, and extending SmartEM from 2D section-wise to 3D computationally guided acquisition. A patent application is noted.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopy at full detail is too slow for whole large samples. RAEM first takes a coarser 3D survey, then sends the microscope back only to the spots that matter, like selected synapses or mitochondria.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopy at full detail is too slow for whole large samples. RAEM first takes a coarser 3D survey, then sends the microscope back only to the spots that matter, like selected synapses or mitochondria.
summaries.intermediate: Chandok et al. (bioRxiv, posted 23 June 2026) describe RAEM, a revisitable multi-resolution ssEM framework. After a low-resolution 3D survey, human or AI knowledge guides high-resolution reimaging at mapped physical sites. Applications named in the abstract are vesicle-resolved human cortical boutons, more than one million human cortical mitochondria, hierarchical nematode nervous-system imaging, and retrospective targeting of a published petabyte-scale human cortical volume. Related prior work is SmartEM, which rescanned pixels within a single field of view.
summaries.advanced: Unreviewed preprint; Harvard patent filing is disclosed. ‘More than one million’ mitochondria is the abstract’s figure; accuracy and completeness metrics for each demonstration should be checked in figures not fully captured here. Repeated-dose tolerance is reported as no detectable degradation in their experiments, not a general limit. Catalog datasets tag includes C. elegans, consistent with the nematode demonstration.

title: Sexual dimorphism in the nervous system: Three principles from the nematode C. elegans
authors: Douglas S. Portman; Chance Bainbridge; Zachary Ward; Jiarui Zhang

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans offers complete developmental lineages and whole-animal connectomes for both sexes, so sexual dimorphism can be dissected at cell-by-cell resolution.
ocar.challenge: Most worm neurobiology has focused on hermaphrodites; male-specific neurons, synapses, and internal-state modulation were historically understudied relative to that convenience.
ocar.action: Portman, Bainbridge, Ward, and Zhang, in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (April 2026), review recent male C. elegans work and organize sexual dimorphism into three overlapping principles.
ocar.resolution: First, sex modulates lineage, neurogenesis, and fate to produce sex-specific neurons and structures. Second, sex changes synaptic topology of circuits. Third, sex acts as internal state, developmentally and dynamically modulating shared neurons. Together these program sex-specific behaviors, tune shared behaviors, and implement dimorphic plasticity. Sex-determination mechanisms differ across species, but the authors argue the principles are likely conserved.
ocar.future_work: Outlook calls for molecular mechanisms linking the sex-determination hierarchy to developmental timing and cell identity, and for connecting those effects to behavior. No new data were generated (data-availability statement).

plain_language_summary: Male and hermaphrodite worms do not have identical nervous systems. This review sorts the differences into three ideas: extra cell types in one sex, different wiring, and the same cells running in a different physiological ‘mode’.

summaries.beginner: Male and hermaphrodite worms do not have identical nervous systems. This review sorts the differences into three ideas: extra cell types in one sex, different wiring, and the same cells running in a different physiological ‘mode’.
summaries.intermediate: Portman, Bainbridge, Ward, and Zhang (Current Opinion in Neurobiology, 2026) review sexual dimorphism in the C. elegans nervous system, especially recent male neurobiology. They group effects into sex-specific cell classes, sexually dimorphic connectivity, and sex as a modulator of shared-neuron physiology. These are tied to sex-specific and sex-shared behaviors and to dimorphic plasticity. The extract is an HHS author manuscript of the April 2026 article (doi 10.1016/j.conb.2026.103175).
summaries.advanced: Opinion/review, not a primary connectome paper. Conservation across species is explicitly a hypothesis despite different sex-determination mechanisms. For comprehensive coverage the authors point to earlier reviews [1–6]. PMC author manuscript.

title: A lightweight data-driven spiking neuronal network model of Drosophila olfactory nervous system with dedicated hardware support
authors: Takuya Nanami; Daichi Yamada; Makoto Someya; Toshihide Hige; H. Kazama; Takashi Kohno

ocar.opportunity: Data-driven spiking networks can test brain computation at cellular resolution, but mammalian models are huge, statistically wired, and slower than real time.
ocar.challenge: Mammalian SNNs often infer topology statistically, obscure region-specific function, and require large computers.
ocar.action: Nanami, Yamada, Someya, Hige, Kazama, and Kohno, in Frontiers in Neuroscience (2024), build a lightweight qualitative SNN of the Drosophila olfactory system with topology taken from connectome data, and implement it on a small FPGA.
ocar.resolution: The FPGA simulation ran in real time, reproduced olfactory associative learning, and reproduced characteristic spiking of different neuron types. They present the pipeline as a general method for building SNNs from biological data that can scale with dedicated hardware.
ocar.future_work: Discussion sketches an ASIC that would simulate the entire Drosophila brain at about 1 watt for insect-like robots; that chip is prospective. A bioRxiv preprint of the manuscript is noted.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly smell circuits are small enough to simulate neuron by neuron. This team built a lightweight spiking model from the fly connectome and ran it in real time on a small custom chip.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly smell circuits are small enough to simulate neuron by neuron. This team built a lightweight spiking model from the fly connectome and ran it in real time on a small custom chip.
summaries.intermediate: Nanami et al. (Frontiers in Neuroscience, 2024) describe a data-driven spiking neuronal network of the Drosophila olfactory system. Network topology is taken from connectome data; neurons are qualitative models chosen to capture key dynamics. Implemented on an entry-level FPGA, the network simulated in real time and reproduced associative olfactory learning plus type-typical spiking. They contrast this with large, slower mammalian SNNs that often use statistical connectivity.
summaries.advanced: ‘Qualitative modeling’ means simplified dynamics, not biophysically complete compartments. Connectome-derived topology should be checked against which fly olfactory reconstruction was used. The ~1 W whole-brain ASIC is a discussion projection, not a device in this paper. Recording data for LN and KC acknowledgements come from collaborators Seki and Inada.

title: Compensatory enhancement of input maintains aversive dopaminergic reinforcement in hungry Drosophila
authors: Eleonora Meschi; Lucille Duquenoy; N. Otto; Georgia Dempsey; S. Waddell

ocar.opportunity: Hunger must keep aversive learning available even while the same dopaminergic system is inhibited so that food-seeking memories can be expressed.
ocar.challenge: In Drosophila, hunger inhibits aversively reinforcing dopaminergic neurons (DANs) via dNPF, which could undermine shock- or bitter-reinforced learning if uncompensated.
ocar.action: Meschi, Duquenoy, Otto, Dempsey, and Waddell, in Neuron (2024), combine behavior, endocrine manipulations, connectomics, and physiology to trace adipokinetic hormone (AKH) effects on aversive reinforcement.
ocar.resolution: Chronic hunger mildly enhances aversive learning; satiated-baseline and hunger-enhanced learning require AKH. AKH acts via its receptor in four ventral-brain neurons, two octopaminergic. Those neurons sit upstream of ascending cells that feed aversively reinforcing DANs; octopaminergic modulation of at least SEZON01 is required for shock- and bitter-reinforced learning. Coordinated input enhancement is proposed to compensate hunger-directed DAN inhibition. Recordings of PPL101 showed reduced baseline DA and enhanced shock-evoked release when hungry.
ocar.future_work: The discussion treats compensation as network homeostasis that preserves reinforcer function during motivational DAN suppression; further sites of AKH action and bitter-tolerance mechanisms are noted as related but not fully mapped here.

plain_language_summary: Hungry flies still need to learn what to avoid, even while hunger quiets some dopamine neurons so they will seek food. This study finds a hormone pathway that turns up incoming signals to keep punishment learning working.

summaries.beginner: Hungry flies still need to learn what to avoid, even while hunger quiets some dopamine neurons so they will seek food. This study finds a hormone pathway that turns up incoming signals to keep punishment learning working.
summaries.intermediate: Meschi et al. (Neuron, 2024) show that adipokinetic hormone supports aversive learning in hungry Drosophila. AKH receptor in four SEZ neurons (two octopaminergic) influences ascending pathways onto aversively reinforcing DANs. Connectomics places those neurons upstream of several ascending classes; SEZON01 output and octopaminergic modulation are required for shock- and bitter-reinforced learning. They propose enhanced input compensates hunger-dependent DAN inhibition (dNPF), a form of network homeostasis. The extract is a Europe PMC author manuscript of the 17 July 2024 article.
summaries.advanced: Animals are Drosophila; DAN class emphasis includes PPL101. ‘Mildly enhances’ aversive learning is the paper’s wording, not a numeric effect size in the extract. Connectomic wiring is used to generate circuit hypotheses tested with genetics and physiology. Author manuscript; present address for Otto is Münster.

title: Connectome-based prediction of functional impairment in experimental stroke models
authors: Oliver Schmitt; Peter Eipert; Yonggang Wang; Atsushi Kanoke; Gratianne Rabiller; Jialing Liu

ocar.opportunity: Experimental stroke models differ in lesion size and location; a mesoscale rat connectome could predict which remote regions, such as hippocampus, lose function even when not directly infarcted.
ocar.challenge: How motor and spatial-memory impairments map onto connectivity change at neuronal-population and parcellation scales was unresolved across MCAO and hemorrhage models.
ocar.action: Schmitt, Eipert, Wang, Kanoke, Rabiller, and Liu, in PLoS ONE (2024), combine two middle-cerebral-artery occlusion models and one intracerebral hemorrhage model with behavior, Fos hippocampal activation, and graph analysis on the neuroVIISAS rat connectome, plus dynamic coactivation modeling.
ocar.resolution: Functional impairment correlated with both extent and location of injury. Lesioned regions coactivated more with motor and spatial-learning regions than with other intact nodes. Weighted bilateral dynamic modeling detected altered hippocampal signal propagation in all three stroke types, predicting hippocampal hypoactivation and spatial-learning/memory impairment. Structural analyses describe changed hub importance that differs by model (dMCAO, ICH, sMCAO).
ocar.future_work: The paper offers an analytical framework for predicting remote diaschisis-like effects; generalization beyond these three rat models is not claimed.

plain_language_summary: A stroke in one place can silence far-away brain areas that were never directly damaged. This rat study uses a whole-brain connection map to predict those remote effects, especially in the hippocampus.

summaries.beginner: A stroke in one place can silence far-away brain areas that were never directly damaged. This rat study uses a whole-brain connection map to predict those remote effects, especially in the hippocampus.
summaries.intermediate: Schmitt et al. (PLoS ONE, 2024) study two MCAO models and one ICH model in rats, measuring motor and spatial memory function and hippocampal Fos. They analyze connection similarities, graph and spatial distances, and regional importance on the neuroVIISAS rat connectome, then run dynamic coactivation models. Impairment tracked lesion extent and location; dynamic modeling predicted hippocampal hypoactivation across all three stroke types. Conclusion boxes list model-specific hub shifts (for example thalamic nuclei after dMCAO; hypothalamic and raphe nodes after ICH/sMCAO).
summaries.advanced: This is a mesoscale atlas-based connectome (neuroVIISAS), not synapse-resolution EM. Fos is a proxy for hippocampal activation. Dynamic-model predictions should be read as in silico signal propagation, constrained by the empirical lesions and behavior. Data are on figshare (10.6084/m9.figshare.26197718.v1).

title: Discriminating neural ensemble patterns through dendritic computations in randomly connected feedforward networks
authors: Bhanu Priya Somashekar; U. Bhalla

ocar.opportunity: If axons from co-active ensembles land as dendritic clusters, single neurons could use dendritic nonlinearities to decode those patterns—even without special wiring rules.
ocar.challenge: It is unclear whether random feedforward connectivity is enough to produce such clusters, or whether brains need activity-dependent targeting.
ocar.action: Somashekar and Bhalla, in a bioRxiv preprint (November 2024 version), combine theory and simulations using rat hippocampal and cortical network statistics.
ocar.resolution: Clustered convergence of axons from 3–4 different co-active ensembles is likely even in random networks, representing arbitrary input combinations in at least ten neurons in a 100,000-cell population. With larger ensembles, spatiotemporally ordered convergence of 3–5 axons is also likely. Clusters yield higher activation when dendritic nonlinearities are strong and background activity is low. They conclude clustered/sequence computation is pervasive, but somatic selectivity needs the right physiology, background, and connectomics together.
ocar.future_work: They discuss testing predictions in EM, viral, and barcoding connectomes, and work an olfactory-bulb-to-piriform example with roughly 40 co-active mitral cells per receptor class as a structurally defined ensemble.

plain_language_summary: Brain cells might read combinations of incoming messages if those inputs land close together on a dendrite. This modeling paper argues that even random wiring is often enough to create those clusters.

summaries.beginner: Brain cells might read combinations of incoming messages if those inputs land close together on a dendrite. This modeling paper argues that even random wiring is often enough to create those clusters.
summaries.intermediate: Somashekar and Bhalla (bioRxiv, posted 9 November 2024) ask whether random feedforward connectivity can cluster axons from co-active ensembles onto dendrites. Using rat hippocampal and cortical statistics, they find 3–4-ensemble clusters are likely, with at least ten representing neurons in a 100,000-cell population, and 3–5-axon sequences given larger ensembles. Expression at the soma requires strong dendritic nonlinearities and low background. They treat this as a bridge from structural connectivity to dendritic computation without invoking special targeting.
summaries.advanced: Theory and simulation, not new EM. Ensemble sizes (~100 for groups, ~1000 for sequences in the discussion) and population size (100,000) are modeling assumptions based on cited statistics. ‘At least ten’ target neurons is the abstract’s lower bound. Olfactory piriform application uses literature mitral-cell counts (~20 per glomerulus, two glomeruli per class). Unreviewed preprint.

title: Dynamic encoding of temperature in the central circadian circuit coordinates physiological activities
authors: Hailiang Li; Zhiyi Li; Xin Yuan; Yue Tian; Wenjing Ye; Pengyu Zeng; Xiao-Ming Li; Fang Guo

ocar.opportunity: Temperature reorganizes daily activity and sleep, but how the central circadian circuit encodes temperature and routes it to locomotion versus sleep was unclear.
ocar.challenge: About 150 Drosophila clock neurons interact with temperature and light; identifying the most temperature-sensitive nodes and their downstream split is hard without combined imaging, tracing, and behavior.
ocar.action: Li, Li, Yuan, Tian, Ye, Zeng, Li, and Guo, in Nature Communications (2024), use in vivo two-photon imaging with a Peltier temperature controller, trans-synaptic tracing, connectome analysis, and behavior in Drosophila.
ocar.resolution: DN1as are identified as the most sensitive temperature-sensing circadian neurons, with responses gated by the clock. They bidirectionally target activity-related E cells (LNds) and sleep-promoting DN3s. The DN1a–E circuit modulates the evening locomotion peak in cold, and the DN1a–DN3 circuit controls warm-induced nocturnal sleep reduction. Upstream inputs include TPN-II (low temperature) and TPN-IV (high temperature).
ocar.future_work: Molecular paths from clock proteins to DN1a temperature sensitivity (receptors, excitability, ER calcium) remain open. Different DN3 subpopulations may use distinct transmitters/receptors.

plain_language_summary: Fruit flies change walking and sleep when the temperature changes, on top of their daily clock. This study finds a pair of clock cells that feel temperature and then push one downstream path for evening movement and another for nighttime sleep.

summaries.beginner: Fruit flies change walking and sleep when the temperature changes, on top of their daily clock. This study finds a pair of clock cells that feel temperature and then push one downstream path for evening movement and another for nighttime sleep.
summaries.intermediate: Li et al. (Nature Communications, 2024) image the Drosophila central circadian circuit during controlled temperature steps. DN1as emerge as the most temperature-sensitive neurons, clock-gated, and they innervate E cells/LNds and DN3s. Behavior assigns cold-evening locomotion to DN1a–E and warm-night sleep loss to DN1a–DN3. Connectome-consistent upstream thermosensory projection neurons (TPN-II and TPN-IV) supply low- and high-temperature information. The authors frame this as a conserved logic for integrating temperature and light across the day.

Bidirectional targeting is anatomical plus functional imaging and behavior. Molecular clock gating of DN1a is proposed, not fully dissected. Publisher extra abstract sentence restates the DN1a result.

title: FISBe: A Real-World Benchmark Dataset for Instance Segmentation of Long-Range thin Filamentous Structures
authors: Lisa Mais; Peter Hirsch; Claire Managan; Ramya Kandarpa; J. L. Rumberger; Annika Reinke; Lena Maier-Hein; Gudrun Ihrke; Dagmar Kainmüller

ocar.opportunity: Instance segmentation of neurons in volumetric light microscopy would let labs jointly analyze morphology and function, but public real-world benchmarks for long, thin, interwoven processes are lacking.
ocar.challenge: Neurons are thin, long-range, and tightly interweaved; light-microscopy noise, partial volume, and uneven illumination break both local disentangling and long-range tracing. ML methods for long-range dependence are often scored on synthetic data.
ocar.action: Mais, Hirsch, Managan, Kandarpa, Rumberger, Reinke, Maier-Hein, Ihrke, and Kainmüller, at CVPR (2024; extract is arXiv:2404.00130), release the FlyLight Instance Segmentation Benchmark (FISBe) with pixel-wise annotations, task-specific metrics, and three baselines.
ocar.resolution: FISBe is presented as the first public multi-neuron light-microscopy dataset with pixel-wise instance labels, from Drosophila FlyLight/MCFO imagery. Baselines include PatchPerPix, Flood Filling Networks, and Duan et al. color clustering; qualitative examples show merges, splits, and coverage failures typical of the difficulty. Metrics are designed for downstream analyses.
ocar.future_work: They invite methods that capture long-range dependencies (e.g. state-space models, continuous CNNs) and self-supervised pretraining on the large unlabeled FlyLight corpus.

plain_language_summary: Computers still struggle to separate individual neurons in 3D light-microscope images, where thin branches tangle together. This paper releases a fruit-fly brain dataset with careful labels so algorithms can be scored fairly.

summaries.beginner: Computers still struggle to separate individual neurons in 3D light-microscope images, where thin branches tangle together. This paper releases a fruit-fly brain dataset with careful labels so algorithms can be scored fairly.
summaries.intermediate: Mais et al. (CVPR 2024; arXiv extract 29 March 2024) introduce FISBe, a FlyLight instance-segmentation benchmark of volumetric multi-color light microscopy of Drosophila neurons with pixel-wise ground truth. They define application-oriented metrics and provide three baselines: PatchPerPix, Flood Filling Networks (with a partial variant), and Duan et al.’s color clustering. title: Generating brain-wide connectome using synthetic axonal morphologies
authors: Remy Petkantchin; Adrien Berchet; Hanchuan Peng; Henry Markram; Lida Kanari

ocar.opportunity: Local EM connectomes and MRI-scale projectomes live at different resolutions; synthesizing axons that are spatially embedded in the whole brain could link them for in silico experiments.
ocar.challenge: Dendrites have been synthesized more successfully than long-range axons that must traverse many regions with realistic morphology and connectivity.
ocar.action: Petkantchin, Berchet, Peng, Markram, and Kanari, in Nature Communications (2025; received 2024), generate whole-brain axonal morphologies for cortical pyramidal cells from sparse experimental reconstructions, then build projectome and connectome predictions.
ocar.resolution: Computationally generated axons are reported to reproduce local and global morphological properties of experimental reconstructions and to yield large-scale inter-regional connectivity. Touches are detected by proximity, filtered by bouton interval, pruned to physiological synapse density, and converted to synapses. Data and code are released (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.13790069; BlueBrain axon-projection).
ocar.future_work: The method is for pyramidal cells in cortex as stated in the PDF; extending cell types and validating predicted long-range synapses against new experiments remain implied next steps.

title: Morphology and synapse topography optimize linear encoding of synapse numbers in Drosophila looming responsive descending neurons
authors: Anthony Moreno-Sanchez; Alexander N. Vasserman; Hyojong Jang; B. Hina; Catherine R. von Reyn; Jessica Ausborn

ocar.opportunity: EM connectomes give exact synapse locations on identified neurons, so one can test how topography—not just synapse count—shapes dendritic integration.
ocar.challenge: In fly looming circuits, retinotopic visual projection neurons (VPNs) synapse onto descending neurons (DNs), but whether synapses stay retinotopic on the dendrite and how that affects encoding was unknown.
ocar.action: Moreno-Sanchez, Vasserman, Jang, Hina, von Reyn, and Ausborn, in an April 2024 bioRxiv preprint, map VPN→DN synapse topography in Drosophila and build multicompartment DN models fitted to physiology using EM morphologies and synapse locations.
ocar.resolution: Synapses of a given VPN type occupy non-overlapping territories on DN dendrites but are near-random within those clusters, not retinotopic. DN dendrite morphologies normalize individual EPSP amplitudes; near-random placement yields linear encoding of synapse numbers from individual VPNs. They propose linear encoding of synapse count as a default from connectivity plus passive properties, on which active conductances and plasticity can later tune.
ocar.future_work: Supplements locate the spike initiation zone downstream of the tether in DNp01, DNp02, and DNp06 using para labeling; active properties and plasticity are left as subsequent tuners of the default linear regime.

plain_language_summary: In the fly, looming-sensitive cells dump synapses onto big descending neurons that drive escape. This preprint finds those synapses sit in type-specific neighborhoods but are shuffled inside them, which helps the cell add up synapse numbers linearly.

Models are fitted to physiology; figure supplements on SIZ location use para-GFSTF. Which DN types (DNp01, DNp03, etc.) carry each result should be read from figures. Passive-property emphasis means active conductances are not the main mechanism claimed here.

title: On human nanoscale synaptome: Morphology modeling and storage estimation
authors: W. Nowinski

ocar.opportunity: A human nanoscale synaptome would be a core object for connectomics and for bounding mental capacity and disease, but its storage cost is unknown.
ocar.challenge: Published neuron and synapse counts vary widely, and a synapse can be stored at different levels of geometric detail.

ocar.resolution: Whole-brain full (simplified) storage ranges from 0.21 (0.14) PB to 28.98 (18.63) PB (topologic), 0.57 (0.32) to 78.66 (43.47) PB (point), and 0.69 (0.38) to 95.22 (51.75) PB (geometric). Cortical ranges are given from tens of TB to several PB. Fly and worm synaptomes are contrasted as MB and kB scale.
ocar.future_work: Hundreds of thousands of human synaptomes would push toward exabytes. The author notes networks of supercomputers or cloud storage as ways around single-machine limits, inspired by SYNAPSE synchrotron mapping efforts.

plain_language_summary: If we listed every human synapse, how much disk space would that take? This paper estimates petabytes—more than most neuroscience supercomputers can hold—depending on how many cells and how much detail you store.

authors: Sarthak Chandra; Mikail Khona; Talia Konkle; I. Fiete

ocar.action: Qiu and colleagues, in Science (2024), reconstruct mouse hippocampal single-neuron projectomes and pair them with spatial transcriptomics, as described in the catalog abstract.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports 10,100 reconstructed projectomes, 341 projection patterns grouped into 43 subtypes, target number and axon-tip placement that depend on soma location along longitudinal and transverse axes, enrichment of subtypes in transcriptomic subdomains, separate wiring diagrams for intra-HPF-only versus intra-plus-extra-HPF neurons, and a general rule that bihemispheric cells usually hit one homologous pair with ipsilateral preference.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the database as a structural basis for combining gene expression with function; specific causal tests of the new projection rules are outside the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Researchers traced the full axon trees of more than ten thousand individual mouse hippocampal neurons. The maps show that where a cell’s body sits in the hippocampus predicts where its axon goes in the brain.

According to the catalog abstract, they separate intra-hippocampal-formation projections from neurons that also leave the formation, and they report that bihemispheric cells generally innervate one homologous target pair with ipsilateral bias. title: Wrapped up: advancements in volume electron microscopy and application in myelin research
authors: Leonie C Schadt; T. Ruhwedel; Constantin Pape; A. O. Sasmita; A. Steyer; Wiebke Möbius

ocar.opportunity: Volume electron microscopy can show myelin’s compacted wraps and axon–glia contacts in three dimensions, and automated segmentation can turn those volumes into quantitative morphology.
ocar.challenge: Classical TEM was the main ultrastructural tool for decades, but it does not easily yield 3-D metrics at tissue scale, while vEM datasets are large and need shared analysis pipelines.
ocar.action: Schadt, Ruhwedel, Pape, Sasmita, Steyer, and Möbius, in Methods in Microscopy (2024; received 5 August, accepted 11 November, published 16 December), review sample-preparation and analysis strategies for vEM and illustrate them with myelin biology and disease.
ocar.resolution: They argue that open vEM datasets plus automated segmentation provide quantitative cellular and organellar readouts and can be reused across questions. The review also points readers to instrumentation, methods, and software developments, including deep-learning segmentation resources cited in the reference list.
ocar.future_work: The piece is a methods-and-application review, not a new volume; it invites use of emerging tools (data-sharing efforts, BioImage Model Zoo, Segment Anything variants) in myelin and other tissues.

plain_language_summary: Myelin is a tightly wrapped insulation that is hard to see in three dimensions with ordinary electron microscopy. This review explains how volume EM and computer segmentation now measure those wraps and their diseases.

summaries.beginner: Myelin is a tightly wrapped insulation that is hard to see in three dimensions with ordinary electron microscopy. This review explains how volume EM and computer segmentation now measure those wraps and their diseases.

title: Connectomes: from a sparsity of networks to large-scale databases
authors: Marcus Kaiser

ocar.opportunity: Whole-brain network analysis began in the 1980s with a handful of connectomes and no human maps. Non-invasive diffusion imaging and related methods now supply structural connectivity in many species and many individuals.
ocar.challenge: Making scientific use of that abundance—comparing organization across species, and moving from one animal to populations—is a different problem from having no data at all.
ocar.action: Kaiser, in Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (published 12 June 2023), reviews available structural connectome data, shared organizational features, and current challenges.
ocar.resolution: He notes that the UK Biobank is on track to record structural and functional connectivity in 100,000 human subjects, and that maps now exist from C. elegans and fruit fly through pigeons, rodents, cats, non-human primates, and humans. The conclusion states that over about 15 years, major databases have given at least one individual connectome for many mammalian and invertebrate species, with human efforts expanding beyond Western samples (e.g., Chinese databases) and across the lifespan. Partial maps (leech, tadpole, mouse retina) are distinguished from whole-brain resources.
ocar.future_work: The review closes on using connectome information scientifically—disease progression and early biomarkers in longitudinal UK Biobank dementia data are given as examples—rather than on a single new analysis.

plain_language_summary: Thirty years ago almost no whole-brain wiring diagrams existed. This review surveys the flood of maps now available, from worms and flies to a planned 100,000 human scans.

summaries.beginner: Thirty years ago almost no whole-brain wiring diagrams existed. This review surveys the flood of maps now available, from worms and flies to a planned 100,000 human scans.
summaries.intermediate: Kaiser (Frontiers in Neuroinformatics, 2023) reviews the shift from a few 1980s connectomes to large structural-connectivity databases. Diffusion imaging is credited for multi-species and multi-individual coverage. The UK Biobank target of 100,000 structural and functional scans is used to illustrate scale. Shared organizational features across species are promised in the abstract; the extract’s conclusion emphasizes population imaging, broader geography, lifespan data, and leftover partial nervous-system maps (leech, tadpole, mouse retina).
summaries.advanced: This is a narrative review of data availability, not a new reconstruction or a quantitative meta-analysis of motif frequencies. The 100,000 UK Biobank figure is a stated trajectory, not a completed release count in the extract. Species coverage is illustrative. Catalog tags include C. elegans (White+); the review is multi-species.

title: Converting Biological Neural Networks to DAGs: Evaluation of Customized Algorithms on C. Elegans
authors: Benjamin Li
journal: 2023 IEEE MIT Undergraduate Research Technology Conference (URTC)

ocar.opportunity: Biological connectomes contain cycles. Turning a recurrent network into a directed acyclic graph can reduce computational load and make sensory-to-neuromuscular pathways easier to read as feedforward chains.
ocar.challenge: Cycle-breaking must not destroy the architecture one cares about. Different algorithms delete different edges.
ocar.action: Li, in the 2023 IEEE MIT Undergraduate Research Technology Conference, customizes depth-first search (DFS) and minimum feedback arc set (MFAS) to remove cycles in the C. elegans adult hermaphrodite connectome, then scores retained edges, sensory-to-neuromuscular-junction pathways, and other graph properties.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports that MFAS retains the structural authenticity of the original graph significantly better than DFS. Mentorship acknowledgements name Constantine Dovrolis and Ross Greer.
ocar.future_work: How these DAGs should be used for simulation or pathway ranking, and how well the result generalizes beyond the hermaphrodite chemical-synapse graph, is outside the extract.

plain_language_summary: The worm’s wiring diagram has loops. This student paper tries two algorithms that cut loops so the network becomes a one-way flowchart, and reports that one method keeps the original shape better.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s wiring diagram has loops. This student paper tries two algorithms that cut loops so the network becomes a one-way flowchart, and reports that one method keeps the original shape better.

The extract notes that feedforward views can lower computational load and clarify downstream pathways.

title: Impact of Retinal Degeneration on Response of ON and OFF Cone Bipolar Cells to Electrical Stimulation
authors: Shayan Farzad; P. Kosta; E. Iseri; Steven T. Walston; Jean-Marie C. Bouteiller; Rebecca L. Pfeiffer; C. Sigulinsky; Jia-Hui Yang; Jessica C. Garcia; James R. Anderson; Bryan William Jones; G. Lazzi
journal: IEEE transactions on neural systems and rehabilitation engineering

ocar.opportunity: In early retinal degeneration, bipolar cells still receive photoreceptor input. Stimulating them with a prosthesis might restore more naturalistic signals than waiting until only inner retina remains.
ocar.challenge: How degeneration changes bipolar-cell responses to extracellular current is not obvious from late-stage devices, and ON versus OFF cone bipolar cells may not behave the same way.
ocar.action: Farzad, Kosta, Iseri, Walston, Bouteiller, Pfeiffer, Sigulinsky, Yang, Garcia, Anderson, Jones, and Lazzi, in IEEE Transactions on Neural Systems and Rehabilitation Engineering (2023), build computational models of healthy and early-degenerate ON and OFF cone bipolar cells using realistic morphologies from healthy and early-stage degenerated rabbit retina connectomes, then apply electrical stimuli while varying pulse duration and electrode distance.
ocar.resolution: OFF CBC membrane potential did not differ significantly between healthy and degenerate cells regardless of position in the model. Healthy ON CBC axon-terminal membrane-potential rising time-constant was shorter (0.29 ± 0.03 ms) than in degenerated cells (0.8 ± 0.07 ms). Axon-terminal calcium current was higher in degenerated cells (32.24 ± 6.12 pA) than in healthy cells (13.64 ± 2.88 pA), independent of cell position.
ocar.future_work: The models address early-stage rabbit CBC biophysics under stimulation; translation to human RP/AMD prostheses and to other bipolar classes is not settled in the extract.

plain_language_summary: Eye implants usually wait until photoreceptors are gone. This study models how remaining bipolar cells in a degenerating rabbit retina respond to electrical pulses, and finds ON and OFF cells do not change in the same way.

summaries.beginner: Eye implants usually wait until photoreceptors are gone. This study models how remaining bipolar cells in a degenerating rabbit retina respond to electrical pulses, and finds ON and OFF cells do not change in the same way.
summaries.intermediate: Farzad et al. (IEEE TNSRE, 2023) simulate healthy versus early-degenerate ON and OFF cone bipolar cells whose morphologies come from rabbit retina connectomes. Electrical stimulation is varied by pulse duration and electrode distance. OFF CBC membrane potentials are reported as not significantly different after degeneration. ON CBC axon-terminal voltage rises more slowly after degeneration (0.29 ± 0.03 vs 0.8 ± 0.07 ms), and terminal calcium current is larger in degenerate cells (32.24 ± 6.12 vs 13.64 ± 2.88 pA), independent of position.
summaries.advanced: These are NEURON-style biophysical models constrained by connectome morphologies, not new EM or in vivo stimulation. Species in the paper is rabbit; catalog organism tags list mouse. Uncertainties are those reported (±) in the abstract. ‘Not a significant difference’ for OFF CBCs is the authors’ statistical claim; test details are not in the extract. Calcium-channel ‘higher concentration and higher current’ should be read as model ionic current, not a measured protein assay.
