title: Eigenvector-based community detection for identifying information hubs in neuronal networks
authors: Ruaridh A. Clark; M. Macdonald

ocar.opportunity: Eigenvectors of a network already highlight central vertices. Extending them to communities tied to those vertices could read information-flow structure from a static connectome without simulating dynamics.
ocar.challenge: Community detection often ignores directed flow, and some have claimed that hubs such as hippocampus cannot be recovered from static graphs.
ocar.action: Clark and Macdonald, on bioRxiv (2018), define eigenvector-based communities, each associated with a prominent vertex, and apply the method to C. elegans, macaque, and a large-scale human MRI connectome of about 1.8 million vertices.
ocar.resolution: In C. elegans, known circuitry appears as separate communities. In macaque, the hippocampus is recovered as an information hub. In humans, prominent pathways from a scan are used as a subject identifier by counting matching pathways between connectomes, including scan–rescan comparison in a twenty-subject dataset named in the discussion.
ocar.future_work: The authors stress that undirected MRI graphs cannot distinguish sources from sinks and that Laplacian analysis of directed graphs would be more informative; cognitive-change tracking via pathway turnover is proposed, not demonstrated as a clinical tool.

plain_language_summary: Some brain regions are hubs that gather or send lots of signals. This methods preprint uses the math of network eigenvectors to find those hubs and their neighborhoods in worm, monkey, and human connection maps.

summaries.beginner: Some brain regions are hubs that gather or send lots of signals. This methods preprint uses the math of network eigenvectors to find those hubs and their neighborhoods in worm, monkey, and human connection maps.
summaries.intermediate: Clark and Macdonald (bioRxiv, 2018) use multiple eigenvectors to define communities, each anchored on a prominent vertex that is a major source or destination of network flow. Applied to C. elegans, the method recovers known circuits as separate communities. Applied to macaque (CoCoMac), it identifies hippocampus as an information hub, which the authors contrast with claims that static graphs cannot yield that insight. On a human connectome of ~1.8 million vertices they extract prominent pathways and argue that matching pathways can identify a subject across scans. Discussion notes that undirected MRI networks hide in/out imbalance.
summaries.advanced: bioRxiv preprint. C. elegans is a nematode; the extract’s ‘flatworm’ wording in the author summary is a taxonomic slip and should not be repeated as fact. Human application is MRI-scale, not synaptic EM.

title: Spatiotemporal ontogeny of brain wiring
authors: A. Goulas; R. Betzel; Claus C. Hilgetag

ocar.resolution: They report reconstructing on average 83% of wiring-principle structure and 80% of global network topology across diverse adult connectomes, including fly and human. ocar.future_work: Activity-dependent refinement is acknowledged as a later sculptor. Pathologies of Notch/BMP timing are suggested as routes to deviant large-scale topology; those links are interpretive.

title: Mapping and Analysis of the Connectome of Sympathetic Premotor Neurons in the Rostral Ventrolateral Medulla of the Rat Using a Volumetric Brain Atlas
authors: Bowen Dempsey; Sheng Le; Anita J. Turner; Phillip Bokiniec; R. Ramadas; J. Bjaalie; C. Menuet; R. Neve; A. Allen; A. Goodchild; S. McMullan

ocar.opportunity: Spinally projecting RVLM neurons generate vasomotor tone and are thought to collect inputs from the entire neuraxis. A monosynaptic map in atlas coordinates would show which levels actually contact them.

authors: Jimin Kim; W. Leahy; Eli Shlizerman

ocar.opportunity: Connectome plus biophysics define a dynome that is too large to explore by exhaustive stimulation. A live graph that can be poked, ablated, and rewound would let hypotheses about function be tested in seconds.
ocar.challenge: Batch simulation of many stimulus patterns yields huge unlabeled time series; empirical search for meaningful stimulations is slow.
ocar.action: Kim, Leahy, and Shlizerman, in Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience (2019; catalogued as a 2017 bioRxiv record), present Neural Interactome, a cross-platform framework that visualizes graph structure together with simulated or recorded neural dynamics, with stimulation, ablation, zoom, review, and preset recording.
ocar.resolution: Implemented on a C. elegans nervous-system model with resolved connectome and dynamics, the tool is used to inspect locomotion-related patterns, revisit experimental touch-response circuits, and explore untested stimulation/ablation scenarios. The design is intended to swap in other connectivity and neuron models.
ocar.future_work: Planned extensions named in the extract include GPU integration for larger nets, connecting the neural model to musculature/body movement, and applying the same UI to other biological or artificial networks.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram sits still; the interesting part is watching it run. This software shows the worm’s nerve net as a live graph you can stimulate or snip, the way an experimenter would.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram sits still; the interesting part is watching it run. This software shows the worm’s nerve net as a live graph you can stimulate or snip, the way an experimenter would.

Catalog metadata list year 2017 and journal bioRxiv; the PDF is the 2019 Frontiers methods paper with the same title and authors.
summaries.advanced: This is interactive simulation software, not new EM. Dynamics come from an existing computational model (279 neurons appear in an equation caption in the extract). Claims about discovering patterns ‘within seconds’ are qualitative. GPU acceleration and body coupling are future work. Open-access Frontiers PDF.

title: Pavlovian Conditioning of Larval Drosophila: An Illustrated, Multilingual, Hands-On Manual for Odor-Taste Associative Learning in Maggots
authors: B. Michels; T. Saumweber; Roland Biernacki; Jeanette Thum; R. D. Glasgow; M. Schleyer; Yi-Chun Chen; Claire Eschbach; R. Stocker; Naoko Toshima; T. Tanimura; Matthieu Louis; G. Arias-Gil; Manuela Marescotti; F. Benfenati; B. Gerber

ocar.action: Michels, Saumweber, Biernacki, Thum, Glasgow, Schleyer, Chen, Eschbach, Stocker, Toshima, Tanimura, Louis, Arias-Gil, Marescotti, Benfenati, and Gerber, in Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience (2017), publish an illustrated manual for Pavlovian odor-reward learning in maggots, with English, German, French, Japanese, Spanish, and Italian versions plus data-analysis tables.
ocar.resolution: The paradigm is described as robust enough for teaching and already adopted by multiple labs. Combined with single-cell transgenes and the forthcoming larval/adult connectome, it is framed as a bridge from behaviour to circuit to genes, including translational biomedicine via shared genetics with humans.
ocar.future_work: The paper is a methods/teaching resource; scientific extensions depend on users applying the protocol rather than new data herein.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly maggots can learn that a smell predicts a taste reward, using a setup simple enough for a classroom. This paper is the how-to guide, in several languages, so more people can run the experiment.

title: Simulating extracted connectomes
authors: J. Gornet; Louis K. Scheffer

ocar.opportunity: Volume-EM reconstructions supply neuron geometry that compartmental simulators such as NEURON are built to run. Closing that loop would test whether extracted circuits reproduce known computations.
ocar.challenge: EM does not give synapse signs or channel models; fully detailed meshes are extremely slow to simulate.
ocar.action: Gornet and Scheffer, on bioRxiv (2017), take Drosophila motion-detection neurons, attach approximate synapses from known/estimated function, simulate direction selectivity in T4, then coarsen geometry from a full compartment model down to a single node.
ocar.resolution: They reproduce T4 direction selectivity, verifying extraction plus simulation. Simplified models, including a lumped single-node neuron, give nearly the same computation. The full model is given as 200,000 nodes, a reduced model 28,000, and a node model 187; the single-node model is at least four orders of magnitude faster. Biologically, they confirm Gruntman that dendritic computation is not required for this detector.
ocar.future_work: Gap junctions and neuromodulators are named as missing. The authors expect reduction to matter more as larger fly EM volumes arrive; reducing every neuron to a point will not always suffice for larger cells.

plain_language_summary: Once a fly neuron’s shape is traced from electron microscopy, you can try to run it as a simulation. This preprint shows that a simple blob model, not a full 3-D tree, is enough for a famous motion-detecting cell.

summaries.beginner: Once a fly neuron’s shape is traced from electron microscopy, you can try to run it as a simulation. This preprint shows that a simple blob model, not a full 3-D tree, is enough for a famous motion-detecting cell.
summaries.intermediate: Gornet and Scheffer (bioRxiv, 2017) simulate EM-extracted Drosophila medulla neurons in the motion-detection pathway. Because synapse physiology is unavailable from EM, they insert approximate synapses with estimated signs and recover T4 direction selectivity. They then compare a fully detailed compartment model (200,000 nodes) with a reduced branched model (28,000) and a single-node model (187). The lumped model is at least 10^4 times faster and still reproduces the main detector operation, supporting Gruntman et al. that dendritic computation is not required. They argue connectivity matters more than detailed shape for these medulla neurons.
summaries.advanced: bioRxiv preprint. Synapse models are approximate, not measured from the EM volume. Node counts and the four-orders-of-magnitude runtime claim are from the extract (full-model times are underestimates because runs were killed after one day). Confirmation of Gruntman is for this T4 on-pathway case. Not a claim about all fly neurons.

title: Statistical Inference on Random Dot Product Graphs: a Survey
authors: A. Athreya; D. E. Fishkind; M. Tang; C. Priebe; Youngser Park; J. Vogelstein; Keith D. Levin; V. Lyzinski; Yichen Qin; D. Sussman

ocar.opportunity: Graphs from connectomes and social networks need inferential statistics analogous to Euclidean data: embeddings, consistency, asymptotic normality, and hypothesis tests.
ocar.challenge: Independent-edge models that are both tractable and flexible enough to approximate block models and latent-position graphs are scarce; spectral methods need a unified theory.
ocar.action: Athreya, Fishkind, Tang, Priebe, Park, Vogelstein, Levin, Lyzinski, Qin, and Sussman, in a 2017 Journal of Machine Learning Research / arXiv survey, review random dot product graphs and inference based on adjacency and Laplacian spectral embeddings.
ocar.resolution: They summarize consistency and asymptotic normality of those embeddings, their use in single- and multi-sample graph hypothesis tests, and applications including community detection in social networks and exploratory analysis of the Drosophila connectome for functional and biologically relevant structure. Open problems in spectral graph inference are outlined.
ocar.future_work: The survey’s later pages in the extract are technical proofs (e.g., Laplacian embedding error bounds); remaining open problems are flagged rather than solved here.

plain_language_summary: A brain wiring diagram is a giant network, and networks need statistics just as tables of numbers do. This survey explains a model that turns a network into points in space so you can test and cluster them.

summaries.beginner: A brain wiring diagram is a giant network, and networks need statistics just as tables of numbers do. This survey explains a model that turns a network into points in space so you can test and cluster them.
summaries.intermediate: Athreya and colleagues (JMLR / arXiv:1709.05454, 2017) survey random dot product graphs (RDPGs) as a tractable independent-edge model spanning stochastic block models to latent-position graphs. The paradigm centers on adjacency and Laplacian spectral embeddings, with results on consistency and asymptotic normality and on building graph hypothesis tests. Applications mentioned include large social-network community detection/classification and exploratory analysis of the Drosophila connectome. The extract’s visible tail is linear-algebraic error bounds (e.g., Frobenius residuals of order O(n^{-1}) with high probability).
summaries.advanced: This is a statistical survey, not an EM methods paper. Drosophila connectome use is an application cited in the abstract, not a new reconstruction. Catalog uuid equals work_id (no DOI). The supplied extract is truncated deep in proofs; biological findings should be read from the application section of the full survey, not invented from the proof pages.

title: Further Insight into the Brain's Rich-Club Architecture
authors: M. Pedersen; Amir H. Omidvarnia

ocar.opportunity: Rich-club organization—hubs densely interconnected with each other—has been reported from human MRI down to C. elegans. A microscale electrophysiology paper could test whether the same architecture carries most information flow among neurons.
ocar.challenge: Macroscale rich clubs do not automatically imply the same phenomenon at single-neuron effective connectivity, and directionality of information flow is easy to confound.
ocar.action: Pedersen and Omidvarnia, in a Journal of Neuroscience Journal Club (2016), review Nigam et al. (2016) on rich-club architecture in neuronal networks, covering in vitro organotypic and in vivo microelectrode effective-connectivity analyses.
ocar.resolution: They highlight Nigam et al.’s finding that a rich club carries a high percentage (~70%) of incoming and outgoing information flow, discuss metrics such as transfer entropy and dynamic importance, and point to Fulcher and Fornito’s mesoscale mouse connectome as bridging macro- and microscale rich clubs, including metabolic-gene associations at hub nodes.
ocar.future_work: They suggest multivariate information-transfer criteria as a path for neuronal rich-club research. The Journal Club itself presents no new data.

plain_language_summary: Some brain regions are like busy train stations that also have extra tracks to each other. This short student/postdoc commentary explains a study that found the same ‘rich club’ among individual neurons and argues most messages travel through it.

summaries.beginner: Some brain regions are like busy train stations that also have extra tracks to each other. This short student/postdoc commentary explains a study that found the same ‘rich club’ among individual neurons and argues most messages travel through it.
summaries.intermediate: Pedersen and Omidvarnia (Journal of Neuroscience, 2016) write a Journal Club on Nigam et al. (2016). After placing rich clubs at macro-, meso-, and microscales (human, newborn, macaque, C. elegans, mouse hippocampus), they summarize Nigam’s effective-connectivity analysis in organotypic cultures and in vivo arrays, including a reported ~70% of incoming and outgoing information flow through the rich club. They discuss directional flow, network drive, and spurious delayed connections as methodological issues. They close by citing Fulcher and Fornito (2016) on a mesoscale mouse connectome in which rich-club nodes associate with metabolic-regulation genes.
summaries.advanced: This is a two-page Journal Club, not original connectomics. The ~70% figure is attributed to Nigam et al. as presented here. Catalog abstract is truncated. PMC PDF. Do not treat commentary citations as new measurements.

title: Microscopy Image Browser: A Platform for Segmentation and Analysis of Multidimensional Datasets
authors: I. Belevich; Merja Joensuu; Darshan Kumar; H. Vihinen; E. Jokitalo

ocar.opportunity: Multimodal 3-D light and electron microscopy are more accessible, but processing, visualization, and quantitative analysis of large volumes remain a bottleneck, especially versus costly commercial packages.
ocar.challenge: Existing freeware tools are fragmented; labs need an open, scriptable segmentation workbench with interpolation, classifiers, and microscopy-aware I/O.
ocar.action: Belevich, Joensuu, Kumar, Vihinen, and Jokitalo, in PLoS Biology (2016), introduce Microscopy Image Browser (MIB), a high-performance open-source package for segmentation and image processing of multidimensional datasets, with plug-in extensibility and tutorials.

The software is free from a dedicated site and customizable in MATLAB.
ocar.future_work: Community plug-ins and new modalities are invited; MIB is infrastructure rather than a biological result.

title: Synapse biology in the 'circuit-age' - paths towards molecular connectomics
authors: D. Schreiner; J. Savas; E. Herzog; N. Brose; Joris de Wit

ocar.opportunity: Anatomical and functional connectomes are becoming high-resolution, but the molecular tags that make synapses specific and physiologically distinct are still hard to list at circuit scale.
ocar.challenge: Genetic tests of chemoaffinity have power and limits; they rarely yield a complete molecular synaptic connectome.
ocar.action: Schreiner, Savas, Herzog, Brose, and de Wit, in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2017 version of a 2016 paper), review genetic approaches to synaptic connectivity and function and discuss proteomic and proximity-labeling methods as a path to a molecular synaptic connectome underlying the neural connectome.
ocar.resolution: They argue that proximity labeling, targeted to specific neurons or even synapses, plus shotgun and quantitative mass spectrometry, can define synapse-type proteomes. Combined with combinatorial genetics, that molecular map is presented as the way to explain anatomical and functional wiring.
ocar.future_work: The conclusion treats these tools as promising rather than as a completed molecular connectome; coverage is explicitly limited by the Current Opinion format.

plain_language_summary: Knowing which cells touch is not the same as knowing which molecular Velcro made that contact. This review sketches how protein-labeling chemistry could catalog the ingredients of specific synapses.

summaries.beginner: Knowing which cells touch is not the same as knowing which molecular Velcro made that contact. This review sketches how protein-labeling chemistry could catalog the ingredients of specific synapses.
summaries.intermediate: Schreiner, Savas, Herzog, Brose, and de Wit (Current Opinion in Neurobiology, 2017; DOI 2016) review paths toward molecular connectomics. After noting that anatomical/functional maps now outrun mechanistic explanation, they discuss limits of genetic analysis of synaptic specificity and highlight proximity-labeling proteomics (down to specific synapses) plus evolving mass spectrometry. The stated goal is a molecular synaptic connectome that accounts for anatomical and functional connectivity. The extract is an NIHMS author manuscript.
summaries.advanced: This is a short opinion/review, not new proteomic data. Sperry’s chemoaffinity hypothesis is background. No protein lists or synapse counts are in the extract. Catalog year 2016; published form February 2017 (volume 42, pages 102–110) as given on the manuscript header.

title: Aldehyde-stabilized cryopreservation.
authors: R. L. McIntyre; G. Fahy

ocar.opportunity: Connectomics and other neuroanatomy need banked brains that keep traceable processes and crisp synapses over long storage, at a scale that perfusion can reach (rabbit to pig).
ocar.challenge: Ice-free long-term storage and excellent ultrastructure have been hard to combine; many banking methods do not scale by perfusion or do not allow cryoprotectant washout for later assays.
ocar.action: McIntyre and Fahy, in Cryobiology (2015), as described in the catalog abstract, introduce aldehyde-stabilized cryopreservation (ASC): glutaraldehyde perfusion fixation of rabbit and pig brains, slow perfusion to 65% w/v ethylene glycol, vitrification at −135 °C, rewarming, and cryoprotectant removal by perfusion or slice diffusion.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports uniformly excellent preservation on multi-region electron microscopy and on FIB-SEM of selected volumes: processes easily traceable and synapses crisp in both species. Advantages claimed: perfusion scaling, vitrification for long-term ultrastructural stability, and a washable, still-perfusable aldehyde-fixed brain for diverse assays.
ocar.future_work: Independent reading of the Cryobiology paper is required for methods detail, quantification, and limits; the mismatched PDF cannot supply them.

plain_language_summary: Brain maps need tissue that can sit on a shelf without ice damage and still show clean synapses. This paper’s abstract describes fixing rabbit and pig brains, filling them with antifreeze, and glassifying them for long-term storage.

summaries.beginner: Brain maps need tissue that can sit on a shelf without ice damage and still show clean synapses. This paper’s abstract describes fixing rabbit and pig brains, filling them with antifreeze, and glassifying them for long-term storage.

They evaluate preservation by electron microscopy across regions and by FIB-SEM of selected volumes, reporting uniformly excellent, traceable processes and crisp synapses in both species. ASC is framed as a scalable brain-banking method for connectomics. Summaries follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.

title: Connectome of the fly visual circuitry.
authors: Shin-ya Takemura

ocar.opportunity: Electron-microscopy connectomes can identify the exact neurons and synapses that implement a classic computation, such as visual motion detection in the fly.
ocar.challenge: Light microscopy only estimates connections from arbor overlap, and incomplete knowledge of the relevant cells and synapses has long blocked a mechanistic account of motion detection.
ocar.action: Takemura, in Microscopy (2015), reviews EM connectomic reconstructions of the Drosophila visual system, as described in the catalog abstract.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports that comprehensive EM reconstruction identified the concrete circuit that computes motion signals, with unequivocal connections and precise synaptic counts that arbor-overlap estimates cannot provide.
ocar.future_work: The abstract frames connectomes as a foundation for relating identified circuits to neuronal function; further functional tests are outside this abstract.

plain_language_summary: Fruit flies detect motion with a small, well-studied visual system, but seeing every synapse requires electron microscopy. This review says those wiring maps finally named the cells that compute motion.

title: Control of synaptic connectivity by a network of Drosophila IgSF cell surface proteins
authors: Robert A. Carrillo; E. Özkan; E. Özkan; K. Menon; Sonal Nagarkar-Jaiswal; Pei-Tseng Lee; Mili Jeon; Mili Jeon; M. Birnbaum; H. Bellen; K. Garcia; K. Zinn

ocar.opportunity: If neurons carry molecular identification tags, a binding code among cell-surface proteins could explain how partner cells find each other in a crowded neuropil.
ocar.challenge: Drosophila has large immunoglobulin superfamily families whose pairwise binding rules, expression, and synapse-level roles were not mapped together.
ocar.action: Carrillo, Özkan, Menon, and colleagues, in Cell (2015), define a Dpr–DIP interaction network, solve a complex structure, and test Dpr11 and DIP-γ in the larval neuromuscular junction and pupal optic lobe.
ocar.resolution: Twenty-one Dpr proteins bind nine DIPs, with specificity attributed to shape complementarity rather than charge pairs. Each of six examined genes labels a unique neuronal subset. Dpr11–DIP-γ interactions affect NMJ terminals and transmission; in the visual system dpr11 marks yR7 photoreceptors and DIP-γ marks Dm8 targets, and mutants send yR7 terminals past medulla layer M6, with DIP-γ also required for Dm8 survival or differentiation.
ocar.future_work: The discussion treats Dpr–DIP pairs as determinants of connectivity by analogy to SYG-1/SYG-2 and IgLONs, leaving the remaining family members and other circuits for later genetic tests.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly neurons use matching surface proteins as name tags when they choose synaptic partners. Breaking one matched pair scrambles wiring at a muscle synapse and in the eye.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly neurons use matching surface proteins as name tags when they choose synaptic partners. Breaking one matched pair scrambles wiring at a muscle synapse and in the eye.
summaries.intermediate: Carrillo et al. (Cell, 2015) report a 21-by-9 Dpr–DIP IgSF binding network whose interface uses shape complementarity, not salt bridges. Six examined genes have distinct larval VNC and pupal optic-lobe patterns. At the NMJ, Dpr11 and DIP-γ regulate presynaptic terminals, trophic responses, and transmission. In the medulla, yR7 (Rh4) cells express dpr11 and their Dm8 targets express DIP-γ; either mutant lets yR7 axons grow beyond layer M6, and DIP-γ is required for Dm8 survival or differentiation.
summaries.advanced: The supplied PDF is a PMC author manuscript (Cell 163:1770–1782). Only six of 30 family genes are expression-mapped here. ‘Survival or differentiation’ of Dm8 is not resolved. Binding specificity is inferred from structure and biochemistry; the visual and NMJ phenotypes show necessity of one pair, not a complete wiring code. Dprs lack clear mammalian orthologs; DIPs are closest to IgLONs.

title: Three-dimensional volume imaging with electron microscopy toward connectome.
authors: N. Ohno; Mitsuhiko Katoh; Y. Saitoh; S. Saitoh; S. Ohno

ocar.opportunity: Serial ultrastructural imaging can in principle reconstruct neuronal wiring in central nervous system volumes large enough to be called a connectome.
ocar.challenge: Conventional serial-section TEM is slow, SEM volume methods trade resolution against speed, and huge image stacks still lack automated segmentation.
ocar.action: Ohno, Katoh, Saitoh, Saitoh, and Ohno, in Microscopy (2015), review SEM-based 3D volume EM and tissue preparation that increases heavy-metal contrast, as described in the catalog abstract.
ocar.resolution: The abstract argues that SEM serial methods have distinct resolution and speed trade-offs and should be chosen by target size, required resolution, and need for re-observation, while automation of segmentation remains the main bottleneck.
ocar.future_work: The abstract awaits improved acquisition and analysis to relate whole-connectome structure to consciousness, intelligence, and memory.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopes can now take 3D pictures of brain tissue instead of one thin slice at a time. This review explains those scanning-EM methods and warns that analyzing the pictures is still the hard part.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopes can now take 3D pictures of brain tissue instead of one thin slice at a time. This review explains those scanning-EM methods and warns that analyzing the pictures is still the hard part.
summaries.intermediate: Ohno and colleagues (Microscopy, 2015) review volume EM toward connectomics. According to the catalog abstract, the key shift is serial imaging with SEM plus heavy-metal staining for contrast, versus classical serial-section TEM. title: Common Connectome Constraints: From C. elegans and Drosophila to Homo sapiens

title: Post-acquisition image based compensation for thickness variation in microscopy section series
authors: Philipp Hanslovsky; J. Bogovic; S. Saalfeld
journal: IEEE International Symposium on Biomedical Imaging

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section EM of entire brains, including Drosophila, is usable for synapse-level reconstruction only if section thickness in z is trustworthy.

ocar.resolution: On a 1000-section FIB-SEM series, similarity estimation took 62.3 s and inference 49.4 s (150 iterations). On 63-section TEM, those steps took 0.6 s and 0.4 s (100 iterations). ocar.future_work: They plan within-section thickness variation via coarse-to-fine estimation, note that the method can flag missing sections but cannot by itself distinguish loss from gaps, and intend to test whether z-correction helps manual and automated segmentation.

plain_language_summary: When you slice a brain for electron microscopy, the slices are not all the same thickness. This method looks at how much the pictures change from slice to slice and puts each slice back at a more realistic depth.

title: Functional allocation of synaptic contacts in microcircuits from rods via rod bipolar to AII amacrine cells in the mouse retina
authors: Y. Tsukamoto; N. Omi

ocar.opportunity: Night vision at absolute threshold must pass a single-photon rod signal through rod bipolar (RB) cells and AII amacrine cells without drowning it in noise.
ocar.challenge: How synaptic contacts are allocated so that amplification is local, rather than averaging noise from a wide surround, was not quantified in 3D.

ocar.resolution: In most cases (94%) each rod contacts two adjacent RB cells; each RB is contacted by 25 rods. Each RB axon contacts four or five AII cells via 53 ribbon synapses, so one rod’s signal can appear as 106 replicates at two RB axons. title: Beyond counts and shapes: Studying pathology of dendritic spines in the context of the surrounding neuropil through serial section electron microscopy
authors: M. Kuwajima; J. Špaček; K. Harris

ocar.opportunity: Because dendritic spines are excitatory synaptic sites, disease-related spine changes are circuit changes in partners, astrocytes, and organelles, not only counts and shapes.
ocar.challenge: Light-level spine metrics miss nanometer relationships that require volume EM.
ocar.action: Kuwajima, Špaček, and Harris, in Neuroscience (2013 version of a 2012 paper), review ssEM studies of pathological neuropil and practical perfusion-fixation for high-quality volumes.
ocar.resolution: They argue ssEM is the best current route to place spine pathology in 3D neuropil context, and they detail adult-rat perfusion (artificial ventilation, up to 180 mmHg, brief oxygenated buffer then mixed aldehydes in cacodylate) versus ≤30 s diaphragm-to-fixative for mice or juvenile rats to limit hypoxia.
ocar.future_work: They caution that animal models capture only some aspects of heterogeneous human disease, so patient ultrastructure should set the context for model findings.

plain_language_summary: Counting how many dendritic spines look stubby or long is not enough to understand brain disease. This review says you need 3D electron microscopy to see each spine with its partner axon and nearby support cells.

summaries.beginner: Counting how many dendritic spines look stubby or long is not enough to understand brain disease. This review says you need 3D electron microscopy to see each spine with its partner axon and nearby support cells.
summaries.intermediate: Kuwajima, Spacek, and Harris (Neuroscience, 2013; DOI 2012) review serial-section EM of spine pathology in surrounding neuropil, including synapses, astrocytes, and organelles. They treat renewed ssEM methods and computational 3D tools as enabling this literature. A methods-heavy section specifies perfusion-fixation aimed at avoiding hypoxia and osmotic artifact (adult rats under ventilation, pressure up to 180 mmHg; mice/juveniles without ventilation, fixative within 30 s). Phosphate-buffer particulates are noted as a reason to prefer cacodylate in their protocol.
summaries.advanced: This is a review plus protocol commentary, not a new pathology cohort. The supplied PDF is an NIH author manuscript (final pagination Neuroscience 251:75–89, 2013). Catalog year is 2012. Quantitative disease-specific spine counts are not synthesized as a single table in the extract. Clinical-network claims are framed as anatomical substrates, not demonstrated here.

title: Combining collation and annotation efforts toward completion of the rat and mouse connectomes in BAMS
authors: M. Bota; H. Dong; L. Swanson

ocar.opportunity: Macroscale wiring diagrams of rat and mouse can be assembled from the tract-tracing literature if names in different atlases can be translated.
ocar.challenge: Independent parcellation schemes rarely define interrelationships, and resliceable 3D atlas alignment was still immature, so studies on different maps cannot be merged naively.
ocar.action: Bota, Dong, and Swanson, in Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2012), present BAMS (Brain Architecture Knowledge Management System) and a rat macroconnectome with more than 50,000 inserted connectivity reports.
ocar.resolution: BAMS stores qualitative comparisons inserted by anatomists or collated from papers, then generates large-scale connection matrices online. The 2012 rat matrix uses a different classification scheme than earlier versions and exceeds the 50,000-report benchmark.
ocar.future_work: They intend spatial attributes (injection and label sites), a re-implemented reliability inference engine, completion of the rat literature connectome, and macroconnectomes for mouse, monkey, and human, plus molecule and cell modules.

plain_language_summary: Rat and mouse brain maps use many different names for the same regions, so connection lists cannot simply be pasted together. BAMS is a public database that translates those names and builds large wiring tables from published tracing studies.

summaries.beginner: Rat and mouse brain maps use many different names for the same regions, so connection lists cannot simply be pasted together. BAMS is a public database that translates those names and builds large wiring tables from published tracing studies.
summaries.intermediate: Bota, Dong, and Swanson (Front. Neuroinform., 2012) describe BAMS (brancusi.usc.edu/bkms) as infrastructure for mammalian macroconnectomes. Incompatible atlases are handled by expert or collator annotation rather than mature 3D resampling. The updated rat macroconnectome exceeds 50,000 connectivity reports under a new classification. The workflow is map rigorously, insert and annotate, then generate matrices online. Macroconnections are axonal links between gray-matter regions treated as nodes.
summaries.advanced: Fifty thousand is a count of inserted reports, not unique verified synapses or a complete matrix fill-in. Strengths are qualitative. 3D inter-atlas models are explicitly not ready. URL longevity should be checked. This is literature collation, not new tracing or EM.

title: The Intrinsic Connectome of the Rat Amygdala
authors: O. Schmitt; Peter Eipert; Konstanze Philipp; Richard Kettlitz; Georg Fuellen; A. Wree

ocar.opportunity: Most tract-tracing exists in rat, so the amygdala’s intrinsic and extrinsic wiring can be compiled into a weighted directed graph for network analysis.
ocar.challenge: Graph statistics depend on how regions sit in an ontology, and original papers often omit injections that would complete the picture.
ocar.action: Schmitt, Eipert, Philipp, Kettlitz, Fuellen, and Wree, in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2012), import a rat amygdala meta-connectome into neuroVIISAS and compute local and global metrics.
ocar.resolution: The intrinsic amygdala graph is described as small-world and scale-free. Highest combined in- and out-degree: anterior cortical nucleus (72), posterior nucleus (45), anterior basomedial nucleus (44). The posterior nucleus has minimal Shapley rate and is called most important. Complete reciprocal motifs exceed randomizations. Superficial regions are flagged as densely interlinked for internal regulation.
ocar.future_work: They note that including non-amygdala-focused papers should raise validity, while synaptic-level spatiotemporal dynamics remain outside this tract-tracing meta-graph.

plain_language_summary: The amygdala is a cluster of nuclei that traffic emotion and memory signals. This team gathered published rat tracing studies into one directed network and asked which nuclei sit at the center.

summaries.beginner: The amygdala is a cluster of nuclei that traffic emotion and memory signals. This team gathered published rat tracing studies into one directed network and asked which nuclei sit at the center.
summaries.intermediate: Schmitt et al. (Front. Neural Circuits, 2012) build weighted digraphs of rat amygdala intrinsic and extrinsic connections in neuroVIISAS. They report small-world and scale-free intrinsic topology; degree leaders anterior cortical (72), posterior (45), and anterior basomedial (44) nuclei; and minimal Shapley rate for the posterior nucleus. They reconstruct a fear-conditioning pathway but find more subregion interconnectivity and reciprocity than some optogenetic circuit sketches assumed. The supracapsular BST lateral part has high Shapley importance despite degree 13, so they warn against reading Shapley in isolation.
summaries.advanced: This is a literature meta-study, not new tracing. Edge presence and weights inherit publication bias and ontology choices. ‘Scale-free’ and ‘small-world’ are authors’ network-statistic claims on the compiled graph. Behavioral roles of hub regions are mapped onto other studies, not tested here. Extract discussion notes synaptic dynamics as a limitation of connectome analysis at this scale.

title: Cell Type–Specific Three-Dimensional Structure of Thalamocortical Circuits in a Column of Rat Vibrissal Cortex
authors: M. Oberlaender; Christiaan P. J. de Kock; R. Bruno; A. Ramírez; H. S. Meyer; V. J. Dercksen; M. Helmstaedter; B. Sakmann

ocar.opportunity: A whisker column in rat cortex is a defined 3D object whose thalamocortical synapses can be counted by cell type and soma location.
ocar.challenge: Somata and dendrites of excitatory types intermingle, so innervation cannot be read from layer labels alone, and structure–function links may differ by type.
ocar.action: Oberlaender, de Kock, Bruno, Ramírez, Meyer, Dercksen, Helmstaedter, and Sakmann, in Cerebral Cortex (2012; advance 2011), reconstruct lemniscal VPM axons and excitatory neurons of a barrel column, objectively classify nine excitatory types, and compare predicted innervation with whisker-touch responses.
ocar.resolution: Thalamocortical connectivity depends strongly on cell type and 3D soma location. Lemniscal afferents can account for some type- and location-specific subthreshold and spiking responses after passive touch in layer 4, but not for other types, for example in layer 5. The result is a quantitative 3D prediction of cell-type-specific VPM wiring.
ocar.future_work: The extract’s conclusions paragraph is truncated; the abstract already implies that additional pathways are needed where VPM innervation does not explain responses.

plain_language_summary: Each whisker on a rat’s snout maps to a cortical column. This study rebuilds the 3D wiring from thalamus onto nine kinds of excitatory cells in one column and asks which cells that thalamic input can actually explain.

summaries.beginner: Each whisker on a rat’s snout maps to a cortical column. This study rebuilds the 3D wiring from thalamus onto nine kinds of excitatory cells in one column and asks which cells that thalamic input can actually explain.
summaries.intermediate: Oberlaender et al. (Cereb. Cortex 22:2375–2391, 2012) reconstruct VPM lemniscal axons and excitatory somata/dendrites in an anatomically defined rat vibrissal column, classify nine excitatory cell types, and estimate thalamocortical synapse numbers and distributions. Overlapping dendritic territories still yield type- and location-specific innervation. Correlation with in vivo passive-whisker-touch responses accounts for some layer-4 patterns but not, for example, layer 5. Keywords: barrel cortex, dendrite morphology, in vivo spiking, VPM innervation.
summaries.advanced: Synapse numbers in the abstract are ‘estimated’ from reconstructions registered to a standardized column, not a fully dense EM connectome. Functional comparison is to passive whisker touch, not active whisking. The supplied extract cuts off in Conclusions, so later caveats in that section are not used. Inhibitory cells are outside the nine excitatory types.

title: Dense, Unspecific Connectivity of Neocortical Parvalbumin-Positive Interneurons: A Canonical Microcircuit for Inhibition?
authors: Adam Packer; R. Yuste

ocar.opportunity: If the largest cortical interneuron class, PV+ cells, follows a simple local connectivity rule onto pyramids, inhibition can be modeled as a dense blanket rather than a fine-scale specific graph.
ocar.challenge: Inhibitory circuit diagrams were still poorly mapped; apparent specificity might be an artifact of sparse sampling.
ocar.action: Packer and Yuste, in Journal of Neuroscience (2011), use two-photon RuBi-Glutamate uncaging to map PV+ interneuron connections onto pyramidal cells across mouse cortical areas and layers.
ocar.resolution: They find locally dense PV+→PC connectivity; in many experiments every nearby PV+ cell connected to every local PC sampled. PV+ cells contacted PC pairs similarly whether or not the pyramids were synaptically connected to each other. They conclude the architecture is an unspecific, densely homogeneous matrix over nearby pyramids, and probably for neocortical inhibition in general.
ocar.future_work: Generalization from PV+ to all inhibition is stated as a conclusion, not a multi-class mapping; other interneuron types remain to be compared with the same method.

plain_language_summary: A major class of inhibitory cells in mouse cortex appears to connect to essentially all nearby excitatory cells, not to a hand-picked few. The authors suggest local inhibition is more like a dense mesh than a precise wiring diagram.

summaries.beginner: A major class of inhibitory cells in mouse cortex appears to connect to essentially all nearby excitatory cells, not to a hand-picked few. The authors suggest local inhibition is more like a dense mesh than a precise wiring diagram.
summaries.intermediate: Packer and Yuste (J. Neurosci. 31:13260–13271, 2011) optically map parvalbumin-positive interneurons onto pyramidal cells with two-photon RuBi-Glutamate uncaging. Connectivity is locally dense across areas and layers; many experiments show complete local PV+→PC sampling. There is no evidence that PV+ cells prefer synaptically coupled PC pairs. The authors propose an unspecific dense matrix as a canonical inhibitory microcircuit. Related prior work from the lab on somatostatin cells in frontal cortex is cited as similarly dense.
summaries.advanced: The extract jumps from introduction to references, so quantitative connection probabilities, distances, and n are not recovered from a Discussion. ‘Probably neocortical inhibition in general’ is an extrapolation from PV+ (and cited SST) maps. Uncaging demonstrates functional connections, not synapse ultrastructure. ‘Unspecific’ means no detected fine-scale PC-pair bias, not that biology is random at all scales.

title: Neuronal Tracing for Connectomic Studies
authors: Ju Lu

ocar.opportunity: A complete wiring diagram requires tracing neuronal processes through enormous optical or EM image sets.
ocar.challenge: Segmentation and tracing remain a major bottleneck; new optical methods add image-analysis problems of their own.
ocar.action: Lu, in Neuroinformatics (2011), reviews automated tracing algorithms for fluorescence and electron microscopy connectomics, as described in the catalog abstract.
ocar.resolution: The abstract surveys recent progress in automated tracing and discusses challenges posed by novel optical imaging.
ocar.future_work: Open tracing challenges under new optical techniques are flagged rather than solved.

plain_language_summary: To map every wire in a circuit you must follow each branch through a mountain of microscope images. This review covers computer programs that try to do that tracing in light and electron microscopy.

title: Reconstruction of complete connectivity matrix for connectomics by sampling neural connectivity with fluorescent synaptic markers.
authors: Y. Mishchenko

ocar.opportunity: A complete connectivity matrix might be recovered statistically from sparsely localized fluorescent synaptic markers instead of tracing every process in EM.
ocar.challenge: Dense EM reconstructions of even C. elegans-scale circuits were still extremely slow; larger animals looked worse.
ocar.action: Mishchenko, in Journal of Neuroscience Methods (2011), proposes randomized genetic targeting of synaptic markers plus compressive sensing to reconstruct the connectivity matrix, tested in simulations on the C. elegans EM diagram, as described in the catalog abstract.
ocar.resolution: The abstract claims the worm wiring diagram could in principle be re-obtained in 1–7 days of imaging and analysis versus at least 1–2 years for alternative approaches then, and discusses possible Drosophila applications.
ocar.future_work: Application to larger organisms is discussed as prospective in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Instead of photographing every synapse with electron microscopy, this paper proposes randomly tagging synapses with fluorescent markers and reconstructing the wiring with compressive sensing. Simulations on the worm map suggest a much faster path, if the method works in real tissue.

summaries.beginner: Instead of photographing every synapse with electron microscopy, this paper proposes randomly tagging synapses with fluorescent markers and reconstructing the wiring with compressive sensing. Simulations on the worm map suggest a much faster path, if the method works in real tissue.
summaries.intermediate: Mishchenko (J. Neurosci. Methods, 2011) describes sampling physical connectivity with anatomical fluorescent synaptic markers placed by randomized genetic targeting, then recovering a high-resolution matrix with compressive sensing. According to the catalog abstract, simulations using the existing C. elegans EM diagram suggest 1–7 days versus 1–2 years for alternative reconstructions of that diagram, with possible extension to Drosophila. Timing claims (1–7 days vs 1–2 years) are from the catalog abstract’s simulations, not a wet-lab reconstruction. Independent reading of the Methods paper is required.

title: Reconstruction of the neuromuscular junction connectome
authors: Ranga Srinivasan; Qing Li; Xiaobo Zhou; Ju Lu; J. Lichtman; Stephen T. C. Wong

ocar.opportunity: The developing mammalian neuromuscular junction is a complete, optically accessible connectome in which synapse elimination and axon layout can be quantified.
ocar.challenge: Automatically tracking individual axons through complex 3D microscopy of the innervation field was unsolved.
ocar.action: Srinivasan, Li, Zhou, Lu, Lichtman, and Wong, in Bioinformatics (ISMB 2010), present AxonTracker-3D, an interactive 3D tracking and labeling tool for reconstructing axonal structures across the innervation field.
ocar.resolution: They argue the tool yields quantitative morphology—trajectories, branching, geometry, spatial relations of axon groups—with a balance of ease of use and accuracy. Availability is given as cbi-tmhs.org/AxonTracker/.
ocar.future_work: They intend data mining on branch number versus segment length, whether axon spatial distributions are random, and optimal motor-neuron layout using extracted wiring diagrams.

plain_language_summary: At the junction between nerve and muscle, you can see whole wiring diagrams in the light microscope, but following each axon by hand is painful. AxonTracker-3D is software to trace those axons in 3D with a person in the loop.

summaries.beginner: At the junction between nerve and muscle, you can see whole wiring diagrams in the light microscope, but following each axon by hand is painful. AxonTracker-3D is software to trace those axons in 3D with a person in the loop.
summaries.intermediate: Srinivasan et al. (Bioinformatics 26:i64–i70, ISMB 2010) introduce AxonTracker-3D for interactive tracking and labeling of axons in neuromuscular-junction connectomes, aimed at synapse-elimination and organizational questions in mammalian CNS development. They emphasize organizational specificity of axons and the need for individual labels. Planned analyses include branch–length relationships and spatial statistics of motor axons. The paper is a software/methods report in the ISMB proceedings issue.

title: Computational inference of the molecular logic for synaptic connectivity in C. elegans
authors: V. Varadan; David M. Miller; D. Anastassiou

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans uniquely pairs a complete wiring diagram with emerging neuron-specific gene-expression profiles, so molecular logic of connectivity can be asked computationally.
ocar.challenge: Connecting those two data types requires identifying synergistic gene sets, not single-gene correlates.
ocar.action: Varadan, Miller, and Anastassiou, in Bioinformatics (ISMB 2006), present EMBP (Entropy Minimization and Boolean Parsimony) and an information-theoretic synergy measure, as described in the catalog abstract.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports preliminary results on public data in which identified gene sets show exceptionally high synergy, taken as evidence of joint pathway involvement, and presents the strategy as improving as more neuron-specific expression appears.
ocar.future_work: The abstract expects more accurate results as expression atlases grow and hopes for clues to universal interconnectivity mechanisms.

plain_language_summary: The worm’s wiring diagram can be lined up with which genes each neuron turns on. This paper’s math looks for groups of genes that together predict who connects to whom.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s wiring diagram can be lined up with which genes each neuron turns on. This paper’s math looks for groups of genes that together predict who connects to whom.
summaries.intermediate: Varadan, Miller, and Anastassiou (Bioinformatics / ISMB, 2006) introduce EMBP to find synergistic gene sets whose joint expression predicts C. elegans neural connectivity, plus a multivariate synergy measure. According to the catalog abstract, preliminary public-data results show exceptionally high synergy, interpreted as joint pathway involvement, with accuracy expected to rise as neuron-specific expression improves. title: Synaptic connectivity in the midget‐parvocellular pathway of primate central retina
authors: P. Jusuf; P. Martin; U. Grünert

ocar.opportunity: The midget–parvocellular pathway is the high-acuity route of primate central retina; its OFF midget bipolar output synapses can be counted across species and color-vision genotypes.
ocar.challenge: Whether dichromatic and trichromatic marmosets, and macaques, use the same midget synaptic numerology was unclear.
ocar.action: Jusuf, Martin, and Grünert, in The Journal of Comparative Neurology (2006), quantify OFF midget bipolar output synapses in marmoset and macaque, as described in the catalog abstract.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports 1:1 midget bipolar to midget ganglion contacts in marmoset, consistent with Old World primates. Output synapses per axon terminal: dichromatic marmoset 10–71 (mean 29.7 ± 12.4 SD, n=104 cells, two animals), trichromatic marmoset 12–86 (28.6 ± 11.7, n=108, one animal), macaque 9–48 (26.5 ± 9.3, n=118, one animal), all unimodal, suggesting comparable midget circuitry.
ocar.future_work: The abstract does not add experiments beyond this comparison.

plain_language_summary: In the center of a primate eye, midget cells carry fine detail toward color vision. This study counts synapses from OFF midget bipolar cells in marmosets and macaques and finds similar numbers whether the marmoset has two or three cone types.

summaries.beginner: In the center of a primate eye, midget cells carry fine detail toward color vision. This study counts synapses from OFF midget bipolar cells in marmosets and macaques and finds similar numbers whether the marmoset has two or three cone types.
summaries.intermediate: Jusuf, Martin, and Grünert (J. Comp. Neurol., 2006) study OFF midget bipolar connectivity in Callithrix jacchus (di- and trichromatic) and Macaca fascicularis. According to the catalog abstract, marmoset midget bipolars contact midget ganglion cells 1:1. Mean output synapses per terminal are about 30 in both marmoset color-vision types and about 27 in macaque, with overlapping ranges and unimodal histograms. Markers: CD15 (marmoset bipolars), recoverin (macaque), ribbon proteins or GluR4, plus retrograde midget ganglion labels from parvocellular LGN in marmosets. title: Nervous system-wide single-cell morphology atlas of excitatory and inhibitory neurons in larval zebrafish
authors: Xu-Fei Du; Zhi-Feng Yue; Ming-Quan Chen; Wan-Lan Li; Tian-Lun Chen; Han-Yang Hu; Hong Wan; Ting Zhao; Yong-Wei Zhong; Xin-Yu Ning; Xiu-Dan Zheng; H. Ren; Ruiqi Wang; R. Zhao; Xiao-Lan Peng; Zhi-Ming Jia; Li-jun Chen; Chen Jin; Jia-wen Huang; Wei Deng; Liu Qian; Li Wang; Meijun Zheng; Wei Zhang; Xiaowen Shen; Xiu-Lian Shen; Xiaoying Qiu; Qimeng Zhao; Dan-Yang Li; Si Wang; Yu-Chen Gong; Yan Li; Yu Mu; Peng Ji; Jie He; Yu-Fan Wang; Jiu-lin Du

ocar.opportunity: A vertebrate morphology atlas with excitatory/inhibitory identity and dendrite–axon polarity would let putative mesoscopic connectomes be built across the whole larval nervous system.
ocar.challenge: Prior vertebrate single-neuron reconstructions were limited in coverage and cell-type labels.
ocar.action: Du, Yue, Chen, and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2025; version posted 24 March 2026), reconstruct a nervous-system-wide larval zebrafish morphology atlas and define morphotypes and putative inter-type and interregional connectomes, served via ZExplorer/iBrAVE.
ocar.resolution: They report more than 20,000 reconstructed neurons from more than 13,400 animals, spanning CNS and PNS, about 24.5% of brain excitatory and inhibitory neurons in a common space, and more than 500 E and I morphotypes. Projection analyses show laterality and directionality biases and modular innervation; network analyses yield motifs, hubs, and sensorimotor pathways. Connectivity is inferred from thresholded dendrite–axon proximity after registration.
ocar.future_work: Limitations include transgene variability, coarse parcellation, and the proximity-not-synapse assumption. They call for EM, transcriptomics, intersectional genetics, and functional tests. Data and code deposits are listed as available upon publication.

plain_language_summary: This team traces more than twenty thousand larval zebrafish neurons, marks them as excitatory or inhibitory, and lines them up in one standard fish brain. From how axons sit next to dendrites they sketch who might talk to whom, with the caveat that nearby is not the same as a synapse.

title: Topological Origin of the Diversity of Timescales in Recurrent Neural Circuits
authors: Marco Zenari; L. Taffarello; Luca Mazzucato; A. Maritan; S. Suweis

ocar.opportunity: Cortical circuits show both heterogeneous degrees (as in the mouse EM connectome) and diverse intrinsic timescales; a mechanistic link would explain multiplexed computation.
ocar.challenge: Standard random recurrent nets treat neurons as exchangeable and do not produce degree-dependent memory.
ocar.action: Zenari, Taffarello, Mazzucato, Maritan, and Suweis (arXiv:2603.04149, 2026) build a configuration-model recurrent net with tunable degree heterogeneity and partial synaptic-weight symmetry, derive heterogeneous dynamical mean-field theory, and instantiate topology from the MICrONS cubic-millimeter mouse connectome.
ocar.resolution: hDMFT yields a degree-scaled non-Markovian self-coupling that broadens activity timescales; degree heterogeneity lowers critical gain and localizes unstable modes on hubs. Under broadband input, slow hubs act as integrators. On MICrONS-matched topology they report a positive Spearman correlation between in-degree and resting-state calcium timescale, ρ ≈ 0.16 (p ≈ 10⁻⁴). In-degree after cutoff kmin = 14 is fit by a truncated lognormal (μ = 3.83, σ = 0.69).
ocar.future_work: The theory identifies hubs in partially symmetric nets as a substrate for multiplexed timescales; extending beyond resting-state calcium and the fitted degree cutoff is implied by the empirical analysis choices.

plain_language_summary: Some neurons in cortex are social hubs with many incoming wires, and some are slow thinkers. This theory says those facts are linked: hub wiring plus partly symmetric synapses naturally creates a mix of fast and slow cells, matching mouse connectome recordings.

summaries.beginner: Some neurons in cortex are social hubs with many incoming wires, and some are slow thinkers. This theory says those facts are linked: hub wiring plus partly symmetric synapses naturally creates a mix of fast and slow cells, matching mouse connectome recordings.
summaries.intermediate: Zenari et al. (arXiv 2603.04149, 2026) introduce a configuration-model recurrent network and heterogeneous DMFT in which partial weight symmetry plus degree heterogeneity produce a degree-dependent memory kernel and a wide timescale distribution. Stability analysis says heterogeneity lowers critical gain and concentrates unstable modes on hubs. Instantiating MICrONS topology, they relate in-degree to intrinsic timescale (HWHM of resting calcium autocorrelation), Spearman ρ ≈ 0.16, p ≈ 10⁻⁴. Calcium filtering is acknowledged as a relative, not absolute, timescale measure.

authors: Matthias P. Christenson; Á. S. Díez; Sarah L. Heath; Maia Saavedra-Weisenhaus; Atsuko Adachi; Aljoscha Nern; L. F. Abbott; Rudy Behnia; A. Sanz

title: The effects of axonal beading and undulation on axonal diameter estimation from diffusion MRI: Insights from simulations in human axons segmented from three-dimensional electron microscopy
authors: Hong-Hsi Lee; Qiyuan Tian; Maxina Sheft; Ricardo Coronado-Leija; Gabriel Ramos-Llordén; Ali Abdollahzadeh; E. Fieremans; Dmitry S. Novikov; Susie Y. Huang

ocar.opportunity: Strong-gradient human MRI (Connectome 2.0 class, ≲500 mT/m) makes axonal-diameter mapping tempting, if the finite transverse diffusivity at high b can be read as a caliber.
ocar.challenge: Real axons are not straight impermeable cylinders: microscopy shows beading (caliber variation) and undulation, both known to bias diameter estimates, including in pathology.
ocar.action: Lee, Tian, Sheft, Coronado-Leija, Ramos-Llordén, Abdollahzadeh, Fieremans, Novikov, and Huang, in NMR in Biomedicine (2024), run Monte Carlo diffusion simulations in axons reconstructed from 3D EM of a human temporal-lobe specimen, using sequence parameters matched to Connectome 2.0.
ocar.resolution: Diameter recovery is accurate for nonbeaded, nonundulating fibers. With realistic caliber variation and undulation, diameter is heavily underestimated because of beading, and that underestimation overshadows the known overestimation from undulation. The authors attribute the underestimation to variations in coarse-grained axial diffusivity. Pathological beading and undulation (e.g. TBI, ischemia) would therefore confound interpretation of apparent diameter change.
ocar.future_work: Relevance to in vivo mapping needs multimodality validation. Alternative encodings, multiple diffusion times, higher-order harmonics, or extra MRI contrasts are suggested as ways to disentangle the biases.

plain_language_summary: MRI can try to guess axon thickness from how water wiggles. Simulations in real human axons from electron microscopy show that bumps and wiggles in the axon itself can make those guesses too small, which matters when reading disease scans.

authors: Ayana M. Hellevik; Philip Mardoum; Joshua Hahn; Yvonne Kölsch; Florence D. D'Orazi; Sachihiro C. Suzuki; Leanne Godinho; Owen T. Lawrence; Fred Rieke; K. Shekhar; J. Sanes; Herwig Baier; T. Baden; R. Wong; T. Yoshimatsu

title: Flexible circuit mechanisms for context-dependent song sequencing
authors: Frederic A. Roemschied; Diego A. Pacheco; M. J. Aragon; Elise C. Ireland; Xinping Li; Kyle Thieringer; Rich Pang; M. Murthy

title: Linking neural circuits to the mechanics of animal behavior in Drosophila larval locomotion

ocar.opportunity: Behavior is neuromechanical: circuit maps alone cannot explain motion unless muscle mechanics and body physics are in the same account.

title: Mapping of Neuronal and Glial Primary Cilia Contactome and Connectome in the Human Cerebral Cortex

Berger; Cailyn Meyer; Cristine Casingal; Ariba Huda; Jiaqi Liu; Tina Ghashghaei; Mikayla Brenman; M. Jiang; J. Scarborough; Art Pope; Viren Jain; Jason L Stein; Jiami Guo; Ryohei Yasuda; J. Lichtman; E. S. Anton

ocar.challenge: Ciliopathies implicate cilia in circuit disorders, but human cortical cilia had not been placed in a layer-resolved contactome or connectome.

A subset of neuronal cilia sit at synaptic clefts, which the authors call a tetrapartite synapse (pre, post, astrocyte, cilium), with more synaptic associations than length-matched axonal controls. plain_language_summary: Tiny antennae on brain cells, called primary cilia, reach into the space around neurons and glia. A human cortex wiring volume shows they touch different partners by layer and cell type, and some even sit in the synapse itself.

title: Neural dynamics and architecture of the heading direction circuit in zebrafish
authors: L. Petrucco; Hagar Lavian; Y. Wu; Fabian Svara; Vilim Štih; R. Portugues

ocar.opportunity: Insect heading circuits are ring attractors with known connectivity; a vertebrate analog with both dynamics and EM architecture would close a mechanistic gap.
ocar.challenge: Vertebrate head-direction cells are well known physiologically, but the connectivity that implements a stable heading bump had not been reconstructed.
ocar.action: Petrucco, Lavian, Wu, Svara, Štih, and Portugues, in Nature Neuroscience (2023), use volumetric light-sheet imaging in larval zebrafish and EM reconstructions of the same stereotyped neurons.
ocar.resolution: A sinusoidal activity bump in the anterior hindbrain (rhombomere 1) rotates with directional swims and is stable for many seconds without landmarks, implying integration of turning efference. Somata sit dorsally; arbors enter the interpeduncular nucleus, where reciprocal inhibition is proposed to stabilize the ring attractor. The neurons are GABAergic and morphologically stereotyped, resembling fly central-complex heading networks.
ocar.future_work: The discussion notes nearby motor-related activity as a candidate integrator input. Full mapping of all attractor components comparable to the insect central complex is still lacking in vertebrates.

plain_language_summary: Larval zebrafish keep an internal compass of which way they are pointing. Imaging and electron microscopy find a small hindbrain circuit whose activity bump rotates with turns and is held in place by cells inhibiting each other.

summaries.beginner: Larval zebrafish keep an internal compass of which way they are pointing. Imaging and electron microscopy find a small hindbrain circuit whose activity bump rotates with turns and is held in place by cells inhibiting each other.
summaries.intermediate: Petrucco, Lavian, Wu, Svara, Štih, and Portugues (Nature Neuroscience, 2023) describe a heading-direction network in larval zebrafish anterior hindbrain. title: Neural mechanisms of dopamine function in learning and memory in Caenorhabditis elegans

title: Sleep benefits different stages of memory in Drosophila
authors: Katherine Marquand; Camilla Roselli; Isaac Cervantes-Sandoval; Tamara Boto

ocar.opportunity: Drosophila’s mapped mushroom-body connectome and sleep genetics make it possible to ask which memory stages sleep helps, and through which cells.
ocar.challenge: Sleep–memory coupling varies with metabolic state, genotype, and memory type; deprivation methods can confound stress with sleeplessness.

Individual sleep amounts vary widely (some flies as little as 4 min/day in a cited study).
ocar.future_work: Whether spontaneous short sleepers have memory defects, and cleaner deprivation devices, are highlighted. Alzheimer’s-model interactions are mentioned as a future setting.

authors: J. Straehle; V. Ravi; D. Heiland; C. Galanis; M. Lenz; Junyi Zhang; N. Neidert; A. El Rahal; I. Vasilikos; P. Kellmeyer; C. Scheiwe; J. Klingler; C. Fung; A. Vlachos; J. Beck; O. Schnell

title: Percolation may explain efficiency, robustness, and economy of the brain
authors: Yang Tian; Pei Sun

ocar.opportunity: A complete fruit-fly brain connectome lets one ask whether functional efficiency, robustness, and wiring economy emerge from a simple physical process on the anatomical graph.
ocar.challenge: Direct evidence that those three properties originate in connectivity has been limited by incomplete maps and missing theory.
ocar.action: Tian and Sun, in Network Neuroscience (2022), treat functional-connectivity formation on the fly brain as a percolation process controlled by the fraction of excitatory synapses λ (E/I balance).
ocar.resolution: Raising λ, a percolation transition appears at λ = 0.3 (E/I 3:7), where the advantageous properties emerge. Near λ = 0.5 (1:1) the giant strongly connected component’s size and growth reconcile, matching prior in vitro predictions of optimal E/I. Beyond λ = 0.6 (3:2) the properties saturate at bounds set by anatomical connectivity. Optimal λ ~ 0.5 is also tied to cortical criticality literature.
ocar.future_work: λ is defined as the excitatory synapse fraction with uniformly generated strengths; mapping onto measured fly E/I physiology is a modeling assumption. Human-brain rhetoric in the introduction is evolutionary framing, not a human connectome analysis.

plain_language_summary: Turn up the fraction of excitatory synapses on a fly brain map and, at a sharp point, the network suddenly becomes good at sending signals, surviving damage, and staying cheap to wire. That physics idea is called percolation.

summaries.beginner: Turn up the fraction of excitatory synapses on a fly brain map and, at a sharp point, the network suddenly becomes good at sending signals, surviving damage, and staying cheap to wire. That physics idea is called percolation.
summaries.intermediate: Tian and Sun (Network Neuroscience, 2022) analyze the then-largest fruit-fly brain connectome with percolation controlled by synaptic E/I balance λ. They report a nondilution percolation threshold at λ = 0.3 (3:7), an operating optimum near λ = 0.5 (1:1) aligning with Shew et al. 2011 in vitro work, and saturation after λ = 0.6 (3:2) set by static anatomy. Efficiency, robustness, and economy are treated as byproducts of the transition. Open CC BY 4.0.

Catalog biological_application/fly tags match; ‘our brain’ in the introduction is rhetoric.

title: Semi-Supervised Neuron Segmentation via Reinforced Consistency Learning
authors: Wei Huang; C. Chen; Zhiwei Xiong; Yueyi Zhang; Xuejin Chen; Xiaoyan Sun; Feng Wu

ocar.opportunity: Unlabeled EM slices are abundant; a two-stage semi-supervised scheme could make neuron segmentation work when dense labels are few.
ocar.challenge: Fully supervised deep nets collapse if the annotation budget cannot cover dense, complex neurites.
ocar.action: Huang, Chen, Xiong, Zhang, Chen, Sun, and Wu, in IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging (2022), pretrain by reconstructing volumes from perturbations, then regularize supervised training with pixel-level consistency between unlabeled images and perturbed copies (SSNS-Net).
ocar.resolution: On representative EM datasets they report up to 400% gain on the VOI metric versus supervised learning with few labels, matching a supervised model trained on ten times as much labeled data. Code is released.
ocar.future_work: Which datasets and label fractions produce the 400% figure must be read from tables not in the extract. Generalization beyond the tested EM volumes is not claimed in the selected text.

plain_language_summary: Drawing every neuron in an electron-microscope stack takes forever. This paper shows a network can learn from a handful of labels plus lots of unlabeled pictures, by insisting that slightly messed-up copies get the same answer.

summaries.beginner: Drawing every neuron in an electron-microscope stack takes forever. This paper shows a network can learn from a handful of labels plus lots of unlabeled pictures, by insisting that slightly messed-up copies get the same answer.
summaries.intermediate: Huang et al. (IEEE TMI, 2022) propose two-stage semi-supervised neuron segmentation: perturbation-reconstruction pretraining, then consistency regularization on unlabeled EM. IEEE Xplore copy licensed to Johns Hopkins University in the extract footer.
summaries.advanced: 400% is the authors’ stated maximum VOI gain, not a mean across all splits. VOI is variation of information (lower is usually better in connectomics; treat the ‘gain’ as their reported relative improvement). Dataset identities are in omitted experiments. This is 2D/3D EM neuron segmentation, not proofreading software.

title: Brain research challenges supercomputing
authors: K. Amunts; T. Lippert

ocar.opportunity: Linking human synapses (nanometres) through cells (micrometres) to the whole organ requires computing and storage that grow with every finer map.
ocar.challenge: The adult human brain has on the order of 86 billion neurons; a C. elegans-level structural–functional model does not yet exist for humans.
ocar.action: Amunts and Lippert, in Science (2021), as described in the catalog abstract, argue that big data from human brain structure push supercomputing, and that those demands may spawn methods useful beyond neuroscience.
ocar.resolution: The abstract contrasts the 302-neuron C. elegans connectome and proposed complete model with the still-distant human case, and treats decoding connectivity, signal transduction, and function as exponentially growing computational problems.
ocar.future_work: Creative computing solutions are invited; the abstract is a perspective, not a benchmark.

plain_language_summary: Mapping the human brain in fine detail creates more data than ordinary computers can handle. This short Science piece says that challenge may force new supercomputing ideas, using the tiny worm connectome as the completeness benchmark we do not yet have for humans.

summaries.beginner: Mapping the human brain in fine detail creates more data than ordinary computers can handle. This short Science piece says that challenge may force new supercomputing ideas, using the tiny worm connectome as the completeness benchmark we do not yet have for humans.

title: Cross-modal coherent registration of whole mouse brains
authors: Hanchuan Peng; Lei Qu; Yuanyuan Li; Peng Xie; Lijuan Liu; Yimin Wang; Jun Wu; Yu Liu; Tao Wang; Longfei Li; Kaixuan Guo; Wan Wan; Lei OuYang; Feng Xiong; Yefeng Zheng; Fang-ming Xu; H. Gong; H. Dong; Qing Luo; Guofang Bi; M. Hawrylycz; Hongkui Zeng

ocar.opportunity: Whole-mouse-brain images from STPT, fMOST, LSFM, VISoR, or MRI must sit in one atlas to type cells and assemble projection diagrams.
ocar.challenge: Cross-modal registration fails when anatomy, clearing, and modality-specific artifacts differ from the Allen Common Coordinate Framework (CCF).

ocar.resolution: They report whole-brain maps of 3D single-neuron morphology and cell types after registration. Comparisons versus MIRACL, ClearMap, and aMAP appear in figures for soma localization and axon mapping (e.g. 162 neurons with L1 apical dendrites; 63 VPM/VPL neurons in one panel). An fMOST average template is iterated and CCF annotations are back-projected.
ocar.future_work: Anatomical variation between fMOST and CCFv3 remains a registration residual. Precise numeric error tables should be read from the published Nature Methods figures.

plain_language_summary: Mouse brains imaged with different microscopes do not line up on the standard atlas by themselves. This method, mBrainAligner, uses landmarks and neural nets to warp whole brains into the Allen map so cells and axons can be compared.

Figure descriptions compare soma and axon accuracy with MIRACL, ClearMap, and aMAP.

Figure-caption neuron counts (162, 63) describe illustrated examples, not the entire BICCN corpus. ‘Coherent landmark mapping’ is the method name, not a claim of zero residual error. Catalog title says ‘cross-modal’; preprint title says ‘cross-modality’—same work.

title: Dopamine Neurons That Cotransmit Glutamate, From Synapses to Circuits to Behavior
authors: Daniel Eskenazi; Lauren Malave; S. Mingote; Leora Yetnikoff; Samira Ztaou; V. Velicu; S. Rayport; N. Chuhma

ocar.opportunity: A subset of midbrain dopamine neurons also release glutamate; mapping that cotransmission from synapse to behavior could yield cell-type-specific therapies.
ocar.challenge: Functional roles of dopamine-neuron glutamate cotransmission were only emerging twenty years after its discovery, despite conservation across species.
ocar.action: Eskenazi, Malave, Mingote, Yetnikoff, Ztaou, Velicu, Rayport, and Chuhma, in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2021), review synaptic, developmental, connectomic, and behavioral evidence for ventral-midbrain dopamine neurons that cotransmit glutamate.
ocar.resolution: Functional connectome mapping shows strong glutamate connections onto cholinergic interneurons in nucleus accumbens medial shell and lateral dorsal striatum. Glutamate markers in dopamine neurons peak embryonically and rise after toxins, suggesting a neuroprotective role. Behaviorally, cotransmission contributes to psychostimulant responses, positive valence, and cognition, with subtler negative-valence effects. Genetic pharmacotherapy (e.g. dopamine-neuron GLS1 reduction) is cited as a schizophrenia-relevant proof of principle.
ocar.future_work: Gene-therapy and intersectional targeting of cotransmitting subtypes are presented as future treatments for addiction, schizophrenia, and Parkinson disease, not as completed trials.

plain_language_summary: Some dopamine cells also spit out glutamate. This review traces that double signal from synapses to circuits to behavior and asks whether it could be a more precise drug target than dopamine alone.

summaries.beginner: Some dopamine cells also spit out glutamate. This review traces that double signal from synapses to circuits to behavior and asks whether it could be a more precise drug target than dopamine alone.
summaries.intermediate: Eskenazi et al. (Frontiers in Neural Circuits, 2021) review glutamate cotransmission from ventral midbrain dopamine neurons. They synthesize in vitro discovery, in vivo confirmation across species, developmental regulation, and a functional connectome onto striatal cholinergic interneurons. Behavioral roles include psychostimulant responses and positive-valence/cognitive systems. Therapeutic framing covers addiction, schizophrenia, and PD, including Genetic Pharmacotherapy via GLS1. Review.
summaries.advanced: ‘Just over 20 years’ dates from the 2021 review. Connectome language here is functional/optogenetic mapping, not EM. GLS1 behavioral effects are cited from Mingote et al., not new data. Disease-treatment claims are translational outlook.

title: FIB-SEM as a Volume Electron Microscopy Approach to Study Cellular Architectures in SARS-CoV-2 and Other Viral Infections: A Practical Primer for a Virologist
authors: Valentina Baena; Ryan Conrad; P. Friday; E. Fitzgerald; Taeeun Kim; J. Bernbaum; Heather Berensmann; Adam Harned; K. Nagashima; Kedar Narayan

ocar.opportunity: FIB-SEM sits in a resolution–volume niche that can quantify virus–cell architecture in 3D, not only 2D snapshots.
ocar.challenge: Virologists rarely have a practical map of room-temperature FIB-SEM: milling/imaging cycles, targeting, and how to turn volumes into viral-density statistics.
ocar.action: Baena, Conrad, Friday, Fitzgerald, Kim, Bernbaum, Berensmann, Harned, Nagashima, and Narayan, in Viruses (2021), write a primer on FIB-SEM in the vEM family and apply it to an in vitro SARS-CoV-2 infection study.
ocar.resolution: Automated mill-and-image cycles interrogate micron-thick samples at tens of nanometres or better. In the SARS-CoV-2 example, quantitation of viral densities and surface curvature shows virions preferentially at plasma-membrane regions of positive mean curvature. Data are in EMPIAR-10677; a supplementary movie reconstructs three infected Vero E6 cells.
ocar.future_work: The authors urge imaginative but realistic virology questions and warn that analysis, not acquisition, of giant volumes is the bottleneck.

plain_language_summary: A focused ion beam can peel a cell like a 3D onion inside an electron microscope. This primer shows virologists how that works and finds SARS-CoV-2 particles sitting on outward-bulging bits of the cell membrane.

summaries.beginner: A focused ion beam can peel a cell like a 3D onion inside an electron microscope. This primer shows virologists how that works and finds SARS-CoV-2 particles sitting on outward-bulging bits of the cell membrane.
summaries.intermediate: Baena et al. (Viruses, 2021) review FIB-SEM as volume EM for virus–cell architecture and include a room-temperature practical guide. Their SARS-CoV-2 in vitro analysis reports virions enriched at plasma membrane with positive mean curvature. Reconstructions of three Vero E6 cells and particle coordinates are deposited as EMPIAR-10677. Open-access review with a primary imaging component. Catalog tags include MICrONS/mouse; the study is cultured primate cells plus a methods primer.

EMPIAR-10677 should be used for quantitative reanalysis. Catalog organism/dataset tags are mismatched to the virology experiment.

title: High-precision targeting workflow for volume electron microscopy
authors: P. Ronchi; Giulia Mizzon; P. Machado; Edoardo D’Imprima; Benedikt T. Best; Lucia Cassella; Sebastian Schnorrenberg; M. G. Montero; M. Jechlinger; A. Ephrussi; M. Leptin; J. Mahamid; Y. Schwab

ocar.challenge: Automated vEM still struggles to find a specific labeled cell after heavy-metal embedding and trimming.
ocar.action: Ronchi, Mizzon, Machado, D’Imprima, Best, Cassella, Schnorrenberg, Montero, Jechlinger, Ephrussi, Leptin, Mahamid, and Schwab, in Journal of Cell Biology (2021), preserve fluorescence through preparation, trim using confocal maps of the resin block, and laser-brand landmarks to position FIB-SEM.

plain_language_summary: Finding one glowing cell inside a big chunk of tissue, then milling only that cell in an electron microscope, is hard. This workflow keeps the glow, marks the block, and aims the ion beam with micrometre aim.
