title: Role of Graph Architecture in Controlling Dynamical Networks with Applications to Neural Systems
authors: Jason Z. Kim; Jonathan M. Soffer; Ari E. Kahn; J. Vettel; F. Pasqualetti; D. Bassett

ocar.opportunity: If the energy needed to steer a network can be written in terms of which edges touch driver nodes, then connectomes can be compared and even edited for control performance.
ocar.challenge: Numerical control-energy calculations do not by themselves yield design rules. Clinical edge deletions (a single tract) need an analytic prediction of how control energy will change.
ocar.action: Kim, Soffer, Kahn, Vettel, Pasqualetti, and Bassett use linear network control theory to derive closed-form expressions linking driver-to-non-driver connections to minimum control energy, then apply them to high-resolution Drosophila, mouse, and human connectomes.
ocar.resolution: They report topological features that raise or lower control energy and, in the preprint extract, that connectomes of increasingly complex species are wired to reduce control energy. Cross-species comparison is used to argue that the human brain supports diverse dynamics at small energetic cost while remaining robust to perturbations. Single-edge removal is presented as a clinically accessible manipulation of control performance.
ocar.future_work: The extract includes a first-order approximation whose error versus unsimplified Gramians is checked numerically (Fig. 2b). Real brains are not linear time-invariant systems; the theory is a linear control approximation.

plain_language_summary: Steering a network takes energy that depends on how the “driver” nodes plug into the rest. Applied to fly, mouse, and human wiring diagrams, this theory suggests more complex brains are built to be cheaper to control and fairly robust if one connection is lost.

summaries.beginner: Steering a network takes energy that depends on how the “driver” nodes plug into the rest. Applied to fly, mouse, and human wiring diagrams, this theory suggests more complex brains are built to be cheaper to control and fairly robust if one connection is lost.
summaries.intermediate: The catalog paper is Nature Physics (2017; nphys4268); the selected PDF is the matching arXiv preprint “Topological Principles of Control in Dynamical Network Systems” (1702.00354). Kim and colleagues derive closed-form linear-control expressions relating driver–non-driver edges to minimum energy and apply them to Drosophila, mouse, and human connectomes. They argue more complex species reduce control energy and that the human brain supports diverse dynamics cheaply while remaining robust, including under single-edge deletions.

Catalog organism is tagged fly; the study is explicitly comparative across fly, mouse, and human. Linear LTI control is an approximation. Numeric energy values are not in the selected extract (later pages are derivations).

title: Structural and functional, empirical and modeled connectivity in the cerebral cortex of the rat
authors: Antonio Díaz-Parra; Zachary Osborn; S. Canals; D. Moratal; O. Sporns

ocar.opportunity: A directed rat cortical connectome from tracing, paired with resting-state fMRI, can test how much empirical functional coupling is explained by anatomical weights and by simulations on that graph.
ocar.challenge: Structure–function correspondence can be inflated or distorted by parcellation mismatches, global-signal regression, motion, and anesthesia.
ocar.action: Díaz-Parra, Osborn, Canals, Moratal, and Sporns, in NeuroImage (2017), combine a curated meta-analysis tracing connectome with rs-fMRI from 14 anesthetized Wistar rats and run neural-mass simulations on the empirical anatomy.
ocar.resolution: Maximum Spearman correlation between BOLD functional-connection strength and anatomical weight was ρ = 0.48. Regions in the same functional community formed more mutual weighted anatomical connections, and functional communities were enriched in dense anatomical motifs not explained by lower-order topology. Simulated FC on the rat connectome reached a maximum Pearson correlation of ρ = 0.53 with measured FC.
ocar.future_work: Limitations discussed include incomplete rat connectome coverage, manual Swanson versus Paxinos matching, aggregating some ROIs, hemispheric averaging of 32 equal-volume ROIs, GSR plus scrubbing (minimum ~9 min windows), and urethane at 1.2 g/kg. They point to more complete tracing (e.g. Swanson et al. 2016) and better physiology as next steps.

plain_language_summary: In rats, the team compares a wiring diagram built from published tracer studies with resting-state MRI. Stronger anatomical links and certain dense motifs go with stronger functional coupling, and a simple simulation on the wiring partly recreates the MRI pattern.

summaries.beginner: In rats, the team compares a wiring diagram built from published tracer studies with resting-state MRI. Stronger anatomical links and certain dense motifs go with stronger functional coupling, and a simple simulation on the wiring partly recreates the MRI pattern.

Same-community regions had more reciprocal weighted connections, and functional communities were enriched for dense anatomical motifs beyond lower-order topology.

title: Using high-throughput barcode sequencing to efficiently map connectomes
authors: Ian D. Peikon; Justus M. Kebschull; Vasily V. Vagin; Diana I. Ravens; Yu-Chi Sun; Eric Brouzes; Ivan R. Corrêa; D. Bressan; A. Zador

ocar.opportunity: EM connectomics is precise but slow and costly; converting synapses into DNA barcode pairs could use sequencing throughput instead of tracing axons across thousands of sections.
ocar.challenge: A 5 mm axon through 50 nm sections would, under the paper’s simple assumptions, need per-section tracing accuracy above 99.999% for even a 36% chance of a correct assignment—illustrating why automation remains hard.
ocar.action: Peikon, Kebschull, Vagin, Ravens, Sun, Brouzes, Corrêa, Bressan, and Zador, in Nucleic Acids Research (2017), present SYNseq: unique RNA barcodes targeted to synapses, protein–protein crosslinking of pre- and postsynaptic partners, extraction, and joining for sequencing.
ocar.resolution: Each biochemical piece (barcoding, protein joining, RNA joining) could be shown to work, including emulsion overlap RT-PCR joining in principle, but they could not recover many barcode pairs. In-droplet reverse transcription efficiency on the order of 1% implies both barcodes succeed in only about 0.01% of properly loaded droplets (0.01²), so joining—not barcoding or crosslinking—limited detection. In its current form SYNseq was unusable for biological circuit tracing.
ocar.future_work: They suggest optimizing droplets (perhaps with barcoded beads), or joining by RNA ligation, gap filling, or immobilization on beads/chips/gels, and co-expressing components via two RNA-binding domains. Catalog journal lists bioRxiv; the PDF is the NAR paper.

plain_language_summary: Instead of photographing every synapse, this method tries to read connections as paired DNA barcodes. The biochemistry mostly works, but stitching the two barcodes together is still far too inefficient to map a real circuit.

summaries.beginner: Instead of photographing every synapse, this method tries to read connections as paired DNA barcodes. The biochemistry mostly works, but stitching the two barcodes together is still far too inefficient to map a real circuit.
summaries.intermediate: Peikon et al. (Nucleic Acids Research, 2017; 45:e115; catalog journal lists bioRxiv) introduce SYNseq: synaptic RNA barcodes joined across engineered protein bridges for sequencing. Components function, but barcode joining failed at usable efficiency. They estimate ~1% in-droplet RT, hence ~0.01% of droplets with both barcodes reverse-transcribed, and therefore blame joining (especially RT) rather than barcoding or trans-synaptic complex formation. The published abstract states that failure to develop efficient joining precludes widespread application.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods paper that reports a negative practical result on joining. The 99.999% EM tracing illustration is a back-of-envelope motivation, not an empirical error rate. No circuit was mapped. Catalog stages include proofreading and graph analysis; those are aspirations, not delivered graphs.

title: Cliques of Neurons Bound into Cavities Provide a Missing Link between Structure and Function
authors: Michael W. Reimann; Max Nolte; M. Scolamiero; Katharine Turner; R. Perin; G. Chindemi; Paweł Dłotko; R. Levi; K. Hess; H. Markram

ocar.opportunity: Without a formal link between network structure and emergent function it is hard to say how cortex processes stimuli in terms of synaptic architecture.
ocar.challenge: Standard undirected graph statistics ignore the direction of synaptic transmission and can miss higher-order organization such as cliques bound into cavities.
ocar.action: Reimann, Nolte, Scolamiero, Turner, Perin, Chindemi, Dłotko, Levi, Hess, and Markram, in Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience (2017), build directed graphs that follow information flow and analyze a local neocortical network with algebraic topology.
ocar.resolution: They report an intricate previously unseen topology: an abundance of neuronal cliques bound into cavities that guide correlated activity. In response to stimuli, correlated activity binds synaptically connected neurons into functional cliques and cavities that evolve in a stereotypical sequence toward peak complexity. They propose that the brain processes stimuli by forming increasingly complex functional cliques and cavities.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents the clique-and-cavity sequence as a proposed processing principle; further tests beyond the local neocortical network are not specified in the catalog abstract.

plain_language_summary: Looking at cortex as one-way streets instead of undirected wires reveals clumps of fully connected cells wrapped around holes. This paper argues those growing clumps and holes are how the network organizes activity after a stimulus.

summaries.beginner: Looking at cortex as one-way streets instead of undirected wires reveals clumps of fully connected cells wrapped around holes. This paper argues those growing clumps and holes are how the network organizes activity after a stimulus.

title: Community detection in networks: A user guide
authors: S. Fortunato; Darko Hric

ocar.opportunity: Many networks of scientific interest, including biological ones, have community structure—groups of vertices more likely to connect internally than to other groups—so practitioners need a critical guide to detection methods.
ocar.challenge: Community detection is ill-defined: there is no universal definition of community, nor agreed protocols for validation and algorithm comparison, which has produced confusion that slows the field.
ocar.action: Fortunato and Hric, in Physics Reports (2016; arXiv:1608.00163), write a user guide covering what communities are, validation (benchmarks, partition similarity, detectability, metadata), methods (spectral, overlapping, statistical inference, optimization, dynamics), software, and outlook.
ocar.resolution: They survey classic and modern views of communities, strengths and weaknesses of popular algorithms, and practical directions for use, emphasizing that identifying communities is not a single well-posed computational problem.
ocar.future_work: The selected extract is largely the introduction and table of contents; the outlook chapter itself is not in the excerpt. The paper’s stated aim is to reduce misconceptions and guide method choice rather than to introduce a new clustering algorithm.

plain_language_summary: Finding clusters in a network sounds simple until you notice nobody agrees what a cluster is. This long guide walks through the definitions, tests, and algorithms so you can pick a method without treating it as magic.

summaries.beginner: Finding clusters in a network sounds simple until you notice nobody agrees what a cluster is. This long guide walks through the definitions, tests, and algorithms so you can pick a method without treating it as magic.

title: Sex-specific pruning of neuronal synapses in Caenorhabditis elegans
authors: Meital Oren-Suissa; Emily A. Bayer; O. Hobert

ocar.opportunity: Comparing hermaphrodite and male C. elegans connectomes shows sexually dimorphic synapses among the 294 neurons present in both sexes, a chance to watch how shared neurons acquire sex-specific wiring.
ocar.challenge: It was unclear whether dimorphic connections are built from scratch in one sex or sculpted from an initially shared hybrid pattern, and whether sexual identity of pre- versus postsynaptic cells is instructive.
ocar.action: Oren-Suissa, Bayer, and Hobert, in Nature (2016), demonstrate sex-specific functions of shared neurons, follow synapse development across sexual maturation, and manipulate sexual identity and dimorphic transcription factors.
ocar.resolution: Many neurons first form synapses in both male and hermaphrodite patterns; sex-specific pruning then keeps a subset. Reversing sexual identity of either the pre- or the postsynaptic neuron alone switches connectivity to the opposite-sex pattern. A dimorphically expressed conserved transcription factor (DMD-5/11 acting with TRA-1 in the extract’s summary schematic) is necessary and sufficient for sex-specific connectivity. Timing of pruning requires additional timer mechanisms because dmd-5/11 are already dimorphic in embryos and L1.
ocar.future_work: The authors hypothesize that other neurons (for example AVA) have their own sex-specific dmd genes controlling pruning, and that heterochronic factors may time the onset of pruning.

plain_language_summary: Male and hermaphrodite worms share most neurons but not all of their synapses. This paper shows many connections are wired both ways at first, then each sex prunes the extras, under the control of the cell’s sexual identity and a conserved transcription factor.

summaries.beginner: Male and hermaphrodite worms share most neurons but not all of their synapses. This paper shows many connections are wired both ways at first, then each sex prunes the extras, under the control of the cell’s sexual identity and a conserved transcription factor.

Cell-autonomous reversal of sexual identity in pre- or postsynaptic cells is sufficient to switch wiring. Dimorphic DMD transcription factors are necessary and sufficient; TRA-1/DMD are discussed as repressors, with extra timers needed because dmd-5/11 expression is already dimorphic early.

title: Chimera-like States in Modular Neural Networks
authors: J. Hizanidis; N. Kouvaris; Zamora-López Gorka; A. Díaz-Guilera; C. Antonopoulos

ocar.opportunity: Chimera states—coexistence of synchronized and desynchronized activity—are a candidate dynamical motif for modular brains, but they had been studied mainly in non-modular complex networks.
ocar.challenge: It was unclear whether a biologically inspired modular graph, with different synapse types inside versus between communities, could produce chimera-like dynamics rather than global synchrony or metastable chaos.
ocar.action: Hizanidis, Kouvaris, Zamora-López, Díaz-Guilera, and Antonopoulos, in Scientific Reports (2015; arXiv extract), simulate chaotic bursting neurons on a C. elegans–inspired network of six communities, with electrical coupling inside communities and chemical coupling across them, and score coherence with the Kuramoto order parameter ρ plus chimera-like χ and metastability λ indices.
ocar.resolution: Coaction of the two coupling types can produce chimera-like states: larger communities synchronize while smaller ones desynchronize. In the (gch, gel) plane, a high-χ / low-λ edge (illustrated at gch = 0.015, gel = 0.5) separates globally synchronous from highly metastable regimes. Similar behavior appears in networks that share features with the C. elegans graph.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the phenomenon as potentially informative for more complex modular brains; living-animal physiology is not tested here.

plain_language_summary: In a computer model inspired by the worm’s wiring, some groups of cells fire together while others fire out of step. That mixed pattern, called a chimera-like state, appears when local electrical coupling and longer-range chemical coupling are balanced just so.

summaries.beginner: In a computer model inspired by the worm’s wiring, some groups of cells fire together while others fire out of step. That mixed pattern, called a chimera-like state, appears when local electrical coupling and longer-range chemical coupling are balanced just so.
summaries.intermediate: Hizanidis and colleagues (Scientific Reports, 2015) place chaotic bursting neurons on a six-community network inspired by the C. elegans connectome, with electrical synapses within communities and chemical synapses between them. Besides the Kuramoto order parameter, they use a chimera-like index χ (synchronization differences among communities) and a metastability index λ (variation over time). Parameter-space maps show a chimera-like regime on the boundary between globally synchronous and desynchronized/metastable dynamics, illustrated at gch = 0.015, gel = 0.5, where some communities lock and others do not. Analogous modular graphs behave similarly under the same assumptions.
summaries.advanced: This is a numerical study of a C. elegans–inspired modular graph, not a claim about living worms. The supplied extract is arXiv:1510.00286v2 of the Scientific Reports paper. Figure 3’s 1–277 neuron index should not be treated as a new biological census. Chimera-like here is defined by high χ and low λ, not by a unique biological mechanism.

title: Comparison of diffusion tractography and tract‐tracing measures of connectivity strength in rhesus macaque connectome
authors: M. P. van den Heuvel; M. D. de Reus; Lisa Feldman Barrett; L. H. Scholtens; Fraukje M.T. Coopmans; Ruben Schmidt; T. Preuss; J. Rilling; Longchuan Li

ocar.opportunity: Human macroconnectomics increasingly treats the number of reconstructed diffusion streamlines (NOS) as a stand-in for cortico-cortical projection strength. A cross-species check against gold-standard tract tracing would say how realistic that metric is.
ocar.challenge: The link between in vivo DWI NOS and invasive measures of anatomical connectivity strength in the same species remained poorly quantified, and deterministic tracking is known to over- and under-represent classes of tracts.
ocar.action: van den Heuvel and colleagues, in Human Brain Mapping (2015), compare GQI tractography from high-angular DWI in 10 rhesus macaques (600 directions total) with projection-strength tables from CoCoMac and the Markov–Kennedy high-resolution tract-tracing dataset.
ocar.resolution: NOS and streamline density correlated positively with tract-tracing strength in both datasets (both P < 0.001), with the clearest relationships after log transformation. NOS was the strongest DWI correlate; radial or mean diffusivity added unique variance in a combined model, whereas FA did not. The authors treat reconstructed streamline counts as a useful approximation of axonal number for in vivo DWI connectomes.
ocar.future_work: The discussion notes that the biological meaning of lognormal connectivity-strength distributions is still unclear, and that systematic under- and over-representation of tract classes remains a limit of deterministic fiber tracking.

plain_language_summary: MRI maps of brain cables are cheaper than injecting tracers, but it is hard to know whether more reconstructed fibers really mean a stronger connection. In macaques, streamline counts from diffusion MRI do rise with classic tracer measures of pathway strength.

(Human Brain Mapping, 2015) compare DWI-derived number of streamlines (NOS) and streamline density from 10 rhesus macaques with CoCoMac and Markov–Kennedy tract-tracing weights. The paper argues that in vivo DWI connectomes can give fairly realistic estimates of white-matter projection strength.
summaries.advanced: Association is statistical, not proof that NOS equals axon count. Deterministic tracking biases (long-range over/under-representation) are acknowledged. The 1.39 factor is for a CoCoMac NOS+RD model versus NOS alone. PDF is a Europe PMC/Human Brain Mapping typeset copy. Species is rhesus macaque, not human.

title: Glial Regulation of the Neuronal Connectome through Local and Long-Distant Communication
authors: R. Fields; D. H. Woo; P. Basser

ocar.opportunity: If a connectome is a complete map of anatomical and functional connectivity, glia belong in it: they shape wiring and signaling from whole-brain white matter down to individual synapses.
ocar.challenge: Connectomics has been framed almost exclusively around neurons, even though astrocytes, microglia, and oligodendrocytes operate on different spatial and temporal scales and use partly shared transmitter systems.
ocar.action: Fields, Woo, and Basser, in a Neuron (2015) Perspective, review glial contributions to long-range networks, local circuits, and synapses, including myelination, metabolic support, blood-flow coupling, and synapse pruning.
ocar.resolution: They argue that all major glial classes influence structural and functional connectivity, that myelin both speeds long-range communication and restricts axonal sprouting, and that glial computation is not well captured by neuronal membrane-potential models. A neuronal-only map is therefore incomplete.
ocar.future_work: The piece closes by rejecting the idea that glial structure and function will fall out automatically from neuronal connectomes; multicellular analysis is required.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram of the brain is usually a map of neurons. This essay argues that support cells—glia—also shape those wires, from whole-brain pathways down to single synapses, so they belong in the connectome too.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram of the brain is usually a map of neurons. This essay argues that support cells—glia—also shape those wires, from whole-brain pathways down to single synapses, so they belong in the connectome too.
summaries.intermediate: Fields, Woo, and Basser (Neuron, 2015) write a Perspective that astrocytes, microglia, and oligodendrocytes should be part of any complete connectome. They survey glial effects on long-range networks (myelination, conduction-time inference from path length and axon diameter), local circuits, and synapses (pruning, neuromodulatory factors). Glia share transmitter-based signaling with neurons but operate on different morphological and temporal scales. The authors warn against assuming glial roles will be revealed as a byproduct of tracing neurons alone.
summaries.advanced: This is a perspective, not a new reconstruction. Conduction-time inference from dMRI path length plus axon-diameter distributions is a proposed measurement strategy, not a delivered atlas. Calcium imaging’s prominence in glial signaling is treated as a methods bias. The extract’s latter pages enter the reference list.

title: Identification of Important Nodes in Directed Biological Networks: A Network Motif Approach
authors: Pei Wang; Jinhu Lü; Xinghuo Yu

ocar.opportunity: Finding which nodes actually matter in directed biological networks—command neurons, global regulators, conserved non-hubs—would give control and pharmacology targets that degree or PageRank can miss.
ocar.challenge: Most importance metrics were developed for undirected graphs; directed biological networks have motif structure (e.g. feed-forward loops) that those scores ignore.
ocar.action: Wang, Lü, and Yu, in PLoS ONE (2014), combine network-motif participation with principal component analysis to rank nodes, and test the index on five real directed biological networks (a neural network, three transcriptional regulatory networks, and a signal-transduction network).
ocar.resolution: The measure recovers biologically important nodes, including command interneurons and non-hub but conserved regulators. ROC curves on the five networks are reported as showing high prediction accuracy. If the feed-forward loop is the only motif, the index reduces to existing motif centrality.
ocar.future_work: The authors note computational cost if more motif types are included, and they propose extensions to electrical and social networks; finding still more effective node features remains open.

plain_language_summary: Not every important cell in a directed biological network is a hub with many links. This paper scores nodes by the wiring triangles they sit in, and reports that the score finds command neurons and key regulators better than simpler rankings.

summaries.beginner: Not every important cell in a directed biological network is a hub with many links. This paper scores nodes by the wiring triangles they sit in, and reports that the score finds command neurons and key regulators better than simpler rankings.
summaries.intermediate: Wang, Lü, and Yu (PLoS ONE, 2014) introduce a motif-plus-PCA importance index for directed biological networks. They evaluate it on five real networks of different sizes and densities: one neural, three transcriptional, and one signal-transduction. They report recovery of command interneurons, global regulators, and conserved non-hub nodes, with ROC analysis described as high-accuracy. The method is offered as an alternative to degree, betweenness, and PageRank. Including more motif types raises computational complexity; unique FFL structure collapses the index to motif centrality.
summaries.advanced: ‘Very high prediction accuracy’ is the authors’ ROC summary, not a single AUC quoted in the extract. Ground-truth ‘important’ labels are network-specific biological annotations. The paper is a methods-and-application study across mixed biological graphs, not a new connectome. Editor was Mark D. McDonnell.

title: Multilayer Analysis and Visualization of Networks
authors: M. Domenico; M. Porter; A. Arenas

ocar.opportunity: Many systems, including neuronal connectomes, are multilayer: several relationship types among the same entities. Analysis and visualization tools for that representation were scarce.
ocar.challenge: Without software that jointly handles interlayer structure, spatial overlays, and standard graph diagnostics, multilayer data are flattened into misleading single-layer graphs.
ocar.action: De Domenico, Porter, and Arenas, in Journal of Complex Networks (2015 version of a 2014 paper; arXiv:1405.0843), present muxViz, an open-source package of multilayer algorithms with interactive visualization, demonstrated on genetic, neuronal, and transportation networks.
ocar.resolution: The software is shown on a C. elegans connectome and on Herpes simplex and HIV-1 genetic-interaction networks, including centrality and other diagnostics (eigenvector centrality is omitted on a DAG layer). Code is released at github.com/manlius/muxViz.
ocar.future_work: The paper is a methods/software demonstration; new biological discoveries are not the claim.

plain_language_summary: Some networks have more than one kind of link between the same players, like different synapse types. This paper releases muxViz, a free tool to analyze and draw those multilayer maps, including a worm nervous-system example.

authors: A. Jorstad; B. Nigro; C. Calì; M. Wawrzyniak; P. Fua; G. Knott

title: The Budapest Reference Connectome Server v2.0.
authors: B. Szalkai; Csaba Kerepesi; Bálint Varga; V. Grolmusz

ocar.opportunity: Individual human MRI connectomes differ, but edges that recur across many subjects could serve as a lower-noise reference graph of the cortex.
ocar.challenge: There is no single ‘graph of the brain,’ so users need a parameterized way to keep only consensus edges and to download anatomically labeled graphs.

ocar.future_work: The consensus graphs are offered as reduced-error references; how they compare to later HCP releases is outside this extract.

title: The Stimulus Selectivity and Connectivity of Layer Six Principal Cells Reveals Cortical Microcircuits Underlying Visual Processing
authors: Mateo Vélez‐Fort; Charly V. Rousseau; C. J. Niedworok; Ian R. Wickersham; E. Rancz; A. P. Brown; M. Strom; T. Margrie

ocar.opportunity: Layer 6 in visual cortex sends both cortico-cortical and cortico-thalamic signals; knowing each cell class’s stimulus tuning and who synapses onto it would explain how context and feature information are routed.
ocar.challenge: L6 principal cells are diverse, and bulk recordings cannot assign sensory selectivity or long-range inputs to identified CC versus CT projection neurons.
ocar.action: Vélez-Fort, Rousseau, Niedworok, Wickersham, Rancz, Brown, Strom, and Margrie, in Neuron (2014), combine whole-cell recording from identified L6 cells in anesthetized adult C57BL/6 mouse V1 with modified rabies monosynaptic input mapping.
ocar.resolution: CC-projecting cells span a broad orientation-selectivity spectrum and are innervated mainly by deep-layer V1 neurons. CT-projecting cells are ultrasparse-firing, sharply tuned for orientation and direction, and receive long-range input from higher cortical areas. The authors interpret this as segregated microcircuits for contextual versus stimulus-specific feedback, including possible stimulus-specific thalamic gain control.
ocar.future_work: Presynaptic functional identity was not recorded, so intra- versus interlaminar contributions to subthreshold tuning remain to be established, as do possible CC subclasses.

plain_language_summary: Deep in mouse visual cortex, two kinds of output cells do different jobs. One talks mostly to other cortical cells and is loosely tuned; the other talks to thalamus, fires very rarely, and is extremely picky about orientation and direction.

summaries.beginner: Deep in mouse visual cortex, two kinds of output cells do different jobs. One talks mostly to other cortical cells and is loosely tuned; the other talks to thalamus, fires very rarely, and is extremely picky about orientation and direction.
summaries.intermediate: Vélez-Fort et al. (Neuron, 2014) record identified layer-6 principal cells in mouse V1 and map monosynaptic inputs with modified rabies. Cortico-cortical cells show a broad range of orientation selectivity and predominantly local deep-layer innervation. Cortico-thalamic cells fire extremely sparsely, are exquisitely orientation- and direction-tuned, and receive long-range higher-area input. Discussion links CT axons to dLGN and TRN as a possible stimulus-specific thalamic gain-control signal, and to modulation of layers 5–6 and upper layers via polysynaptic routes.
summaries.advanced: Animals are anesthetized 5–8-week C57BL/6 mice (fentanyl/midazolam/medetomidine). ‘Ultrasparse’ is qualitative in the extract. Functional identity of rabies-labeled presynaptic cells is not measured. Open-access Neuron PDF (© 2014 The Authors).

title: Wiring patterns in the mouse retina: collecting evidence across the connectome, physiology and light microscopy
authors: Felice A. Dunn; R. Wong

ocar.opportunity: The retina is the first stage of vision and a proving ground for whether parallel channels are exclusive microcircuits or unique combinations of shared parts.

ocar.action: Dunn and Wong, in Journal of Physiology (2014), review mouse retinal wiring, diagramming current knowledge and open puzzles and urging multi-method verification.
ocar.resolution: They argue that parallel channels more likely emerge from unique combinations of microcircuits than from exclusive pathways, and they collect structural and functional evidence across serial EM, electrophysiology, and light microscopy for the mouse retina.
ocar.future_work: The review’s stated need is to test proposed connectivity with more than one method so that circuits are verified both structurally and functionally.

plain_language_summary: The eye’s retina was thought to send visual features down separate private cables. This review of the mouse retina says the channels share parts, and that electron microscopy, physiology, and light microscopy must be combined before we trust a wiring diagram.

summaries.beginner: The eye’s retina was thought to send visual features down separate private cables. This review of the mouse retina says the channels share parts, and that electron microscopy, physiology, and light microscopy must be combined before we trust a wiring diagram.

title: Large-scale network organization in the avian forebrain: a connectivity matrix and theoretical analysis
authors: M. Shanahan; V. Bingman; Toru Shimizu; Martin Wild; O. Güntürkün

ocar.opportunity: Birds can match some ape-level cognitive feats despite a nucleated, non-laminar telencephalon. A large-scale wiring diagram would test whether avian and mammalian brains share organizational principles after ~300 million years of separate evolution.
ocar.challenge: Macro-scale connectivity matrices existed for humans and macaques but not for a bird, so graph comparisons were unavailable.
ocar.action: Shanahan, Bingman, Shimizu, Wild, and Güntürkün, in Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience (2013), assemble the first large-scale pigeon forebrain connectivity matrix and analyze it with graph theory.
ocar.resolution: The pigeon telencephalon is reported as a modular small-world network with a connective core of hubs that includes prefrontal-like and hippocampal structures, plus disassortativity and characteristic motifs. Top-level modules are described as functionally analogous to human ones but more anatomically distributed. Hub membership is supported by betweenness, degree, k-core, rich-club, and knotty-centrality analyses.
ocar.future_work: Implications of disassortativity for robustness are flagged as unresolved; the matrix is a literature-collated wiring diagram, not a new tracer census.

plain_language_summary: Bird brains look different from ours—they are built of clumps, not layers—yet some birds are strikingly smart. A wiring diagram of the pigeon forebrain is reported to follow the same high-level network rules as mammal brains: modules, short paths, and a core of hub regions.

title: A tutorial in connectome analysis: Topological and spatial features of brain networks
authors: Marcus Kaiser

ocar.opportunity: As high-throughput connectomes arrive, newcomers need a map of which graph and spatial statistics are meaningful at regional and neuronal scales.
ocar.challenge: Metrics at node, module, and whole-network scales are easy to misapply, and spatial wiring-length constraints are often ignored when only topology is reported.
ocar.action: Kaiser, in NeuroImage (2011), writes a tutorial on topological and spatial connectome analysis from microscopic neuron graphs to macroscopic region graphs.

title: OsO2 as the Contrast‐Generating Chemical Species of Osmium‐Stained Biological Tissues in Electron Microscopy

ocar.future_work: The abstract presents this assignment as an opening for improved high-contrast staining protocols.

title: Perineuronal Net Microscopy: From Brain Pathology to Artificial Intelligence
authors: M. Paveliev; Anton A Egorchev; Foat Musin; N. Lipachev; A. Melnikova; Rustem M. Gimadutdinov; Aidar R. Kashipov; Dmitry Molotkov; Dmitry E. Chickrin; Albert V. Aganov

ocar.opportunity: Perineuronal nets (PNNs) encapsulate synapses on many CNS neurons and change in schizophrenia, epilepsy, Alzheimer’s disease, stroke, and trauma. High-resolution microscopy plus AI could relate mesh microstructure to synapses and disease.
ocar.challenge: The functional meaning of PNN microstructure had been understudied, and tracing mesh units around boutons is laborious.
ocar.action: Paveliev and colleagues, in International Journal of Molecular Sciences (2024), review PNN microstructural changes in brain disorders, high-resolution studies of mesh units around synaptic boutons, PNNs as drug targets, and they report a machine-learning-assisted tool for PNN mesh contour tracing.
ocar.resolution: The review links PNN alterations to several pathologies, discusses ECM–synapse mutual regulation at mesh resolution, updates pharmacological targeting, and presents an ML-assisted contour tracer as a first AI-assisted PNN microscopy step matching the multi-scale complexity of PNN biology.
ocar.future_work: Broader AI models that span synapse to whole-brain PNN organization are proposed rather than demonstrated as a finished connectome tool.

plain_language_summary: Many brain cells wear a lattice of sugars and proteins, a perineuronal net, around their synapses. This review explains how that lattice looks under the microscope in disease, and it introduces a machine-learning helper for tracing the lattice’s outlines.

title: Synaptic connectome of a neurosecretory network in the Drosophila brain
authors: Theresa H. McKim; Jayati Gera; Ariana J. Gayban; Kevin W. Christie; Joel Shin; Nils Reinhard; Giulia Manoli; Selina Hilpert; Patrick Callaerts; Floris van Breugel; Charlotte Helfrich-Förster; Meet Zandawala

ocar.opportunity: Hormones from brain neurosecretory cells (NSC) coordinate sleep, feeding, growth, metabolism, and reproduction. A synaptic connectome of those cells would show how sensory and descending systems regulate endocrine output.
ocar.challenge: NSC dendrites sit in the subesophageal zone, yet it was unclear whether peripheral gustatory neurons synapse on them directly, and NSC synaptic outputs looked sparse relative to their physiological reach.
ocar.action: McKim, Gera, Gayban, Christie, Shin, Reinhard, Manoli, Hilpert, Callaerts, van Breugel, Helfrich-Förster, and Zandawala, on bioRxiv (2024; FlyWire v783), reconstruct the synaptic connectome of adult Drosophila pars intercerebralis/pars lateralis NSC classes, with dynamical modeling and functional tests of corazonin NSC and DNg27.
ocar.resolution: Diuretic hormone 44 NSC emerge as a major integrative hub. Gustatory inputs to NSC are largely indirect despite SEZ dendrites; diverse olfactory paths are mapped. Linear dynamical modeling ranks enteric neurons as the strongest influencers of NSC activity among sensory modalities. Descending neurons provide substantial NSC input, suggesting coordinated endocrine and motor output. Synaptic output is sparse and mostly from corazonin NSC; both CRZ NSC and downstream DNg27 influence egg-laying. Paracrine peptide paths are explored via single-cell transcriptomes.
ocar.future_work: The authors offer the map as a platform to disrupt endocrine pathways relevant to diabetes, hypertension, and infertility; those disease links are prospective.

plain_language_summary: Flies, like us, use brain hormones to run the body. This preprint charts who synapses onto the fly’s hormone cells and finds that gut-related neurons are especially influential, while the hormone cells themselves make few conventional synapses—except a corazonin pathway tied to egg-laying.

summaries.beginner: Flies, like us, use brain hormones to run the body. This preprint charts who synapses onto the fly’s hormone cells and finds that gut-related neurons are especially influential, while the hormone cells themselves make few conventional synapses—except a corazonin pathway tied to egg-laying.
summaries.intermediate: McKim et al. (bioRxiv, 2024; updated 2026 in the extract header) analyze the FlyWire v783 synaptic connectome of adult Drosophila neurosecretory cells. DH44 NSC are implicated as a major coordinator. Peripheral taste inputs are largely indirect. Olfactory pathways to NSC are deciphered. Dynamical modeling identifies enteric neurons as the strongest sensory-class influencers. Descending neurons synapse heavily onto NSC. Output synapses are sparse and mostly from corazonin cells; CRZ NSC and DNg27 affect egg-laying (Kir2.1 and optogenetic tests in methods). Transcriptomes address putative paracrine peptide routes.
summaries.advanced: This is a bioRxiv preprint using an existing FlyWire snapshot (v783), not a new EM volume. ‘Strongest influencers’ comes from linear dynamical modeling, not in vivo ranking of all senses. Disease language in the outlook is translational framing. The selected extract’s latter portion is methods (strains, immunohistochemistry).

title: A cerebellar disinhibitory circuit supports synaptic plasticity
authors: Changjoon Park; Jawon Gim; Sang-kyu Bahn; Gyu Hyun Kim; Yoonseok Im; Sang-Hoon Lee; Kisuk Lee; Minsu Kim; Kea Joo Lee; Jinseop S. Kim

ocar.opportunity: Cerebellar learning is thought to require long-term depression at granule-cell to Purkinje-cell synapses when climbing-fibre error signals arrive. A circuit that briefly lifts inhibition at those moments would protect LTD.
ocar.challenge: Inhibitory inputs to Purkinje cells can disrupt LTD, so it was unclear how depression proceeds when interneurons are active in the molecular layer.
ocar.action: Park, Gim, Bahn, Kim, Im, Lee, Lee, Kim, Lee, and Kim, on bioRxiv (2023), analyze synaptic connectivity among neurons reconstructed from serial EM of cerebellar molecular layer and test a computational model of a feedforward disinhibitory motif.
ocar.resolution: They report synapses from climbing fibres onto a subset of inhibitory interneurons (IN1) that synapse onto remaining interneurons (IN2) that in turn inhibit Purkinje cells, redefining interneuron types by connectivity. Together with CF-to-PC synapses this is a feedforward disinhibitory circuit argued to suppress inhibition whenever CF input—and thus LTD—should occur. A model is used to validate the hypothesis.
ocar.future_work: The authors generalize to a principle that disinhibition supports synaptic plasticity; in vivo confirmation of the IN1/IN2 split is implied.

plain_language_summary: The cerebellum learns by weakening some synapses when an error signal arrives, but nearby inhibitory cells can block that weakening. An electron-microscope wiring map suggests the error fibres also turn off those inhibitors at the right moment, giving learning a clear shot.

summaries.beginner: The cerebellum learns by weakening some synapses when an error signal arrives, but nearby inhibitory cells can block that weakening. An electron-microscope wiring map suggests the error fibres also turn off those inhibitors at the right moment, giving learning a clear shot.
summaries.intermediate: Park et al. (bioRxiv, 15 September 2023) reconstruct cerebellar molecular-layer connectivity from serial EM. Climbing fibres synapse onto a subset of inhibitory interneurons (IN1) that inhibit another subset (IN2) that inhibit Purkinje cells, forming a feedforward disinhibitory loop alongside CF-to-PC synapses. Interneuron types are redefined by this connectivity rather than only morphology or molecules. A computational model is used to argue that the motif secures granule-to-Purkinje LTD when CF input arrives. Extended Data compare IN1/IN2 dendrite density, axon complexity, and synapse distances (Mann–Whitney tests).
summaries.advanced: This is a 2023 preprint; the selected extract is front matter plus extended-data figure captions rather than a full discussion. IN1/IN2 labels are connectivity-based in this volume. Extended Data p-values (e.g. axon complexity p=0.023, N=20 vs 6) are fragment/cell samples, not a whole-cerebellum census. Catalog dimension is neuroai; the paper is EM plus a model.

title: Axonal energy metabolism, and the effects in aging and neurodegenerative diseases
authors: Sen Yang; J. Park; Hui-Chen Lu

ocar.opportunity: Human imaging consistently finds glucose hypometabolism in aging and neurodegenerative disease, especially in densely interconnected long-range hubs of the connectome. Understanding axonal bioenergetics could explain early axonopathy.
ocar.challenge: Long-range axons have high metabolic demand and are vulnerable to injury, toxins, proteostatic and lysosomal stress, yet local energy failure as a driver of connectome disintegration is under-synthesized.
ocar.action: Yang, Park, and Lu, in Molecular Neurodegeneration (2023), review axonal energy metabolism across axon initial segments, myelinated segments, and presynaptic arbors, NAD+ homeostasis, and perturbations in aging and NDAs (AD, PD, HD, ALS).
ocar.resolution: They argue that metabolically expensive, long-range axons in topological hubs are innately vulnerable, that local bioenergetic dysregulation can precede frank degeneration, and that NAD+ imbalance, network hyperactivity, and glial pathology can exaggerate deficits in a still-asymptomatic phase. They call for metabolically oriented neuroprotection and for tests of causal links among metabolic vulnerability, axonopathy, amyloid/tau pathology, and cognition.
ocar.future_work: Interventional strategies to normalize bioenergetics in NDA models are encouraged; this article is a review, not a trial.

plain_language_summary: The long cables of the brain are energy-hungry, and in aging and diseases such as Alzheimer’s they often fail first. This review explains how axons make and use fuel, and why the most connected brain regions may be the most metabolically at risk.

summaries.beginner: The long cables of the brain are energy-hungry, and in aging and diseases such as Alzheimer’s they often fail first. This review explains how axons make and use fuel, and why the most connected brain regions may be the most metabolically at risk.
summaries.intermediate: Yang, Park, and Lu (Molecular Neurodegeneration, 2023) review axonal bioenergetics in aging and neurodegenerative diseases. They link human glucose hypometabolism to disintegration of long-range, hub-like connections, then survey energy supply in the axon initial segment, myelinated internodes, and presynaptic boutons, including glial support. A second focus is NAD+ biosynthesis, recycling, and consumption. They argue that innate metabolic vulnerability of the connectome is worsened by NAD+ disruption, hyperactivity, and glia, and they advocate metabolically oriented neuroprotection research.
summaries.advanced: This is a review; disease mechanisms are literature synthesis. The selected extract’s end is abbreviations and declarations (no competing interests; accepted 8 June 2023). Catalog stages (segmentation, graph_analysis) do not describe the paper. Causal chains among metabolism, axonopathy, and proteinopathy are posed as future tests.

title: Development and circuitry of the tunicate larval Motor Ganglion, a putative hindbrain/spinal cord homolog
authors: K. Piekarz; Alberto Stolfi
journal: Journal of Experimental Zoology Part B: Molecular and Developmental Evolution

ocar.opportunity: A complete chordate larval connectome, together with invariant cell lineages, lets motor circuits be studied cell by cell in a vertebrate sister group.
ocar.challenge: Tunicate larvae have only a brief window to swim and settle, and it has been unclear how their small Motor Ganglion relates to vertebrate hindbrain and spinal cord.
ocar.action: Piekarz and Stolfi, in Journal of Experimental Zoology B (catalog year 2023; published form 2024), review development, connectivity, function, and identities of Motor Ganglion neurons, drawing mostly on Ciona.
ocar.resolution: They treat the Motor Ganglion, formerly called visceral or trunk ganglion, as a putative rhombospinal homolog at the base of the tail. In Ciona intestinalis the larval CNS has 177 neurons plus about 50 peripheral sensory cells; the Motor Ganglion core is a network of 7–8 bilateral pairs. The review argues that this cellular simplicity plus the first complete chordate connectome makes the ganglion a model for how chordate central pattern generators are assembled.
ocar.future_work: The conclusion asks how those CPGs generate rhythmic swimming and how the circuits are set up within a chordate developmental program; the article reports no original data.

plain_language_summary: A sea-squirt larva swims with a tiny cluster of motor neurons at the base of its tail. This review explains how that cluster develops and is wired, and why it may be a miniature version of the vertebrate hindbrain and spinal cord.

summaries.beginner: A sea-squirt larva swims with a tiny cluster of motor neurons at the base of its tail. This review explains how that cluster develops and is wired, and why it may be a miniature version of the vertebrate hindbrain and spinal cord.

title: Gap junctions desynchronize a neural circuit to stabilize insect flight
authors: S. Hürkey; N. Niemeyer; Jan-Hendrik Schleimer; S. Ryglewski; S. Schreiber; C. Duch

ocar.opportunity: Asynchronous insect flight is used by more than 600,000 species, yet the central-pattern-generating circuit that times wing power has been hard to pin down in a miniaturized nervous system.
ocar.challenge: Electrical synapses are classically expected to synchronize coupled neurons, which would not produce the staggered motoneuron firing needed for stable wingbeat power.
ocar.action: Hürkey, Niemeyer, Schleimer, Ryglewski, Schreiber, and Duch, in Nature (2023), combine electrophysiology, optophysiology, Drosophila genetics, and mathematical modelling of the five identified dorsal-longitudinal motoneurons (MN1–5).
ocar.resolution: The CPG is those motoneurons linked by electrical synapses that, contrary to doctrine, splay activity in time rather than synchronizing it. Weak gap junctions plus neuron-intrinsic excitability (including Shab delayed-rectifier current) can desynchronize small networks and convert unpatterned premotor input into a fixed activation sequence. The authors report the mechanism as conserved across multiple species and argue that connectomics must detect electrical synapses, not only chemical ones.
ocar.future_work: The paper frames a wider versatility of electrical synapses in circuit dynamics; how generally the desynchronizing regime applies beyond flight motoneurons is left as an implication rather than a mapped inventory.

plain_language_summary: Flies beat their wings with a tiny motor circuit. This Nature paper shows that the electrical synapses in that circuit do not lock the cells together; they stagger them, which helps keep flight stable.

summaries.beginner: Flies beat their wings with a tiny motor circuit. This Nature paper shows that the electrical synapses in that circuit do not lock the cells together; they stagger them, which helps keep flight stable.
summaries.intermediate: Hürkey, Niemeyer, Schleimer, Ryglewski, Schreiber, and Duch (Nature, 2023) study the Drosophila asynchronous-flight CPG formed by motoneurons MN1–5 of the dorsal longitudinal muscle. Using electrophysiology, optophysiology, genetics, and modelling, they find that electrical synapses among these motoneurons desynchronize rather than synchronize firing. Weak coupling plus specific excitability dynamics, including Shab potassium current, produce stereotyped sequences that stabilize wingbeat power. The authors present this as a generic small-network mechanism conserved across several insect species and as a reason to score gap junctions in connectomes.
summaries.advanced: Open-access Nature article. Extended-data numbers in the extract (Shab ~50% of delayed-rectifier current in MN1–5; RNAi and overexpression replicate counts) are from figure legends, not a single summary statistic for the whole CPG. ‘More than 600,000 species’ is the paper’s stated scope for asynchronous flight. Chemical-synapse maps alone would miss the coupling they study.

title: Hunger- and thirst-sensing neurons modulate a neuroendocrine network to coordinate sugar and water ingestion
authors: Amanda J. González-Segarra; G. Pontes; Nicholas Jourjine; Alexander del Toro; Kristin Scott

ocar.opportunity: Hunger and thirst compete, so a wiring diagram of how internal state is turned into ingestion choices can show how animals prioritize nutrients.
ocar.challenge: Food and water circuits are often studied separately, leaving the downstream path from shared interoceptive neurons unclear.
ocar.action: González-Segarra, Pontes, Jourjine, Del Toro, and Scott, in a June 2023 bioRxiv preprint, use the fly brain connectome plus in vivo manipulations to trace partners of the four Interoceptive Subesophageal zone Neurons (ISNs).
ocar.resolution: ISNs synapse onto a Bilateral T-shaped neuron (BiT) that projects to neuroendocrine centers and, like the ISNs, oppositely regulates sugar versus water ingestion. Downstream peptide cells include insulin-producing cells and CCAP neurons (both bidirectional for sugar versus water) and CCHa2R-RA neurons (water only). The authors conclude that the ingestive decision is implemented by a broad peptidergic network that integrates nutritional state.
ocar.future_work: How this network generalizes beyond the assayed peptides and how it maps onto mammalian hunger–thirst interactions are framed as comparative implications of a preprint.

plain_language_summary: Flies decide whether to drink sugar or water using a few brain cells that sense hunger and thirst. This preprint follows those cells into a hormone-releasing network that pushes the two choices in opposite directions.

summaries.beginner: Flies decide whether to drink sugar or water using a few brain cells that sense hunger and thirst. This preprint follows those cells into a hormone-releasing network that pushes the two choices in opposite directions.

title: Network inference from short, noisy, low time-resolution, partial measurements: Application to C. elegans neuronal calcium dynamics
authors: Amitava Banerjee; Sarthak Chandra; E. Ott
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

ocar.opportunity: If synaptic links could be recovered from calcium time series, functional recordings could be turned into wiring hypotheses even where electron microscopy is unavailable.
ocar.challenge: Real recordings are short, noisy, sparsely sampled, and often miss nodes, so link scores may not split cleanly into true edges versus non-edges.
ocar.action: Banerjee, Chandra, and Ott, in a PNAS inaugural article (2023), compare Granger causality, transfer entropy, and a reservoir-computer method on Lorenz-oscillator networks and on C. elegans neuronal calcium data with known ground-truth connectivity, and they test surrogate data for confidence.
ocar.resolution: On synthetic data the reservoir method improves with shorter sampling interval, longer duration, fuller node coverage, and lower noise. On C. elegans, limitations prevent clean two-group score separation; the authors argue that failure of scores to bimodally separate is itself a diagnostic, and that related simulated networks can be used as confidence-building tests when the true graph is unknown.
ocar.future_work: They present the worm tests as especially relevant to other calcium-imaged systems such as Drosophila and zebrafish, not as a finished inference of the hermaphrodite connectome from calcium alone.

plain_language_summary: Can you guess which neurons are wired together just from how their calcium signals wiggle? This paper tests three guessing methods on worm data and on toy chaotic networks, and shows why messy, short recordings make the job hard.

summaries.beginner: Can you guess which neurons are wired together just from how their calcium signals wiggle? This paper tests three guessing methods on worm data and on toy chaotic networks, and shows why messy, short recordings make the job hard.
summaries.intermediate: Banerjee, Chandra, and Ott (PNAS, 2023) score directed links with Granger causality, transfer entropy, and reservoir computing. They systematically degrade Lorenz-network time series (sampling interval, duration, noise, partial nodes) and apply the same tools to C. elegans calcium fluorescence with known synaptic ground truth. Reservoir inference on the synthetic data tracks experimental quality; C. elegans scores do not cleanly separate links from non-links. Surrogate data are assessed as a route to statistical confidence when ground truth is unavailable.

title: Re-formation of synaptic connectivity in dissociated human stem cell-derived retinal organoid cultures
authors: Allison L. Ludwig; Steven J. Mayerl; Yu Gao; Mark Banghart; Cole Bacig; Maria A. Fernandez Zepeda; Xinyu Zhao; D. Gamm
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

ocar.opportunity: Human stem-cell retinal neurons will only restore vision if they can form new synapses after they are taken out of organoids and placed in a new environment.
ocar.challenge: Intact organoids show calcium signs of synapses, but direct evidence that dissociated cells reconnect had been lacking, and animal xenografts are limited by species differences in synaptic machinery.
ocar.action: Ludwig, Mayerl, Gao, Banghart, Bacig, Fernandez Zepeda, Zhao, and Gamm, in PNAS (2023), apply rabies-virus monosynaptic retrograde tracing to dissociated early human pluripotent stem-cell retinal organoid cultures, with a high-throughput labeling and counting pipeline.
ocar.resolution: Dissociated organoid neurons form de novo connections. Photoreceptors and retinal ganglion cells are the two largest traced presynaptic populations among cell types of therapeutic interest. Tracing demonstrates connectivity plasticity, not mature ribbon-synapse physiology; the authors used a pre-ribbon stage and pseudotyped virus to avoid a known barrier to rabies spread at adult ribbons.
ocar.future_work: They position the assay as a complement to animal grafting and as a platform for future work on later-stage photoreceptors and on enhancing synaptogenesis for cell replacement.

plain_language_summary: Lab-grown human retinal cells only help if they can plug back into a circuit. This study uses a tracing virus to show that after the cells are pulled apart, photoreceptors and ganglion cells do form new synapses.

summaries.beginner: Lab-grown human retinal cells only help if they can plug back into a circuit. This study uses a tracing virus to show that after the cells are pulled apart, photoreceptors and ganglion cells do form new synapses.

title: Regional and cell-type-specific afferent and efferent projections of the mouse claustrum
authors: Quanxin Wang; Yun Wang; Hsien-Chi Kuo; Peng Xie; Xiuli Kuang; Karla E. Hirokawa; M. Naeemi; Shenqin Yao; M. Mallory; Benjamin Ouellette; Phil Lesnar; Yaoyao Li; Min Ye; Chao Chen; Wei Xiong; L. Ahmadinia; Laila El-Hifnawi; Ali Cetin; S. Sorensen; Julie A. Harris; Hongkui Zeng; Christof Koch

ocar.opportunity: A cell-type-resolved wiring diagram of the mouse claustrum would let its proposed roles in attention and cortex-wide coordination be tested at cellular resolution.
ocar.challenge: Claustrum borders in mouse are disputed, and bulk tracing mixes cell types and can contaminate neighboring insular cortex.
ocar.action: Wang, Wang, Kuo, Xie, Kuang, Hirokawa, and colleagues at the Allen Institute, in Cell Reports (2023), combine multimodal references with bulk anterograde/retrograde viral tracing and single-neuron reconstructions registered to CCFv3.
ocar.resolution: They delineate the claustrum as one neuronal group embedded in agranular insular cortex. Prefrontal cortex supplies more projecting cell types than other cortical modules, with layer 5 intratelencephalic neurons predominating. Nine morphological types of claustrum principal neurons innervate functionally linked cortical targets, preferring midline cortex, secondary motor area, and entorhinal cortex.
ocar.future_work: Limitations they list include rabies TVA leak, incomplete transsynaptic coverage, injection-site contamination, registration error, and axons of passage inflating anterograde terminal fields; they urge cross-checks with anterograde, single-cell, and BARseq data.

plain_language_summary: The claustrum is a thin sheet of cells tucked beside cortex and wired to much of the brain. This mouse map shows which cortical cell types talk to it and how its own cells send axons back to matching sets of areas.

summaries.beginner: The claustrum is a thin sheet of cells tucked beside cortex and wired to much of the brain. This mouse map shows which cortical cell types talk to it and how its own cells send axons back to matching sets of areas.

The discussion catalogs viral-tracing and registration artifacts rather than claiming a complete EM connectome.
summaries.advanced: PMC author manuscript. ‘Nine morphological types’ and the prefrontal/L5-IT bias are stated in the summary; the extract does not list per-type synapse counts. This is mesoscale viral tracing plus light-level single-cell morphology, not synaptic EM.

title: Brain-wide analysis of the supraspinal connectome reveals anatomical correlates to functional recovery after spinal injury
authors: Zimei Wang; Adam Romanski; Vatsal Mehra; Yunfang Wang; Matthew Brannigan; B. C. Campbell; G. Petsko; P. Tsoulfas; Murray G. Blackmore

ocar.challenge: Most studies profile a handful of motor command populations and ignore dozens of autonomic and modulatory supraspinal groups.
ocar.action: Wang, Romanski, Mehra, Wang, Brannigan, Campbell, Petsko, Tsoulfas, and Blackmore, in eLife (2022), combine optimized retrograde viral labeling, 3D imaging, and atlas registration in adult mice, and release a web resource.
ocar.resolution: Tens of thousands of supraspinal neurons are assigned to 69 identified regions. The workflow is used to map topographic brain-to-spinal-level relationships, population-specific injury sensitivity, and links between spared regional neurons and variable functional recovery. Nuclear-localized fluorophores and confocal 3D imaging yield higher dual-innervation estimates than some prior reports (examples in the discussion: 8% in cerebellospinal versus prior complete segregation; over 50% in corticospinal versus almost none; more than 40% in gigantocellular versus about 20%).
ocar.future_work: They argue that regenerative and clinical work should include understudied autonomic and postural populations, and they note that dual-innervation rates depend strongly on detection threshold.

plain_language_summary: Many brain regions send axons into the spinal cord, not just the famous motor pathway. This mouse study labels those cells brain-wide after injury and asks which leftover groups go with better recovery.

Editors highlight tissue clearing and viral labeling for spinal-injury research.

title: Differences in the critical dynamics underlying the human and fruit-fly connectome
authors: G. Ódor; G. Deco; Jeffrey Kelling

ocar.opportunity: If brain-wide dynamics sit near criticality, comparing a modular human connectome with a denser fly map can show which graph features create an extended critical regime.
ocar.challenge: Prior human-connectome simulations suggested Griffiths-phase (subcritical, rare-region) criticality driven by heterogeneity; it was unknown whether the fruit-fly central-brain graph would behave the same.
ocar.action: Ódor, Deco, and Kelling, in Physical Review Research (2022), run the Kuramoto synchronization model on the 21,662-node fruit-fly connectome and compare the transition with the KKI-18 human connectome and with random graphs.
ocar.resolution: They describe the fly graph as less heterogeneous, lacking modular structure, and high in topological dimension. Its synchronization transition is mean-field-like: the transition region is wider than in random graphs but much narrower than for KKI-18. They attribute the difference to modularity and dimension.
ocar.future_work: The introduction notes that such numerics do not prove whole-brain criticality and remain inside model assumptions; the fly result is offered as a basis for understanding human critical dynamics, not as a neural recording study.

plain_language_summary: Some theories say brains hover near a tipping point between quiet and fully locked-together activity. This physics paper compares a fly wiring diagram with a human one and finds the fly’s tipping point is sharper.

summaries.beginner: Some theories say brains hover near a tipping point between quiet and fully locked-together activity. This physics paper compares a fly wiring diagram with a human one and finds the fly’s tipping point is sharper.
summaries.intermediate: Ódor, Deco, and Kelling (Physical Review Research, 2022; arXiv title prepends “What makes us humans”) simulate Kuramoto oscillators on a 21,662-node fruit-fly connectome (hemibrain-scale resource cited in the bibliography). Relative to prior KKI-18 human-connectome work, they find a mean-field-like synchronization transition whose width exceeds random graphs but is much smaller than the human case, which they link to weaker modularity and higher topological dimension in the fly graph.
summaries.advanced: Same paper as the catalog record; the PDF title adds a popular prefix. Node count 21,662 is the authors’. This is a dynamical simulation on an anatomical graph, not new EM or physiology. Criticality claims are model-dependent, as the authors state.

title: Glassy phase in dynamically-balanced neuronal networks
authors: Kévin Berlemont; G. Mongillo

ocar.opportunity: Balanced cortical networks are a standard explanation of low, irregular, weakly correlated spiking; a theory that allows realistic connection symmetry could show extra dynamical phases cortex might use for computation.
ocar.challenge: Classic balanced-network theory assumes uncorrelated random connectivity, whereas local cortical wiring includes reciprocal and other symmetric structure.
ocar.action: Berlemont and Mongillo, in a March 2022 bioRxiv preprint, develop a mean-field theory for balanced rate networks whose synapses have an arbitrary symmetry level, find the fixed point, and locate its stability boundary.
ocar.resolution: Above a critical synaptic gain that depends on symmetry, and for positive symmetry, they report a previously unreported phase: many marginally stable fixed points, non-exponential relaxation, and broken ergodicity—a glassy phase. They discuss it as a candidate for cortical dynamical and computational regimes.
ocar.future_work: Relevance to cortex is proposed rather than fit to a particular dataset; Dale’s-law constraints and full spiking networks are noted as theoretical context in the notes.

plain_language_summary: Brain models often assume random wiring that keeps excitation and inhibition in a tight tug-of-war. This theory paper shows that when connections are a bit symmetric, the network can freeze into a glassy landscape of many almost-stable states.

summaries.beginner: Brain models often assume random wiring that keeps excitation and inhibition in a tight tug-of-war. This theory paper shows that when connections are a bit symmetric, the network can freeze into a glassy landscape of many almost-stable states.
summaries.intermediate: Berlemont and Mongillo (bioRxiv, 2022) give a mean-field theory for balanced rate networks with tunable synaptic symmetry (log-normal efficacies; threshold-linear transfer). They locate the balanced fixed point and a symmetry-dependent critical gain. For positive symmetry beyond that gain they describe a glassy phase dominated by marginally stable fixed points, slow relaxation, and broken ergodicity. The extract presents equations and the phase claim; it does not fit in vivo spike statistics quantitatively.
summaries.advanced: Unreviewed preprint. ‘Previously unreported phase’ is the authors’ claim. No connectomic reconstruction is performed. Cortical interpretation is conceptual.

title: PointNeuron: 3D Neuron Reconstruction via Geometry and Topology Learning of Point Clouds
authors: Runkai Zhao; Heng Wang; Chaoyi Zhang; Weidong (Tom) Cai
journal: IEEE Workshop/Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision

ocar.opportunity: Automatic tracing of neurons from 3D light-microscope volumes is needed for morphology and connectomics, but voxel segmentation plus tracing is memory-heavy and sensitive to gaps and background.
ocar.challenge: Convolutional segmentation followed by tracing inherits image noise and disconnected arbors; dense voxels spend compute on empty background.
ocar.action: Zhao, Wang, Zhang, and Cai, in WACV (catalog year 2022; arXiv 2022), introduce PointNeuron: point-cloud graph convolutional networks that predict skeleton points and then their connectivity, writing SWC files, evaluated on the Janelia-Fly subset of BigNeuron.
ocar.resolution: They report competitive reconstruction versus voxel deep-learning baselines, fewer false-positive branches than APP2 in visualizations, about 95.6% lower input memory by dropping background voxels, and a proposed-model F1 of 71.7±17.48 in their ablation table. They suggest the geometry/topology approach may transfer to other 3D medical surfaces.
ocar.future_work: The conclusion positions the method as a pipeline for automatic reconstruction rather than a completed fly-brain connectome.

plain_language_summary: Turning microscope pictures of neurons into stick-figure traces usually means slicing a huge 3D grid. This computer-vision paper treats the neuron as a cloud of points instead, which is lighter and can follow thin branches through gaps.

summaries.beginner: Turning microscope pictures of neurons into stick-figure traces usually means slicing a huge 3D grid. This computer-vision paper treats the neuron as a cloud of points instead, which is lighter and can follow thin branches through gaps.
summaries.intermediate: Zhao, Wang, Zhang, and Cai (WACV / arXiv, 2022) convert 3D neuron image volumes to point clouds, then use one GCN to predict skeleton points and another to predict their links, exporting SWC. On Janelia-Fly (BigNeuron) they report competitive accuracy, reduced false-positive arbors relative to APP2, and a large memory cut versus voxel networks (95.6% less input memory in the extract). Ablations compare loss terms, PointNet++, DGCNN, and downsampling; the proposed setting lists F1 71.7±17.48.
summaries.advanced: Conference/arXiv methods paper, not a biological reconstruction of a whole fly brain. Metrics are on BigNeuron Janelia-Fly; they should be read from the tables, not treated as a universal tracing accuracy. Code link is given as GitHub PointNeuron.

title: Imaging Three-Dimensional Brain Organoid Architecture from Meso- to Nanoscale across Development
authors: J. Rodriguez-Gatica; Vira Iefremova; L. Sokhranyaeva; S. W. Yeung; Y. Breitkreuz; Oliver Bruestle; M. Schwarz; U. Kubitscheck

ocar.opportunity: Human brain organoids contain 3D circuits, but conventional light microscopy cannot jointly capture whole-organoid layout and synaptic-scale contacts.
ocar.challenge: Organoids are millimeter-scale and opaque; high-NA optics have short working distance, and slicing destroys 3D context.
ocar.action: Rodriguez-Gatica, Iefremova, Sokhranyaeva, Yeung, Breitkreuz, Brüstle, Schwarz, and Kubitscheck, in a December 2021 bioRxiv preprint, combine tissue expansion with light-sheet fluorescence microscopy (LSFEM), using CHAPS permeabilization to preserve fluorescent proteins.
ocar.resolution: Expansion of about 1.5- to 4-fold lets them move in one session from mesoscopic views to super-resolution, including mitotic cleavage planes and aligned pre- and postsynaptic proteins. They report imaging organoids up to 15 mm after preparation, following labeled cells for up to 14 months of culture, and effective resolutions they cite as laterally under 100 nm and axially down to 300 nm after 4× expansion. They note batch-to-batch developmental variability and that a 1 mm³ organoid expanded 4× imaged at that sampling would be an enormous (they estimate 340 TB) dataset.
ocar.future_work: They expect LSFEM to support developmental and disease studies; full-organoid synaptic maps at Nyquist sampling remain data-limited.

plain_language_summary: Mini-brains grown from stem cells are too big and cloudy for ordinary microscopes to see both the whole lump and single synapses. This preprint swells the tissue and uses a light-sheet microscope to zoom from the whole organoid down toward synaptic scale.

summaries.beginner: Mini-brains grown from stem cells are too big and cloudy for ordinary microscopes to see both the whole lump and single synapses. This preprint swells the tissue and uses a light-sheet microscope to zoom from the whole organoid down toward synaptic scale.
summaries.intermediate: Rodriguez-Gatica and colleagues (bioRxiv, 2021) combine expansion microscopy with light-sheet imaging of human brain organoids (LSFEM). CHAPS-based clearing/expansion (about 1.5–4×) preserves autofluorescent proteins and antibody stains in large samples (they cite up to 15 mm). They illustrate cleavage-plane geometry and pre/postsynaptic alignment, and they discuss previously reported effective resolutions after 4× expansion (laterally <100 nm, axially ~300 nm). Culture periods up to 14 months and strong batch variability are noted. A back-of-the-envelope 340 TB figure illustrates why whole-organoid Nyquist volumes are impractical.
summaries.advanced: Unreviewed preprint. Expansion factors and resolution figures are those stated in the extract. 340 TB is an illustrative calculation, not a dataset they acquired. Not an EM connectome.

title: Integration of signals from different cortical areas in higher order thalamic neurons
authors: V. Sampathkumar; Andrew J. Miller-Hansen; S. Sherman; N. Kasthuri
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

ocar.opportunity: Higher-order thalamus is a candidate hub for mixing cortical messages on a cortico-thalamo-cortical route, but whether single relay cells actually receive drivers from different cortical areas was untested at synapse resolution.
ocar.challenge: Light-level tracing cannot prove that sensory and motor layer-5 terminals converge on the same thalamic neuron.
ocar.action: Sampathkumar, Miller-Hansen, Sherman, and Kasthuri, in PNAS (2021), dual-label layer 5 of mouse S1 and M1 with ascorbate peroxidase in Rbp4-cre mice and reconstruct synapses in posterior medial nucleus (POm) with serial EM.
ocar.resolution: Nineteen of 33 reconstructed POm cells received convergent S1 and M1 layer-5 input. As a population, labeled layer-5 synapses were larger and more proximal on dendrites than unlabeled synapses. The authors conclude that many of these thalamic neurons integrate disparate cortical signals rather than relaying a single source.
ocar.future_work: They note incomplete labeling and incomplete dendritic reconstructions, so true convergence rates would likely be higher, and they treat driver status of M1→POm as less established than S1→POm.

plain_language_summary: Messages from touch cortex and movement cortex were thought to stay on separate lines through the thalamus. This electron-microscope study finds that many thalamic cells in the mouse actually collect both.

summaries.beginner: Messages from touch cortex and movement cortex were thought to stay on separate lines through the thalamus. This electron-microscope study finds that many thalamic cells in the mouse actually collect both.
summaries.intermediate: Sampathkumar, Miller-Hansen, Sherman, and Kasthuri (PNAS, 2021) combine genetic/viral peroxidase labeling of layer 5 in mouse somatosensory and motor cortex with serial EM in POm. Nineteen of 33 reconstructed relay cells receive both labeled input classes; layer-5 terminals are larger and more proximal than unlabeled synapses. They interpret this as integration in a transthalamic corticocortical path, contrasting with a pure-relay view modeled on LGN. Driver/modulator language is presented as a useful but partly hypothetical framework.
summaries.advanced: Convergence fraction 19/33 is from partial reconstructions and partial labeling; the authors say it is a lower bound. M1 driver identity is explicitly less certain than S1. ‘Connectomics’ here is targeted EM, not a whole-thalamus volume.

title: Petabyte-Scale Multi-Morphometry of Single Neurons for Whole Brains
authors: Shengdian Jiang; Yimin Wang; Lijuan Liu; Sujun Zhao; Mengya Chen; Xuan Zhao; Peng Xie; Liya Ding; Zongcai Ruan; H. Dong; G. Ascoli; M. Hawrylycz; Hongkui Zeng; Hanchuan Peng

title: Small, correlated changes in synaptic connectivity may facilitate rapid motor learning
authors: Barbara Feulner; M. Perich; Raeed H. Chowdhury; L. Miller; J. A. Gallego; C. Clopath

ocar.opportunity: Animals adapt reaches within minutes, and motor-cortex activity changes with them; knowing whether those changes come from local rewiring or from altered inputs would constrain what a connectome can explain about rapid learning.
ocar.challenge: Synaptic weights cannot be measured densely in vivo during adaptation, and preserved neural covariance has been taken as evidence against local connectivity change.
ocar.action: Feulner, Perich, Chowdhury, Miller, Gallego, and Clopath, in Nature Communications (2022), train a modular recurrent network (PMd- and M1-like modules) on visuomotor perturbation tasks, comparing plasticity in inputs (Hinput) versus local recurrent weights (Hlocal).
ocar.resolution: Hinput yields small activity changes and largely preserved covariance, as expected. Hlocal needs only small, correlated weight changes and produces activity and covariance shifts still within experimental range. Larger behavioral remapping (a target–reach reassociation) separates the two. Experimental patterns—larger activity change in PMd than M1—better match Hinput, supporting plasticity upstream of motor cortices for rapid visuomotor adaptation.
ocar.future_work: They suggest designing tasks with bigger behavioral change to distinguish the hypotheses empirically; the model does not measure synapses in animals.

plain_language_summary: When you quickly adjust a reaching movement, motor-cortex activity shifts. This modelling paper asks whether that means the local wires changed, and finds that small, structured weight tweaks—or changes in incoming signals—can both look a lot like the recordings.

summaries.beginner: When you quickly adjust a reaching movement, motor-cortex activity shifts. This modelling paper asks whether that means the local wires changed, and finds that small, structured weight tweaks—or changes in incoming signals—can both look a lot like the recordings.
summaries.intermediate: Feulner et al. (Nature Communications, 2022) use a modular RNN as a qualitative stand-in for primate motor cortex during visuomotor rotation. Learning via input weights (Hinput) preserves covariance; learning via local connectivity (Hlocal) also stays within recorded activity and covariance ranges because successful adaptation uses small, low-dimensional, correlated weight updates. A reassociation task splits the hypotheses more clearly. Matching to data (larger PMd than M1 activity change) favors Hinput for rapid VR adaptation, unlike multi-day skill learning where M1 rewiring is reported.
summaries.advanced: Simulation study; no new connectome or synaptic physiology. ‘Within the range of experimental recordings’ is the authors’ qualitative comparison. Covariance preservation is not proof of frozen synapses.
