title: Synaptic recognition molecules in development and disease
authors: Dhrubajyoti Chowdhury; Katherine E Watters; T. Biederer

ocar.opportunity: Connectomic reconstructions show precise partner choice in dense neuropil; the molecules that implement that choice are the complementary explanation of how those graphs form.
ocar.challenge: Many adhesion systems look similar at the domain level yet act at different times and places, so a single ‘synaptic recognition code’ is easy to oversimplify.
ocar.action: Chowdhury, Watters, and Biederer, in Current Topics in Developmental Biology (2021), review vertebrate synaptic recognition molecules along a developmental sequence: initial wiring, rejection of wrong partners, synapse specification, and removal of inappropriate synapses.
ocar.resolution: They survey cadherins, immunoglobulin-superfamily proteins, Semaphorins/Plexins, leucine-rich-repeat proteins, and neurexins with their binders, plus secreted factors. Recurring themes are cell-type-specific expression, combinatorial action, alternative splicing, and post-translational modification. Laminated structures such as hippocampus and retina are highlighted as advantageous assays; proteomics and single-cell expression are noted as methodological advances. A closing section links aberrant recognition to neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disease.
ocar.future_work: The outlook calls for deeper accounts of how these systems yield the precision and diversity of connections; the chapter is a review, not a new screen.

title: Untangling the cortico-thalamo-cortical loop: cellular pieces of a knotty circuit puzzle
authors: G. Shepherd; Naoki Yamawaki

ocar.action: Shepherd and Yamawaki, in Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2021), review cell-type-specific synaptic connections among major cortical and thalamic neuron types across sensory, motor, and cognitive areas.

title: An efficient analytical reduction of detailed nonlinear neuron models
authors: Oren Amsalem; Guy Eyal; Noa Rogozinski; Michael Gevaert; Pramod S. Kumbhar; F. Schürmann; I. Segev

ocar.opportunity: Realistic neurons with thousands of synapses are needed to interpret micro-connectomes and to build biologically grounded networks, but full compartmental models are too slow.
ocar.challenge: Rall’s equivalent-cylinder collapse does not apply to trees with unequal lengths, conductance-based synapses, or active dendrites.
ocar.action: Amsalem, Eyal, Rogozinski, Gevaert, Kumbhar, Schürmann, and Segev, in Nature Communications (2020), introduce Neuron_Reduce, mapping synapses and active channels onto a reduced cable that preserves transfer impedance to the soma and merging equal-impedance synapses while keeping their activation times.
ocar.resolution: They report 40–250-fold faster simulations for several cell types with 10,000–100,000 synapses, while closely replicating voltage dynamics and specific dendritic computations. Thirteen morphologies are used in the methods extract, with 1,250–10,000 synapses in the accuracy tests described there. The tool is public for NEURON.
ocar.future_work: They present reduced cells as enabling unprecedented network scale, including micro-connectomic circuits and biologically inspired deep nets.

plain_language_summary: Detailed digital neurons are slow to simulate because every twig is a tiny electrical compartment. This method folds the tree into a simpler shape that still behaves like the original at the cell body, so big networks become computable.

summaries.beginner: Detailed digital neurons are slow to simulate because every twig is a tiny electrical compartment. This method folds the tree into a simpler shape that still behaves like the original at the cell body, so big networks become computable.
summaries.intermediate: Amsalem et al. (Nature Communications, 2020) present Neuron_Reduce, an analytical reduction that preserves somatic transfer impedance when placing synapses and active conductances on a simplified morphology, merging synapses that share impedance. Headline speedups are 40–250× for realistic synapse counts (10,000–100,000). Methods in the extract mention 13 cell models and 50-second test simulations. Frequency parameter ω=0 gave best performance in their supplementary tests.
summaries.advanced: Open-access methods paper. Speedup range and synapse counts are the authors’ reported spans, not a single benchmark. Accuracy is relative to the parent compartmental models, not to in vivo voltages. Reduction is not a connectome.

title: Analysis of Synaptic Microcircuits in the Mushroom Bodies of the Honeybee
authors: Claudia Groh; W. Rössler

ocar.opportunity: Honeybee mushroom bodies are large multisensory learning centers whose synaptic microglomeruli visibly remodel with experience, offering a social-insect window onto structural plasticity.
ocar.challenge: Causal links from microglomerular change to specific behaviors remain incomplete, and work is spread across development, sensory exposure, and associative memory.
ocar.action: Groh and Rössler, in Insects (2020), review plasticity of calyx microcircuits, focusing on synapses from sensory projection neurons onto Kenyon cells, and compare honeybee results with other insects.
ocar.resolution: They synthesize evidence that differential brood care, sensory exposure, age-related hive-to-foraging transition, and associative long-term memory all associate with structural change in olfactory and visual calyx compartments, paralleled by physiological changes after learning. Mushroom bodies are framed as recoding high-dimensional sensory input into value-based codes.
ocar.future_work: The review closes on open questions about causal neuron–behavior links and colony-level sociality, and on promising integrative approaches.

plain_language_summary: A honeybee’s learning centers are packed with tiny synaptic knots that change as the bee grows up, leaves the hive, and forms memories. This review gathers what those knots look like and how they rewire.

summaries.beginner: A honeybee’s learning centers are packed with tiny synaptic knots that change as the bee grows up, leaves the hive, and forms memories. This review gathers what those knots look like and how they rewire.
summaries.intermediate: Groh and Rössler (Insects, 2020) review mushroom-body calyx microglomeruli in Apis. They cover projection-neuron to Kenyon-cell synapses in olfactory and visual compartments and relate structural plasticity to brood care, sensory exposure, interior–exterior transition, and associative LTM, alongside physiological retuning after learning. The honeybee is emphasized as a social-behavior model, with comparative notes to other insects. This is a review, not a new EM volume.
summaries.advanced: Open-access review. No single synapse census for the bee MB is given in the extract. Plasticity associations are those reported in the cited literature as summarized here.

title: Determinants of seeding and spreading of α-synuclein pathology in the brain
authors: Martin T. Henrich; Fanni F. Geibl; H. Lakshminarasimhan; Anna Stegmann; B. Giasson; Xiaobo Mao; V. Dawson; Ted M. Dawson; W. Oertel; D. Surmeier

ocar.opportunity: If Parkinson’s Lewy pathology spreads like a trans-synaptic agent, then connectomic maps should predict where injected α-synuclein fibrils go—and where they do not.
ocar.challenge: It is unclear whether uptake is cell-type specific and whether connection strength sets how much pathology appears downstream.
ocar.action: Henrich, Geibl, Lakshminarasimhan, Stegmann, Giasson, Mao, Dawson, Dawson, Oertel, and Surmeier, in Science Advances (2020), inject preformed α-synuclein fibrils into mouse pedunculopontine nucleus and compare resulting pathology with anterograde and retrograde maps, including ChAT-Cre tracing of PPN cholinergics.
ocar.resolution: Within PPN, pathology is robust in Parkinson-vulnerable cholinergic neurons but not neighboring noncholinergic cells. Nearly all neurons that project to those cholinergics show pathology, yet kinetics, amount, and persistence of propagated pathology are unrelated to connection strength. Phenotype governs somatodendritic uptake; the afferent connectome restricts where pathology can go but not how severe it becomes.
ocar.future_work: They argue that connectivity plus other cellular/regional factors together explain clinical Lewy distributions and may suggest control strategies.

plain_language_summary: Parkinson’s protein clumps are thought to hop along brain wiring. In mice, this team seeds the clumps in one brainstem region and finds that cell type decides who takes them up, while the wiring map only loosely predicts how bad the spread looks.

summaries.beginner: Parkinson’s protein clumps are thought to hop along brain wiring. In mice, this team seeds the clumps in one brainstem region and finds that cell type decides who takes them up, while the wiring map only loosely predicts how bad the spread looks.
summaries.intermediate: Henrich et al. (Science Advances, 2020) inject α-synuclein preformed fibrils into mouse PPN and compare phospho-synuclein pathology with viral connectomic maps. Cholinergic PPN neurons, not neighbors, accumulate pathology. Afferent neurons are broadly affected, but magnitude and time course do not track coupling strength. The authors reject connection weight as the sole spreading rule. Methods in the extract include WT and ChAT-Cre mice and biotinylated fibril preparations.
summaries.advanced: Open-access. ‘Nearly all’ afferents is the paper’s wording; the extract does not give a percentage table in the selected text. Mouse PFF seeding is a model of spreading, not a human connectome. Two prior papers arguing strength-dominated spread are cited as the view they challenge.

title: DIP/Dpr interactions and the evolutionary design of specificity in protein families
authors: Alina P. Sergeeva; Phinikoula S. Katsamba; F. Cosmanescu; Joshua J. Brewer; G. Ahlsen; S. Mannepalli; L. Shapiro; B. Honig

ocar.opportunity: Drosophila DIP and Dpr proteins help axons pick synaptic partners; understanding how a shared interface encodes many orthogonal specificities would explain a molecular layer of the fly connectome.
ocar.challenge: Family members are similar in sequence and structure, yet only a few of the many possible DIP–Dpr pairings bind strongly.
ocar.action: Sergeeva, Katsamba, Cosmanescu, Brewer, Ahlsen, Mannepalli, Shapiro, and Honig, in Nature Communications (2020), combine sequence, structure, energy calculations, and SPR affinity measurements across the family.
ocar.resolution: DIPs/Dprs fall into seven specificity subgroups. Binding of each subgroup is controlled by negative constraints—interface residues that block non-cognate pairs—distributed across most of the canonical interface rather than a single specificity patch. Each non-cognate subgroup pair uses a unique constraint set (steric clashes, unsatisfied charges, packing defects). They discuss this as a general evolutionary route to specificity in multi-protein families.
ocar.future_work: Implications for designing or interpreting other recognition families are conceptual; switching specificity in tests required altering at least three constraints in cases they examined.

plain_language_summary: Fly neurons use families of look-alike surface proteins to choose partners. This paper shows that what often matters is not a special ‘on’ switch but many small ‘don’t bind them’ features scattered over the same handshake surface.

summaries.beginner: Fly neurons use families of look-alike surface proteins to choose partners. This paper shows that what often matters is not a special ‘on’ switch but many small ‘don’t bind them’ features scattered over the same handshake surface.
summaries.intermediate: Sergeeva et al. (Nature Communications, 2020) partition Drosophila DIP and Dpr proteins into seven SPR-defined specificity subgroups. Homology models, FoldX, and binding measurements indicate that orthogonal pairing is enforced by negative constraints covering most of the shared Ig interface. Physical origins include charge repulsion, buried unsatisfied charges, and hydrophobic packing defects. Intra-subgroup affinities in the extract are generally described as in the 10 μM range. The work is structural/biophysical, not a circuit reconstruction.
summaries.advanced: Open-access. Seven subgroups and the 10 μM KD remark are the authors’. Catalog pipeline tags include segmentation; this paper is protein biochemistry of recognition molecules used in neuronal targeting.

title: Drifting assemblies for persistent memory: Neuron transitions and unsupervised compensation
authors: Yaroslav Felipe Kalle Kossio; Sven Goedeke; Christian Klos; Raoul-Martin Memmesheimer
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

ocar.opportunity: Memories can last while synapses and which cells fire for a memory turn over; a circuit mechanism that keeps representations consistent without a teacher would reconcile plasticity with persistence.
ocar.challenge: Standard assembly models assume a stable neuron set, yet experiments show spontaneous synaptic change and drifting codes, including in long-term memory areas.
ocar.action: Kossio, Goedeke, Klos, and Memmesheimer, in a September 2020 bioRxiv preprint (catalog venue PNAS), simulate assemblies that exchange neurons because of synaptic turnover and noisy spiking, with STDP plus homeostasis compensating without teaching signals.
ocar.resolution: Assemblies drift completely—no preserved core—yet representational structure, inputs, and outputs stay consistent, supporting persistent memory and simple computations. Interior neurons switch which memory they join; periphery neurons are more stable. The model is used to explain evolving fear-memory representations.
ocar.future_work: They argue memory systems must be understood as complete input–assembly–output loops because parts constantly change.

plain_language_summary: We often picture a memory as a fixed club of neurons. This theory paper says the club’s membership can turn over completely, while unsupervised plasticity keeps the memory itself intact.

summaries.beginner: We often picture a memory as a fixed club of neurons. This theory paper says the club’s membership can turn over completely, while unsupervised plasticity keeps the memory itself intact.
summaries.intermediate: Kossio, Goedeke, Klos, and Memmesheimer (bioRxiv 2020; catalog lists PNAS) propose drifting assemblies: spontaneous remodeling and irregular spiking exchange neurons, while STDP and homeostasis keep assemblies aligned with inputs and readouts without external error. There is no stable core connectivity or invariant cell set. They contrast this with models that preserve a core, retrain, or use feedback, and they link the idea to changing fear-memory engrams. The extract is the preprint text.
summaries.advanced: Preprint extract of work catalogued as PNAS; treat bibliographic venue as the catalog record and the PDF as the bioRxiv version. No new experimental connectome. Drift and compensation are simulation results.

title: Macroscopic gradients of synaptic excitation and inhibition in the neocortex
authors: Xiao-Jing Wang

ocar.opportunity: If cortex is built from a repeated canonical circuit, systematic regional gradients in excitation and inhibition could explain how areas acquire qualitatively different functions.
ocar.challenge: Slice physiology has been dominated by sensory cortex, so differences along the hierarchy have been under-documented and treated as noise.
ocar.action: Wang, in Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2020), reviews experimental and theoretical evidence that synaptic excitation and inhibition vary as macroscopic gradients across neocortex and that those gradients are abnormal in mental illness.
ocar.resolution: Quantitative gradient differences can yield qualitatively new dynamics via bifurcation. He reports an increasing excitation gradient along hierarchy (spine counts, NMDAR-related gene expression) and a shift in inhibition toward more input-controlling SST+/CB+ versus output-controlling PV+ interneurons in higher areas. Gene-expression variation is described as low-dimensional and aligned with T1w/T2w hierarchy.
ocar.future_work: He notes that a multi-area NMDAR excitation gradient still needs direct elucidation, that PV/pyramidal ratios and SST subtypes need fuller mapping, and that gene expression is only an indirect link to function.

plain_language_summary: Every patch of cortex looks a bit like every other, yet they do different jobs. This review argues that excitation and inhibition change smoothly from sensory areas to association areas, and those slopes can flip circuits into new kinds of behavior.

summaries.beginner: Every patch of cortex looks a bit like every other, yet they do different jobs. This review argues that excitation and inhibition change smoothly from sensory areas to association areas, and those slopes can flip circuits into new kinds of behavior.
summaries.intermediate: Xiao-Jing Wang (Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 2020) reviews macroscopic gradients of cortical excitation and inhibition. Canonical minicolumns are the starting motif; area differences are treated as structured, not random. Headline claims in the concluding section are a hierarchy-aligned increase in recurrent/NMDA-related excitation and a rising SST+/CB+ to PV+ inhibitory ratio. Bifurcation is the mathematical bridge from quantitative slopes to qualitative function. Psychiatric disruption of the gradients is discussed.
summaries.advanced: PMC author manuscript of a review. Gradient evidence is synthesized from cited studies; this paper does not report a new connectome. NMDAR gradient ‘remains to be elucidated’ is the author’s own caveat.

title: Rapid mesoscale volumetric imaging of neural activity with synaptic resolution
authors: Rongwen Lu; Yajie Liang; Guanghan Meng; Pengcheng Zhou; K. Svoboda; L. Paninski; Na Ji

ocar.opportunity: Cortical neurons integrate synapses over millimeters and two hemispheres; activity imaging that is both mesoscale and spine-resolving would link dendrites to large circuits in awake mice.
ocar.challenge: Point-scanning two-photon imaging that is fast enough for volumes usually sacrifices either field of view or synaptic resolution.
ocar.action: Lu, Liang, Meng, Zhou, Svoboda, Paninski, and Ji, in Nature Methods (2020), add a Bessel-beam module to a two-photon mesoscope and perform calcium imaging in awake mice.
ocar.resolution: They demonstrate volumetric activity imaging with synaptic resolution over mesoscale fields, including entire dendritic arbors and ensembles in multiple cortical areas across both hemispheres. A density bound in the methods discussion illustrates when Bessel projection remains unambiguous (example: 25,000 somata/mm³ upper bound under stated GCaMP6s assumptions versus 3,402 GABAergic neurons/mm³ in their Fig. 3). Thorlabs licensed related IP from HHMI.
ocar.future_work: Labeling density, sensor kinetics, and Bessel length jointly limit separable structures; the paper is a methods demonstration, not an all-cortex functional connectome.

plain_language_summary: Watching synapses fire across a wide stretch of mouse cortex is usually a choice between zooming in or seeing the big picture. This team shapes the laser into a long thin focus so they can do both, even across two hemispheres.

summaries.beginner: Watching synapses fire across a wide stretch of mouse cortex is usually a choice between zooming in or seeing the big picture. This team shapes the laser into a long thin focus so they can do both, even across two hemispheres.
summaries.intermediate: Lu, Liang, Meng, Zhou, Svoboda, Paninski, and Ji (Nature Methods, 2020) insert a Bessel focus module into a two-photon mesoscope for rapid volumetric calcium imaging at synaptic resolution in awake mice. Applications include full dendritic spans and multi-area, bi-hemispheric ensembles. Automatic ROI detection uses CNMF-E-style code. A labeling-density inequality in the extract sets when only one active structure occupies the projected volume. Mesoscope and Bessel IP were licensed to Thorlabs.
summaries.advanced: PMC author manuscript of a brief methods paper. Density numbers are hypothetical bounds and one reported GABAergic density, not a cortex-wide census. Synaptic resolution refers to optical spines/synapses in fluorescence, not EM.

title: SEQUIN multiscale imaging of mammalian central synapses reveals loss of synaptic connectivity resulting from diffuse traumatic brain injury
authors: A. Sauerbeck; Mihika Gangolli; Sydney J. Reitz; Maverick H. Salyards; Samuel H. Kim; Christopher Hemingway; Maud Gratuze; Tejaswi Makkapati; Martin Kerschensteiner; David M. Holtzman; D. L. Brody; Terrance T. Kummer

ocar.opportunity: Counting and classifying central synapses across mesoscale volumes in animals and archived human tissue would show how injury and neurodegeneration disconnect circuits.
ocar.challenge: Synapses are small and densely packed; many super-resolution workflows are slow, specialized, or require large section arrays.
ocar.action: Sauerbeck, Gangolli, Reitz, Salyards, Kim, Hemingway, Gratuze, Makkapati, Kerschensteiner, Holtzman, Brody, and Kummer, in Neuron (2020), introduce SEQUIN, a super-resolution imaging and analysis workflow for synapse quantification and nanostructural/molecular characterization.
ocar.resolution: SEQUIN identifies delayed cortical synapse loss after diffuse traumatic brain injury. Similar loss appears in three murine Alzheimer-related models, where mesoscale mapping shows regional synaptic vulnerability. The method uses standard histology and exogenous labels, enabling human tissue and archived samples. It does not measure physiology directly but can quantify nanostructural correlates of strength (separation, size).
ocar.future_work: They compare SEQUIN’s niche with EM, array tomography, and STED/SMLM, and suggest pairing with activity reporters such as SynaptoZip or SynTagMA.

plain_language_summary: Synapses are tiny and packed like sand, so counting them in a chunk of brain is hard. This paper offers a practical super-resolution recipe and uses it to show that diffuse head injury, like some Alzheimer models, quietly deletes cortical connections.

summaries.beginner: Synapses are tiny and packed like sand, so counting them in a chunk of brain is hard. This paper offers a practical super-resolution recipe and uses it to show that diffuse head injury, like some Alzheimer models, quietly deletes cortical connections.
summaries.intermediate: Sauerbeck et al. (Neuron, 2020) present SEQUIN for rapid super-resolution synapse counts in animal and human tissue without large histological arrays. They report delayed cortical synapse loss after diffuse TBI and comparable loss with regional vulnerability in three mouse Alzheimer-related models. Discussion places SEQUIN as accessible and artifact-resistant relative to more specialized modalities; EM remains superior for ultrastructure, array tomography for multiplexing. Holtzman disclosures are listed in the extract.
summaries.advanced: PMC author manuscript. The extract’s summary does not give a single percent-loss figure. ‘Three murine models’ is the paper’s phrasing. SEQUIN infers synapses from labeled puncta geometry, not from EM.

title: Ubiquitin-dependent regulation of a conserved DMRT protein controls sexually dimorphic synaptic connectivity and behavior
authors: Emily A. Bayer; Rebecca C Stecky; Lauren A. Neal; Phinikoula S. Katsamba; G. Ahlsen; Vishnu Balaji; T. Hoppe; L. Shapiro; Meital Oren-Suissa; O. Hobert

ocar.opportunity: Sex differences in synapse maps of shared neuron classes would show how the same connectome template is edited for sex-specific behavior.
ocar.challenge: How a conserved DMRT transcription factor could act only in one sex in shared neurons was unknown.
ocar.action: Bayer, Stecky, Neal, Katsamba, Ahlsen, Balaji, Hoppe, Shapiro, Oren-Suissa, and Hobert, in eLife (2020), study C. elegans dmd-4 in sex-shared phasmid sensory neurons.
ocar.resolution: dmd-4 is expressed in two phasmid classes in hermaphrodites, not males, and promotes hermaphrodite-specific synaptic connectivity and function. Sex specificity is posttranslational: ubiquitin binding to the conserved DMA domain stabilizes the protein in a sex-specific way. A human DMRT homolog is reported to be controlled similarly, suggesting broader relevance.
ocar.future_work: The discussion places DMRTs as a rare shared sexual-differentiation family across animals and contrasts dmd-4’s ubiquitin/DMA logic with transcriptional sex-specificity of other worm DMRTs such as mab-3 and dmd-3.

plain_language_summary: Male and female worms share many of the same neurons but wire some of them differently. This paper finds a switch protein that is kept stable only in hermaphrodites, and that stability is enough to build the female-like connections.

summaries.beginner: Male and female worms share many of the same neurons but wire some of them differently. This paper finds a switch protein that is kept stable only in hermaphrodites, and that stability is enough to build the female-like connections.
summaries.intermediate: Bayer et al. (eLife, 2020) show that the DMRT gene dmd-4 is expressed in two classes of sex-shared C. elegans phasmid neurons in hermaphrodites only, where it supports sex-specific synapses and function. Regulation is via sex-specific protein stability through ubiquitin engagement of the DMA domain, not solely transcriptional on/off. They report analogous control of a human DMRT homolog. The study links molecular sex determination to dimorphic connectivity in an otherwise shared nervous system.

title: Correlated states in balanced neuronal networks.
authors: Cody Baker; Christopher Ebsch; I. Lampl; R. Rosenbaum

ocar.opportunity: Relating spike-train correlations to synaptic wiring is central to interpreting population recordings and connectomes together.
ocar.challenge: Balanced-network theory of the asynchronous state assumed uncorrelated feedforward input; real upstream spike trains are often correlated.
ocar.action: Baker, Ebsch, Lampl, and Rosenbaum, in Physical Review E (2019), as described in the catalog abstract, analyze balanced networks that receive correlated feedforward spike trains.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports that correlated feedforward input produces much larger downstream correlations than the classical asynchronous state, yielding a ‘correlated state’ with tight excitatory–inhibitory balance consistent with in vivo cortex. Earlier work is summarized as showing very weak average correlations that can still hide some strong pairs when feedforward input is uncorrelated.
ocar.future_work: Extensions beyond the abstract’s scope are not specified here.

plain_language_summary: Brain models often assume incoming spike trains are independent, which keeps cortical cells nearly uncorrelated. This theory paper, summarized from the catalog abstract, says that if those inputs are themselves correlated, the whole network enters a much more correlated state.

summaries.beginner: Brain models often assume incoming spike trains are independent, which keeps cortical cells nearly uncorrelated. This theory paper, summarized from the catalog abstract, says that if those inputs are themselves correlated, the whole network enters a much more correlated state.
summaries.intermediate: Baker, Ebsch, Lampl, and Rosenbaum (Physical Review E, 2019) study balanced networks with correlated feedforward input. According to the catalog abstract, that input drives a correlated state with larger spike-train correlations and a tight E–I balance matching in vivo observations, unlike the weakly correlated asynchronous state obtained with uncorrelated feedforward spikes. title: Expansion Microscopy of Lipid Membranes
authors: Emmanouil D. Karagiannis; Jeong Seuk Kang; T. Shin; Amauche Emenari; Shoh M. Asano; Leanne Lin; Emma K. Costa; A. Marblestone; N. Kasthuri; E. Boyden

ocar.opportunity: Lipid membranes define organelles and neurites, but expansion microscopy had lacked a validated lipid tag, limiting optical nanoscale views of membranes relevant to connectomics.
ocar.challenge: Standard ExM visualizes proteins and nucleic acids; lipids need a gel-anchorable stain, and protease digestion destroys epitopes needed for protein–lipid overlays.
ocar.action: Karagiannis, Kang, Shin, Emenari, Asano, Lin, Costa, Marblestone, Kasthuri, and Boyden, in a November 2019 bioRxiv preprint, introduce a chemical membrane tag and membrane expansion microscopy (mExM) with post-expansion antibody labeling after heat/detergent homogenization instead of proteinase K.
ocar.resolution: They image protein–lipid relationships in ER (calnexin), Golgi (giantin), mitochondria (Tom20), nuclear envelope (NUP98), and myelin (MBP), with lipid and antibody signals colocalized. The protocol is proposed for cell–cell interactions, intracellular transport, and neural connectomics. Expansion after antibody buffer is about 2× before full ~4.5× water expansion.
ocar.future_work: Utility for connectomics is prospective; the extract focuses on organelle membranes and myelin rather than a dense synaptic map.

plain_language_summary: Expansion microscopy usually lights up proteins or DNA, not the fatty membranes of cells. This preprint adds a membrane stain and a gentler expansion recipe so lipids and proteins can be seen together at nanoscale with a light microscope.

summaries.beginner: Expansion microscopy usually lights up proteins or DNA, not the fatty membranes of cells. This preprint adds a membrane stain and a gentler expansion recipe so lipids and proteins can be seen together at nanoscale with a light microscope.
summaries.intermediate: Karagiannis, Kang, and colleagues (bioRxiv, 2019) describe mExM: a lipid-optimized expansion protocol using a gel-compatible membrane tag (pGk5b in the extract) and post-expansion antibodies after SDS/DTT heat homogenization rather than proteinase K. They show colocalization with organelle membrane proteins (ER, Golgi, mitochondria, nuclear membrane) and myelin basic protein. Linear expansion is the usual ExM ~4.5× after water, with ~2× in antibody buffer. Kasthuri and Boyden are among the authors; connectomic use is listed as a motivation.

title: Impact of higher order network structure on emergent cortical activity
authors: Max Nolte; Eyal Gal; H. Markram; Michael W. Reimann

ocar.opportunity: Neocortical microconnectomes contain both pairwise (first-order) statistics and higher-order motifs such as cliques; isolating their dynamical effects would show what morphological diversity buys a circuit.
ocar.challenge: First- and higher-order structure usually covary, so their impact on activity is confounded.
ocar.action: Nolte, Gal, Markram, and Reimann, in Network Neuroscience (2020; catalog year 2019), compare the Blue Brain NMC microcircuit with a ‘cloud-model’ control that keeps first-order connectivity (including distance dependence and m-type strengths) but derives excitatory connections from average morphologies, reducing common-neighbor bias.
ocar.resolution: Morphological diversity within types yields more heterogeneous degrees, more directed cliques, small-world topology, and hub neurons—features weakened in the cloud-model. Spontaneous and evoked dynamics look similar at first glance, but spike counts follow in-degree, population responses become more excitatory and less reliable, and the hierarchical dependence of pairwise correlations on clique position is weaker without higher-order structure.
ocar.future_work: They conclude that models matched on first-order statistics can still differ drastically in higher-order structure and in nuanced activity statistics.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram is more than who connects to whom on average; clumps of all-to-all connected cells also matter. This modelling study keeps the simple connection rules the same but removes those clumps, and some firing patterns change.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram is more than who connects to whom on average; clumps of all-to-all connected cells also matter. This modelling study keeps the simple connection rules the same but removes those clumps, and some firing patterns change.
summaries.intermediate: Nolte, Gal, Markram, and Reimann (Network Neuroscience, 2020) contrast the neocortical microcircuit (NMC) model with a cloud-model that preserves pairwise connection statistics while flattening morphological diversity. Higher-order features (cliques, hubs, small-worldness, heterogeneous degrees) drop in the control. Average activity remains similar, but correlation structure tied to directed simplices weakens. The study is in silico on reconstructed morphologies, not a new EM volume.
summaries.advanced: Published Network Neuroscience article (DOI netn_a_00124); catalog lists bioRxiv/2019. ‘Drastically different higher-order structure’ is the authors’ phrasing. No new experimental recordings.

title: Methods for analysis of brain connectivity: An IFCN-sponsored review.
authors: P. Rossini; R. Iorio; M. Bentivoglio; G. Bertini; F. Ferreri; C. Gerloff; R. Ilmoniemi; R. Ilmoniemi; F. Miraglia; M. Nitsche; F. Pestilli; M. Rosanova; Y. Shirota; C. Tesoriero; Y. Ugawa; F. Vecchio; Ulf Ziemann; Mark Hallett

ocar.opportunity: A classified human brain connectome that combines anatomy with neurophysiology would help relate structure to function and to clinical mapping.
ocar.challenge: Many connectivity methods exist across EEG/MEG stimulation, imaging, and graph theory, and they are not automatically commensurate.

title: Microstructure-Informed Connectomics: Enriching Large-Scale Descriptions of Healthy and Diseased Brains
authors: S. Larivière; Reinder Vos de Wael; C. Paquola; Seokjun Hong; B. Mišić; N. Bernasconi; A. Bernasconi; L. Bonilha; B. Bernhardt

ocar.opportunity: Macroscale structural and functional connectomes now describe healthy organization, individual differences, and lifespan change, and they are being recruited to conceptualize brain disorders.
ocar.challenge: A shift toward high-level network models can sideline regional microstructure, local circuits, and non-imaging cellular, genetic, or chemical properties that actually constitute nodes and edges.
ocar.action: Larivière, Vos de Wael, Paquola, Hong, Mišić, Bernasconi, Bernasconi, Bonilha, and Bernhardt, in Brain Connectivity (2019), review how MRI tissue-microstructure markers, local function, and extra-imaging data can be integrated with large-scale connectome models.
ocar.resolution: They argue that enriching nodes and edges this way clarifies connection strength and better specifies the substrate of disorders in which local anomalies interact with network perturbations, including stroke, autism, and drug-resistant epilepsies. Conclusions highlight multivariate methods (canonical correlation, partial least squares) and connectome-informed in silico models of lesion consequences.
ocar.future_work: The piece is a program for microstructure-informed pathoconnectomics rather than a new reconstruction; prognostic use of lesion-effect models is cited as promising, not demonstrated here.

plain_language_summary: Whole-brain wiring maps are useful, but they often treat regions as simple dots. This review argues that adding tissue texture and local cell biology to those maps would better explain healthy brains and diseases such as epilepsy, stroke, and autism.

summaries.beginner: Whole-brain wiring maps are useful, but they often treat regions as simple dots. This review argues that adding tissue texture and local cell biology to those maps would better explain healthy brains and diseases such as epilepsy, stroke, and autism.
summaries.intermediate: Larivière and colleagues (Brain Connectivity, 2019) review human MRI connectomics alongside meso- and microscale features: tissue-microstructure markers, local function, and cellular, genetic, or chemical data. Integrating those measures is presented as a way to define nodes and edge weights more realistically and to capture how focal anomalies interact with network-level change in stroke, autism, and drug-resistant epilepsy. The conclusions point to canonical correlation and partial least squares as formalisms for linking structural, functional, microstructural, and behavioral spaces, and to connectome-informed dynamical models as tools for lesion prognosis.
summaries.advanced: This is a narrative review, not an empirical connectome. Disease examples are illustrative. The selected extract’s conclusions run into acknowledgments, so multivariate and in silico claims are those stated there rather than a full methods comparison. No new numeric network statistics are reported.

title: Molecular basis of synaptic specificity by immunoglobulin superfamily receptors in Drosophila
authors: Shouqiang Cheng; J. Ashley; J. D. Kurleto; Meike Lobb-Rabe; Y. J. Park; Robert A. Carrillo; E. Özkan

ocar.opportunity: Stereotyped fly circuits are thought to be wired by cell-surface identity proteins. Two immunoglobulin superfamily groups, Dprs and DIPs, are strong candidates for synapse targeting.
ocar.challenge: How Dpr–DIP binding specificity is encoded in structure, and whether those interfaces can be engineered to probe particular circuits, was unknown.
ocar.action: Cheng, Ashley, Kurleto, Lobb-Rabe, Park, Carrillo, and Özkan, in eLife (2019), determine five crystal structures of Dpr–DIP and DIP–DIP complexes and use structure-guided mutations to retune specificity and affinity, testing engineered Dpr10 and DIP-α in the Drosophila neuromuscular circuit.
ocar.resolution: The structures show how gene duplication diversified recognition: distant duplications created specialized subclasses, whereas recent duplications largely yielded redundant interactions. Engineered receptors with novel specificities or modified affinities can be used to study circuits that require Dpr–DIP interactions, and both homophilic and heterophilic binding contribute to neuromuscular wiring.
ocar.future_work: The discussion calls for a comprehensive arthropod Dpr/DIP census to test whether receptor family expansion tracks neural-network complexity, and for matching connectomic and transcriptomic maps to accurate protein-interaction and structural data.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly neurons use matching surface proteins to choose synaptic partners. This team solves several of those protein structures and redesigns them to show how the matches help wire a muscle circuit.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly neurons use matching surface proteins to choose synaptic partners. This team solves several of those protein structures and redesigns them to show how the matches help wire a muscle circuit.
summaries.intermediate: Cheng and colleagues (eLife, 2019) report five crystal structures of Drosophila Dpr–DIP and DIP–DIP complexes and use them to engineer receptors with new specificities or affinities. They test engineered Dpr10 and DIP-α in the neuromuscular circuit and find roles for both homophilic and heterophilic binding. The discussion frames Dprs/DIPs as an arthropod-expanded toolkit whose older duplications specialized interactions while newer ones remain mostly redundant.
summaries.advanced: Five complexes are solved, not the full 21×11 Dpr–DIP matrix. Functional tests in this extract focus on one engineered pair in the neuromuscular system. Evolutionary claims about network complexity versus gene number are speculative. Connectomic matching is positioned as a future opportunity, not a result of this paper.

title: Neural mechanisms of contextual modulation in the retinal direction selective circuit
authors: Xiaolin Huang; M. Rangel; K. Briggman; Wei Wei

ocar.opportunity: On–Off direction-selective ganglion cells (DSGCs) are a classic motion encoder, but their responses are also shaped by surrounding motion context.
ocar.challenge: The synaptic mechanisms of that contextual modulation, and whether On and Off pathways use the same motifs, were unknown.
ocar.action: Huang, Rangel, Briggman, and Wei, in Nature Communications (2019), combine synapse-specific genetics, patch clamp, and connectomic analysis in the mammalian retina to trace circuits that modulate posterior-preferring DSGCs (pDSGCs).
ocar.resolution: pDSGCs are sensitive to discontinuities of moving contours via contextually modulated cholinergic excitation from starburst amacrine cells. Distinct motifs upstream of On versus Off starbursts are required for bright versus dark contrasts. Wide-field amacrine cells with straight, unbranching dendrites act as “continuity detectors” of moving contours, extending DSGC encoding beyond direction selectivity.
ocar.future_work: The selected extract’s discussion is not captured (the tail is the reference list), so remaining experimental caveats and quantitative effect sizes should be read in the full paper.

plain_language_summary: Some retinal cells that report motion direction also notice whether a moving edge is continuous or broken. This study finds separate inner-retina circuits for bright and dark edges that create that extra sensitivity.

summaries.beginner: Some retinal cells that report motion direction also notice whether a moving edge is continuous or broken. This study finds separate inner-retina circuits for bright and dark edges that create that extra sensitivity.
summaries.intermediate: Huang, Rangel, Briggman, and Wei (Nature Communications, 2019) show that posterior-preferring On–Off DSGCs are modulated by motion context through cholinergic excitation from starburst amacrine cells. Synapse-specific genetics, electrophysiology, and connectomics identify distinct upstream motifs for On versus Off pathways and a class of wide-field amacrine cells with unbranching dendrites that detect contour continuity. Divergent On/Off motifs therefore add discontinuity encoding on top of direction selectivity.
summaries.advanced: The extract’s discussion was not captured (tail is references and license text), so circuit claims follow the abstract and introduction. Species is mammalian retina (mouse methods are implied by the author list and typical DSGC genetics, but not named in the selected front matter). No numeric synapse counts or reconstruction volumes appear in the extract. Briggman’s role indicates EM connectomics, but volume size is not stated here.

title: A macaque connectome for large-scale network simulations in TheVirtualBrain
authors: K. Shen; G. Bezgin; S. Everling; A. Mcintosh

ocar.opportunity: Whole-brain simulators such as TheVirtualBrain need anatomically constrained connectomes; macaques can supply multi-scale data that rodents and humans do not jointly provide.
ocar.challenge: Existing tracer resources are incomplete or only categorically weighted, and diffusion tractography has well-known biases, so a usable macaque cortex-wide connectome for simulation is nontrivial to assemble.
ocar.action: Shen, Bezgin, Schirner, Ritter, Everling, and McIntosh, in Scientific Data (2019; catalog year 2018), combine axonal tract-tracing with macaque diffusion tractography to build a macaque (Macaca mulatta and M. fascicularis) connectome for whole-cortex TVB simulations, then simulate resting-state BOLD and fit it to empirical fMRI.
ocar.resolution: Best-fit simulated functional connectivity used G = 0.298 and sigma = 0.0255, with cosine similarity 0.75 versus empirical grand-average FC (greater than null networks, p < 0.001). PCA of simulated BOLD recovered frontal, superior-temporal/auditory, and visual networks. Individual-animal cosine similarities were 0.47–0.80 and were not significantly different when using each animal’s own connectome versus the canonical one (paired t-test p = 0.35); individual specificity instead appeared in biophysical parameters.
ocar.future_work: The extract flags limitations of probabilistic tractography. Canonical versus individual connectomes captured similar FC fits, so subject-specific structure is not shown to be required for this resting-state use case.

plain_language_summary: This team builds a macaque brain wiring map for a whole-brain simulator and shows that the simulated resting activity resembles real fMRI, including familiar frontal, auditory, and visual networks.

summaries.beginner: This team builds a macaque brain wiring map for a whole-brain simulator and shows that the simulated resting activity resembles real fMRI, including familiar frontal, auditory, and visual networks.
summaries.intermediate: Shen and colleagues (Scientific Data, 2019) construct a macaque cortical connectome for TheVirtualBrain by enhancing tract-tracing resources with diffusion tractography. Simulated resting-state BOLD best matched empirical FC at G = 0.298 and sigma = 0.0255 (cosine similarity 0.75; p < 0.001 versus nulls). Simulated networks resembled previously reported macaque resting-state systems; nodal strengths correlated with empirical FC (r = 0.51, p < 0.001). Fits to nine individual animals (cosine similarity 0.47–0.80) were similar with a canonical versus individualized connectome (p = 0.35), with more subject-specific parameter sets in the individualized case.
summaries.advanced: Catalog year is 2018; the PDF is the 2019 Scientific Data descriptor (received December 2018). Markov et al. coverage of 29 of 91 regions is cited as a limitation of an existing weighted tracer set, not as this paper’s parcellation size. Nine subjects appear in the individual-fit analysis; the extract does not state a single node count for the released connectome. Tractography limitations are acknowledged; cosine similarity is the reported fit metric, not Pearson r of full FC matrices except for nodal strength (r = 0.51).

title: A Survey of Methods for 3D Histology Reconstruction
authors: Jonas Pichat; J. E. Iglesias; T. Yousry; S. Ourselin; M. Modat

ocar.opportunity: Serial histology sees cells but destroys 3D topology; reconstructing stacks, with or without 3D medical imaging as shape prior, can recover spatial relationships and link MRI contrast to microstructure.
ocar.challenge: Cutting, staining, and imaging introduce artefacts; realistic shape is hard without an independent 3D ground truth; and the problem spans histopathology, physics, computer vision, and medicine.
ocar.action: Pichat, Iglesias, Yousry, Ourselin, and Modat, in Medical Image Analysis (2018), survey almost three decades of methods for 3D reconstruction from serial sections, covering pipelines with and without 3D medical imaging, registration, validation, and applications.
ocar.resolution: They organize methods around recovering histology’s original topology, characterizing MRI signals from tissue, and building high-resolution anatomical atlases, and they stress that image registration is the workhorse for automated correspondence. Closing sections emphasize interdisciplinary workflow (histopathologist, physicist, computer scientist, physician) and remaining multimodal alignment challenges, including emerging CNN-based correspondence.
ocar.future_work: Trends flagged include better control of tissue alteration over time, ex vivo MRI interpretation after fixation or freezing, and learning-based multimodal registration; none is a new algorithm introduced here.

plain_language_summary: Slicing tissue for a microscope flattens a 3D object into a stack of 2D pictures. This review surveys decades of computer methods that restack those slices, sometimes using MRI as a shape guide.

summaries.beginner: Slicing tissue for a microscope flattens a 3D object into a stack of 2D pictures. This review surveys decades of computer methods that restack those slices, sometimes using MRI as a shape guide.
summaries.intermediate: Pichat and colleagues (Medical Image Analysis, 2018) review nearly three decades of 3D histology reconstruction from serial sections, with and without 3D medical imaging. They summarize how specimens become digitized sections, the artefacts that follow, registration-based reconstruction, validation, and uses such as recovering topology and building atlases. The extract’s later discussion stresses cross-disciplinary coordination and remaining multimodal correspondence problems, including possible CNN approaches.
summaries.advanced: This is a survey (Medical Image Analysis 46:73–105), not a new reconstruction benchmark. The supplied PDF is a King’s College accepted manuscript with publisher portal front matter. Quantitative method rankings are not in the selected extract. “Almost three decades” is the authors’ scope statement.

authors: M. Abdellah; J. Hernando; Stefan Eilemann; Samuel Lapere; N. Antille; H. Markram; F. Schürmann

title: Sexually dimorphic unc-6/Netrin expression controls sex-specific maintenance of synaptic connectivity
authors: Peter Weinberg; Matthew Berkseth; D. Zarkower; O. Hobert

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans has sex-shared neurons whose synapses are pruned or maintained in a sex-specific way, giving a cell-resolved model of sexually dimorphic connectivity.
ocar.challenge: The molecular signal that maintains male-specific synapses between the phasmid sensory neuron PHB and the sex-shared AVG interneuron was not known.
ocar.action: Weinberg, Berkseth, Zarkower, and Hobert, in Current Biology (2018), show that UNC-6/Netrin acting through UNC-40/DCC and CED-5/DOCK180 is required and sufficient for male-specific PHB>AVG maintenance, and they map the transcriptional logic of unc-6 in AVG.
ocar.resolution: unc-6 is transcribed in AVG in both sexes in juveniles, then downregulated in hermaphrodites at sexual maturation via TRA-1 antagonism of the LIM homeobox activator lin-11, while remaining on in males. Ectopic unc-6 in hermaphrodite AVG maintains PHB>AVG synapses. Intersectional transcriptional control of unc-6 is therefore necessary and sufficient to pattern this sexually dimorphic connection cell-autonomously.
ocar.future_work: The selected extract’s later pages are methods rather than a discussion of generality; whether the same Netrin logic patterns other dimorphic synapses is not established in this card.

plain_language_summary: Male and female roundworms keep different synapses between the same named cells. This study shows that a well-known guidance cue, Netrin, is left on in one male cell to preserve a male-specific connection.

summaries.beginner: Male and female roundworms keep different synapses between the same named cells. This study shows that a well-known guidance cue, Netrin, is left on in one male cell to preserve a male-specific connection.
summaries.intermediate: Weinberg, Berkseth, Zarkower, and Hobert (Current Biology, 2018) identify UNC-6/Netrin, UNC-40/DCC, and CED-5/DOCK180 as required and sufficient for male-specific maintenance of PHB>AVG synapses in C. elegans. Sex specificity comes from transcriptional downregulation of unc-6 in hermaphrodite AVG at maturation, via TRA-1 opposing lin-11. Ectopic unc-6 in hermaphrodites preserves the male-typical synapses. The PDF is an author manuscript (PMC 2019).

Sufficiency is shown for this PHB>AVG pair via ectopic unc-6, not for the whole sexually dimorphic connectome. Catalog tags this as connectomics; the experiment is genetic and anatomical, not a new EM volume.

title: Whole Mouse Brain Structural Connectomics using Magnetic Resonance Histology
authors: Nian Wang; R. J. Anderson; Alexandra Badea; G. Cofer; Russell Dibb; Y. Qi; G. A. Johnson

ocar.opportunity: Diffusion MRI histology could quantify whole-mouse-brain structural connectivity in disease models if scan time and spatial resolution were less tightly traded off.
ocar.challenge: Fully sampled high-resolution diffusion volumes are slow; accelerating acquisition must not destroy scalar metrics or graph measures of the connectome.
ocar.action: Wang, Anderson, Badea, Cofer, Dibb, Qi, and Johnson, in Brain Structure and Function (2018), apply compressed sensing to whole-mouse-brain diffusion MRI, reconstruct tensors, run DSI Studio tractography, and build connectomes with a 166-ROI atlas.
ocar.resolution: Compared with fully sampled data at the same scan time, compressed sensing at higher spatial resolution better visualized cortical layers, dentate gyrus, and cerebellum. Versus fully sampled data at the same resolution, FA and MD error stayed below 6.0% even at 8.0-fold acceleration, and node properties (strength, clustering coefficient, eigenvector centrality, local efficiency) correlated better than 95.0% with fully sampled connectomes. Color FA/DWI/MD at 45 μm isotropic CS were visually comparable to 90 μm fully sampled scans.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the acceleration as enabling routine application to mouse disease models; that application is prospective in this methods paper.

plain_language_summary: High-detail MRI of a whole mouse brain usually takes too long. This team uses compressed sensing so they can scan finer and still keep the wiring-map numbers close to a full slow scan.

summaries.beginner: High-detail MRI of a whole mouse brain usually takes too long. This team uses compressed sensing so they can scan finer and still keep the wiring-map numbers close to a full slow scan.
summaries.intermediate: Wang and colleagues (Brain Structure and Function, 2018) accelerate whole-mouse-brain diffusion MRI with compressed sensing. At matched resolution, FA and MD error remained <6.0% at 8.0× acceleration, and connectome node metrics correlated >95.0% with fully sampled graphs using a 166-ROI atlas (Calabrese et al. 2015). Figure 3 compares 90 μm fully sampled versus 45 μm CS tensors. The PDF is an author manuscript.

title: An intersectional gene regulatory strategy defines subclass diversity of C. elegans motor neurons
authors: Paschalis Kratsios; S. Kerk; Catarina Catela; Joseph Liang; Berta Vidal; Emily A. Bayer; Weidong Feng; Estanislao Daniel De La Cruz; L. Croci; G. Consalez; Kota Mizumoto; O. Hobert

ocar.opportunity: Neuron classes often split into subclasses that share many features but differ in select traits such as connectivity along the body axis.
ocar.challenge: Transcription factors that specify class identity were not clearly shown to also generate subclass diversity, and regional cues that could intersect with pan-class factors were incomplete.
ocar.action: Kratsios, Kerk, Catela, Liang, Vidal, Bayer, Feng, De La Cruz, Croci, Consalez, Mizumoto, and Hobert, in eLife (2017), analyze cholinergic ventral-nerve-cord motor-neuron classes in C. elegans and the roles of the terminal selector UNC-3 and Hox cofactors.
ocar.resolution: UNC-3 controls both shared class traits and subclass-specific genes along the anterior–posterior axis. Three of six worm Hox genes (lin-39, mab-5, egl-5) are expressed in subsets of DA, VA, and AS neurons and intersect with broadly expressed unc-3 to co-activate subclass effectors in post-mitotic motor neurons. The authors propose this intersectional logic may be conserved from nematodes to mice.
ocar.future_work: Conservation in mice is a stated possibility, not a result of this paper. How many subclass traits beyond the assayed genes follow the same logic remains open.

plain_language_summary: Motor neurons that look like one type still differ along a worm’s head-to-tail axis. This study shows a general identity gene working together with position genes to create those subtypes.

summaries.beginner: Motor neurons that look like one type still differ along a worm’s head-to-tail axis. This study shows a general identity gene working together with position genes to create those subtypes.
summaries.intermediate: Kratsios and colleagues (eLife, 2017) show that the COE-type terminal selector UNC-3 specifies both pan-class and subclass features of C. elegans cholinergic ventral-cord motor neurons. Region-restricted Hox proteins (lin-39, mab-5, egl-5) intersect with unc-3 in subsets of DA, VA, and AS neurons to co-activate subclass-specific effectors after mitosis. The discussion frames subclass diversification as more elusive than interclass specification and offers this intersectional strategy as a possible conserved principle.

Connectivity differences along the A-P axis are part of the subclass definition, but this paper is gene-regulatory, not a new EM connectome. White et al. 1986 is cited as the anatomical classification backdrop.

title: Cell biology of astrocyte-synapse interactions
authors: N. J. Allen; C. Eroglu

ocar.opportunity: Astrocytes are abundant regulators of synapse development and physiology, so a cell-biological account of how they contact and remodel synapses would clarify circuit construction.
ocar.challenge: Large gaps remain in astrocyte cell biology and in the mechanisms of astrocyte–synapse communication, leaving their role in brain function still poorly specified.
ocar.action: Allen and Eroglu, in Neuron (2017), review seminal findings on the cellular and molecular basis of astrocyte–neuron communication, focusing on synapse development and remodeling, and they list open questions.
ocar.resolution: They treat astrocytes as integral circuit components and essential regulators of synaptic development, summarizing morphological classes and known signaling interactions. The conclusion states that addressing the posed cell-biological questions is a step toward understanding how brains work.
ocar.future_work: The review explicitly defers mechanistic completeness to future work on the questions it raises; no new connectome or quantitative synapse census is provided.

title: Efferents of anterior cingulate areas 24a and 24b and midcingulate areas 24aʹ and 24bʹ in the mouse
authors: C. Fillinger; Ipek Yalcin; M. Barrot; P. Veinante

ocar.opportunity: Mouse anterior and midcingulate areas 24a/24b and 24a′/24b′ are implicated in cognition, emotion, and pain; a complete afferent–efferent map would give an anatomical basis for those functions.
ocar.challenge: Afferents of these areas had been described, but efferents needed a matching anterograde-tracing survey to finish the cingulate connectome and to compare ACC versus MCC and dorsal versus ventral subdivisions.
ocar.action: Fillinger, Yalcin, Barrot, and Veinante, in Brain Structure and Function (2017), as described in the catalog abstract, inject anterograde tracers into mouse areas 24a/24b (ACC) and 24a′/24b′ (MCC) and chart cortical and subcortical projections.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports a shared projection pattern to cortex, basal forebrain, hypothalamus, thalamus, brainstem, and spinal cord, with denser ACC than MCC output and topographic differences between dorsal (24b/24b′) and ventral (24a/24a′) areas, suggesting shared plus area-specific roles.

title: Pyramidal cell-interneuron circuit architecture and dynamics in hippocampal networks
authors: D. English; S. McKenzie; Talfan Evans; Kanghwan Kim; E. Yoon; G. Buzsáki

ocar.challenge: Synaptic connectivity is hard to study in vivo, and pairwise coupling estimates can be contaminated by background network co-modulation.
ocar.action: English, McKenzie, Evans, Kim, Yoon, and Buzsáki, in Neuron (2017), infer CA1 pyramidal-to-interneuron connectivity from spike transmission, and validate the inference with juxtacellular and optogenetic control of presynaptic spikes in behaving mice.
ocar.resolution: Neighboring CA1 cells had stronger connections; superficial pyramids projected more to deep interneurons. Connection probability and strength were skewed, with a minority of hubs. Divergence promoted interneuron synchrony; convergent synchrony boosted postsynaptic drive. Short-term depression and facilitation implemented diverse spike-transmission filters, and transmission depended on prior postsynaptic spike timing. Evoked spike-transmission probability tracked spontaneous coupling.
ocar.future_work: The discussion treats spike-timing inference as a complement to anatomical connectomics for dynamic synaptic parameters; a full anatomical census of the same pairs is not provided here.

plain_language_summary: This team infers which hippocampal cells talk to which inhibitory cells from the tiny delays between spikes, then checks the guesses by forcing single cells to fire in mice that are behaving.

title: Sparse synaptic connectivity is required for decorrelation and pattern separation in feedforward networks
authors: N. A. Cayco-Gajic; C. Clopath; R. Silver

ocar.action: Cayco-Gajic, Clopath, and Silver, in Nature Communications (2017), build cerebellar input-layer models with spatially correlated inputs, systematically vary synaptic connectivity, and score pattern separation by how fast a classifier learns input versus output patterns.
ocar.resolution: Sparse synaptic connectivity was essential for separating spatially correlated inputs over a wide activity range. Expansion and correlations, rather than sparse activity, were the major determinants of pattern separation.
ocar.future_work: The extract’s tail is references; generality beyond cerebellar input-layer architecture should be checked in the full discussion rather than assumed.

authors: L. Yang; Yizhe Zhang; Jianxu Chen; Siyuan Zhang; D. Chen
journal: International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention

title: Toward a neurocentric view of learning
authors: Heather K Titley; N. Brunel; Christian Hansel

ocar.opportunity: Optogenetic engram studies emphasize which neurons fire and join ensembles, not only which synapses potentiate, suggesting a broader cellular view of learning.
ocar.challenge: Synaptic plasticity (e.g., LTP) is often treated as the cellular correlate of learning, which can underweight cell-autonomous excitability changes.
ocar.action: Titley, Brunel, and Hansel, in Neuron (2017), review evidence that ensemble integration can arise from LTP or from intrinsic membrane-excitability plasticity, and they propose distinct roles for the two.
ocar.resolution: They argue that synaptic plasticity sets connectivity maps while intrinsic plasticity, possibly separated in time, amplifies responsiveness and acutely drives engram integration—a move from an exclusively synaptocentric toward a non-exclusive neurocentric view. They note a lower induction threshold for some intrinsic plasticity (Purkinje-cell examples inducible within 3 s) and that excitability changes can contribute to a memory trace with little ongoing synaptic involvement after induction.
ocar.future_work: Whether intrinsic plasticity commonly supports single-experience learning in adult associative systems remains a proposed scenario. Adult synaptic rewiring is described as typically slower, over days.

plain_language_summary: Learning is often explained as stronger synapses. This review argues that neurons can also join a memory by becoming easier to fire, even without rewriting their connections first.

summaries.beginner: Learning is often explained as stronger synapses. This review argues that neurons can also join a memory by becoming easier to fire, even without rewriting their connections first.
summaries.intermediate: Titley, Brunel, and Hansel (Neuron, 2017) review engram-cell studies and intrinsic plasticity. They propose that synaptic plasticity determines connectivity maps while intrinsic plasticity amplifies responses and can acutely integrate neurons into ensembles, possibly on a faster timescale than synaptic rewiring. authors: Johnny Phong Hoang Do; Min Xu; Seung-Hee Lee; Wei-Cheng Chang; Siyu Zhang; Shinjae Chung; Tyler J Yung; Jiang Lan Fan; Kazunari Miyamichi; L. Luo; Y. Dan

authors: G. Zamora-López; Yuhan Chen; G. Deco; M. Kringelbach; Changsong Zhou

title: Sexually dimorphic differentiation of a C. elegans hub neuron is cell-autonomously controlled by a conserved transcription factor
authors: Esther Serrano-Saiz; Meital Oren-Suissa; Emily A. Bayer; O. Hobert

ocar.opportunity: Cortical population activity occupies a lower-dimensional space than the combinatorial explosion of spike patterns; a simple per-neuron coupling statistic could summarize that structure.
ocar.challenge: It was unclear whether neighboring neurons share the same relationship to the population, and whether that relationship reflects stimulus preference, behavior, causality, and synapses.
ocar.action: Okun, Steinmetz, Cossell, Iacaruso, Ko, Barthó, Moore, Hofer, Mrsic-Flogel, Carandini, and Harris, in Nature (2015), record visual cortex in mouse and monkey and relate each cell’s population coupling to behavior, optogenetic drive, in vitro synaptic counts, and pairwise correlations.
ocar.resolution: Neighbors ranged from strongly coupled “choristers” to weakly coupled “soloists.” Coupling was largely independent of sensory preference and invariant to stimulus conditions. Highly coupled cells were more affected by non-sensory variables such as motor intention. Coupling predicted responses to optogenetic increases in local activity and predicted in vitro neighbor-synapse counts. Knowledge of n neurons’ couplings predicted a substantial portion of their n² pairwise correlations; residual correlations still tracked orientation similarity after removing nonspecific connectivity predictions.
ocar.future_work: The extract’s tail is figure/supplementary-style correlation analyses; a full circuit model of how coupling is wired is not a new EM reconstruction.

plain_language_summary: Even neighboring visual-cortex cells differ: some fire with the crowd (“choristers”) and some do not (“soloists”). That simple difference predicts extra synapses, sensitivity to movement, and much of the pairwise correlation structure.

summaries.beginner: Even neighboring visual-cortex cells differ: some fire with the crowd (“choristers”) and some do not (“soloists”). That simple difference predicts extra synapses, sensitivity to movement, and much of the pairwise correlation structure.
summaries.intermediate: Okun and colleagues (Nature, 2015) define population coupling in mouse and monkey visual cortex. Coupling is a stable cellular attribute, largely independent of sensory tuning, higher in cells more affected by motor intention, causally predictive of optogenetic population drive, and predictive of in vitro synapses from neighbors. Coupling of n cells predicts much of the n² correlation matrix; leftover correlations still depend on orientation difference, matching a specific-plus-nonspecific connectivity picture. In vitro synapse counts are subsequent estimates on the same neurons, not a complete connectome. Species are Mus musculus and Macaca mulatta. Catalog dimension is connectomics; the measurements are physiological plus slice connectivity, not volume EM.

title: Fast Approximate Quadratic Programming for Graph Matching
authors: J. Vogelstein; John M. Conroy; V. Lyzinski; L. J. Podrazik; S. Kratzer; Eric T. Harley; D. E. Fishkind; R. J. Vogelstein; C. Priebe

ocar.opportunity: Graph matching, a quadratic assignment problem, is needed to align large brain-graphs such as C. elegans connectomes as graph-valued data grow.
ocar.challenge: QAPs are NP-hard; prior approximations were too slow or too inaccurate for big-data graphs.
ocar.action: Vogelstein, Conroy, Lyzinski, Podrazik, Kratzer, Harley, Fishkind, R. J. Vogelstein, and Priebe, in PLoS ONE (2015), introduce the Fast Approximate Quadratic assignment (FAQ) algorithm and benchmark it on QAPLIB and on matching C. elegans connectomes.
ocar.resolution: FAQ was faster and achieved a lower objective value on over 80% of the QAPLIB library versus the previous state of the art, and it efficiently achieved performance on the worm connectome matching task. The discussion lists extensions: parallel LAP subroutines, sparsity, vertex attributes (position, cell type), and matching more than two graphs.
ocar.future_work: Multiple-graph matching is described as in progress. Incorporating biological vertex attributes is proposed, not demonstrated as a completed brain-atlas pipeline.

plain_language_summary: Lining up two wiring diagrams is a hard matching problem. This algorithm does it faster and, on a standard test set, better than the previous champion, including on worm brain graphs.

title: Frustrated hierarchical synchronization and emergent complexity in the human connectome network
authors: Pablo Villegas; P. Moretti; M. A. Muñoz

ocar.opportunity: Synchronization on the empirical human connectome could explain flexible access to many dynamical repertoires without fine-tuning to a critical point.
ocar.challenge: Standard Kuramoto dynamics on simpler networks miss the hierarchical modular structure and frequency heterogeneity of the connectome.
ocar.action: Villegas, Moretti, and Muñoz, in Scientific Reports (2014), study Kuramoto synchronization analytically and computationally on the human connectome and on synthetic hierarchical modular networks, using spectral graph theory to interpret slow modes.
ocar.resolution: They report an intermediate phase between order and disorder, arising from hierarchical modules plus quenched frequency heterogeneity: frustrated synchronization, metastability, and chimera-like states. Structural bottlenecks at many scales produce anomalously slow dynamics; even the coarse-grained connectome shows non-degenerate Laplacian eigenvalues at the lower edge as a fingerprint of that heterogeneity. Without frequency dispersion, synthetic hierarchies synchronize bottom-up; bottlenecks alter that cascade.
ocar.future_work: Relating these mesoscopic chimera-like regimes to cognitive flexibility is interpretive. The connectome used is a coarse-grained mapping, not cellular resolution.

plain_language_summary: When simple oscillator models run on a map of human white-matter connections, they do not just lock together or fall apart. A messy in-between regime appears, with parts of the network aligning while others drift.

summaries.beginner: When simple oscillator models run on a map of human white-matter connections, they do not just lock together or fall apart. A messy in-between regime appears, with parts of the network aligning while others drift.
summaries.intermediate: Villegas, Moretti, and Muñoz (Scientific Reports, 2014) simulate and analyze Kuramoto dynamics on the human connectome and on hierarchical modular surrogates. Hierarchical organization plus frequency heterogeneity yields frustrated synchronization, metastability, and chimera-like states between the usual coherent and incoherent phases. Spectral graph theory links the slow dynamics to structural bottlenecks and to non-degenerate small Laplacian eigenvalues. The discussion treats this complexity as a way for the brain to access many attractors without sitting exactly at criticality.

No subject count or parcellation size appears in the selected extract. arXiv version in the file is 1402.5289v2 (3 Jul 2014). Catalog year is 2014.

title: Rapid Golgi Analysis Method for Efficient and Unbiased Classification of Dendritic Spines
authors: W. C. Risher; T. Ustunkaya; Jonnathan Singh Alvarado; C. Eroglu; C. Eroglu

ocar.opportunity: Golgi-Cox staining visualizes dendritic spines across species, including humans, with simple optics, so an objective classifier would make developmental and disease studies more comparable.
ocar.challenge: Manual spine typing is slow and inconsistent because categories are loosely defined.
ocar.action: Risher, Ustunkaya, Singh Alvarado, and Eroglu, in PLoS ONE (2014), define a geometry-based hierarchical formula on measurements exported from RECONSTRUCT and test it on mouse primary visual cortex during development.
ocar.resolution: The formula conveyed the maturational shift in spine types. Versus a trained observer on the same dendrites, filopodia density did not differ (0.07±0.01 versus 0.06±0.01 per unit length; p = 0.50) nor did mushroom density (0.25±0.02 versus 0.28±0.02; p = 0.37). Spreadsheets implement length-to-width ratio and type rules. Remaining drawbacks include stain time up to 2.5 weeks.
ocar.future_work: The method still depends on Golgi-Cox’s incomplete labeling and on 2D measurements from light micrographs, not EM-verified spine classes.

plain_language_summary: Sorting dendritic spines into shapes by eye is slow and disagreeable. This paper uses simple length and width rules in a spreadsheet so the typing is faster and less subjective.

title: Morphology and Physiology of Excitatory Neurons in Layer 6b of the Somatosensory Rat Barrel Cortex
authors: M. Marx; D. Feldmeyer

ocar.opportunity: Neocortical layer 6B is heterogeneous and understudied; a quantitative morphological–physiological classification would enable later connectivity work.
ocar.challenge: Prior names for the layer are not interchangeable, and few studies used unsupervised classification focused on excitatory L6B cells.
ocar.action: Marx and Feldmeyer, in Cerebral Cortex (advance access 2012; issue date December 2013), combine whole-cell recording and biocytin filling in P17–24 rat somatosensory barrel cortex, then unsupervised cluster analysis on physiology plus axonal and dendritic metrics.
ocar.resolution: Three excitatory clusters emerged: (C1) pyramids with pia-directed apical dendrites; (C2) cells with a prominent “apical-like” dendrite not aimed at the pia (further split into inverted, tangentially oriented, and horizontally oriented); (C3) multipolar spiny neurons. title: Spatial profile of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic connectivity in mouse primary auditory cortex
authors: Robert B. Levy; A. Reyes

ocar.opportunity: Knowing how far excitatory and inhibitory connections spread in mouse A1 would show whether local circuits favor lateral inhibition or co-tuned excitation and inhibition.
ocar.challenge: In vivo reports disagree, most dual recordings sampled only neighbors closer than about 100 μm, and slicing truncates processes.
ocar.action: Levy and Reyes, in Journal of Neuroscience (2012), use multiple intracellular recording in mouse primary auditory cortical slices to map connectivity among pyramids, fast-spiking (FS), and non-FS cells in the principal input layer, fit distance dependence with Gaussians, and estimate truncation effects from anatomy.
ocar.resolution: Connection probability was distance-dependent with comparable Gaussian spreads of 85–114 μm across cell types. FS-formed unitary synapses were stronger than other classes during brief trains; strength did not correlate with distance. Anatomy qualitatively matched physiology. Slicing reduced overall connectivity but did not change the spatial pattern. Comparable E and I spreads plus strong E–I interconnectivity are consistent with models in which either lateral inhibition or co-tuning can dominate depending on input structure. Facilitating pyramid-to-GIN (non-FS) synapses are argued to contribute little to transient onsets.
ocar.future_work: Which regime dominates in vivo is left to the structure of thalamic/cortical input, not decided by this slice map alone.

plain_language_summary: In mouse auditory cortex, excitatory and inhibitory cells connect over similar short distances. Depending on the incoming pattern, that layout can either sharpen tuning or keep excitation and inhibition balanced.

summaries.beginner: In mouse auditory cortex, excitatory and inhibitory cells connect over similar short distances. Depending on the incoming pattern, that layout can either sharpen tuning or keep excitation and inhibition balanced.
summaries.intermediate: Levy and Reyes (Journal of Neuroscience, 2012) map local synaptic connectivity in the principal input layer of mouse A1 slices among pyramids, FS, and non-FS interneurons. Gaussian fits to connection probability give comparable spreads (85–114 μm). FS synapses are stronger in brief trains; synapse strength is distance-independent. Process truncation reduces connection rates but not spatial shape. The authors argue this architecture can support either lateral inhibition or co-tuning depending on input, and that facilitating non-FS (GIN) inputs are weak at stimulus onset.
summaries.advanced: Spreads are Gaussian fit parameters, not hard wiring cutoffs. “Principal input layer” is the mapped lamina; exact layer numbering should be read from the full methods. GIN/non-FS onset-quiescence is an interpretation from facilitating, initially weak EPSPs plus cited in vivo/in vitro transients. Catalog dimension is connectomics; this is slice paired recording, not volume EM.

title: Statistical Inference on Errorfully Observed Graphs
authors: C. Priebe; D. Sussman; M. Tang; J. Vogelstein

ocar.opportunity: Connectomes and other graphs are inferred from imperfect edge evidence, so statistical tasks such as labeling neurons should account for that observation error rather than treating the reconstructed graph as ground truth.
ocar.challenge: More informative edge features cost more, so one cannot assess every possible edge at high quality; the quantity/quality operating point for the intermediate edge-classification step is usually chosen ad hoc rather than to maximize the downstream inference task.
ocar.action: Priebe, Sussman, Tang, and Vogelstein (arXiv 2014; later Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics) formulate errorfully observed graphs in a stochastic blockmodel, derive an optimal quantity/quality operating point for a simple but optimal vertex classifier, and apply the trade-off to errorful observations of the C. elegans connectome.
ocar.resolution: Optimal operating points are surprising: methods for the intermediate edge task should be chosen to maximize subsequent vertex classification, not edge accuracy itself. The C. elegans connectome is used as a scientific case of this quantity/quality trade-off.
ocar.future_work: The extract’s later sections analogize the same trade-off to social-network topic modeling (e.g., Enron email) and do not report a numeric C. elegans accuracy table in the selected text.

plain_language_summary: Wiring maps are built from noisy guesses about which cells touch. This paper asks how carefully you should check each possible connection if the real goal is to label the cells, not to get every edge perfect.

authors: H. Akil; M. Martone; D. V. Van Essen
